The game starts with an unskippable cutscene, which can't be paused.
Stupid story.  Words cannot describe how much I don't care about anything that happens.  There's nothing to make me the least bit interested in the bizarre lore of this game.
Bad character model design.  It kinda' reminds me of Warhammer, but not in a good way.  It's like it was all designed by someone who has seen a few video games, but doesn't know which ones are good, or what people like.
Bad character animations.  For exmple, it always looks like their legs are moving way too fast for their current speed.
Sub-par voice acting.
No control tips in-game for controllers.  If you're using a mouse and keyboard, it's fine.  If you're doing couch gaming with a controller, have fun figuring out the controls on your own.
The controls are also not as easy as they should be to adjust.
The gameplay is horrible.  You basically just stand out in the open, taking damage with no effect, while using a number of unimpressive weapons on only a few equally unimpressive enemies.  There should always be a challenge, with ways to make mistakes and fail, but ways to learn and then succeed without it being excessively difficult.  This game's designers know literally nothing about that.
Not long after the beginning of the game, the player is introduced to customization options they can't use.  It would make sense to have a few lesser options available, then unlock more later, but you can't buy anything when you start.  They basically say "Hey, look at all these nearly-as-ugly armor options.  Want to upgrade?  Too bad, you can't.  You can't use any of this.  No go out there and grind until you've earned these pointless customization options."
Summary:
There are no redeeming qualities.  This game is a polished turd.  It is literally the worst game every made.  Ever.

After a potential reviewer downloads and starts playing the game, they stop responding to emails.  They're hoping people will start playing for free, then buy the expensive add-ons later.  I've always known this game is pure garbage, but now I also know the developers are liars, and will stoop to new lows to promote their polished turd.

Frederic: Resurrection of Music (F:RoM) has probably one of the strongest premises of any rhythym game. The music industry has become so commercialized that it literally causes classical pianist and composure Frederic Chopin to rise from the dead. Disturbed by the modern day music industry's quest for fame and fortune, Frederic sets out to school all of these wannabe musicians about what it truly means to be an artist. Or something like that. I honestly couldn't really tell what was going on most of the time because narratively the execution is a little wonky.
But who cares about that! It is all about the music man! It is the strength of song selection that makes or breaks a rhythym game and F:RoM shines in this department. Each track is a genre breaking remix of one of Chobin's classical pieces. Ever wonder what Chobin would sound like if he smoked pot and took influence from Bob Marley? How would his music be affected if he binged old Western movies for a weekend? It is an insanely clever idea that makes picking up this game worthwhile.
The actual gameplay is not great but merely acceptable. Other reviewers claim that there are problem while playing on keyboard but I cannot comment on this because I played using the touch controls on my Windows 8 Surface Pro. It is a nice litte pick up if you are playing on a tablet like device. Other than that, however, I cannot recommend it whole heartedly.
Controls aside the story does leave much to be desired. I feel like the developers could have done a lot more with the set up but for less than $3 I believe to be Frederic: Resurrection of Music to be worth your time and money.

I found this game quite enjoyable, though it did indeed have it's bugs to deal with. I can forgive that much with the witty story and the cheap price. List of bugs at the end!
ART
+I found the simplistic cartoon art very charming.
+Has a bit of a "homemade" feel to it, which I really liked personally.
MUSIC
+Music was fitting (except for few expections in my opinion) and set the mood
-Very limited soundtrack, pretty much keeps repeating a few select songs throughout the game
STORY AND CHARACTERS
+I ABSOLUTELY fell in love with the characters. They had their own personalities and quirks, and all appeared interesting in one way or another.
+The dialogue was witty and interesting, and the story had me hooked all the way till the end.
+Voice acting was impressive, wasn't expecting such good quality (English)
+The humor is definitely one of the strong points of this game and the main element.
GAMEPLAY
+Loved the "wrong" interactions. Not just the standard "I don't know what you want me to do", but rather every single interaction had its own reaction, which I found quite entertaining.
+At a couple points I had to cheat, I admit, but mainly the puzzles were logical and there would be enough hints to keep you going if you keep looking long enough.
-The bugs, bugs, and bugs.
-The controls were kinda tiring at times, when you'd have to first select whether you want to "Look at...", "Talk to...", "Pick up", "Use..." the item and then you'd have to click the item itself. Though if you got the interaction wrong the dialogue following would be amusing enough to make me forgive it.
BUGS
- Java crash, when starting the game --> I went to the game folder and started the game for the first time without using steam launcher, and it worked fine. After that it would also start normally through steam launcher for me.
- The famous kitchen menu bug--> Fix available through steam community. I was unfortunate enough to run to this without saving my game, and it prevents you from doing so, but after forcibly closing the game and restarting after the fix, it let me continue from the menu part, this time with the fix :)
- The Enging bug (? Never got to experience since I fixed it along with the kitchen menu bug)
- Occasional crashes, where the game would just shut down on me. REMEMBER TO SAVE OFTEN NOT TO LOSE PROGRESS!
Without the bugs, 9/10. Definitely one of my favorite point-and-click adventures.
With the bugs, 7/10.

Basically, you (Edna) and your little pyromaniac stuffed rabbit (Harvey) are trapped in an asylum and you have no clue why. So you have to find a way to break out and get your memories back. On your way you will meet a lot of crazy people, which are helping you out (one more, one less).
The voice acting (just played the german version) is well and fits perfectly to the witty dialogues and its characters. Sometime you can hear that not all of the voice actors are professionals, but that's no big harm to the game. You can literally talk to everything and you will always get a unique answer. Even if you combine things, you will always get an impertinent comment. All is attended by catchy music. The puzzles are creative, but never unfair. At some parts I had to riddle for a while, but I've never really stuck or was forced to use the internet to get the solution. The game is basically divided into two sections. The first is bright, colorful and the pure joy of life. The second part is dark, morbid and almost serious. Especially the second part shows that
But, no matter which part, both are detailed made with heart and fantasy.
But, there are some downsides as well...
The game crashes a lot. Because it uses Java underneath, it's doomed to perform badly. So the strategy is "save early, save often". The resolution is low and if you play the game in fullscreen mode, everything becomes a little bit blurry. Also the animation and drawings are miles away from being technically perfect. But on the other hand, if you know that the most of the game is made by only one lousy german student (now a cofounder of Daedalic), it starts to feel "authentic" and charming.
Conclusion
If you are able to overlook the few rough edges its a 10/10.
And beside that, if the game is on sale its a must buy for every p-a-c adventure lover.

The concept for this game is subtly brilliant.  At first glance it seems to be a call back to the old style point-and-click adventure games; the sort of stories that used nonsensical "Nintendo logic" to solve the puzzles, while reveling in their own ridiculousness.  I admit, I totally bought into that.  I had so much fun with the carefree tone and witty dialogue that I would often forget the serious nature of the setting.  Everything from the wonky art style, to the jazzy music, to the over-the-top character personalities is initially played for laughs, and it's all so well done that you may forget you're playing as a mental patient surrounded by crazy people.  This is done towards a very deliberately effect, but the result so crafty that you may end up playing through the entire game without ever consciously realizing what hit you.  For the sake of spoilers, I will say no more, because this is a game that should be experienced by lovers of the genre.
As a wonderful bonus, this game is fully voice acted, with the acting varying in quality.  However, since 80% of the characters are insane, even the most hammy and ridiculous of performances feels appropriate in context.

Guild of Dungeoneering is a dungeon crawler card game  where you play as a guildmaster sending different heroes into a dungeon, one at a time.  When your start  a dungeon quest, your chosen hero begins as level 1, and gains experience and gear as they progress through the level. Luck and randomization determine how your fare
in the dungeon, and the mechanics get a bit repetitive, as you start each new dungeon
again as a level 1 with no gear that carries over.
If your hero dies, you and your guild are not punished in any way, and another hero
of the same class appears in your guild to take the place of the fallen. This endless
supply of heroes that don't interact of coordinate with any of your other heroes gives
the game a disjointed feeling, and takes away a sense of progression as you level up your guild.
Because your heroes do not level up as your progress, and you are unable to bring any sort of gear into a dungeon with you, or have any choice in what cards you bring with you, the game relies heavily on luck and repetition. When it comes to beginnning a new dungeon, you are essentially thrown into battle with no ability to prepare for different types of enemies. The leads to having to repeat levels hoping for the right random cards, and a grinding feel.
The concept of this game, and the way this game was presented was very appealing, but at the end of the day, upon playing the game, the extreme repetitiveness and grinding nature of the game make it frustrating and time consuming to play. You have no emotional ties to any of the heroes, and have to start out each new dungeon at square one. There is virtually no deck building, and no depth to the game. This was a great concept, but it fell short of it's potential.

Guild of Dungeoneering is a game that rewards progress without giving the player reliable means to do so.
The game is a dungeon-crawling, deck-building, rogue-like RPG, but a character's progression is limited to the start of a map to the end of it. After winning or losing, you lose all of your items, your levels, and any sort of progress, bringing along a small amount of gold back to base to unlock more characters to do the same.
There are a few presistent elements for sure, like temporary buffs at the start of the map or items you can unlock to appear in dungeons, but this was done better by Rogue Legacy, whereas Guild of Dungeoneering still demands that you start in a rather poor and dismal state.
While I enjoyed the game a little at the start, it became clear that as time went on, progress was going come to a grinding halt. I have not played the game in weeks, and I regret not applying for a refund as a result.

I don't usually break my habit of lurking, so that should say something about this game. I've been playing this game for years now, having joined just after it got out of beta testing, way before it made it on steam. This game is, at its core, a game with brawling combos. If you don't like those, or sidescrolling, don't play this game. Otherwise, there's no reason not to give it a try.
That being said, I've been witness to many "problems" people have with the game, so I'll go ahead and list them, as well as my reasons why people shouldn't be quite as put off by them as they are:
1. Stamina - Stamina is infamous. When it's depleted, your character no longer has the ability to enter dungeons (disregarding the special boss rush dungeon Henir). I'm honestly not as put off by this one as many, as it allows you to focus on multiple characters without burning out one by playing that for days on end. In addition, weekends have unlimited stamina, so push your mains all you want on those days.
2. The field system - this is only a issue with other players who miss the old system. I don't actually have many oppinions on this other than that the fields provide an incredible source of exp, which will prove handy later on.
3. Exp tables - I will admit that the exp tables for this game seem rediculous at some times, especially when viewed in comparison to the original KR version. That being said, the fields, as well as the 15% exp medal obtainable from killing field bosses, alleviate this fairly well, and despite what many might try to tell you, NA does not have the worst tables. In the end, though, this is an MMO. What were you expecting?
4. Cash Shop - Yes, we have a cash shop. The main value of the cash shop is for costumes, accessories and the like. There are items in there to let you bypass certain grinding quests for class changes and the like, but these aren't that big of an issue. There is one bigger issue, though, and that is the B-slot. Plainly stated, this item increases your skill holding section by 4 slots, which sounds like it would be a massive help. It really isn't all that much. Especially given that the field revamp made it possible to switch skills while in a dungeon, this item has become a luxury. On top of that, I've actually lost pvp matches becuase my mind couldn't keep up with the B-slot's additional buttons. Get it if you want it, but don't think it gives you a broken advantage ala play-to-win.
5. Skills - This is the one most people who used to play the game before the revamp have issues with. Originally, you were limited by prereq skills rather than having to make choices. The end result was cookie cutter skill builds for everyone playing the same class. Under the new system, you have to pick one of two skills every five levels. Some people see this as limiting, but I feel it improves the uniquness of your character compared to the many others. That being said, KR recently implemented a multiple page system, allowing you to hold two skill pages where you can pick the other of the two options if you feel like it. All in all, a revamp was necessary given how the old system was abused, and for all the people who feel that classes they play are worthless now that they have to choose, I can only say I'm still enjoying my TT, who went from top tier to near bottom as a result. Deal with it.
There may be more reasons people don't like the game, but all in all, most of them a tiny preferential things. This being said, there is no reason no to give this game a try, as although many of the afore mentioned people have attempted to "rage-quit" elsword, they have yet to find any game quite like it.

Just went through the first act (Classic mode) with the following team: Elementalist / Warrior / Ranger / Scoundrel and here are some thoughts.
Pros:
- First of all, this game is basically "Divinty, Original Sin" done right (or at least better). This does not reinvent the previous game from the ground up but instead provides you with an improved experience of what the previous episode was.
- The soundtrack performs flawlessly, the ability to change a part of it by selecting an instrument gives the right feeling of customization.
- By the looks of the first act, the story seems compelling, the personal story aspect of the four main characters seems to bring a good amount to replayability.
- There are many graphical improvements when compared to the previous D:OS, level design has also been improved, with a lot of clutters and many details to be found here and there (again, this is based by the looks of the first Act, not the entire game).
Cons:
- This may be due to the Early Access aspect of this release, but a lot of quests seem buggy / unfinished / unclear. At the end of the first act, I had a lot of remaining entries in my quest logs for quests that I had clearly finished, but didn't fetch any reward from.
- This release is still buggy (as expected from an early access release). However, due to the timeline and the currently announced release date of this game, I'm not entirely sure that D:OS 2 will release entirely bug-free. This goes from fairly anecdotic issues (such as the stealth ground highlights not disappearing when going out of stealth) to fairly game breaking bugs (such as quests that cannot be completed due to missing elements).
- Some people may regret the lack of new features regarding the combat system. So just be advised that this is a "more of the same" from D:OS and not a complete rework.
TL:DR
All things considered, I would strongly recommend this game if you liked D:OS. If you didn't played this game, you may very well try it before (it's much cheaper now and it's well woth the money IMHO).
However, I'm not sure I will be playing this day one after release. Maybe wait for a patch or two and some reviews to make sure the final release is mainly bug-free.

Ok...so beat act 1, and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥larian out did themselves. Everything from the atmosphere to the character building has been improved, using the same formula as before and making every aspect better. The combat is the same style but with many subtle at first differences that expand into a lot more combat flexibility.
Update (Release): The game has finally released and I really have to say...Larian has out-done themselves. Playing through the game on Tactician and seeing how the AI does its best to break the combat system like a real player would, ending their turn with their back to a wall so your rogue is inefective, reversing your moves by throwing water on the enemy you just shocked and stunning your entire party, it's an incredible system that Larian has created so much flexibility, every move of every fight becomes a question of "did that just happen? can I really do this?" which is something no other game can capture.
Gone are the supercharged ridiculous characters of the first game, replaced with smarter and more adept enemies that force you to make better decisions. The flexibility in character creation and the much more intuitive world makes me excited every chance I get to jump on and uncover just a bit more of the world. The inclusion of a darker story and races adds a much needed party diversity and the lore being less silly pulls you in far more to the atmosphere (which is beautiful...from the musical score to the graphics) creating a much more enjoyable transition from combat to exploring, and giving you more to WANT to explore.
The beautiful score and excellent voice acting talent (so far) has been an incredible treat in an age when games have been spending less and less time and devotion to world building and character development. The party while smaller than some CRPGs, is fully fleshed out with interesting characters who I actually want to talk to and interact with.
So far I am incredibly excited with the release and looking forwarding to simply getting through ACT 1 on tactician and exploring the unknown. Well done Larian, you have brought art back into the gaming industry.

FIrst thing you need to know: this is a very short game. Even taking it slow and going back for 100% achievements I only got about 4 hours out of it. On that basis alone you probably want to wait for it to go on a pretty major sale. In fact the length of the game is one of the main reasons I'm not recommending it. For a game to be so short I feel that it needs to make up for it by being either increadibly good or extremely original. Or very very cheap. I seem to be in the minority, but I don't think Contrast quite made up its length on any of these.
As far as the game itself; it was fairly good but there were a few things I felt let it down. The story was a little childish, naive, and predictable. While it delt with some darker topics, things turned positive way too quick to seem real or satisfying. The world in which the game was set was interesting and had some great ideas, but also suffered from a slight vagueness which I think was meant to be mysterious and intriguing but didn't ring true to me. Personally  I'm used to my fictional worlds being a little more conrete and storylines a little less sickly sweet, but given the other ratings that seems to be a matter of taste.
The platforming integrated with the shadow mechanic which the game centres around was both novel and enjoyable if straitforward. The levels were fairly pretty, and the jaz theme throughout suited it very well, but they were also quite small and sparse. Honestly if it was longer (both for playtime and to stretch the conclusions to storylines) it could have been a very good game. As it is, it turned out fairly good but not something I'd recommend. Excepting on sale.

It is my belief that ARK: Survival Evolved as an amazing, open world experience that is a must-have for this year's holiday~! I've been playing a long time. I did have my breaks from the game due to school, playing LoL, or Diablo III seasons, but I always kept in touch with the patch notes and how the game as developed in the years leading up to now. Playing with friends, or making new ones with tribes is a great feeling of teamwork and cooperation, and the PvP between tribes feels very intense in combat. I recommend this game to anyone with a high-end laptop or mid-level desktop for the best experience.
As for gameplay, it does have a steep learning curve after you're upgrading from stone and metal building and tools, and does take some learning, and certainly a lot of grinding to reach end-game. The early game of spawning in can feel a bit slow, or even frustrating if you're inexperienced, but the game definetly picks up around level 40-50 in terms of what you can do, tame, and acomplish in the game itself. If you're not on a PvP server, late game can feel pretty boring and pointless when you've tamed everything, built everything, and basically have a prehistoric monopoly, so I recommend playing on a PvP, or at least a PvPvE.
As for tribes, there are a good amount of politics involved with managing, joining, or creating tribes, espically high-level and/or active and populated tribes. Raiding can be fun depending on how the server feels about it or if it's an official server or not, but you don't need to♥♥♥♥♥♥and pillage to have a good time, although it does help!
A few tips I would have that aren't really based off of gameplay, are joining an official server when it's freshly wiped, so you don't run into level 80+ players when you're just spawned in. Also, being an overall alturistic person in the game, when in a position of immence power, or a pesent really helps if you get into some heat with other tribes or specific members.
Lastly, I have very fond memories of this game, and I'm hoping of making new ones every day. It's an active game with a good amount of updates and attention from devs, so it's my opinion that getting into this game would be great for the longhaul. And if you need help with game mechanics or are stuck, either ask someone in the server, fourms, or there are plenty of YouTube guides on where to build bases, what dinos to tame, being efficiant in mining, etc. Thanks for reading my review and feel free to add me if you need somone to play with!

Kitty Powers' Matchmaker is fun and addicting!  This game is completely unique to anything I've ever played before, and it combines so many elements!  Let's start with clientele!  First you choose a location (disco, gym, comic book store, ect.) for Kitty to set up fliers to attract customers.  The locations you pick determine the type of clients that arrive; for example, choosing the comic book store will bring in the "Geeky" types.  Each client is different, varying in looks, personality, and interests.  Because of the uniqueness of each character, it can be hard finding the right match for your client, but that's what makes it so much fun!  Will your client swing a home-run of strike out on their date(s)?
The actual dates are the most intricate part of the entire game.   Literally everything has a part in determining the success of the date, from choosing a restaurant to holding in your farts!  There are fun mini-games to be played that vary with each establishment you go to.  Leveling up unlocks new restaurants for clients to visit and different features in the salon to beautify your client before the big date!
There is quite a lot of memorization involved in the game, so it can get tough once you reach the higher scoring dates, but I don't believe it distracts from the overall entertainment of the game.
My favorite thing about the game is the mailbox feature.  After successfully setting up your client with a hot date, you will receive mail from he or she updating you on how things are progressing in their new relationship.  Sometimes things go sour and the couple breaks up, but sometimes they'll end up with children and even name one of the babies after you!  It all comes down to how well you do when playing matchmaker.

This is a fun take on the deckbuilding genre. The presentation is simple but very functional. Extra praise has to be heaped on the atmospheric music and snarky lyrics that pervade play. The game is simple enough to certainly not need external reference or strategy guides, but hard enough to require forethought. Each run is short enough that dying 10 times isn't detrimental or particularly aggravating, which is fortunate because the game does not hold your hand and sometimes successive random chance dictates a no win scenario.
Each dungeon run consists of turns with the player placing up to 3 cards of 5 in their hand. These consist of map tiles, gold, and monsters. Once placed, the dungeoneer then moves through the dungeon (prioritizing treasure, monsters and exploration of new tiles). Assuming the dungeoneer does not encounter a monster, this cycle completes until the specific mission objective is completed (kill a boss, kill X monsters, escape before X turns etc...they are rather varied).
Battle consists of playing against an AI deck with each playing a single card per turn. Cards vary widely and include mechanics for two damage types, first strike, blocking, unblockable, card drawing and discarding, healing etc. The players deck is based off their class start deck and is augmented by "loot" captured from previous battles and chests. All loot give bonuses to one or more "skills" (such as Holy, Fire, Quick, Slashing etc). Extra cards are added to your deck based on the totals of these various skills (eg if you have Fire II and  Fire I items, you get the cards for Fire I, II and III).
You have a central guild that you upgrade with the winnings from individual runs. Available upgrades include classes (base battle decks of a dozen or so cards and one special ability), packs of boosters that expand the potential pool of loot items, and a charm that adds a special ability.

Dustforce is a lovely game for those that enjoy speedy platformers with an emphasis on control over one's character.  The janitors in Dustforce can jump off walls, run up walls, run up ceilings, and perform multiple double jumps by defeating enemies.  Gameplay consists of mastering the route through a level to sweep up all the dust while continuing one's combo (which can be done by running over dust or hitting enemies) and avoiding spikes, pits, and enemy attacks.  The game employs a ranking system that judges based on completion (how much dust was ran over and how many enemies were defeated) and finesse (how few hits and restarts taken).  This game is perfect for those who go for perfect ranks in modern Sonic titles.
However, later levels in the game approach unfair difficulty, spamming spikes and requiring jumps and dashes to be timed down to the millisecond to succeed.  Thankfully, it is not necessary to play any of these levels, and the game can be obtained at a price cheap enough to warrant playing only the well-designed levels in the first half of the game.

Disappointing for such a game that really could have been amazing. The general premise of the game, both story-wise (Didi and parents) and gimmick/mechanics-wise (using shadows to navigate and solve puzzles), was interesting enough for me to give the game a shot in the first place. I also enjoy the noir style and going back almost a century ago to a different type of world.
However, the game really let me down. There's just too many issues that all stack up against it, and the quality of the game seems to bounce back and forth as you play. The story starts off without much information, though I did get into it once I started picking up what was happening. But there are a lot of weird background details that are never explained at all, and nothing much seems to fit together. I also did not think there was much of a climax, and the ending of the game felt very cheap.
There is no real environment to the game, as the world is weirdly disconnected and with missing areas and emptiness. Basically, there is no "life" to it, is a better phrasing. You just go through hollow areas to get to the next mini-cutscene, and then solve a puzzle. While the visual art style of the game great, and some places look very beautiful, the lack of anything actually inhabiting the areas ruins it. And though the game's gimmick, as I mentioned before, is dealing with shadows, I didn't enjoy every character except you and Didi being shown as shadows. It just felt cheap and as if the developers didn't want to do that design. It only furthers the lack of "life" in the game. And the dialog and sound of the game also was nothing special. Nobody gave any performance that was great, and I think a good few scenes actually lacked any good emotion.
Then you have the mechanical problems, showing that the game wasn't fine-tuned or even tested that well. Your character's movement is pretty far from good, and I often found myself glitching around, especially when you are in the shadows. One of the things about the shadows is that if certain moving shadows are about to crush you, then the game pops you out of the shadows, which is understandable; however, I found myself popping out of the shadows at random points without anything touching me, causing me to fall down and making me start parts of puzzles over and over again.
When it comes to Didi, who you are following around, they were very lazy in her movement as well. I would often see her animations entirely stop, so she would "walk" without any motion. She doesn't move her mouth when talking, at least as far as I saw. And half the time you were supposed to find her somewhere, I would walk into the room or area and see her in "generic 3D model" form, standing in place with arms and legs rigidly stretched out as if someone is in the middle of editing her design.
And in terms of actually playing, it seemed like "Saving" didn't actually mean the game was saving, whenever it popped up. At least twice, I exited the game to stop playing after it had finished saving, and I came back each time to find that the game jumped back at least 10-15 minutes, so I would have to redo some section. For instance, it did this in one of the carnival areas after I completed it and then quit the game.
Finally, the length of the game - it is way too short, and with all of the issues, it all made it even worse. I don't know if the developer just didn't have enough money at the time, or they just chose not to clean things up or test enough, but the game is very lacking in pretty much every area. It could have been a really great game if they had put in more work.

I want to like this game.  I really, really want to like this game.
When I initially started playing, I was having a lot of fun playing against the CPU.  Learning how to play the game, trying to figure out the timing of shots, and playing through the tournaments.  However, I knew that this fun would not last forever, as the real crux of these kind of games is the multiplayer.  So I finally jumped on to play some online games and what do I get?  Probably one of the most frustrating experiences I've ever had playing a basketball game.
I played multiple matches, and it all boiled down to this:  The opposing team would send their Steph Curry to the opposite side of the cart, wait for the clock to run down, and shoot from 90 feet away.  They'd make it about 25% of the time, which is already a big giant red flag for me.
Okay, you'll say, but if that's all he's shooting you can easily outscore them.  That would work, except that rebounding is inherently broken.  If you don't control the rebounder, your teammate's AI decides to run out to the three point line to contest the shot, then realize they can't and run back under the basket which is always later than the opposing player's AI.  If you ARE controlling the rebounder, you can expect the AI to never play defense on the other side of the court, and grabbing a rebound is incredibly frustrating.  It's impossible to jump and grab a rebound, because your player will just go flying into the air towards god knows where.  You have to walk towards where the ball is going to be which, again, wouldn't be an issue if the opposing player's AI didn't somehow magically know where the ball was going to bounce and get to it before you.
Even with Dwight Howard, I'd be standing directly underneath where the ball was going to land and the opposing team's Steph Curry would casually walk over and go into what I call the rebounding animation of stupidity.  The game decides who's going to get the ball before the ball is grabbed. That player will then look upwards and very, very slowly walk towards the ball.  It doesn't matter if somebody else gets to the position before that player since that player has already been prematurely chosen as the rebounder.
Then there's the shooting.  I had to go online and do research on what the shot timing is supposed to be.  I've played basketball games all my life from NBA Jam to 2k17, and I've never had an issue with shot release timing.  In this game, it seems the shot release has nothing to do with your actual player's animation.  It's much easier to stand in the corner and shoot a three than it is to try and time a layup in this game, which is ridiculous.
Then there's the powerups.  A fun but gamebreaking (see what I did there) addition to the NBA Street games, in Playgrounds the powerups are not created equal and can therefore single handedly win a team a game.  Oh look, I got the powerup that allows me to score a shot with 100% accuracy.  The opponent gets the powerup that doubles their dunk points... and it lasts multiple possessions.  Takes a lot of the skill out of the game.
Finally there's the stealing.  It happens in about 50% of the games.  The opposing team will be about five feet away from me, mash the steal button, and knock the ball away 100% of the time.  I mean it.  Literally 100% of the time steal mashing would work for those players.
Again, I would absolutely love to be able to enjoy this game, but with online broken like it is I just can't see myself playing it again any time soon.  Because of that, I'll be asking for a refund.
tl;dr:  Fun concept, but the online is broken in incredibly frustrating ways.  Would not recommend.

Crusader Kings II is a grand strategy. Let my stress the word "grand." This game requires investment. Not just a monetary investment, but the investment of your time. Its a game that will take quite a long time to learn, let alone master. But in Crusader Kings II, is one of the richest, and deepest grand strategy experiences in a video game of all time.
In Crusader Kings 2 you play as an individual during a year of your choosing, I believe anywhere from 866 AD to around 1499, plotting for more power in a Medieval Court, Game of Thrones style. The game is riddled with depth and intrigue, and you're going to have to be willing to get your hands dirty if you want to make it to the proverbial top of the pile. Did I say get your hands dirty? I meant filthy. You're going to have to do some heinous, treacherous things if you want to end up at the top. You can't really trust anyone - not even your own flesh and blood in this one. You may have fathered good ol' Johnny for 19 years, but Johnny is rather ambitious, and will take you out of the spotlight if it means he can have his spot at the throne. It's ruthless.
Crusader Kings II is a game where you can send your brother to his death atop the sands of Syria by the hands of Jihadists, bang his grieving wife, make her bare your children, and then plot the murder of the little runts too. Oh, and you get to secretly arrange plots against people you don't like, get everyone else in on it, and then pull a Gaius Julius Caesar-esque everyone-run-up-and-collectively-stab-Henry-to-death type of thing. It's a great game, and if you have the time and effort to invest into it, I suggest you purchase it.

Frederic: Resurrection of Music Director’s Cut is a game about Frederic Chopin, travelling around the world and reviving “real” music.
If you don’t know Chopin, you can read about him here:
But if you already know about him or even like his music, then there is no need of reading the Wiki page and you can go into the game right away and enjoy the music.
This game is much like Guitar Hero, played not with a guitar but a piano. You use your keyboard to control the piano: A, S, D and F for the white keys. W, E and R for the black keys. The goal is to press the right key in the right moment. The notes on the screen will show you what key to press. Some notes are special: there are notes with arrows, notes you have to hold for a while and golden notes you have to catch before they fly away. Time after time you can use your super attack to crush your enemy.
You play as the ghost of Frederic, battling other musicians of different nationalities, subcultures and music styles (hip-hop, techno, Bollywood and more). There are many cut scenes telling with storytelling before and after each song. Frederic gets to know more and more information and after every music battle he travels to another country where new opponents are waiting for him. But what’s next? Well. Play it and you will know. :)
The graphics are quite okey. The cut scenes are well drawn and the world map has a beautiful design.
The music is also very pleasant and doesn’t get annoying as the songs differ very much from each other.
But I had some problems. Sometimes I had no sound in the cut scenes and I didn’t get to know much of the story. Also the game offers you to play it with the mouse or play it with the help of the mouse AND the keyboard, but for some reason only the first level supports the mouse controls. That was a big problem, as I’d need the mouse to catch those golden notes. Then I tried to reassign the control buttons but I didn’t succeed. I gave it some tries, restarted the game several times, but it didn’t want me to change the controls.
Positive:
+ a game about Frederic Chopin
+ nice gameplay
+ beautiful world map
+ very pleasant songs
+ different subcultures and music styles
Negative
- many cut scenes without sound
- couldn’t rebind the keys
- mouse doesn’t work after the first level
All in all I really liked the music, the gameplay and the parts of the story I could hear but the problems I pointed out are quite heavy and affect the game much. I hope this gets patched soon, so everybody can enjoy the full spectrum of the game.

SpeedRunners allows for a fast-paced, blood boiling, and vocal chord tearing experience that's easy to pick up and play but terrifyingly difficult to master. Up to four players, local, online, or bots are placed in a single screen within a 2D map. The goal is to race around the map until a character falls behind the screen. After the first goes, the screen quickly grows smaller as the music and mood intensify. The first person to three victories is crowned the winner of the match. Tools such as grappling hooks, remote explosives, dashes, and rockets aide in the fight for first place. While each match may only last minutes, you'll surely find yourself promising "only one more game," again and again. No game will more quickly transform four friends into vengeance seeking animals all maniacally laughing at their own victorious, however short-lived they may be.

is a by the number 2D adventure game. If you've played one you've probably played them all. Roughly perfected during the hayday of LucasArts' offerings such as
and
,
copies their formulas directly.
The interface is veryslimmed down. Everything is done through a single click. There's not "Look", "Talk", or "Open" button, the interface just gives the one option. On one hand this may seem like it limits the options the player has to solve puzzles, but veterans of this genre will know this makes the game easier.
And it is easy, at least for veterans. This is easier than the LucasArts games, and easier than more recent high quality offerings like
. But with ease comes logic, puzzles are not esoteric or impossible, and a decent number will leave you scratching your head long enough until you get that "Ah ha!" moment so crucial to the feedback loop for these kind of games. If you're new to adventure games, this is a good start.
Graphically the art is clean, polished, and objects are easy to identify without having to go pixel hunting. The story is unfortunately dull. Kelvin travels to 3 different times periods to locate 3 famous men from the post-Renaissance era. Kelvin plays your typical awkward Unlikely Hero we've seen countless times in well, pretty much every Adventure game (Deponia, Monkey Island, etc). Humor does suffer and there are very few laugh out loud moments. Think Michael Cera movies and you have a good idea what to expect.
So call this a provisional thumbs up. It's rather short, but as an introduction to the genre or just a time-waster for veterans you could do worse.

Kelvin and the Infamous Machine is a witty point and click adventure starring lab assistant Kelvin who has to change history to correct mistakes introduced by a mad professor. The settings are clever, and the gameplay is good, but the best thing about the game is the dialogue. The dialogue is very witty, full of references and jokes, and the voice acting is superb. I highly recommend the game if solely for the dialogue. On top of the dialogue, the gameplay was nice and smooth. The character movement was paced well, so I rarely felt like I had to wait for Kelvin to walk from point A to point B, and interactable items show titles when hovered over, which eliminates searching via random clicking as is necessary in some similar games.
The difficultly of the game was also well choosen. Only once or twice did I feel like I was stuck with no idea of where to go, and I later realized this was due to me missing something obvious. The game does a good job giving subtle hints as to the purpose of items and what is necessary where, and the items you collect themselves often provide a decent clue. There is also some replayability to the game, at least more so than normal with this kind of game. I completed the game in around 3.5 hours, and when playing back through the chapters to get the achievements I'd missed, I discovered lines and jokes I'd missed the first time (although being a second playthrough I knew exactly what to do to progress, that didn't change).
In terms of achievements, some come from progression, and some come from meeting certain conditions when interacting with objects in game. If you read through the achievement descriptions ahead of time, you can probably get most of them on your first playthrough, but a second will almost certainly be necessary anyway. If you're unsure about any of them, there is an excellent community guide that gives descriptions for each, but certainly play through the game on your own first. One requires a little something outside the game, but it is easily done (saying exactly what I mean would spoil it a bit).
This game was highly enjoyable and although there are many great aspects of the game, it is worth playing for the dialogue alone.

500 hours at least gone, at least another 500 are going to be taken out of me and probably much more. You want to know why ARK: Survival Evolved has longstanding mixed reviews? I'll give my experience.
I didn't play ARK because I chose to on my own. I got surrounded by people who have sunk more hours into it than I have; I've only started to surpass them in that. Primarily, I've been on Ragnarok because that's what we've played together. Still working on getting my Alpha Ascenscion on the Island in Singleplayer. Dove into Scorched and the Center for a good week.
I hate this game.
Even from when I first started playing ARK, it was apparent that it was unoptimized. My current download of the game takes up 128gb, a sizeable amount that I eventually bought an external hard drive for when I had to start using only my laptop after my computer died. Always having a sizeable amount of storage open for the amount of temporary space you need to have for each update so that it will occur is beyond stupid. The reason that I used to have so many hours is because ARK is the only game I could have downloaded at any point in time. Even after getting in, the loading takes ages and walking around in the world is certain to be accompanied by uneven framerate, graphical glitches, and a motley of screen freezes, a quarter of which may be a crash.
Yet, I love this game.
Despite it's shortcomings, it has been a long time since a survival game had taken my breath away with long rolling environments, large, towering creatures, and a sense of wonder. Figuring things out was something I had to take time to do, though, because I grouped in with people that already knew what to do. I merely got taken in for the ride, trying to figure out what engrams to take, what I should do for stats, and how to tame my first creature. Now I'm able to build up an army of powerful rexes and take down creatures many times my size and strength, such as a dragon, a giant ape, a huge spider, and a
manticore. Yet, even with all of this knowledge that I've gained, I feel like there is still more I can learn after 500 hours. Even with all that I know, every time I start the game again, I still know the feeling of danger around every corner.
But still, I hate this game.
It's the constant never-ending war in my heart with this. If Wildcard gave a
about anything other than profit, it would make me overjoyed. Simple fixes, optimization, and listening to the community is
what they'll do. They won't care as long as they keep making money, and with the release of Aberration, they're brimmed with more. The simple wishes we have are futile. Accounts of eggs and items slipping and disappearing through the ground are rife from when the game was announced in Early Access ages ago and are
present. An egg from one of my dilophosaurs slipped through the ground and hatched.
On top of that, Wildcard has a terrible sense of balance. Viability in dinosaurs is few. Most of what you need is rexes, filling the gaps with whatever else is strong. TEK is so far beyond the abilities of mortal men. If balancing in ARK was a see-saw, it would be sitting nearly vertical with how much weight stuff like this carries.
Unfortunately,
ARK in essence is more like a job. Tames take hours in most cases, incubating eggs and breeding takes longer, and raising babies takes immense amounts of time. For some lifeless slob of a girl that is me, this isn't a big deal. I enjoy sinking my hours away because I have nothing better to do and I feel like I accomplish something. I don't care that it took me two hours to tame a shark, because I'm
well going to ride it around underwater and kill some of those
mantas. I'm the stupid
that sat around for a large portion of my day taking care of
baby rexes. Modding makes the game so much more than it is, especially when you have people to play those mods with. I know how easy it is to lose a month to ARK and then watch that progress get taken away in less than an hour. Inversely, I know how fun it is to blow someone else's base sky high and kill hundreds of dinosaurs. It's a rex eat rex world out there and we're all wearing prime meat pants.
So how does this tie in to people that haven't bought this yet? I've given you the information you need, despite not recommending it. This game is loads of fun, especially with your friends, and you'll lose hundreds of hours to it. However, it's a bug-riddled, unoptimized heap of disappointment that'll wear on your system and your storage. People can erase your work in under an hour and it defeats your hope.
If you buy this,
It is
worth the $60 price point they slapped on after official release. In the end, though, that decision is on you. Shop smart, buyers.

I picked up this game during a sale, literally for just a few dollars. By far the best purchase I've made on Steam.
This is an open-world game set in 1949 Los Angeles. You play as a detective working your way up the ranks, digging deeper and deeper into a world of murderers, corrupt politicians, shady businessmen, and dirty cops. You investigate cases involving drugs, murders, arsons, insurance fraud, as they all tie up together into a web of crime that leads all the way to the top (just like in real-life). All this on a back-story of WW2 GI's returning home and reintegrating into civilian life, all the while unable to escape the psychological traumas incurred during the war.
The gameplay becomes somewhat repetitive after a while, but the solid realistic story, combined with fragments of a WW2 backstory, manage to keep things interesting all the way to the end.
The game does a decent job of transporting the player into the world of 1940's LA. The city, the music, the cars, the characters, all blend together nicely. The cast include actors from Mad Men and Fringe, and apparently many of the cars were from Jay Leno's collection.
From the cast, to the motion-scan and motion capture technology used in the making of this game, LA Noire really is a blend of game and film. In the end, it becomes an interactive movie where you control the main character. In fact I read somewhere that it was actually screened at the Tribeca Film Festival.
But don't let all those artsy overtones deter you from playing it. In the end, it's still a Rockstar game. The game could be described as a GTA for grown-ups. But it still provides a lot of the silliness you'd expect from a Rockstar game. For example, just like in GTA, as you walk down the street you can overhear fragments of conversations; the people of LA Noire often express some of their deepest thoughts and observations, such as:
"If olive oil comes from olives, where does baby oil come from?"
"They say I have bad taste in men, but I still like you. "
"I used to be indecisive; Now, I'm not so sure. "

Crusader Kings II can hook you in on a historic strategy gameplay. There are tons of possibilities of fame and shame on this game. Essentialy you play as a dynasty, whether your dynasty be the line of kings and emperors, or be just vassals, that is your choice. Though you start small as a lowly vassals, it is possible for you to become emperors, and it's also possible to be "demoted" to dukes at the same time.
This game have quite deep (and quite correct) simulation of kingdom life. You have to have a heir to continue your dynasty, keep your vassals weak, keep your liege happy, and so on. You can't wage war on every kingdom, you have to have a valid cause of war for that. To gain that cause war, you have to work hard. You can send your steward to create some fake claim, or you can start a holy war, or you can combine assasination and marriage so you can press your claims, etc.
There are so many mechanics in this game. The problem is that this game's help and tutorials are next to useless in explaining this or that to you. But on the other hand, the tooltips are really handy. You can know why this vassal is mad, or why that vassal is happy. Nearly all components in this game can be explained by the tooltips, though the mechanics is still hard to learn.
In the end, this game should be bought. For me, it's 9.25/10, slightly beaten by EU IV.

Frederic: Resurrection of Music is a music rhythm game where you play as Frederic Chopin on a quest to free music from an evil overlord.
The story begins in France where Frederic is buried as he is resurrected by three muses who give a simple task, free music and after that you travel around the globe fighting people in musical battles to get one step closer to restoring music.
So how is Frederic: Resurrection of Music ? Well it's not bad, but it's not great either.
Let me go over through everything good first:
The art style is really really good. It's a comic book like style of visuals and all of it is really pleasing to the eye. A lot of care went into creating the art style which is great.
The gameplay itself takes some time getting used as the controls are kinda meh. You use the A,S,D,F and W,E,R keys to control the piano and hit notes like Guitar Hero. This builds up a meter on the top of the screen where if you have the most of the bar filled means you win and if you don't you lose.
The game also let's you grant special abilities which I'm not sure what they do so can't really explain it here.
The game is also rather tough so even if you're slightly off rhythm you might lose the fight.
The Music is also really good and I had a great time listening to the tracks in game.
Now for the bad things:
As stated the controls are really really tough to master and it's really card to hit combos in the game.
The game is also really really short, just barely an hour long. But there is a ton of replay value. Completing the game on certain difficulties will unlock arena levels which I have not tried out.
Also for people interested on knowing the difference for the Director's Cut and regular is that in the director's cut there are two bonus story missions.
In the end I like my time with Frederic Resurrection of Music. It's a short and sweet time and on a sale it cost me 50 cents which is a steal. It's definitely worth a pick up.
Final Rating:
7/10
Pros:
+ Great Art Style
+ Great music
Cons:
- Short
- Controls are tough to master

This one is a little different, however, because rather than going on dates yourself, you pair up other lonely hearts and send them on dates in an attempt to help them find their soulmate.  It's set up in a game show-type fashion, where you watch your client and their date through secret cameras and tell them what to say to their date in an attempt to impress them.  If you can't impress them, however, you will lose reputation points and undoubtedly hold your head in shame.  One negative thing that I must bring attention to is that this game gets stupid hard later on.  It may just be the fact that my skillz just aren't mad enough, but I'm a little too dense to figure out the date's type based on their interests, which is something you must know for maxium chances of success.  It would be nice if you could see their type along with the rest of their info.  Another thing that I'm not so keen on is the randomness of the mini games which can get pretty frustrating.  Sure, you can cheat, but only if you have enough coins.  But I suppose the random aspect is all part of the fun, kinda like Mario Party.  Overall, this is a fun, simple game that I must admit is pretty addicting, even if it is a little difficult.  It doesn't take itself seriously at all, which I something I value in life as well as games, so if you think this is the sort of game you would be interested in, I'd definitely give it a shot.

Crusader Kings II is a grand strategy. Let my stress the word "grand." This game requires investment. Not just a monetary investment, but the investment of your time. Its a game that will take quite a long time to learn, let alone master. But in Crusader Kings II, is one of the richest, and deepest grand strategy experiences in a video game of all time.
In Crusader Kings 2 you play as an individual during a year of your choosing, I believe anywhere from 866 AD to around 1499, plotting for more power in a Medieval Court, Game of Thrones style. The game is riddled with depth and intrigue, and you're going to have to be willing to get your hands dirty if you want to make it to the proverbial top of the pile. Did I say get your hands dirty? I meant filthy. You're going to have to do some heinous, treacherous things if you want to end up at the top. You can't really trust anyone - not even your own flesh and blood in this one. You may have fathered good ol' Johnny for 19 years, but Johnny is rather ambitious, and will take you out of the spotlight if it means he can have his spot at the throne. It's ruthless.
Crusader Kings II is a game where you can send your brother to his death atop the sands of Syria by the hands of Jihadists, bang his grieving wife, make her bare your children, and then plot the murder of the little runts too. Oh, and you get to secretly arrange plots against people you don't like, get everyone else in on it, and then pull a Gaius Julius Caesar-esque everyone-run-up-and-collectively-stab-Henry-to-death type of thing. It's a great game, and if you have the time and effort to invest into it, I suggest you purchase it.

Music: 8.2/10
Great to listen to in and out of Dustforce, and is relaxing enough to not make you frustrated.
Overall: 8.6

Guild of Dungeoneering looks like a fun deck building dungeon crawling turn based strategy game. That's exactly what it is. First of all, don't get me wrong; it's fun, but there's not much depth to it beyond realizing that it's a deck building game and choosing your aquisitions accordingly.
If you like the gameplay you've seen of this game, you'll like playing it. That said, there are many pros and cons.
Pros:
1: Turn based gameplay - play on your time!
2: Effect stacking and interaction is fun and rewarding.
3: Class diversity is nice - different heroes have unique decks and effects to reward playing through multiple times and in different ways.
4: Gameplay is unique and engaging.
5: It's pretty replayable if you don't mind replaying mostly the same content.
Cons:
1: The constant reliance on RNG for most of the game can be a blessing and a curse, having to restart over and over because you keep pulling bad cards is no fun but that perfect find feels so good.
2: You can't save progress in the middle of a dungeon.
3: Early in the game you have to save up for the next tier purchases for a long time and some people end up getting stuck because they end up getting countered by certain enemies and dying over and over.
4: Once you unlock the next tier hero, the one you were using ends up never getting used due to difficulty scaling, which sucks if you like a tier 1 or 2 hero.
5: In my experience, some of the heroes are just weaker than other heroes of the same tier (especially at certain parts of the game.)
After playing through multiple times, I still feel like this game is incomplete. Everything is so temporary it feels like a beta or a game made under a time limit for a competition. There's no individual hero character stats or experience or consequence for their death. The story is pretty sparse, as well. Also, once you beat the game you can't even fight anything anymore. Dungeons close off when you beat them.
Even after all that, I still think it's worth it. This game has entertained me longer than I thought it would, and I can see myself returning to it in the future to play through again. At $15 this game is a little costly for what it delivers (nowadays) in my opinion, but it's a fun, novel experience. I'd give Guild of Dungeoneering a D- for amount of content, C for content diversity, and B+ for overall gameplay and personal enjoyment.

I rather liked Guild of Dungeoneering.  It's got a great asthetic and it knows how to get the most out of it.  The 'drawn' art style goes wonderfully with the bard voice over, and the playful style and theme of the classes and cards.
The combat is very simple to learn, but has enough depth to it to keep you interested and strategising.  The animations for the card-based combat ensure that you know where everything is coming from and what is causing what effect.  I was surprised when I watched some video reviews of the game on its release where the combat didn't have any animations, but thankfully that is no longer the case, since they add so much to the clarity of the game.
The out-of-combat gameplay is also surprisingly deep and strategic, with smart enemy placement giving you buffs: for example a bandit who has the "loner" special gets -1 hp if you place him in a dead end.  However, as you reach the final levels in the game you really have to know your way around the game, using every special to best effect.
I have some minor concerns about late game balance and a few classes under/over performing, as well as the progression of gold, but these are pretty minor as far as the whole game goes.
Overall, a great game that's a welcome change of pace.  Just enough tactical depth to get those gears turning in your mind, without requiring a huge ton of memorization or learning before you can get into it.

You play as a detective working your way up the ranks, digging deeper and deeper into a world of murderers, corrupt politicians, shady businessmen, and dirty cops. You investigate cases involving drugs, murders, arsons, insurance fraud, as they all tie up together into a web of crime that leads all the way to the top (just like in real-life). All this on a back-story of WW2 GI's returning home and reintegrating into civilian life, all the while unable to escape the psychological traumas incurred during the war.
The gameplay becomes somewhat repetitive after a while, but the solid realistic story, combined with fragments of a WW2 backstory, manage to keep things interesting all the way to the end.
The game does a decent job of transporting the player into the world of 1940's LA. The city, the music, the cars, the characters, all blend together nicely. The cast include actors from Mad Men and Fringe, and apparently many of the cars were from Jay Leno's collection.
From the cast, to the motion-scan and motion capture technology used in the making of this game, LA Noire really is a blend of game and film. In the end, it becomes an interactive movie where you control the main character. In fact I read somewhere that it was actually screened at the Tribeca Film Festival.
But don't let all those artsy overtones deter you from playing it. In the end, it's still a Rockstar game. The game could be described as a GTA for grown-ups. But it still provides a lot of the silliness you'd expect from a Rockstar game. For example, just like in GTA, as you walk down the street you can overhear fragments of conversations; the people of LA Noire often express some of their deepest thoughts and observations, such as:
"If olive oil comes from olives, where does baby oil come from?"
"They say I have bad taste in men, but I still like you. "
"I used to be indecisive; Now, I'm not so sure. "

This is a platform adventure game with a twist.  The 3-D setting is nice to look at, but the scope of it is limited.  Most of your focus will be on how to properly manipulate light and shadows to get around obstacles and reach "hidden" items that are actually quite visible but hard to reach.  In most cases, the solution is obvious.  There are no enemies to defeat.  You are an acrobat, not a fighter!  As for the setting and plot:  it is the 1920's (think film noire but in color) and you are the imaginary friend of a little girl with a broken family.  The girl is trying to find a way to keep her family from splitting up, and you are trying to help.  Most of the hidden items you find are clues to what is happening in the real world while the poor girl slowly goes "crazy" because she sees the world differently from the grown-ups.  Her madness is evident in the twisted and broken state of the world in which you travel, which is a reflection of the girl's mental state and memories.
The game is VERY short, you can finish it in just a few hours.  The path is always obvious and you have strict limits about where you can go; you can never stray much outside of the world known to the little girl because you will find great chasms at the edges of her memories.  The way you can become a shadow when you stand against any well-lit surface is pretty cool though.  In many instances you will need to move objects in the 3-D world in order to open a new path in the shadows in order to progress in the game.  It really is a unique and fun game mechanic.
So, the bottom line...
yeah this game is fun, but very short and straightforward.  There are no enemies, no boss fights, no NPCs to talk to or get side quests from, no level-up system... just platforming with travel through shadows.  The story is a nice mix of sweet and sad but really nothing to write home about.  The setting and graphics are stylized and cute, but not exactly beautiful.  So, I'd say go ahead and grab this game if it's available for a really cheap price.  If you pay more than $5 for it, you're paying too much.

GoD is a fun little rogue-like with a lot of character, but not a lot of content.
The card based gameplay is very straight forward compared to a traditional TCG, so the mechanics shouldn't be a stumbling block for most players for very long. Each of the different character classes (13 in total, I believe) has their own starting decks. These decks are expanded in battle by collecting equipment dropped after each battle. As with most RPGs, the common drops are low quality, only granting you a single card or buff, while the rare and epic loot drops can grant you 5 powerful cards and multiple buffs. You can also equip your Dungeoneer with a special item or blessing before exploring a dungeon, and these can offer advantages like extra hit points, larger starting hand sizes, or increased damage.
Your role in the game is not that of the Dungeoneer! You are actually the guildmaster sending these freshly recruited dungeon crawlers in to fetch you treasure, to defeat boss monsters to give you bragging rights over a more successful rival guild, and more often than not, to die.
This is where a lot of people are complaining about the game. Instead of this being a traditional RPG when you play as the same protagonist throughout, leveling up and accumlating new powers, your Dungeoneers die quite frequently and are replaced just as easily. There is no individual character progression in the game... Only the Guild benefits from the adventurers labors. You may find yourself getting attached to a particular Guildie after they survive a few expeditions, but trust me...
THEY ARE ALL EXPENDABLE.
Once you have that in mind, you will find a fun and stylish game! The maps are partially laid out for you, and you get to fill in the blanks with the random dungeon tiles you are given each turn. Same thing with treasure and enemy placement. Some things are already on the map for that particular mission, and you get to place the rest to your own liking. You don't directly control the Dungeoneer once they are on a mission, but you can influence their path by tempting them with gold or putting a monster in their path. GoD actually reminds me of the tabletop tile game Boss Monster, and that is a favorable comparison!
The biggest downside of the game is that it is very short. I beat the game with nearly 100% unlocked in a little over 15 hours. There is no end game content, and you cannot re-run old missions in the same game. There is no New Game +. The selection of classes and items is limited. There is little replay value. As such, the game does kind of let you down because there is the potential for so much more!
Apparently an expansion entitled Pirates Cove is in the works, so that is a plus. The ability to mod the game would bea welcome addition. I, for one, would love to create some of my own classes or even do different genres, like a Warhammer 40K-style sci-fi version or super hero style set up.
If you don't mind the relatively small amount of content, then yes, I recommend this game. Just be aware that you're going to be paying about a dollar per hour of content. Fun content, yes!
Just not a lot of it...

My experience with Ark has been a real mixed bag. I've experienced some real highs and some astounding lows. The game is diffucult and extremely unforgiving for new players. Learning what to do is daunting and doing it while dodging hostile players and an extremely hostile environment can be as discouraging as you could possibly expect. I played ark for my first time in the begining of 2017 and after a few short hours I quit and didn't touch it again untill now. My experience was a clunky game with zero guidence and nothing but a multitude of ways to die, loose all your gear and start again. Since then, not very much has changed other than my mind set going in.
I decided to try it again and stick with it till i learned at least the basics. For this I used offline single player and I managed to very easily put together several videos of a thousand ways to die. After about a week on and off I decided to take a chance and see what online multiplayer was like. I met some nice people on a PVP server and all seemed great. We tamed several large dinos and began building a thriving community. Death soon followed, our town was burnt down and all our dinos killed without mercy. Our supplies looted and our pitiful defence over run like they weren't even there. The is no mercy on PVP servers. You will die, a lot and then you will die some more.
At this point my enthusiasm for this game was dwindling quickly. I decided to join a new PvE server and try avoid the mindless bloodshed. Well, the PvE servers are without a doubt the single most boring gaming experience you could ever hope for. The island map looked less like the island I was familiar with and more like a crazed building simulator with no point. Players build pillars all over the map since this is the only way you can stop other player from building next to your base in PvE since you cant attack other players. They also build extremely large walls, for what, I dont know. I left that server quicker than a windows CTD.
At this point I'd all but given up on Ark and was ready to reconcile it to the rubbish bin of games never to be played again. Before that I decided to give PvP one more chance. I've become an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I steal from everyone, I raid any base thats got a weakpoint. I have no base of my own and literally every item of gear I have was stolen or made using stolen matrials in other players forges while they slept or bled to death. It has become the high point of my day, stalking, hunting, moving through the jungle like silent death. If you are timid, uninformed, peace loving or in any way not willing to kill, steal, rob and savage your way to survival you will not survive. How you chooe to survive is up to you. Get a team, work hard, build a base and maybe. just maybe you'll luck out and be one of the few alpha tribes who dominate each server. For the rest of use lowly scum, its kill or be killed, eat or be eaten, steal or be left destitute. This game has taken me to hell and back again. Buy this game, get used to dying and dont turn you back for a single minute. 9/10 I'd have given it 10/10 but their are a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of bugs to deal with aswell...get used to crashing as much as dying. But my god, its been one wild ride.

I’m really excited about the potential for Youtubers Life. I’ve always enjoyed Life Simulation games, and Youtubers Life, a new game on Steam, puts an interesting twist on Life Simulation games.
In the game, you play as a person trying to get famous by creating YouTube videos. The game is currently in Early Access, and some of the features haven’t launched yet. Right now, the only channel you can have is on video games, but in the future you will be able to choose to do them on fashion and food as well. Considering how well-developed the video game portion is, I’m really excited to see what the developers will be able to do with those other categories.
Overall, this is the sort of fun, relaxing game that I could really get invested in. The social aspect to it seems a little underdeveloped currently, but I love all the little elements that the creators added to make the game feel realistic, and I’m anxious to see where they go with it as they finish developing it. For a first look, I’m feeling pretty positive.
Most Enjoyable Element: I’ve found editing the videos you make to be one of the most enjoyable parts of the games. It’s an interesting aspect that hasn’t been done before: You have reaction cards that you can use to amp up your video, and then you edit the pieces together to fit as best as possible.
Least Enjoyable Element: The venues to go out with friends seem rather limited right now and a little droll. There doesn’t seem to be any consequence to leaving a movie in the middle of it, for example. And I seem to be stuck in the friend zone with everyone, which is a little depressing. Additionally, waiting for some of the updates to the game, such as the ability to create fashion & food channels.

Hence some people's conception that this game would be p2w, which it most definitely is not). And then, just try it out.
