I confess I purchased this mainly for the nostalgia factor. After completing 1993:SM  I really can say the tagline "celebrating games like Gradius, R-Type and Life Force" was at least partially misleading: those were great shooters indeed, but no (half) bullet hell they were.
Bullet hell did surface in year 1993 but was not a popular subgenre until the second half of the decade. What we have here, to summarize, is a part classic / part bullet hell horizontal shooter cast in Amiga-style graphics, what with all the Xenon2 Megablast references. Well, let's be honest here: I venerate Amiga, and 1993's art and sprites and (shyly used) parallax background are average Amiga fare; but obviouly not even a pumped up A4000 could have pushed so many high-color animated objects on a scrolling screen at once: not without major slowdowns and other problems.
tech demo (grandfather of 1993; look for it on youtube), while remarkable for its time, could not even come close to the level of complexity on display here. I like the archaeological side of the project the developers explained, but the game is clearly coded with modern hardware in mind.
Since Amiga had many great scrolling shooters, but never a bullet hell (unless you count some modern homebrew attempt of a game), you could say this is a sort of
approach at retrogaming: interesting, for sure, but not completely succesful.
I admit that bullet hell is not my cup of tea, not even in hybrid form: I prefer 100% standard scrolling shooters, by far. I find bullet hells tend to overcrowd the screen with unnecessary debris, particles and tiny bits of whatever that serve only one purpose: a mere trick to distract the player's eye and to unfairly increase difficulty level. 1993 is no exception in this, but fortunately it doesn't have that other typical bullet hell issue: primary-colored, fluoresecent, lisergic, anime-style characters and graphics :-) (which usually I quite appreciate, but not when they make your eyes bleed).
As for 93 game mechanics, you don't have a clear indication of your status (no classic energy bar) and I found this to be a little off-putting: yes, your life depends on the 8 rotating barrier dots - they regenerate after they're hit, they decrease when your ship is hit. But some projectiles can apparently take your ship down at once, even if you still have dots: better instructions explaining this, maybe? Either this, or I was not able to distinguish what exactrly hit me and how many times it did it - and we're back to bullet hell issues.
Speaking of instructions, I completely missed that you could summon the armory vessel *during* a level by hitting a small beacon (shame on me!), so I completed 1993 on a much higher difficulty  (big me!) but this granted me no special achievement (hint, hint). So, my 200+ deaths could have been less, for sure, If I had purchased some weapon ehancement in the middle of a level  - because of this, I cannot really express a fair judgement on difficulty and frustration level. For me it was high until I finally beefed up my ship, then it decreased and was up again on last level, but your experience could definitely be much different.
Lastly, audio: contrary to others, to me the game sounded not that great. Average (again) techno fare, no real personality to show. 90s shooters had way better music and melodies and all, but this is a general problem with today gaming.
All in all, I appreciate the effort and the meaning of the whole operation here, but recommending the game is no easy choice: if you are an avid retrogamer you'll probably really like its graphics; if you are a 2D shooter completist, definitely go for it; and a really diehard bullet hell fan could enjoy its different approach and  unusual setting. For all the others it could be too niche.
As for me, I'd prefer to give no thumb, but alas, Steam allows no draw.  So, thumbs up - but by an invisibly thin hair.

The difficulty with reviewing this game is that I'm also obligated to mention its spiritual predecessor.
, a cult-classic beatemup released in 1996, is one of my Top 10 Favorite Games of All-Time. Naturally, this should cast a very large shadow on my opinion of Degica's latest release. Is
a better game? Is it worse? This is why I've never been a fan of comparison reviews, because they do a disservice to both games. Nevertheless, I'm going to say something that some readers will believe to be a cop-out answer:
is different. This isn't a game designed to build upon
or the changes/additions made in its 2011 re-release. Instead, this game is a unique take on Treasure's multi-plane fighting/beatemup series, one that started with
on the Sega Mega-Drive.
Beatemups, like any other videogame genre, consist of ideas. The first entries involved fights between street gangs, rescuing kidnapped girlfriends, and finding freshly-cooked turkeys inside of barrels. Today's beatemups haven't strayed too far from these humble roots, but they have developed outward through the accumulation and expression of ideas.
is a very unique game. The characters are a collection of quirks. Their move-sets range from the typical to the absurd. Instead of 5 to 8 levels of side-scrolling action, this game is divided into well over 100 short quests.
Now when I call the characters a collection of quirks, I'm not just referring to their odd attire. Solange dresses like she inherited the contents of her mother's underwear drawer, and she swings a sword that must weigh twice as much as she does. Next we have Ali, her partner, a thief who doesn't just attack with a dagger. She can also throw bombs, whistle to get the enemy's attention, and teleport. Zozo is a necromancer who built herself out of spare body-parts, and she fries everyone with magic. The blind samurai Tsukikage fights with typical slashing attacks, but he also "flies" across the screen like the heroes from the movie
. The 2,000 year old bard Allegro swings an electric guitar... and you get the idea.
This motley assortment of heroes is further bolstered, by the plethora of enemies that you'll unlock. Everyone, from the final boss to the tiniest slime, has a set of moves. Of course, with over 50 playable characters, there are also a handful of stinkers. On the other side of the coin, a few opponents border on overpowered. That's the price of freedom, and I gladly accept it. Having so many fighters to experiment with is really entertaining. Furthermore, every hero, monster, or otherwise, can improve their stats through level-ups. Some characters can use equipment that improves their stats and bestows special abilities. This lends a unique approach to combat depth, though some weapons and armor... border on overpowered.
On the field, there are a few factors that set this game apart from other beatemups, even
. Your "burst" ability allows you to stun opponents and do more damage. This ability costs 100 mp to activate, and is cancellable at any time. However, while this ability can be abusable in the right situation, even a stunned opponent can respond with a burst of their own. Every character has a lock-on attack. When an enemy is locked onto, the player can do more damage to them. Certain special moves also have homing properties when performed during a lock-on. Last and certainly not least is your armor. When you take damage, your armor (green meter) is reduced. When this is gone, you have 0 defense, and attacks do far more damage to your life (red meter). This is one of those times where bursting is very handy, because it restores armor. Certain attacks do more damage to armor than life, so it's worth switching tactics if enemies are taking far too long to beat.
The combination of characters, stats, and equipment lend
a "sandbox" feel. Now when I talk about the sandbox, I don't mean in the sense of
or
. It's more along the lines of exploring the mechanics of a beatemup. Think of it as finding out the effects of certain moves, the properties of attacks, and combining abilities to destroy adversaries as quickly and creatively as possible. These aspects of the game are very compelling, and will keep players coming back long after the story mode is completed.
Alongside the campaign, you can unlock a wealth of bonus quests. These challenges are targeted at the advanced players, and can have unique win conditions. I hate to say it, but there are a few escort-missions in this game. Sometimes it's best to go back to the character-select menu, and choose someone apt for the task. Now I could use the mighty dragon, but his attacks cause a lot of collateral damage. Instead I went with someone fast, who quickly reaches enemies, so that they can't immediately crush the idiot townsperson I'm trying to protect.
also has a bevy of multiplayer modes, for both competitive and cooperative players. The versus mode offers something for everyone. If you're looking for a "fair" fight, without all of the high-stats and special equipment, then there's no need to worry. Alternatively, if you have to put all of that experience grinding to use, then you're also covered. However, the cast of this game isn't balanced very well. For one, a handful of characters have infinites, which is something to look out for. There are also some exclusive quests aimed squarely at co-op gamers.
If you're a fan of the traditional arcade-style brawler, this probably isn't the game for you. While there are options to fight versus matches with default-strength characters, the bulk of the game is designed with the expectation that players will level-up, allocate stats, and decide on equipment. In short, there might be too many RPG elements for some. Bursting can also bring down the pacing of a versus match. Since they can be executed at any time, some fights will devolve into bursts countering bursts. Bursting can be an effective tool, like using
V-ism activation to counter moves. However, I don't think allowing the player so many opportunities to burst is a good idea. As far as nitpicks are concerned, certain large-scale attacks can cause the screen to shake a little too much. The soundtrack is also really bland.
is like I said, a beatemup with ideas. Not all of them are great, but they're creative and lend the game a lot of flavor. It helps that the mechanics are pretty solid, and there's fun to be had in beating enemies up. It also can't be stressed enough; having this game run at a playable frame-rate is a huge boon in itself. I owned the 3ds version for a spell, and on average it ran three to ten(!) times worse. All in all, I think that this game is worth checking out.

I was hoping this screen would allow the use of the Page Up, Page Down, Home and End keys for quick navigation but unfortunately that is not the case. They also show armor that your current character can't equip, which serves no purpose but to add more scrolling and make things tedious.
Music is forgettable, sound effects do their job. There is no English dub despite it being in the 3DS version.

I never got the chance to play Code of Princess on the 3DS, but always wanted to. I was and am very excited for this PC port. The frame-rate stays at a steady 60fps and even though the resolution is 720p it never bothered me since I was having so much with the game-play. You also have the option to have dual-screens with the 3DS menu features.
There are so many characters you can unlock and play in co-op mode with friends, but only four of them can be used in the campaign. There is so much customization you can easily make your character a powerhouse, a speedster, or even both. Combos are a blast to keep going and taking advantage of character's unique move sets keeps each stage exciting.
The campaign's story is loose and a great satire of the rpg-genre from the half-naked heroine to the plot of being "chosen ones" all done with a terrific Japanese dub. But, I do wish there was an option for English voice-overs due to some mis-matched subtitles and loose translation.
Overall, I felt this was a great port of a 3DS game. The graphics might be chunky in places, but that's what it is; a port, and if you'd wanted to try out Code of Princess, but don't want to go digging up a small screen 3DS copy, the Steam version is fun and has online co-op/vs. to keep you invested.
(Disclaimer: I was a beta tester and received a early access of the game.)

1933 Space Machine looks like an early 90s Amiga game because it literally is - it was unfinished and in storage for about two decades before the owner finally completed and put it on Steam Greenlight. While I'm not too familiar with Amiga games, this clearly shows inspiration from Stargunner and Raptor: Call of the Shadows. It's a moderatly paced, side-scrolling shmup where destroyed enemies drop currency that you can use to upgrade your ship between missions and at mid mission checkpoints.
There's a half a dozen different ships, and about two dozen different weapons that you attach to the top, left, right, and bottom of your ship. I find this annoying, since I found myself losing track of where my ship was in more hectic moments.  These weapons will help you deal with enemies at various distances and angles, so you sometimes need to watch you back. Thankfully, your ship can take a few hits and you have a rotating shield that can take a few hits and partially regenerate. You can also manually rotate this shield if you desired. Lives are unlimited, and instead the game will count your deaths per mission and over the entire playthrough. Each level usually has about 2 checkpoints as well.
The checkpoints, unlimited lives, moderate game speed, and managable bullet patterns makes this much easier to suggest to casual shmup fans versus the bullet hell games out there, which are too overwhelming for some gamers.

If you enjoyed the arcade basketball classics such as NBA Jam and the NBA Street series, this game is definitely for you.
NBA Playgrounds is like a combination of both series, with fast-paced gameplay, arcade controls and a wacky artistic style, which I find pleasing to the eye.
PROS:
- Fast-paced basketball gameplay, focusing on quick possessions and dunks.
- Arcade-style feel
- Official NBA licensing, including a whopping 150-man roster, with more players planned in the future.
- Unique graphical feel I haven't seen in a basketball video game before.
- Easy to pick up and play for the most part.
CONS:
- The timing on the shooting is a little hard to get used to if you have played other basketball titles.
- Not many graphical options (Resolution and a quality slider, that's it.)
- Loading can take slightly longer than expected.
- Down time between scores (AKA inbounds) are extremely long, I hope this'll be changed in the future.
- Seem to be having a hard time with online matchmaking in Australia.
In summation, if you're a fan of arcadey basketball titles like the ones mentioned above, or even a fan of NBA and basketball in general, NBA Playgrounds is a nice title to pick up and play to satisfy the itch you may not fix by playing 2K17.

This isn't the usual tycoon or even the usual dating sim. This is Kitty Powers's Matchmaking and believe me, it's harder than you think.
The one thing that it has in common with other dating/matchmaking games is the ... well, dating and matchmaking. But how you go about it and that fact that you will have all possible couple combinations (which is amazlingly refreshing for once) is different ... and can be quite difficult.
There is some guess work and some unexplained features that can make this a little more difficult - for example who is what 'type'. No, not sexuality wise but life style wise. How do you best figure that out. Then you start having to guess some more and make conclusions until you finally realize that someone who loves Halloween might just like someone who enjoys costume parties.
It's not black and white - it is not match the same with the same but it is a but find the middle ground.
The rest of the set up dates are won or lost with a serious of mini-games and a good memory or the ability to right things down fast. Some are a lot of fun, some not so much  - and some are simply depending on luck.
Depending on your matchmaking skills, memory and luck, the couple will hit it off or not.
Coins, XP and reputation are awareded. XP unlocks additional features via level - Coins are required to buy the features, cheat or get hints - and Reputation ... well I only know that the tip you receive for a sucessful case increases with reputation ... but that's all I know.
For now, the game does get slightly repetitive but I am hoping to unlock some additional features to spice things up with time. Kitty Power's comments, the ... unusual ways of talking, crazy hobbies and the likes are currently still making up for it.
One thing that I am really missing is the means to reset the account. I have the feeling I invested some money in the wrong things at the beginning and would have loved to start over.
All in all - it's addictive and challenging and I am bent to crack a good bunch of the achievements.
So yes, for the price, I would recommend the game.

This game is like eating three pints of ice cream while watching your favorite movie. You have this sinking feeling that something or someone may judge you, but you know what? It tastes good and it just FEELS SO RIGHT.
This is a very well thought out dating sim game and I'm happy to still be waist deep within it. Your task is to help your boss, Kitty Powers, make perfect matches. Send your clients off on their dream dates and make sure they don't blow it.
Simple enough, right? Not quite. There are types of people to mix and match together while hoping that date goes perfectly. Will it take one perfect date or do you want to steam it out with three dates? Guide your clients by playing mini games to make sure they succeed in winning the affections of their date.
If you succeed, you get promotions and you get paid. Getting paid means better restaurants to take dates to, better ways to fancy up your clients (because they REALLY need your help), and other little perks like kicking out the more troublesome clients.
The tutorial makes things look incredibly easy, but once that's done, you are almost completely on your own and left figuring out things for yourself. You'll have to understand clients interests and how your little black book works. You'll either figure this out through dumb luck or failing. Either way, there's no harm in making a few mistakes at first. No one's perfect starting out. Even I have a completely ruined relationship from a client that I thought were totally into each other. Oh well, win some and lose some.
I love that you get updates from satisfied customers and you get perks from their continuing relationships. I thought that this was a great touch and another incentive to get things right the first time. Another thing that I loved? Making my own profile to send out myself to be a "mystery shopper" for my own dating life. Can't wait to see the results to have a good laugh over that.
The graphics are bright and inviting, reminding me of traditional time management games. And those games? Those games remind me of addiction. They remind me of "just one more level". That's what I noticed immediately. I wanted one more date conquered just because I needed the ego boost. Just to say I was Kitty's best employee (I have no friends playing this so this is my wild imagination), I needed to do more work for more upgrades. Just ONE MORE client! It's very friendly and I'm almost happy that Kitty isn't cartoony because that would take away from the humor that is our wonderful and loving boss. She is quite sassy and pixels just wouldn't suit her, after all.
I especially appreciated that there was a bit more inclusion in this game. It's not just limited to man-seeking-woman or woman-seeking-man, the devs did realize there's more than man and woman relationships so I must say I appreciated that option. Thank you. It means a lot that you did that.
There is a bit of stereotyping...but more so on the personality types of "sporty", "nerds", "hippies", etc. If that offends you then I have no idea what to say. If you have trouble with characters who are supposed to be "punk alternative" speaking with what seems like (forgive if I read it in the wrong accent!) a Cockney/London accent then steer clear. Seriously. British Punks from London stereotypes. I can't imagine anyone hating that but hey, they're there amongst a few other cliches. I thought they were all incredibly adorable characters I really, desperately wanted to see happy. They're very "human" with wants and needs and the need to be validated.
Even for cartoon people without souls, yes. I'm entirely serious.
The more things you buy for your matchmaking business, the harder things get. If you buy better restaurants, you get paid more, but the games get harder and sometimes slightly lewd. Yes there is a game to hold in your fart. The fact I can write a review complimenting a game for recognizing that yes, you have to hold in your gas during a date and it is indeed a game of chance is astounding. I never thought I'd have to compliment a fart mini game.
Buy a salon for your business and you can alter your appearance for a better potential mate for your client. Wouldn't that one guy or gal be great IF ONLY your client dyed their hair lilac? Now you can...if you do it quickly. Does that guy/gal prefer a more chic style? Quickly change clothes after you buy an add-on for your salon. They say you shouldn't change for anyone but hey, let's make an exception, right?
It's an easily accessible game that truly anyone can play. While I'd keep this for the crowd that can understand dating, I'd honestly say this is really a decent game for anyone to play. It's cute. It's bubbly. You can play against your friends and compare scores. You can even send your friends personas on dates if they're playing. You get bonus points for making matches with real life people and you'll tell who they are by the little globe by their profile as you match them up to people.
I can't find a single thing bad about this game, really. It's a little tycoon/sim on dating and it really illustrates the whole luck/chance and repetition that is dating. And I'm not bored! There's always some new curve ball coming at me!
Plus Kitty Powers is the best boss I have ever had. If I could just do this in real life with Kitty as my real boss, this would be great.

Do you like the idea of re-starting everytime without any special equipment and levels (think spellunky)
Do you like cards and daring your luck .?.
Do you enjoy exploring a game .?.
Do you enjoy neck and neck battles that might go either way .?.
Do you like supporting indie developers that are in turn caring and updating their product .?.
If the answer is YES, in at least 3 of those questions, then buy this game :D

A charming deck building game that oozes character. An amusingly callus and jealous guild leader sends droves of hapless and probably brainless 'dungeoneers' into foul and dangerous places to try and show up those Ivy League ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
Your equipment and some classes/blessings give points in a variety of combat disciplines, up to a maximum for 4 points per style. Each consecutive point in a style grants the next (and more powerful) attack card of the style. Consequently specialiseation in 1/2 styles will make you reliably powerful while attempting to jack of all trades will leave you with a large deck full of weak attacks.
Stratagie in and out of combat is simple, often simply having an obvious 'best' option. Due to the small numbers used in game failure to identifiy or misstep from the 'best' tactic can get easily you killed. While possible to tailor your style to give optimum results for each dungeon my own experience suggests this to be of dubious value.
The basic gameplay loop is very simple and best suited to short play sessions.
The game balance is a little wonky in that:
- It is possible to be forced into suboptimal and even leathal situations by the random nature of the cards through no fault of your own.
- Each group of classes is objectively more powerful than the group preceeding it.
- Some of the combat disciplines seem less effecitive than others.
- The difficulty progression of dungeons can be subverted by gaining access at a class/gear above the intended level, which is an issue because...
- The movement system can be abused to indeffinitly extend a dungeon attempt to farm, dull but easy to accomplish
Sound assets are in theme but very limited. The bardic narrator is well voiced but sometimes frustratingly slow spoken.
Visually strong asthetic, if you happen to like the handdrawn look.
My bottom line:
If you want a simple, rouge light deck builer with basic stratagie then grab it. If you aren't down for all those things or something mentioned above puts you off in a noteworthy way, wait till a sale.

I played through a bit of DOS 1 and really enjoyed the concept, but couldn't create a character I was happy with. I also feel like they did a better job this time around of peppering "town time" with (usually avoidable) combat and/or puzzles to solve. The game is clearly designed to be played the way you want to play it. So if you liked the first game, you'll love this game. If you liked the style of the first game but couldn't get into it, give it a shot. If you didn't like the first game at all, probably a pass.
[Edit] I have now played the released product for over 50 hours and I expect to enjoy it for much longer. I strongly recommend this game for anyone who likes challenging RPGs with an emphasis on story and character. Some people will find the pacing to be a little slow but the game is simply a masterpiece if you have the patience to play. You can really tell they have improved their writing by leaps and bounds since DOS1.

This is a fun and challenging shoot 'em up. Originally developed in 1993 (although only recently released) it uses a retro style it reminds me of games like Xenon II. The weapons are fun and unique and each level has a different design providing interesting challenges.
This game feels like old school shooters you used to play on your Megadrive (or Genesis), only updated for the modern era. The weapon options are interesting, each one providing an interesting way to make bad guys explode. The level design is fantastic, each level having a specific theme and an interesting challenge. It's not the most hardcore bullet hell I've played, but it still provides an interesting challenge for fans of the genre.
The shield mechanic is interesting - you can leave it spinning or you can take control of it. It only protects you from specific angles and can be used to prevent small bullets from making contact. As you take more damage your shield shrinks, so it also acts as an indicator of your current health.
The game also has checkpoints, saves, and you can play the four different worlds in any order so it is less challenging than old-skool shooters in that respect. This is probably a good thing for the modern gamer in my opinion, and doesn't detract from the experience in my opinion.
It has some interesting achievements that provide extra challenges, which helps to increase its replay value.
If you're a fan of old school shoot em ups and want a sense of nostalgia with something fresh at the same time, I highly recommend this game.

Crusader Kings II is the ultimate medieval strategy game, period.  And this is coming from a guy that has a BA in history from Rhodes College with a focus on medieval studies.  It is the type of game that you won't instantly love or even understand.  That's because it's an incredibly deep and complex game that has almost infinite replayability.  You can play as a lowly count of a single territory and try to work your way up to king (or emperor).  You can also start as a duke, king or even William the Conqueror and try to hold onto England as a Norman! Along the way, there will be treachery, fighting with your vassals, fantastic feasts (where you even choose the food and entertainment), religious crusades, crazy random events, arranged marriages, succession wars, family and court politics, etc. etc!   For those of you who have played Europa Universalis IV, this game has some similarities but is more focused on personal relationships.  You play as a dynasty from a single bloodline.  If all of your heirs of the bloodline die out, it's game over!  When your ruler dies, depending on the laws you set, your heir takes over.  To top it off, this game has TONs of fantastic expansion packs.  Play as the vikings starting even early in the 900s or play as a merchant republic, etc. etc.  The game is so deep and detailed that you don't even need the expansions, but they will keep you busy for hundreds of hours more.  They really nailed the feudal system and all of its complex and crazy relationships.  I once built a castle in my home territory.  I gave it to a relative and thought I was safe.  They married a powerful princess from Norway who kept her title.  All of a sudden, I had a single foreign castle right in the middle of Ireland!  It reminded me of the French castle in Monty Python's Holy Grail! The music is fantastic and really fits with the period.  The one negative I will say is that the learning curve is steep and the tutorials are prettymuch awful.  To really play this game, you'll need to invest some time either reading a few guides or watching some tutorial videos.  (I recommend Ck2 guide for newbies youtube series by SeeKayEm99.  There's a ton of parts and a few things are outdated but it's still great for learning.  You only need to watch the first few to get the hang of things)  So, I would heartily recommend this game to someone who loves strategy games and a challenge as well as history.  Be warned that there's some micromanagement involved.  Sometimes, your heir will need a royal marriage and you'll need to spend some time looking at various matches and alliances around the world.  Anyway, pick this game up if you have patience, love strategy games, and don't mind a steep learning curve.

The game is a puzzle-platformer and your character must use the shadows cast by real objects (and people) to achieve her goals. This often involves moving light sources in such a way as to line up shadows just right to reach a ledge or time a jump over the shadows of moving people. I never thought the original BioShock could be improved upon.
Guess what - I was right.
Don't get me wrong, this game is absolutely fantastic. The story is rich, the combat is satisfying. Everything you need for a good BioShock game. Even multiplayer in the non-remastered version. However, I do have a few nitpicks with this game, although I still recommend it.
For one: the combat
I did say that the combat in BS2 is good, and I stand by that. But it feels like some weapons are either underpowered or not emphasized. A good example of this is the spear gun. Essentially a sniper rifle, the speargun is a long-range weapon that does good damage but has a small clip. The problem I have with this is that 90% of the combat in BioShock 2 is close-ranged, so it is pretty useless. The camera is also bad. Instead of simply photographing your foes for research, you have to photo them and then attack them within a set period of time. The plasmids now have alternate abilities, and some are pretty good. But some, like 'Eruption!' for 'Incinerate!' seem really bad and drain your EVE like a frickin' hose.
For two: the little sister system.
This is what annoys me most about this game. In order to get the most ADAM out of a single little sister, you have to:
1) Kill the big daddy protecting it
2) either adopt or harvest it. For the most ADAM, adopt.
3) Follow the sister's commands to the nearest ADAM-filled corpse. Proceed to place her down and get attacked by waves of splicers.
4) Repeat one to two more times. When done, place the little sister in the vent for ADAM or harvest her for more ADAM.
5) Do this procedure for EVERY LITTLE SISTER IN THE LEVEL.
6) When you put the last little sister in her vent/harvested her, a VERY POWERFUL ENEMY will come after you called a Big Sister, a plasmid-wielding, extremely agile Big Daddy. Although she does drop ~40 ADAM, the ammo and EVE shots/health packs consumed doesn't seem worth it.
7) Repeat steps 1-6 for almost EVERY LEVEL IN THE GAME.
Regardless of these things, I still love this game and think you should get it and its DLC, but try to do it when it's on sale

While this obviously lends itself to easily written silly games, this is one probably the most fun - if dopey - casual/tycoon game I've ever played. I honestly don't even know how to describe what I like about it. It's just plain fun. Instead, here is the small list of things I don't like about it, compiled over my admittedly meager 1.5 hours played (in my defense, I bought this at 1 AM on a Monday morning).
-Loading seems to happen all the time. If there's a different 2D background for the 2D characters, there will be a load screen, and they're often relatively long. I can usually load a new area in heavily modded Skyrim at least as quickly as KPM can load the lewdly named American restaurant. I feel like load screens and load times both should be pretty minimal for something like this, but I'm no expert, and it's not horrid. Just annoying.
-It can get a little samey, and it's probably not something most people want to sit down and play for more than a couple hours because of that. The dialog is modular (i.e. there are probably 5-10 different ways of saying "I like your hair" and any other conceivable saying), but you see them a lot. After 30-45 minutes of playing, I stopped reading the unimportant dialog because it wasn't funny or interesting after seeing it a few times in that time. It was still fun, just a little less immersive, especially because it felt like the same people talking. Also, unless things change further in, the dates are all just dinner at a restaurant that consist of a few random minigames from a small pool. While they do vary from each other a little and it's a good formula, it does get old.
-A lot of the difficulty of the game seems to stem from its randomness. Randomness is kind of a necessity in a game like this, but I think it has a little too much influence. It's very hard to predict how your client's date is going to react to what you say or the decisions you make, and I think there should be more reliable guesswork, if that makes sense. But maybe I just need to play more to understand. I do like that failing a client too much makes them leave and hurt your rep a lot - I almost got to a third strike with one client and I had to do everything I could to make their last date work out.
-I'm not sure if I'd pay the full $10 for this game, just because it remains to be seen to me how much the gameplay fleshes out, but I got it on GMG for $6 and that was definitely worth it. At time of posting, it was $7.49 on Steam, which I would have paid if not for the GMG deal.
All that said is just overanalysis of things that weren't big deals. The art is fitting, the voice work and images for the one persistent character is hilarious and well done, and the gameplay is enjoyable and error-free. If you're looking to play a game all day, this probably isn't it, but it's definitely something you can keep on hand and get a few hours of fun out of. It also throws your friends' characters in the game as potential clients/dates, so you can have some fun with that if you can convince someone else to play it. I also plan to break it out at LAN parties so my friend Brian can laugh at me and call me rude names.

I can recommend ARK if you're the kind of player that likes being dropped into a survival map with no real objections besides explore and survive and nothing to really explain mechanics in the game. So you're probably going to die more than a few times before you figure out the basics, especially as it's only semi-balanced to make the game easier to survive. There are mulitple spawn points to choose from in case a dinosaur ends up spawn camping which, while useful, shows off more of the balancing issues. I died 8 times trying to find my friends on their private server when I first started playing and ended up waiting for them to come to me when it got so dark I could barely see anything.
Like many games of this genre the difficulty curve drops once you've managed to get a basic base up, which at that point the game becomes enjoyable. Being able to tame dinosaurs and other creatures in the world is a neat feature but it's something I've not been able to do reliably myself. For me ARK lacks the fun building of something like Minecraft and the survivability chance of Don't Starve. I think also the cost at $59.99 is going to be a sticking point for some people as is that you need fairly good computer specs for the game.
Ultimately if you're the type of person who likes hardcore survival games you probably love this. If you're the type of person who is more into casual survival with an actual difficulty curve you're probably going to have problems with ARK.

Excellent game.
The playstyle is slow, so you can take your time, leave and come back, or sit and think.  It's perfect if you want a slow-paced day.  The advancement, though, is incremental.  Each battle will set you ahead, but not in epic proportions.  It's a nice, linear rise in power.
The art style is cute, sort of like Don't Starve.  The music is very much styled after what you might hear at a RenFair.  There's little bits of vocal commentary with each new addition and after each battle, win or lose, and it's pretty good.
The playstyle is Rogue-like.  Your characters don't seem to carry and advancement from one instance of a dungeon to another; all equipment and abilities are gained inside each dungeon.  That can offer some excitement as your favorite weapons or gear pops up, and keeps things from becoming a min-max grind.  What does advance through the game is what sort of loot you can find; as you unlock that, your little Dungeoneer finds nicer and nicer things.
Overall, it's a really fun game if you like something that's a turn-based game with a cutesy art style and good voice acting that will take you several dozen hours to get through.  They're also adding an "endless" version instead of just standard dungeons, so that ought to help replay value.

Guild of Dungeoneering is fun, challenging and addictive, the art style is cute, the backstory is humorous.  Don't take the below criticism as disapointment, it is only my desire to make a great game even better.
The pacing could use some fine tuning, there is alot of downtime between actions, and it can start to get tiresome, especially if your hero dies and you have to start the level over.  The dialog becomes more than a little samey, your hero makes a comment before every step and it doesn't take long before they start repeating lines.  The turorial is unskipable, if you chose to start over (I haven't found a total fail state yet) you'll have to sit through a good bit of unneeded hand holding before  getting into the action.
An indicator as to whether the current card will affect hero-pathing would be a welcome addition.  By now I feel like I understand what will and will not alter a hero's course, yet I still occasionally waste moves on an action I was sure would redirect them.
The hero panel blocks the quest objectives, this is a minor UI issue, but it's one of those things that a will drive a layout designer nuts.  Also, stop hiding my hero panel, I prefer to play with it open, but many events auto-close it for no reason.
I would love the ability to customize a hero's starting deck, maybe a training room where we spend gold to swap out cards.  This would also give the game a sense of permanence, right now there is no feeling of loss when a hero dies because the replacement hero has the exact same cards and stats (I do get that they're supposed to be disposable "chumps", but there should be at least some penalty for letting them die).

I know there's not a whole lot of people that even know what Mah Jong is, but, for those that do, this is not the usual game you've played in the past. The game uses the Antique Road Show as a backdrop and uses tilesets like antique items that you match with a few treasures thrown in. The player follows the board like a MB board (Life or Sorry etc) and you follow it around to various antique shows and flea markets, each one having a different layout and tileset, though some tiles are common to all the stops on the way. The end goal is to make it to the big TV show called Antique Road Show where people bring stuff in and appraisers tell them the value, some are worth a little and some items are worth a small fortune.  I consider it money well spent (IMO) as I bought it on sale and I'm still playing it. The graphices are good, the tile sets are clear and the controls are easy and responsive, though a few times I have clicked on a tile and the input (LMB) did not seem to take, it did on the second try though.
If you like the game Mah Jong, IMO, this one is worth getting.

There was a time where I could really recommend this game 100%. But not anymore.
As time has passed more people got good at the game resulting in a lot of higher ranked players.
Now you might think that that's a good thing. Well no, in this community it isn't.
Instead of good players playing against each other you have 90% of highranks (45+) playing in team objective servers and rank stacking on the same team (usually attack side). So basically instead of having balanced fun matches most high ranked players purposefully join the team with more highranks which ends up in very unbalanced teams and an almost guaranteed win for the stacked team.
You really only need to look at the rank distribution at the start of a match and you can predict which team wins with 99% certainty.
Not only is it unfair for the players on the other team but it makes matches just overall very boring. As someone who reached rank 50 I either join the stack and will not be challenged at all (imagine a pro soccer player playing against a 5 year old) or I join the other team and stand no chance at all.
It has been like this for quite a while but it's reached it's peak lately where you really have to search hard for a server where this doesn't happen every match. Sometimes I don't find such a server and end up not playing at all because of it.
The game has a lot of little flaws but in my opinion it's the community who in the end really ruins it. They call it a skill-based game but there is no skill involved in unbalancing teams as much as possible and winning without effort. In fact a lot of people who think that they are particularly good only think so because they simply stack all the time.
The only way to enjoy this game nowadays is if you like to play in a clan. If you are into that I can recommend it even though I'm not a huge fan of clans. Otherwise you can only join the stacking or lose nearly every match if you don't. I dont enjoy either of it and therefor this review.

It's balanced much more fairly than all the other scrolling shmups I've played, touching the floor isn't an instant death, and there is no lives system, only checkpoints. If you've ever played a scrolling shooter in your life you'll probably do just fine here. The weapon system works wonderfully and the shield is an interesting mechanic that allows you to tank a few hits if you've got it facing the right direction, a nice break from dying in one hit with no exceptions. VIDEO REVIEW:
Scores: [Graphics] 6/10, [Music] 8/10, [Story] 5/10, [Controls] 9/10, [Gameplay] 8/10, [Content] 6/10
1993 Space Machine is a classic arcade style shoot em up that you don't see much anymore. Using a 2d design that felt empty at time, leaving large portions of the background bair with just a gradient for a sky. The background felt out of place and made it hard to see enemies as well. When fullscreened, 1993 had a black border that felt unnecessary, especially for a game released in 2016. The sprite work however looked familiar reminding me of megaman and metroid with its pixelated cross hatching, giving things a shiny look.
Music -The music is quite good and didn't get old even when the gameplay became repetitive. The sound effects felt thrown in as if they were an afterthought, leaving some sounding incredible strange and out of place. This department could've used some definite improvement overall.
When it comes to story, 1993 has little to offer. To even get an understanding of who you're killing and what for, you have to visit there website. The pop ups while you play are just helpful tips and offer little story. According to the website your are an acclaimed combat pilot on a mission to infiltrate Nestor, a space pirate who stole a device called 1993 space machine used to terraform barren planet making them habitable. Nestor then used then newly habitable planets to raise his army. Even with this explanation I wouldn't say this is a story driven game.
1993 has different challenges in every level forcing you to change your loadout and playstyle. Loadouts can be changed to accommodate the strenuous levels but only if you find an item that lets you go to the shop or restart from the beginning of the level. You start with a small stage 1 ship with up to 2 mountable guns. After saving enough money, you can purchase a stage 2 ship that will give you 4 weapon slots. The weapons vary from a cannon that shoots behind you to multiple lasers that hit different enemies at once. 1993 had so much to offer when it comes to content, leaving you up to the decision making.
While holding down the fire button isn't the funnest thing to do, the movement with the joystick is. Controlling your ship is incredible challenging. One wrong move and you're dead. The ships movements require precision to guide your bullets into the enemy while also avoiding their fire. You have a shield that you can move yourself or let spin around you. The shield can come in handy in the bullet hell sections forcing you to move it where you need it most. With that in mind, navigating through even the toughest sections controls smooth holding you accountable for any mistakes.
This shoot ‘em up was originally designed for the Amiga in 1993. The game is challenging since each new level is composed of different obstacles that create  anticipation and interest for the player. 1993 offers different weapons combinations that give the player a sense of creativity. If multiplayer is your thing you can have up to 4 player at once but keep in mind, more enemies will spawn and the game overall will become more difficult. The boss battles are interesting as well, with their difficulties varying from simple to difficult. The Boss battles can also seem repetitive at times due to the placement of checkpoints being far away.
1993 Space Machine is a simple old school arcade shooter that offers just that. This is one of those rare games that can make you go "just ONE more try." If you like classic arcade side scrolling shoot em ups, this is one to check out!

If you like minesweeper and teleporting, I'd give it a whirl for the 30 minutes to few hours before you get bored. It's pretty hard until you figure out what to do, then it becomes trivially easy, in my experience. The maker probably has to tweak something in order to make it difficult.
Once you know what you're doing... here's how to make the game laughably easy. If you're near shadow and nothing is showing up on your intuition (which identifies whether the danger is a trap or a shadow), teleport 1 space diagonally into more darkness until you find a hidden danger. Then toss a beacon 2 spaces away into the darkness and it'll show blurs where there are traps/shadows. If you know which is which, right click and throw a torch or a rock to disarm it, and keep the chain going by teleporting/throwing beacons. You can keep a chain going by teleporting even into light spaces, and I think that's probably a design flaw, because a beacon doesn't break a chain, so basically your chain will net you hundreds of courage and you'll be unstoppable if you do it right.
If the creator wanted to make this somewhat difficult, he'd have to do one or multiple of these: make beacons break a chain, make teleporting into light spaces break a chain, give less starting courage, and/or make long halls so you can't teleport indiscriminately (there are a couple levels like this, but there's still darkness across a wall and you can just throw a beacon to see where it's safe to tele there and continue a combo).
I'm guessing people couldn't figure it out and this was made easier, based on former reviews. I think it's an interesting concept, and a fun use of 30-90 minutes.

Guild of Dungeoneering is fun, challenging and addictive, the art style is cute, the backstory is humorous.  Don't take the below criticism as disapointment, it is only my desire to make a great game even better.
The pacing could use some fine tuning, there is alot of downtime between actions, and it can start to get tiresome, especially if your hero dies and you have to start the level over.  The dialog becomes more than a little samey, your hero makes a comment before every step and it doesn't take long before they start repeating lines.  The turorial is unskipable, if you chose to start over (I haven't found a total fail state yet) you'll have to sit through a good bit of unneeded hand holding before  getting into the action.
An indicator as to whether the current card will affect hero-pathing would be a welcome addition.  By now I feel like I understand what will and will not alter a hero's course, yet I still occasionally waste moves on an action I was sure would redirect them.
The hero panel blocks the quest objectives, this is a minor UI issue, but it's one of those things that a will drive a layout designer nuts.  Also, stop hiding my hero panel, I prefer to play with it open, but many events auto-close it for no reason.
I would love the ability to customize a hero's starting deck, maybe a training room where we spend gold to swap out cards.  This would also give the game a sense of permanence, right now there is no feeling of loss when a hero dies because the replacement hero has the exact same cards and stats (I do get that they're supposed to be disposable "chumps", but there should be at least some penalty for letting them die).

I recommend this game, but you should be aware of how much game you are buying.  I just finished it, and I've got a total of 17.8 hours played.  The 17.8 hours was fun, but I expected more.  Still, that's less than a dollar an hour.  Just be aware there's not a lot of game here if you just want to play though it once and be done.
When I finished the game, I only had 3 of the 3rd level classes unlocked, all of the gear unlocked, and one of the 3rd level bonus affect items unlocked.  Don't remember how much of the other 1st and 2nd level stuff I had unlocked.  After the last mission, I got enough gold to buy most of the things I hadn't unlocked, but since you can't go back and replay any of the dungeons even after the credits have rolled, I can't do anything with what I unlocked.  Maybe that's for the expansion?  Still, would have liked to go replay old dungeons after the credits rolled just to try things out.
As for the game itself, this is a deck building card game.  All the rules for deck builders apply.  It's not about the number of cards in your deck.  It's about the quality of the cards.  You want as lean a deck as possible, not one cluttered up with junk cards that hurt you more than they help when you play them.  Each class' base deck is designed with a strength in mind, usually a dungeoneer's special ability.  Pick up gear that gives you cards that play to that strength and junk the rest.  Don't take an item just to fill an empty slot.  Take the gold and use it to influence you dungeoneer's movement.
Speaking of dungeoneer movement, I read about what is supposed to influence movement, but something still seems broken.  I've been on a timed mission, right next to the exit with 1 turn to go, placed gold on the exit with no monster there, and my dungeoneer still runs off to fight a level 3 monster on an unexplored tile and dies because time ran out.  The mission would have been won if he'd just moved to the exit tile with the gold and no monster.  What's that all about?
Other than that, I had 2 crashes in my 17.8 hours.  Nothing I couldn't live with.
So, to recap, good deck buildler.  I just wish it had lasted more than 17.8 hours.
Still, given that it costs me 20+ dollars every time I go to the movies to be entertained for 2-3 hours, that doesn't make it overpriced by any means.

In Dustforce speedruns aren't the meta-game, they ARE the game. If you can enjoy the precision and timing involved in such endeavors you won't be disappointed. If you enjoy watching other players' speedruns you won't be disappointed (and in a sense, this is your reward for at least finishing a level).
I think Dustforce stands out in the design more than actual gameplay (you can get a similar challenge from e.g., Super Meat Boy). The game is distilled in the art design, character design, and level design. That's not to say it's sparse, the levels are often beautiful, but there is very little that doesn't directly serve the game. There's very little narrative. There's not a lot of moving parts and gimmicks. It's simply: here's an obstacle course, find the shortest course and execute perfectly (with a few exceptions for arena stages; here's a room full of enemies, flawlessly defeat them).
The soundtrack to the game is excellent, and one of my all time favorites. Definitely check out the composer's web page.
This is a game for all ages and abilities. I often play this with my 2.5 year-old son. He likes to watch the colorful characters run around cleaning and making the animals and people happy. In the hubs he will just make the people sweep and jump around and narrate the action. He likes the music, too. Older kids will be able to finish a lot of the levels and have fun doing it. Parents might be interested to know there's next to no violence in single player, since the sweeping "attacks" are really cleaning off the inhabitants of the stages and they are largely greatful for it.
The biggest drawback to me, is that progression is entirely linked to perfecting skills. Most of you will eventually reach a plateau where you've unlocked every level you can and you're stuck trying endlessly to improve your times and combos on the hardest levels. There's no "grind" to "brute force" your way forward, you either get good or accept defeat. Judging from the global achievement (there's only one) stats, around 90% of players will not unlock the highest levels. Less than 1% have perfected every level. You can't see everything even as just a tourist.
I'm disappointed there isn't a wider set of achievements to build some meta-game around.

This is a triple A game that is free and its as fun as a 3rd person shooter gets. Haz loot. Haz gunz. Haz swords and bows and maces and knives and throwing stars and MACHINE GUNS and shotguns and.... Haz u controlling a GODLY SPACE NINJA.
This game is as fun as a 3rd person shooter gets.
It has this amazing ability to make you feel powerful when you're controlling your character without making you feel cheap. It accomplishes this by giving your warframe (what the character you control is called) AMAZING mobility. And it's not difficult to pull off, or way too easy. It gets it just right. No complex button combinations to memorize to pull off a soaring jump that flings you forward through the air, glide for a distance, then double jump out of that glide in to another direction, and grabbing on to a ledge.
There's tons of weapons to get your hands on. And different warframes with different abilities as well.
And the best part? It's free. Paying money only serves to get you different weapons and frames NOW. The game has another avenue for these items, and thats loot drops and missions that award different components. Once you farm up your parts, you pop them in to a "Foundry" on your ship and hit the craft button. It will cook for some real world time, and when its done, you have your item. The crafting time ranges from 1 minute for small items like keys or ciphers up to 3 days for completion of a frame. Don't want to wait? Spend some of the game's purchased currency and instantly complete the item. Don't want to farm? Go in to the market through the in game menu to pull up whatever you're looking for and buy it with platinum.
The feeling you get when your warframe or shiny new machine gun is completed after a few days is like christmas morning. It is fun, satisfying, and downright replayable. I love this game, and I am picky as hell. There are a few games I've loved enough to play this much in the past. Elder Scrolls Morrowind, Diablo II, Diablo III, World of Warcraft, DOTA (original and 2). And now, Warframe is easily among the AAA titles on the list.

Try to imagine Super Meat Boy as a racing game with Mario Kart style pickups.  SpeedRunners is pretty close to that, though unlike Meat Boy, missing a step doesn't always lead to failure.  The game is still in development, as such not everything is finished; currently two stages are untextured but all the maps are fully functional and new content is being added often.
The idea of the game is to outrun your opponents.  Unlike traditional racing games where you aim to be the first to cross the line, here you just keep platforming until your opponents fall too far behind.  The camera keeps all four players on screen at once so going off screen is bad.  Once one player falls behind, the visible screen area starts shrinking and the play area can become really small; often times this forces you to play by memory since it becomes impossible to see what's ahead and above you.
It's a whole lot of fun and well worth the price.  Even more fun if you have friends to play with, though there is online quickplay and bot support if you don't.

Dustforce is a relentlessly unforgiving platformer, even moreso than Super Meat Boy. In most platformers, there are usually a few different ways to approach problems. In Dustforce, however, you are forced into a single kind of "perfect run" to progress normally through the game. You can complete stages without these perfect runs, but by doing so, you lock yourself out of so many stages. Perfection is demanded of you in this game.
I'm the kind of person that really enjoys a challenge, but the level of timing, reaction, knowledge, and control demanded of the player is so insane that I made it about 75% of the game before finally stopping to retain my sanity. When you can pull off what it demanded, it is an amazing feeling. But sometimes the game feels incredibly inconsistent, and I know that's only because the timing on everything in this game is on a hair-trigger.
I find it really hard to recommend this game except to anyone who is masochistic about challenging games. I did actually really enjoy it myself (I am one of those people), but I also know this is not the kind of game that almost anyone else would be able to enjoy the way I was able to.

The game itself is nice enough. The levels have multiple solutions and fly by at a comfortable pace. There's nothing all too challenging, but it didn't feel boring.

This is just completely moronic. It's an incredibly lazy way to try and get people to play your game. I'm personally someone who likes achievements. I think they're a fun reason to keep playing a game past its end. There's none of that here. I tried the game out because the screenshots looked similar to other puzzle games I really enjoy, and since it was free I didn't see why I shouldn't give it a shot. If this developer comes to his senses and removes this stupid part of the game, I'd wholeheartedly recommend this game as a simple, relaxing puzzle game, but until that day it's a disappointed "No" for me.

Lines Free by Nestor Yavorskyy is exactly what it looks like and advertises to be: a relaxing, straightforward Numberlink game. With a simple line drawing mechanic akin to the puzzles of LYNE and Unium, it's inviting to play in a single quick session or bit by bit in between.
The game doesn't introduce anything new to learn, special squares or rules. It's a classic Numberlink game and therefore suitable for anyone slightly interested in puzzle games. Albeit a little too easy overall, the design of the puzzles is more often than not quite compelling and does indeed require the acquisition of principles on how to assess and handle certain situations. Some, if not the majority, of the puzzles do have more than one solution, but that doesn't lessen their appeal.
As the game focuses on simplicity, its visual and auditory presentation mirrors that. The colour schemes can be interchanged, which
help some colour blind players. The sound effects are delightful and the music is decently modest to the point that it completely blends into the background with the passing of time.
To sum up, it's a nice and short collection of Numberlink puzzles with a rather low difficulty level.

Contrast is a very beautiful game, it has a unique and interesting art style, the music is top notch, and the game play is pretty unique with using light and shadow to travel. The game has a few somewhat open areas to play through in each Act, the game is comprised of 3 acts,  each act will probably take about an hour or so.  The puzzles are fairly simplistic, although that isn't really a bad thing.
The story centers around a little girl known as Didi, she has an imaginary friend named Dawn, often being left alone at night so her mother can preform Didi enlist the help of her friend Dawn to sneak around in a landscape which is set in 1920.  Going along with Didi, the player (Dawn) will be introduced to numerous interesting characters shown only via their shadows.
The length of the game is rather short, I have 11 hours clocked in but over 8 of those hours were from  idling cards while I slept.  I played the game completely and got all the achievements in a little under 3 hours.
I'd recommend this game for the gameplay, interesting art style and compelling story.  I personally found it well worth the price I paid, but if you are a stickler for games having a lot of meat and potatoes, I'd think you may be better off skipping out on this one.  Fans of good games will enjoy this in spite of it's short length..

In the second type, you have a board with only a few dots and the challenge lies less in figuring out how to connect than and more in trying to cover the board in lines, a Coloring puzzle. Shadow Hunter is an isometric dungeon delver that should be a catch for anyone who's a fan of Minesweeper, but it's a work in progress.
You play as an eponymous Shadow Hunter, who seeks to purge the encroaching darkness. Unfortunately, there's not much more in the way of story just yet. Side missions, or “Tasks,” are few and repeat rather quickly. The satisfaction of completing the game is to see your final gold count, as there isn't a real end.
The key player in the game's system is Courage. It's a consumable stat that can be recovered and drained by various actions. Lose too much of it, and you'll have to camp, thereby triggering a fight and potentially getting Courage in return. Fights are so trivial, and Courage is so abundant, that you'll likely never find this an issue no matter how things turn out, however.
There are a couple mini-games on display. The encounters, engaged either randomly or through events, are Simon Says/Memory style affairs. The Shadow Hunter intuits the enemy's moves, but only briefly. It's then up to you to copy the pattern displayed. Success grants a flawless battle, whereas missing a “Match” allows the enemy to get a hit in, simultaneously jogging the Shadow Hunter's memory and allowing you to try again.
The other game manifests in the locked doors throughout the levels. Each game's take on lock picking is a little bit different; here, it plays out like Mastermind. You have a number of tries to get the order of the tumblers right, with each wrong position highlighted in red, and each correct assignment in blue. Failing to decipher the sequence, or deliberately pulling the spring, will trigger an encounter automatically. At present, however, the threat of failure is mitigated entirely by the fact that you can just click the door again or walk away and come back with no penalty or remembered actions.
The graphics aren't going to wow you. The tileset is an odd hodgepodge of mismatched pieces, without artistic consistency. The interface is a clash between retro sensibilities and newly-minted 3D art. What few NPCs exist appear as portraits of decently made 3D models. Encounters all have the same icon to indicate “enemy” during battles.
While the tutorial is stashed away for easy reference, it's a tad front-loaded.
Bugs, while not game-breaking, do mar the experience, such as when a roving enemy skips all of its turns to get to you upon completing a random encounter. Balancing issues still exist from the changes that have been made already. Perhaps the greatest example: the score board. You can, theoretically, play through the levels repeatedly, amassing obscene amounts of untold wealth. Thus, the fact that the score board uses your gold as a marker of how well you do is a bit moot. There are some convenience/design features not quite implemented, such as a notification for the player that they never retrieved all of the shards.
The game has a way to go yet, and you may not be keen on joining the ride. So why, then, might this game still have merit for some?
Simply put, it's intriguing when basic gameplay gets a practical spin, becoming a part of a larger whole. In Shadow Hunter, the MC “repels the darkness” through Minesweeper-like game play. The Hunter's pulse pounds, and “intuition” shows when danger is nearby: traps, shadow creatures, or events. The “flags” from Minesweeper appear automatically, but it is possible for you to “guess” where traps or shadows are, or rather to dispel them from a spot that they're likely to be. Adding a layer of depth to the game is the manner in which tiles are cleared. Simply stepping into the darkness isn't enough, as squares cleared in that way become “fear tiles,” and thus remove your Courage even after being cleared. In order to avoid creating fear tiles, you have to teleport, and either keep the combo of teleportation going, or walk out of the square you've teleported to. The greater the combo, the better the rewards, but also the greater risk of “missing” and creating a field of fear tiles. Very few other games take advantage of this mechanic, and Shadow Hunter's clever implementation of it makes for an interesting Minesweeper variant, if nothing else.
As it stands, I can't recommend Shadow Hunter but to those looking for a little variation on the standard Minesweeper formula.

I bought this of sheer boredom.
And I hate to admit it, but it's actually a lot of fun, challenging, and incredibly addictive, though it's nothing more than a gloryfied memory game.
Played 4 hours in my first session, and I'm nowhere near having everything unlocked, and have yet to get my first achievement.
Basically, you run a dating service, and your job is to pair up couples successfully, by comparing attractions, interests and personality types.
Take them on dates, pay sincere compliments (or lie), and keep dates interesting by selecting different conversation topics.
While on dates, you get to play different mini-games (mostly memory oriented, as far as I can tell after playing 4 hours).
And occasionally, something incredibly funny happens, and it actually made me LOL af few times.
Personalities consist of 5 different traits, each with 2 different mindsets and behaviors connected to them.
Combining these with a ton of different interests, jobs, hair styles and colours, clothes style, eye colours and make-up (for women), and facial hair (for men), and different accessories, makes up a dating pool with tremendous variety.
And this variety is what makes the game interesting.
The really brilliant part of this game is, that you start of by creating your own character, by customizing looks to your own preferences, and answer a series of questions to determine your own personality type.
And (if you allow) this character will then become a dating option for other players to pair you up.
And the game will then send you notifications on how your 'virtual self' does in the dating world, depending on other players choices and skills to determine your personality type.
Your character is given a fake name if allowed in other players games.....just in case you're the kind to worry about such things.
And as you successfully pair up couples and earn reputation, you unlock different things to add further variety to the game.
Such as extented dating options, different restaurants with different difficulty levels, and pre-dating alteration options that allows you to change clothes or hair styles, colours, make-up, or buy gifts to impress your date.
This is a well constructed casual game, well worth the price tag, if you're into games you can pick up and leave at any time.
I have no problems recommending this game - much to my own surprise.

Also it is very easy to break the game with the arcane skill tree, since nothing in the game normally hits higher than 3 (and only a few bosses can hit for 4 once per cycle) you can effectively get infinite HP and unlimited damage, especially so with the Alchemist and Mathemagician who both have their own damage buffs and are generally easy to use on their own. This game breaking becomes especially apparent with the cartomancer who, when combined with arcane 4 and the "wise" effect, becomes an unkillable and unstoppable death machine who can hit enemies for 13 damage without damage buffs and can effectively attain infinite damage with enough patience due to the "Focus" card in the Arcane set.
That said, I also found a few classes were notably underpowered and simply unable to do some missions without getting a perfect and lucky run, namely the Ranger, Artificer, Berserker and the Most Holy Grail Knight.

Dustforce takes every one of these (admittedly small) complaints and addresses them: the technical skills required to beat some of the levels that ensure you can't set it down and come back to it without having to remaster things, the decision to design the game from the get-go with speed-running in mind, and a soundtrack that is as catchy as it is lovely...the list goes on and on.
Without gushing on for too long about it, I recommend Dustforce as highly as I can recommend anything, provided that you know what you want in a platformer. This game will be hard and it will be unforgiving, assuming you attempt to play it at the highest level. The level design will keep pulling you back in, making you wonder if you could have shaved off a second or two by doing this loop slightly differently. The technical skill required will make you consider purchasing a keyboard that actually works (Apple keyboards are now my chief complaint with Apple computers). In short, if mountains were video games, Everest almost compares to Dustforce.

For its length and number of different worlds and characters available, Dustforce offers almost no variety at all. Worlds are only thematic variations, repeating the same kind of level structure over and over with no unique mechanics between them, while the characters themselves all play pretty much the same, with some minor tweaks from one character to another (with some of the more subtle changes not even being hinted in-game).
If that wasn't enough, the game demands "perfect" double-S scores for players to be able to make standard progress. Scores that in any other game would exist only as a side challenge to those who truly want to spend their times mastering it. Here, you'll have to clear every single stage flawlessly if you ever hope to see those final levels, and there are MANY stages to be mastered — enough to make one feel like the game overstayed its welcome after only a few hours.
Bottom line is: Dustforce gets old. Fast. It offers almost no variety in its gameplay and the absurd requirement to progress through stages is a cheap way of stepping up the difficulty, which only helps to add to the incessant repetition the player will experience. I cleared one world + a bunch of other stages and saw no point in continuing. It offers no reason to go on beyond getting a good performance on stages, so you can move on to more stages and repeat the process in the exact same way, everytime. I felt like I had already seen all the game had to offer, and that more arrangements of the same stage elements weren't really worth stressing over.
It's a shame, really. Dustforce has tight controls and a unique core theme and aesthetics (though it keeps the same kind of mild/serene atmosphere all the way through. I got bored of it after a while). If it just presented new mechanics for each world and/or character and reduced the overly-demanding difficulty a tad (a double-A ranking requirement to get keys for further stages would be a huge improvement) this review could have been a "Yes" instead. The way it is, though, I'd only recommend this game to the most time-attack obsessed players with plenty of time to burn and that wouldn't care much for a more varied and rich experience.
For everyone else looking for an interesting platforming experience, you're better off looking elsewhere.

I enjoyed it but my biggest gripe with this game and a lot of games today is the morality system. Metro Last Light probably has the single worst morality system I have ever seen in +1k hours of gaming. What is the point of designing and implementing so many various post-apocalyptic style guns and improvised weapons if the game penalizes you for using them? Now granted, you can throw caution to the wind and kill every single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you come across with your bloodlust and accept the "Bad/Evil ending" as your penance for the brutal, anarchaic, warmongering, murdering ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you are...
But that ending is♥♥♥♥♥♥
A breath taking and death defying adventure with danger at every corner coupled with the anxiety over your dwindling supplies as you trudge through the darkest of Moscow's subway system brutally cut off at the end. And there is absolutely no forgiveness. It's completely all or nothing. Yes, you can spend 11 hours tediously sneaking up behind every guard, spare everyone's life, give every bit of your money to the poor, kiss babies, and volunteer at the soup kitchen every wednesday of the month, But then you get that one lapdance. Suddenly, you're the antichrist himself.
Okay, I exaggerate. Still there's no indication how far to one side you're leaning. You maybe be shooting for the good ending, and suddenly get surprised with the bad ending. The decision ultimately feels arbitrary, and it comes off like the game only wants you to play it a certain way. No, I don't want that in my games. The morality system soured the whole experience. An ending is supposed to leave you wanting more, but this has left me wanting to go play something else.
I give it a 5/10. However, if I played through the game and Alt F4'd out of the final scene to go watch the ending I want on youtube, I would give it an 8/10. Or better yet do away with the morality system altogether and I would give it an 8/10. This game could have been massively improved with one awesome ending as the grand finale.
The game was gorgeous and a lot of love was put into the story, but it's merits were over shaddowed by the morality system.
TL;DR watch the ending on youtube.
