Dusforce is a 2D indie platform game developed by Hitbox Team. The game is short, simple, and tells the story of four custodial protagonists who attempt to sweep away a world corrupted by dust and filth. The game was released on Steam in January of 2012 and will be pushed to the Playstation 3, Playstation Vita, and Xbox 360 consoles in January of 2014.
The game consists of roughly 50 levels in which the player has to use a number of acrobatic skills in order to clean up small sections of leaves and defeat filth-covered creatures to score and progress though the level. Some of the skills that the player will have to master to complete each level in an efficient manner are the double jump, wall jump, mid-air dash, and the ability to cling to the walls and ceiling. The player also has the choice of a light or heavy attack with which to defeat the enemies in the levels. The levels themselves are laid out very well and tend to vary from horizontal to vertical design, which pushes the player to master the controls of Dustforce (a game best played with a controller, if possible). The game tracks your progress through each level with the combo meter, which is influence by the player's ability to move through the level and eliminate both enemies and leaf piles in an efficient manner. At the end of each level, the player is "ranked" by their abilities to achieve a high combo and how quickly they moved through the stage. The game also comes with a four-player multiplayer system with some typical variants such as Survivor and King of the Hill, along with a level editor that was introduced via patch after the games initial release.
While it's certainly an interesting way to promote level completion, the biggest problem with Dustforce's ranking system is that in order to access many levels of the game, the player is required to complete each previous level in a near-perfect manner. I found myself running through previous levels over and over just so I could access the next one. This certainly speaks volumes about Dustforce's ambitious gameplay, but also says a lot about how the game is put together. Forcing a player to run through previous levels 10-15 times will often make it feel as if the developers are simply padding out their game. It's a fantastic experience, but it would be a lot better if it were only longer and if it were easier to progress through the game. Also, the acrobatic abilities are hard to master, and it will take a lot of time with a controller in hand in order for an average player to perfect the play style that Dustforce presents.
However, there are many things about Dustforce that makes it an indie game that you should experience for yourself. The game has a unique art style that is gorgeous to look at, especially when a player is whizzing through a level at top speed. The colors blend together in a fantastic way that makes the game visually stunning. Also, the techno soundtrack was created by lifeformed, and it is nothing short of amazing. The music is stunning, and is some of the best I've ever heard in an indie game. Since it's release, Dustforce has been compared to other indie games, such as Super Meat Boy and N+, and while it shares a similiar style, Dustforce is a game that stands alone. It's innovations seperate it from other games like it, and it's penchant towards speedrunning implies that the developers knew exactly what market Dustforce would do best in.
Unfortunately, while Dustforce is a fantastic game, it is one that is more difficult than it's predecessors, and to the players that have never experienced fast-paced platforming gameplay, I would have to recommend that they play Super Meat Boy or N+ before this one. Those games are simpler, and typically will be a more casual experience than the one Dustforce provides. That being said, if you have experienced either of those games and hunger for more, then Dustforce is the game for you. Dustforce will impress and, hopefully, amaze you.

I'll start off by saying I love this game. Really, really do. But holy crap, how you go from near perfect (Mid-EA) to an unfocused mess so fast.
1. What you'll hear much about, is the damage resist system that blocks status effects. At first sounds like a good idea, but dig a little deeper into the mechanics and you realize this is a terrible system. Stunning, burning, knocking enemies down keeps the fight in balance, and a big part of the first game. Now it's a DPS fest.
And it's not only that, but since the beginning, there's been skills that remove these statuses. Is your fighter bleeding, poisoned, and on fire? Off the top of my head, Geomancer, Hydrosophist, Huntsman have abilities that remove these statuses. Why would we need an additional layer of armor just to slow things down?
2. RNG loot. It's not a matter of "did you get a two handed sword or a dagger". It's "did you get anything or an empty chest". This is obviously tied to:
3. Lack of money in the early game. Just so you understand, it's not only a matter of better gear, but the game's skills need to be bought too. You'll be collecting loot worth 4-20 gold, but an individual skill book costs 300. And the loot is very much finite. Now these books, you need to buy at least 1-5 for every character, to make them be able to do anything.
You watch any thread, any video, and notice a pattern "steal the books". Why? Because it's the only way to get a working group going. There's just not enough money otherwise.
4. Source skill system sucks. You need two resources to use later skills, Source points (one shot and it's gone, boom) and extra Memory slots (normal skills use 1, maybe 2 slots, these things 3). And these spells/skills really aren't that good, like really underwhelming. You'd expect an end of the world kind of spell, but nope.
So what happens with these skills then? You just plain don't use them, and instead branch out your character to Polymorph or whatever.
5. The voice acting is terrible. Not even funny bad, just bad.

1993 Space Machine, as the name implies, is a retro vertical-scrolling shmup. The kind where you control a spaceship and shoot a ton of weird looking creatures and machines hell-bent on destroying your fragile vehicle. I can't say I have played very many shmups in my time, a genre that has always been more popular in the arcades and on consoles. If there are any clever references to genre classics then I can't say I have gotten any.
At its core it's a fairly standard shmup. Instead of weapon power-ups, you collect cash from destroyed enemies and upgrade your ship between levels. There's actually a number of basic ship models to choose from but as far as I can tell they all behave identically. You get two special weapon slots to fill aside from your standard blaster and there's a large variety of weapon types to choose which resemble typical shmup power-ups: vertical shot, diagonal shot, continuous laser, etc.. Additionally there are three advanced ships which have four special weapon slots and they can equip an even greater variety of weapon types. However, these ships are considerably slower than the standard ships and I did not find that to be a worthwhile trade.
A  big problem with the upgrade system is that you don't really know what you get when you buy something. Most of the weapon descriptions are vague and you only see the spray pattern and effectiveness once you start a new level. I think it would have been good to see a short animation of the pattern or at least some numbers. Nothing like going into a level and figuring out the weapon you just bought is useless. Even though you can sell your gear again (at a loss), you don't get that much money that you can really experiment.
Otherwise there is not much to say about 1993 Space Machine. The level design is solid, the story is not much more than an excuse plot and the music is rather unremarkable. The controls are a bit too sensitive when using a 360 controller. It's also very short at about two hours (13 levels)but I suppose this type of game is more about skillful play than sightseeing - there is a hard mode.
Overall I would recommend 1993 Space Machine but only to people who already like shmups. I don't believe it would convert anyone who doesn't.

Giving the wolf varience on how it behaves as you progress may improve the quality of the wolf, and not leave it as a "running scary thing coming at you" that gets repetitive. Next, I initially thought that the wolf hated the light, or "lack of sin", which is why I ran to them for safety. While being safe was not the case, I feel as if adding a torch to shine the wolf's eyes and having safety in the lights would be a better option than to simply look at him. You can apply to those quick reactions I was talking about, but have players save up the oil they use for the encounters, and have every 25 milestones have an oil container of some sort.
-I didn't quite understand why almost every single bit of the game had to be some sort of audio freak-out or rock-hard music. I would've understood if it was a tech-based monster or something, but it was a werewolf. As overused as they may seem, there are still ways you can apply different but similar sounds to them: snarls, growls, etc. Or if you wanted a quiet wolf, give some subtle noises/short music when it's approaching. I noticed the warnings of how scary the game was in a community announcement, but the only thing people had to fear was the sudden loud techo/death metal music that would play for no real reason. Sounds and music could use some improvement.
-The navigation is exploitable to an extent, as I could almost remember where to go without the milestones. When I was using them, they had this weird ordering about them, and sometimes they'd be out of your view because of the too-dense fog. I understand that you recieved comments saying "too easy" about the wolf, and maybe perhaps the navigation, but it's a pain to die and have to start all the way from the beginning when I almost made it to 122. I'd say to make the milestones less obscure by lowering the fog just enough to see each one's glow to make navigation a tad bit easier. However, if you take my idea into consideration about the torch mechanic, making the lights more distant and allowing some use of a lantern may also be an option. It's all tweaking and trying new things out.
Overall, it's meh. A few flaws, but that's because the game was focusing more on looks than anything at the time. So I'd hold off on getting this until it feels a bit more unique.
Thank you for reading! If you found this review helpful, then that's awesome. Give it some upped thumbs and all that. As for you, Nicholas Bernard, don't be afraid to get even more innovative and try out even more things. My video will be up Saturday for you to watch, and if you want to talk about anything, leave a comment below. Thank you again, and have a great day!

LA Noire is a detective game published by Rockstar and Bondi. It has some adaptations from the GTA series but they are not as large. One of them is a funny one, in GTA you were stealing cars, in LA Noire you can get inside any car by just stopping them and entering. It is developed by Rockstar so you'll have to deal with Rockstar Social club which can end in save file corrupting, losing accounts and things among those lines.
The game is set in Los Angeles, as you might have guessed by the title, right after World War II. As our main character Cole Phelps, is an ex-marine, this opens up for some WW2 flashblacks and some returning co-marines that are connected to Cole. LA allows for a big setting for a game and you can also opt for a Black and white mode which is definitly as beautiful as with colours. Unfortunately the problem with a big city as big as LA is that it can lag quite a lot rendering parts of the map which makes driving not always as smootly. The music is a mixture of investigation music or music from shootouts which is the same the whole game and whenever you driving you can enjoy songs from that time mostly popular ones. If you are into that kind of music or heard such music before you'll recognise a lot of songs. The story is more the character trying to redeem himself from the actions he done in the war with a sad ending. I think the sad ending made the main character shine even more because he didn't get the respect he deserved for a big part of the game. I can't say I didn't enjoy it, although theres one part that I really found unnecessary.
The gameplay is worked out very well, the work fits right into the setting and the cases are very good overall. The work you do in this game is detective work, which means you'll be solving cases. Or when you don't want to for a while you can solve street crimes. Before each case, at least in most of them, you get shown a cutscene showing us how the crime happened without showing faces and giving clear clues away. In the cases themselfs you find clues to help solve your case, requires you to sometimes brawl or shoot your suspects. Brawling in this game is amazing it feels like a boxing game. You sometimes also have to chase suspects or how they call it in this game subduing. It is a very bland objective since sometimes shooting in the foot doesn't fail the case for killing them and sometimes it does kill them. You are on thin ice trying to shoot a suspect you are chasing because it is not clear if it is allowed. In the cases you also get help from a partner depending on what desk you are in, I'll be mentioning the different partners and desks later. Whenever you are driving with the partner it starts a conversation with them about the case giving you side information or their insight. You could also use them as a sort of GPS. Do remind yourself that once you choose to reveal a new side mission that the partner will direct towards that. You also get to question your suspects which is for me the best part of the game. They have really spent an amount of detail to the facial expressions in an interview although the mouth may go out of synch with the voice sometimes. You have three options after you asked your question, whetether you believe him or doubt him or believe that he is straight up lying. You can recognise in the facial expressions in the small details what direction it is going in although making out a doubt from a lie depends how much you have progressed in the case and how much you can charge against him. When you are finished you get shown a case reports with the amount of clues you found and the amount of questions you have done correctly. Aside from that and the rating, in stars, you get some side information sometimes revealing what you missed.
Desks:
Patrol is the standard police work before we get a real taste of the detective work. This is mainly an overextended interactive tutorial more meant to show us the ropes of the game and to intrest us in the rest of the game. It also makes us more acquaintanced with the main character. Traffic surprised me more or less. If you do not know what Traffic means in cop terms, it mainly is about solving hit and runs. What surprised me that every case contained the hit and run with that little element extra what didn't make an ordinary hit and run. In Traffic you get partnered with Stephen Bekowski. He is a pretty rookie cop in the Traffic department but so are you so you learn a lot from each other making it both to Homicide eventually.Homicide is probably the longest rank you have in the game. It is twice as long as any other desk in terms of cases, unless you count the DLC cases, and the missions themself are also longer compared to Traffic. Homicide is researching and solving murders. I like how they managed the endings of the cases, giving the player an open ending, and also the question if you did the cases right. The open endings made the final case even better which was mainly designed around missing clues from other cases and most of the landmarks in LA. You get partnered up with Rusty Galloway in Homicide. He is a good cop who can't wait on his pension and he expresses that most of the time. The conversations about the cases were definitly the most interesting in the game since it was more a discussion which made me doubt too. Ad Vice is trying to stop the drug empire from happening. The Ad vice story itself is pretty short, again without DLC, but the cases are pretty lengthy on themselfs. The surprise to me whas the shoot first then ask questions later mentality in this desk. Which made it more exciting, I also think the drug empire in this game is pretty interesting how it works. They also connect with Cole his backstory , his time in the war as a marine, giving a chance to see most of the ex-marines back again. Roy Earle is impressed by your work in Homicide that's why he pulls you over to Ad Vice to be his partner. Roy Earle is a detective we already met an Homicide case and I didn't like him then and I still don't like him. He is by a landslide my least favourite parnet in any game with a buddy system. He thinks the only way to solve things is by being rude and aggressive. He does know the drug community inside out and teaches us a lot about that and also how the LAPD really operates. Arson desk is the solving of domestic fires and finding out how they happened. These cases are only meant to connect with the ending so that all the pieces fit togheter. I wouldn't mind that they had added some extra, non-DLC, but I like the appearance of the ex-marines again and the whole scandal around them. I also like that Cole isn't the only one investigating in this desk, what I mean with that will be clear once you play this desk fully. You get partnered with Herschel Biggs in Arson. Herschel has been in the war too but not the second one, which gives you an idea of how old he is at the time. Herschel is a very grumpy character but he is the only one who would never question a decision made by Cole without helping him in any way. That is how a partner needs to be. What I missed with Herschel is the conversations, they are there but very short.
LA Noire is in my eyes a must pick up, if you love the setting of the 1940-1950's America with the classic detective with interactive cases which are sometimes pretty confusing to solve. I do not know if the DLC's are worth picking up, can't wait to find out for myself.

I like this game, and I see the potential. I hope that it grows into a fully-fledged strategy game one day, but for now, it seems like a 20 minute experience that will only frustrate the player.

This game is absolutely amazing, allowing you to explore a faithfully-recreated long-dead Los Angeles in its 1940s heyday, while solving crimes and unraveling a well-written story. Remarkably, the developers managed to create a world that actually feels like 1947, rather than just feeling like a 1940s-flavored game world that doesn't fully convince you a la Mafia II. What adds to the realism is that the characters, particularly some of your partners, are astoundingly politically incorrect for any medium from the 2010s (although certainly a historically accurate portrayal of how people might have behaved).The face-replication technology creates, for the first and only time in my gaming experience, faces so realistic that real-life actors can be easily recognized in many cases.
The only downside to this game is that the developer went under, and while they were planning a second game in this mold,  titled ♥♥♥♥♥ of the Orient and set in the political turmoil of 1930s Shanghai, it was finally officially canceled in 2016. I am deeply saddened by this and I hope that one day there will be a sequel to this game. Had a series of these games come out over the past few years, we may have seen a mini-revival of the adventure genre, but unfortunately this will stand alone, and in my case will be replayed every year or so.

Shadow Hunter is primarily Minesweeper, if you played a minesweeper who had to physically navigate the board to clear spaces.  And there were two types of mines, each with their own disarming item.  And walls restricted your movement.  And there were lockpicking puzzles and memory-based combat.  And a food counter that decreased with movement.
Shadow Hunter's primary flaw is that boards repeatedly put you into situations where your next move is random chance.  Walls restrict your movement, with rooms entered from corridors that are a single space wide.  If one of those spaces is safe, then you have to guess to progress.  You can start, or be teleported into similar situations.  You can clear shadows and still end up in such situations.
While mistakes do not mean instant failure, they do drain resources.  Stepping into a trap drains health, limiting how often you can take such chances.  Using the wrong disarming item costs you that item, which requires camping to restock.  Card spaces have no item that disarms them, but also deal no direct damage, instead triggering some effect.
You are rewarded with bonuses for disarming multiple spaces without taking damage.  This works okay.  You are rewarded with bonus food for clearing multiple spaces within a single move.  This does not work okay.  When you move multiple spaces in a turn, you can only move in a straight line.  The board layout restricts how many places even have the potential to let you move enough to trigger the food bonus.  When you do attempt such a move, you are almost guaranteed to be moving into spaces for which you hold no information, and thus it is random chance whether or not you actually have a clear path or will instead hit a trap (which will reset the counter.)
There is a lockpicking minigame for opening locked doors.  You have five chances to find the correct order of the five pins.  Failure only means that you gain no bonus gold, while the fewer the tries required means the greater the bonus you receive.  While logic and memory can greatly increase your odds of clearing this puzzle, it is still random chance as to how fast you will clear it, and thus how large your reward will be.
Combat (as combat can be triggered by stepping into card spaces, or seemingly just by chance when moving) is a memory game.  At the start of combat you are shown, in order, the attacks that the opponent will make.  You have to perform the same attacks in the same order, while the enemy sequence is removed from view after you start.  Feedback for this combat is poor.
In theory, minesweeper where you move through the board sounds interesting.  In practice, it just doesn't work that well.  Setting it in a fantasy world gives it some meaning, but seems to have also lead to the game implementing several awkward or ill-fitting mechanics together.
The game is a free game, so it costs nothing but time to try.  But mechanically, it just doesn't hold up.

Dustforce is a game about 4 heroic cleaners out to clean up some sort of sentient filth.  Leaves, dust and slime all coat the floors, walls and ceilings of each level and it’s your job to sweep, dust or vacuum it all away.  To do so requires precise, difficult control and levels are designed to be completed with finesse.  The game shines in its difficulty which drives the player to finish each level as quickly and elegantly as possible, striving for an elusive SS Rank.
Dustforce is not a game without some fault, however.  The controller support is limited, requiring some menu fidgeting to get it to work and the d-input controls override the keyboard inputs.  The game also doesn’t do a great job of guiding the player or setting a level curve, despite the door and key mechanic for some of the harder levels.  But really, those are minor gripes.
Despite its minor flaws, I’ve really been enjoying this game.  The beautiful visuals and vibrant music have quite a grip on me.  The animation uses a lot of fluid animation smears and the the music presents a feeling of adventure without being over the top.  It’s very relaxing, which can be very important when dealing with a particularly difficult run.
One of the better mechanics also lies in the replay mechanic.  When looking at the leaderboard, simply click on any of the camera icons (including the one by your own run) to view a replay of that run in its entirety.  This is a cool way to see how your friends compare, how you can improve your own run and what the top players are doing to get such good runs.
In the end, this game is fantastic, and somewhat reminiscent of something like N+ or perhaps even Super Meat Boy.  If you’re into that sort of tough platforming, Dustforce is worth your time and money.  And buy the soundtrack edition; it’ll save you a step later.

THe Guild of Dungeoneering is a really, REALLY simplistic game. Pretty much you watch as some vengeful♥♥♥♥♥♥ who was kicked out of his previous guild, tries to get revenge and be better than his last. That involves building his own guild and then hiring nimrods who are (According to the game) dense, stupid, greedy, and all-around feeble. Not a great cast huh? Well, it doesn't matter because all the characters you unlock are expendable and when they die, it just pops out another for you to use. No penalty. None. I'm nut even sure that 'leveling' a character (or whatever it tracks outside the dungeons) actually matters other than what gets written on their tombstone.
Now, the game isn't stupidly difficult. No, instead it relies on a fantastic random number generator that, even with a high level character (They level in dungeons), a great hand, a good strategy, and all the patience in the world IT COULD ALL GO UP IN FLAMES. All progress on that quest lost and POOF. Start over. Mook dead. Aww well.
The problem is that this "quest, level, die, repeat" thing has me wonder if I'm not missing SOMETHING. I feel like my mooks could be stronger or something. I beat the first dungeon and a handful of quests, but the rest just curb stomp me with crap luck.
The art style is neat, it looks handdrawn, but oddly enough ALL the characters look female. Even the first mook it give you, despite it may be a man, has visible boobs. What's up with that? Otherwise, the characters fall under the typical "Jack, Warrior, Mage, Thief, Bard (Or mime)" formula where Jacks are the crap starter, warriors are all physical, thiefs have potent extra effects, mages use magic, and bards (or mimes) use a mix of magic and physical. It's nothing new or revolutionary.
I wish I could give this game like a middling score. I would say 6/10, the graphics are neat, the premise (simple but effective) works, but the faux difficult keeps me from trying and failing repeatedly. So, yeah, 6/10.
Would I recommend it? Probably not.

This game is... interesting. You create a character, that is supposed to be "You". You choose your looks, your personality traits, your birthday which is also your star sign (Gemini, Aquarius, etc.) Your first date you set up you cannot mess up, as it's the tutorial that's running you through how to play.
You choose your venue that you want to act as a matchmaker for. Each venue has different people's personalities. You do kinda feel like a third wheel on the dates, since you're just silently watching them. The goal is to pick up on verbal cues by the dates and give them the best experience. Make the right comments, order the right food based on the hints they give, etc. You can date other peoples character profiles as well.
You get coins that are used as a currency to buy upgrades and other things to help you. The better you do, the more coins you are tipped at the end, the higher your reputation goes up, and the more you matchmaking you can do.
All in all, it's a pretty interesting game and if you like the idea of setting people up on the perfect date, then it's worth a try.

Dustforce is an interesting little side-scrolling platformer where you play as one of four (approximately equal) characters to literally clean up various levels. To me, this game is a lot like Sonic the Hedgehog with smaller levels and more specific goals. All you really need to do is get to the end of the level and clean the 'boss'. However, to progress you need to meet certain goals: % of the level cleaned and point value, which you get by maintaining a combo for as long as possible.
The graphics are interesting but nothing terribly special- I think it could be best described as artistically minimal. The audio is there, but neither good nor bad. The story... well, a game like this doesn't really need much of a story.
Mechanically the game is pretty solid. There are times when it feels like the controls aren't as tight as they could be, and the objective-based advancement means you find yourself doing many iterations of the same frustrating levels. The game does have controller support, but you'll have to do a lot of rigging to make it work right.
Its an interesting challenge game, but lacks a certain something. It doesn't make it bad, just... not something I play at for long periods. This indie title is still worth playing though, so consider picking it up if it happens to be on sale.

Yay, I mean, it's free for real!
I really love these kind of logic puzzle games.
This one is a concept not that new, but definitely enjoyable.
It's a basic minimalistic game that requires  you to connect the dots through the game square and of course to fill it and, in later levels, to match blue dots, red dots and so on with the respective color lines.
It's very simple and I'm sure everyone has already seen some versions of this game!
Don't expect anything but the graphics you see in the store page, 'cos it's really super minimalistic and it's great as it is. Super relaxing.
I'm aware that connect-the-dots games are way easier to play on a touchscreen, but I'm still having fun with my mouse nonetheless.
And as I said it can get challenging, even if it's definitely short, but it's free and we all really hope to see new 1€ games like these :)
As always, I'm pointing out some nonsense in other reviews. Those who say this is a rip-off of something else, plagiarism, seriously? It's a minimalistic puzzle game, there's no copyright on games that have millennias of age! And those who complain about the few levels we have, ok, it's true, but it's free and everything runs perfectly so what can we expect more? 200 levels? Maybe in the next games! :)
And for those who complain about the achievement spam.. I mean, the game runs full screen greatly, the game table is centered, what's the problems with the achievements on the lower right?! XD
But this isn't a demo to me, this is a full free game and can also be very interesting in order to introduce players to puzzle games of this sort, so, definitely recommended :)

This is the arcade classics’ trailing sibling. Had it been born in 1993 it would have been the Swedish apostle around the table of worshipped shoot ‘em up games. However, the 23-year age gap, an eternity within this industry, puts it in the genre of today’s retro games. Gladly, as such, it is actually possible to play on a regular computer. Having been of topmost gaming age in the 80s and 90s, it was a pleasure to play 1993 Space Machine, reviving joyous feelings from my adolescence. Graphically, it is an impressive work of art. I was flying around and admiring the views, as well as the music and sounds. But as a superannuated player I had a hard time staying alive, using the keyboard controls. With a joystick or a gamepad would be the right way to play this. I’d like to experience all the delights of this game. I’m glad it was brought out of the basement after all these years. Well done!

I felt that 1993 Space Machine was a pretty good example of what the SNES library really consisted of - mostly shooters, with varying degrees of innovation that seldom inspired confidence in the industry at large.  Honestly, it plays exactly like what you'd expect from an SNES game.
Against genre classics like R-Type and Gradius, 1993 Space Machine doesn't really hold up. Sure, it works pretty well as an introduction to the genre at large, but really doesn't innovate or present anything interesting that you've not seen before.
The only thing I can say 1993 Space Machine really has right is the weapon system - it's interesting.  It's not complex, but it presents a number of interesting options, and I really enjoyed it.  There are plenty of ways to kit your ship and become more than the level can handle, meaning your loadout really determines your difficulty.

2) Master Hacker
3) All Weapon Upgrades
4) Research Master
5) Master Gatherer
6) Trap Master
7) Big Spender
8) Rapture Historian
Over the years, I've run into a handful of games that have failed to give me an Achievement (each).  But, there's no excuse for a game that has 8 broken Achievements.
The longer version:  even though the game has a good story and mechanics (though I had to change the keymappings a bit), and even though I'm apparently one of the rare ones who didn't suffer from graphical glitches or the fatal "Press Space to Continue" crash, along with those broken Achievements, the game is just as tedious as BioShock 1 (assuming you're going for Achievements).  The biggest difference between BioShock 1 and BioShock 2 is the change to the hacking mini-game:  now, it's a mindless muscle-twitch activity instead of the "make a tube" activity of before.  At first, I thought that might have relieved the tedium a bit.  But, no.  It's actually worse.  So, I'm sad to say that I've got to Not Recommend the game.  If they ever fix the Achievements, it might be OK.  But, with them broken, nope.

Contrast is a puzzle based platform game, developed by Compulsion Games.
In this game you follow the story of a small girl Didi Malenkaya who has an imaginary friend called Dawn.
No one else can see Dawn, but that does not mean she does not exsist.
Didi found herself in a world where she only sees people as shadows.
Her parents are having relationship problems and many debts to pay off.
They both are too busy to take care of Didi, her mother Kat Malenkaya works as a singer at the Ghost Note cabaret while her father Johnny Fenris has been kicked out of the house because of doing business with gangsters in order to make some money.
Child services have threatened to take Didi away from her mother.
Didi can't stand this situation anymore and together with Dawn she sneaks out of the house to save the situation between her parents.
Contrast is set in a 1920 Nior atmosphere.
In this game you play as Dawn who has the ability to shift into the 2D shadow world and back into the 3D world.
Throughout the game you have to help Didi solve puzzles that vary from moving objects between the physical 3D world and the 2D shadow world.
Manipulating light sources in the 3D world such as spotlights, film projectors etc. will create shadow paths.
These paths will lead Dawn to new areas containing collectibles like Luminaries (light sources) and Documents that reveal more about the story.
Contrast felt like a very unique game because the ability of shifting between the physical 3D world and the 2D shadow world was something I have never seen before in games.
Everything I already knew about puzzles games couldn't always match up to the puzzles in Contrast.
This will make you think more out of the box, requires a little more creative thinking and raise the bar of puzzles.
I must admit that Contrast has a short length of gameplay and the story itself does not have that much depth than I expected it to be.
I really recommend Contrast for its unique experience but I don't think it's worth the full price, purchase the game when it's on sale.

Dustforce is a bipolar experience. Sublimely calming throughout with an insurmountable skill level.  The things that make Dustforce one of my favorite games are things that seem obvious a few years out now, but they're worth saying for someone who hasn't experienced it.  The soundtrack, by Lifeformed, is transcendent.  It has trappings of dubstep and chillwave but so much attention gets paid to cohesive textures and melodies that no song becomes just a genre-piece.  You will listen to this soundtrack outside of the game, and I've played this sountrack at work, heard it used on NPR, and my friends who have never played Dustforce have heard it.  The visuals are  better than they need to be.  They could have been retro 8 or 16-bit, which would make sense with the pizel perfect gameplay, or they could have been bulky flash graphics, or boring minimalist nonsense, or they could have been cheesy 3D graphics, or anything else that you'll find by flipping through the other platformers on Steam.  Instead, what they are are a beautiful flat colors, equally evoking 16-bit clarity and Gamecueb-era cel shading.  The game could have been a linear experience, lacking a hub-world and natural progression like Super Mario 3D Land.  But what we get is a branching, growing, player-guided progression through multiple worlds in a hubworld that is more of a sequel to Peach's Castle from Super Mario 64 than anything.  In order to access certain levels, you have to develop the skills necessary to play through those levels by traversing increasingly difficult areas of the hub world, accomplishing not only training a new player but evoking exploration and the unique atmospheres of each world.  It's these reasons that make Dustforce an experience that's larger than it's parts, a charming, sublime experience that respects the skill of whoever plays it without trying to intimidate you or restrict your experience.  Absolutely required.

Very much in two minds about the game. As it is, I refunded after playing for abour an hour, and would say, briefly:
For ME it was not what I had hoped to get, but if YOU are just looking for a nice, simple dungeon crawler and can live with some of its limitations, you might enjoy GoD much more than I did.
---
The game's concept, while not unique, is really pretty cool. You have an AI-controlled hero exploring a dungeon, which YOU build around him. You place down corridors, monsters, special events, and your hero then acts accordingly. Sounds great, doesn't it? I expected there to be all sorts of tiny differences between hero classes- maybe a Thief would always go for gold, maybe even putting himself into danger? Or a Ranger would probably move themsleves into good sniping positions? I saw myself considering how to place cards so that my hero would survive and level up and that sounded amazing.
Nothing of that. The main idea is: Room with monster is a no-go. Room with same monster and any amount of treasure however: Let's go there. It's almost irrelevant how you place down stuff. Your hero will always act more or less the same.
Even worse: Not only are all heroes the same, even the classes make relatively little difference, at least early on you just don't get that much of a difference between a Bruiser and a Mime, yet on paper they are "Fighter" and "Spellcaster". I admit, I did not play very long, and there probably is more to the class system, but after spending my hour throwing Hero after Hero into a dungeon where my building made little difference, I lost hope a bit.
There's also no permanence to anything. You keep no equipment, your Hero resets to level 1, you just return with some gold. That made it even harder to actually get invested into my tiny AI lemmings.
Still, I admit that the game just disappointed ME, probably because I expected such a lot of it. The core rules are simple and easy to get into. The combat, while simple, works just okay. And the art IS charming as hell.

The biggest issues I had were light shafts reducing frame rate in a small area or combat actions occasionally becoming "delayed" which seems to be related to animations or other actions getting stuck in a temporary loop.
Not much else to add. This is probably the best RPG I've ever played. Only shortcomings it has compared to Original Sin (Enhanced Edition) is some lack of voice acting, but due to the game's narrative and character origin/tag system, it's understandable - full voice acting of this game would require immense effort and resources, especially time. Twenty five levels of relatively simple puzzles and exactly one hundred “achievements” which will unlock at the rate of one third a dozen per level. Kinda close to achievement spam games, but actually fun to play with and free without that nasty “to pay” part. Well, theoretically since it's a demo of a paid version of the very same game from the very same developer, but half the levels and quarter the achievements. I guess paid version will unlock latter at the rate of two fifth a score per level. Maybe. Probably. Last time I checked there were a free Halloweenesque DLC with as many levels as here. So, that achievements per level rate might be somewhere in between and more fractional than necessary.
Puzzles may look simple, but the main point is not to connect all the colored dots with colorful lines, but also cover the whole game board with these connections on the way which essentially turns and twists the most obvious solutions through and all around themselves. Not sure I want to buy a paid version even though it's cheap and free one were rather nice, but if you want to write your motto in profile with achievements then you may want to get a paid one since it have more words to play with. You won't be able to write “Halloweenesque” with either, though. Anyway, try this one first. You'll lose nothing but your time and even that is a given for puzzles.
Ah, right, the main point of achievements in this and paid version of this game is to write some potentially meaningful sentences in your profile with them. Meaningful. Potentially. Eeyep. Hey, at least that isn't main point of the game. Unlike the rest achievement spam “games” this one is actually playable and interesting.

My review;
This is a turn based 4x sci-fi space strategy game, and this one is very, very good.
Right off the bat, I recommend, highly, especially for those that like turn based games, 4x games, space games, etc.
The graphics, style and gameplay are all top notch.
I've encountered no crashes or what I would call game breaking bugs in my time playing.
I play with an i5 and GTX 970 and it sticks to 60fps just about all of the time, no issues with performance for me.
In extremely long games (300+ moves), the AI can take a couple seconds to decide the next move, but all 4x games I've played have this.  This is my biggest complaint and I only mention it to keep my review accurate.
The replayability of the game is crazy.
Every race has very unique ships, features, traits etc.
Some of them are truely alien too, not just reskinned humaniods.  Alien ships look alien.
Every race has different motivations and ending goals and are very different to both play as and against.
This is the first game I've played in a LONG time that had me watching Youtube vids for stratagies and gameplay training and loving every bit of it.
This game repays taking the time to learn its mechanics, the more you learn about how the game actually works the more you find that you really CAN take nitpicky control of waaay more aspects of what fleets do, how they do it, etc.  Same with planets, what citizens are on which planet and tweaking the returns and synergies are DEEP and rewarding once you spend the time to learn them.  Again, the different races behave very differently regarding its citizens and taking that level of control, while the game will handle it for noobs, allows you to really milk every drop out of a system if you take direct control and guide it correctly.
I feel that many players will play the game without any knowledge of its mechanics and still have a ton of fun all while learning the details.  This, to me, only draws out the true gem of a game that this is.  The more you play it and figure out its idiosynchronsy's the more it will grow on you.

ENDLESS SPACE 2: a sapce opera rivalled by no other.
While the kings of 4X =  Master of Orion, Galactic Civilizations 2, and maybe stellaris are all great 4Xs, endless space 2 has a few key differences that may make this game better or worse than these champs.
*TLDR*
Graphics: 9.5/10 - great to look at, especially the minor details in ships/planets/ the combat scenes (the black hole combat zone is my favorite), By far the pretiest 4X to date, helps out a lot when you need to stare at screens all the time (the moving minimalist backgrounds in the various management screens are great).  The sheer number of in-game cutscenes from a 4X ( looking at you stellaris, gal civ) gives this game some great atmosphere. The whole game is like a massive dream of space on LSD.
GUI: 8/10 - easy to use, flush transitioning from screen to screen , though the buttons may be small-ish. overall very streamlined and clean. Designing ships is a fun thing to do in this game, and the screen is great.
Combat: 7/10 - outside visual appeal, combat is focused on more or less who has the more advanced ship and is (unfortunately) less tactics based (the battle cards as great as they (sometimes)  are , are quite minimal in selection) , though the flottila system is quite interesting. However endless space 2 is one of the few 4X games to have decent combat system with a great "everything else". (Most 4X with great combat are subpar in their more civ mechanics). The faction shsips could be more varied as well.
Races + Story: 10/10 - simply outclasses all other space sim out there in how unque every race is and their accompanying storylines are great. (Though I'll highly doubt the cravers would help any aliens even if they are in stasis). Some people may not like their imagiantions pre-built however.
Replayability: 9/10 - a sapce opera with great story and decision choices alongside great races and quests make this game one of a kind in it's genre. It doesn't beat stellaris in terms of what you can do however. The differences in playstyle between the avrious races keeps the agme from ever being stale, in the management side of things.
Difficulty: 7+/10 - the lack of game-changing disasters and an innate hostility between you and your opponents make the game quite predictable... this becomes less ofa  problem with teh avrois mods available however (such as the official G2G balance mod)
Overall :  9 /10 - a great 4X space opera with more story than you'd expect, a brilliant universe, diverse races held back only by lacklustre AI and combat (to be fair most 4X's suck at combat). Highly recommended.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
To begin endless space 2 presents with very disntict races that all have unque gameplay perks that drastically change the way you play.
1.The religous Vodyani aim to spread their culture around the world while ascending other aliens into their own. Also colonisation arks. Probably the most distinct;y unique race in the history of 4X, they're ability to gatehr essence and change systems anytime is a powerful mechanic if used properly.
2.The Cravers literally eat planets for a living (which I personally still don't know how to effectively play them).
3.The sterotypical humans aren't as stereotypical in this game, having the funnest story in my opinion and a faction perk that just screams flexibility.
4.The Sophons arguably the most beginner friendly race are equipped with the power of science, and will be more advanced than their adverseries 90% of the time.
5.The Unfallen are diplomatic trees, that spread intergalactic vines across star systems (how that works I have no idea)
6. The Amphibian-like Lumeris are money hoggers that will smash an economic victory faster than you can say "what is trade?"
7. The megalamoniac Horatio and his army of well ... himself will become the perfect enemy ... or ally.
8. and lastly are the riftborn, who are literally from a rift of another universe altogether.
These disntinct factions all ahve their unque storylines that can sometimes create massive gameplay changes (especially the Raians). Additionally they make a game that otherwise has too much story for a 4X into a decent competitor to the previous champs in terms of replayablity.
For a 4X, endless space 2 is a lot easier to pick up, but it makes up for this decreased complexity with deep mechanics (which unfortunately do not include espionage), which are well integrated into the "spacebar for more details" feature. You will find how usefull the global marketplace is. How usefull luxury resources are (which are special resources that boost certain aspects of your race and they are A LOT to choose from) . The importance of heroes in combat and system management (which can easily turn extrremely overpowered if you know what you're doing).
Additionally I highly recommend enabling the pirates gameplay feature as they provide a very good challenge from the early to mid game ( so you can't just spam build setller ships). They make the game a lot more fun in my opinion.
The random quests that appear al the time contain nice tidbits on the endless universe ( mind you endless sapce 2 is part of an endless universe with all the other endless games), and are great to add to the game overaching story. I will admit they aren't that many however (will likely change).
The developers over at Amplitude studios of SEGA, are keen on providing free DLC that can sometimes add a whole lot of changes to the game (such as fighters and bombers - HELL YEAH). They also made a custom official balance mod on the workshop to balance the game.
The ship designs may be great + the battle cutscnes are gerat to watch a few times but the combat systems could still be improved with more battle cards ( a card system to dictate the strengths of your ships/smallcraft) and probably less of a decisive factor on who has the more advanced ships. The ground battle is nothing special unfortunately.
The quests that do exist do lack the oppurtunity to massively disrupt anything however, such as major disaters present in the civilzations agmes or the more recent Mars Colony game, making every game a direct competition between the other factions, which may cause some staleness after a while (not forgetting the AI usually hates you can diplomacy is very lacklustre in this game - giving endless coins doens't do anything really). This makes the agem stale as you rapidly overexceed your opponents.
Altogether counting the games inherent falls in difficululty, predictable AI, limited drastic game-influencing quests and decent-ish combat make endless space 2 slighly less than perfect but if you're looking for a space opera like no other , endless space 2 is a very very good title on your list of options.
Oh did I forgot to add that the game's soundtrack is great. Also modding in a 4X is always great (just see stellaris)
PS: Don't be fooled by the 41 hour playtime, I have played this for at least 150+ hours offline :D

Well, this game is a diamond in the rough. As a huge fan of survival games, you just can't beat something like this. Especially at it's price point. It is a freaking steal.
I went into the game with very low expectations. Survival games have been becoming very cliched. This game, also, is your typical survival, but what makes this different is there's an end game. What's the reward when you complete the game? Multiplayer! That is pretty cool for its genre.
The game does have a story. Very small so far that I have seen. You come in on a ship and happened upon an island where experiments were or is being ran. The mission is to make it to the center and turn off teslas so your life can go back to normal. But you must survive, grind, and craft so you can prepare for the threats that lie towards the center. Wolves, bears, zombies, and others I'm sure. When they hit you, it hurts. I had to run back to camp after every melee fight so far. I've learned to fight from a distance. The threats in the game are very much real and resources seem to be very hard to come by. But that brings me to another of why I enjoy this game. To proceed, you must hunt down these creatures that want to kill you. You may need the bear fur or bones, wolf's pelt, zombie may have a weapon. You do what you must to proceed.
Now the cons.
-There are a few bugs. But they are more nitpicky bugs to me. Nothing to where it is game ruining.
-Time in the day. It's hard to tell how much time you have until it gets dark. From the story in the game, it's dangerous when night falls and I've never been stuck out there to find out how dangerous it is. But when night comes, you have about 20 secs from the moment you realize its dusk til it is completely dark. But it was mention in-game that the island is messing with the day and night cycle so it could be part of the game.
-The map. There's two different maps. One full view of the island then one map that is more zoomed in. I can't move the map in any direction to see when way I need to go. Sense of direction is all messed up for me because the sun seems to be running North and South according to the map.  There's no compass, So i tend to get turned around here and there and have to open my map every 10 seconds. I know I could run straight but the island is full of mountain terrain and threats of the creatures always stop me.
-Melee. It's impossible to melee attack and not get hit back. In other words, no way of dodging theirs. When they hit you, it hurts.
From those cons, they are more nitpicky cons than actual cons. I could actually say, I haven't experienced one bad moment.
Pros
-Price point. 3 dollars and you get an amazing game. This game is worth more and I appreciate the devs for making it this low to try to get attention.
-Survival aspect. This is par with all the good survival games out there right now. Only difference is it being single player. But I love that.
-The unknown. I can't help but just have the sense of not knowing what is just over that hill. For once, I am happy to fear the things in the woods than to fear a random player killing me for my stuff.
-Last note, price point.

4. I mean, yeah, there was a game developed in the nineties that looked like this. There is recorded proof of this but the idea that this is at all just a straight out up-port to a new engine doesn't hold water.
5. You have infinite lives and there's checkpoints you can restart from w/o penalty always. This is not how things worked in 1993. In 1993, you got however many lives they give you, there was no checkpoint before the epic final boss of each level and if you ran out of lives you could restart the level if you had continues (or quarters) left.
6. The new way, with checkpoints, is enormously better for everyone but arcade owners.
7. This being said, this truly does have an old school field. It smartly did away w/ 4:3 for 16:9 widescreen but the graphics and sound are legit. The controls are tight and gameplay is nutty and intense.
8.  This game does have controller support (recommended by me) but it is not enabled by default. You gotta go into the menus and enable it. It give you a recommended configuration but does not map it by default so you then have to map it yourself manually. Maybe in 1993 you could get away w/ that garbage but it seemed kinda lazy to me.
9. I found this did not mix well w/ drinking all that much beer which I suspect is why it took me about 50% longer than average to beat it. You win some, you win some more slowly while drinking beer.
10. The weapons upgrade system is kinda borked. You buy upgrades permanently rather than find upgrades in the level. There were tons of things to try but rather than try new things out, I just upgraded basically two random weapons and my starting ship and the mid-game of this was the easiest thing I've done in my entire life.
11. The rest of it was not so easy.
12. If I have one major complaint it's that the boss fights were not properly epic. As per number 6, you got a checkpoint right before and could replay the boss over and over w/o going through the whole level again. I will take a less frustrating (and, yeah, easier) experience for the sake of my sanity but it does ease the tension in kind of a bad way. Furthermore, none of the bosses had like six forms that got more and more ridiculous as you go through them.
13. This said, after the final boss in this one, I felt sooooooo good beating it. I don't think you can ask for anything more in a shmup. It is kind of a pure gaming experience. There is a story you ignore and then you kill things. If it's hard enough and you win, you feel good. Heck yes!

Solid 4x with an overloaded GUI that is both, elegant yet crowded. Still managable though, but the reliance on tooltips is a bit over the top, so you are constantly moving your mouse over stuff and wait some milliseconds for the tooltip to appear. This is a bit annoying in terms of game-flow.
Besides that, when it comes down to the game itself, there is a lot of content, quests, anomalies, etc. so the content is there and the variation in races and playstyle is quite nicely done.
Science has a lot of options in a huge tech tree, but unfortunately it does not offer that many real game-changers. Quite a big chunk of the tech tree is just incremental boosts to the basic resource system.
Generally speaking the game is similar to other 4X and does not do anything extremely innovative, but delivers a solid overall experience without any major hickups. Nice mood, nice soundtrack, clean presentation.

Endless Space 2; well I'm going to give out a bunch of pros and cons. hopefully this will help you out.
Pros:
1) customization is better and balanced out. in Endless Space one and Endless Legends you could easily build a very ridiculous build because beside the point limitation and traits being unable to conflict each other there was no limit. you can pick all the positive traits you ever wanted as long as you got enough negative traits to balance out the point limitation. here in endless space 2 however you have a limit of 8 traits for your custom factions. this balances custom factions out FAR FAR better than in either endless space one or endless legends.
2) it plays fairly similar to endless space one so if your familiar with endless space one you should get the hang of it pretty fast.
3) there is actual meaning to the government and law system. for example dictator ships give you 2 law slots but essentially a guaranteed party victory because dictator ship. this means you get to keep your industrial windfall law if your party is industrious and so on. however each government type has its own draw backs. for example with dictatorship if your people are not happy they will start to rebel much sooner and quicker than with other governments. some governments allow more law slots as well.
4) customization of ships is more meaningful. in endless space one you had something called tonnage; this allowed you to spam missiles, plasma, slugs, shields, armor, flak, etc. because your limitation was only that of your tonnage. now however in endless space 2 it is more like the endless legends customization. you have slots and some slots are specialized so you have a limit to how many shields and armor and guns you can have on your ship.
5) there are exclusive tech; in endless space one you could just get everything you wanted outside of faction tech but now there is a exclusive tech so you research one but can not get the other. this goes back to customization and which direction you want to take your fleets to.  (to be honest this is a bit more iffy for me but I can see its intent and felt fine the way it was done and there is not that many exclusive techs so it stops it from any potential of ruining the tech tree)
6) minor factions; this is a thing that comes from endless legends. there are minor factions and if you assimilate them they give you bonuses (although you can not recruit them like endless legends)
7) ground battles; I like the added layer of ground battles that's all there is for me to say.
8) you can change your government. if you don't like your government or laws you can change it so your not stuck with a choice.
9) market: in endless legends you had something known as the trade market where you could buy and sale strategic and luxery resources. its in endless space 2 here and it helps when you are not very resource rich in your territory. (granted it helps to build towards what you have but if you need a boost or two there is the market)
Cons:
1) no ground troop customization. I would have liked customizing my ground troops but you can not. it is just like endless space one where you just straight out upgrade your troops.
2) pirates...don't really like them..they are...annoying..espically when its early game and you find your self in the unlucky spot of being sandwiched between two pirate bases. it helps isolate you from other empires but the pirate fleets are going to get stronger and stronger and so on. it kinda forces you into an early aggression because you need to del with those pirates one way or another because they will destroy your fleets, blockade your planets, and so on.
3) minor factions....hold on let me finish...to be more specific the lack of factions from endless space one. for example the aomeba and the bird samurai guys. they are minor or background factions you just can not play which I liked the aomeba and the bird people. I also liked the harmony the intelligent rock people.
4) to repair things or buy out things with dust you must research it first.
5) faction trait limitation; the 8 trait limitation does not give you much wiggle room. at least 10 trait limitation for the extra wiggle room is what I personally would want.
6) weak starter ships...in endless space one this was less of an issue because there were no pirates and even in the case of early aggression you had the tonnage system which allowed you to quickly assemble fairly effective frigates. with this new system however your starter ships are far weaker and this matters because pirates will attack your fleets and blockade your planets and so on.
7) colonization...I don't mind the module thing but I don't like the colonization module being exclusive for certain ships. in endless space one you could have essentially super colony ships that could colonize multiply planets and star systems. the way it is in endless space 2 you just can not do that anymore to the same effect.
8) heros...I don't like the way it is done in endless space 2...ide prefer being able to go in whenever and get whatever hero instead of waiting for another hero slot to open before I can get another hero/governor/admiral. other than that heros have a slightly bigger impact because they come with their own ships instead of inhabiting one of your ships in endless space one. (which also kinda makes them more vulnerable but it is a decent trade off).
9) faction specific tech and affinity does not really exist outside of the visual affinity stuff. in endless space one the bird people had their bushido effect and several faction specific tech which added onto them. the aomeba could tell you were all the planets are and the harmony could tell you where all the resources were regardless of your tech level/usage of these resources. you could pick and choose BOTH the visual style and the affinity. they were SEPERATE choices. here not so much when you choose a visual style your also choosing the affinity essentially as well. it was a better system when they were separate. An no the omniscience and all that other stuff don't count as affinity by my book they count as an additional faction bonus on top of the other 3 you could get right below your political arrangement by making 3 policy choices.

Side-scrolling space-shooters of the 90’s were ruthless. Checkpoints were few and far between and the sheer amount of enemies you’d battle would be relentless. 1993 Space Machine takes us back in time to a time when games weren’t meant to be easy and tutorials were portrayed by a single window showing you what powerups did when picked up. Watch our 1993 Space Machine gameplay and review video on YouTube below!
I remember as a kid playing games, like R-Type and Fantasy Zone, and having a hell of a hard time progressing beyond a certain point. These games were cut-throat, but a good way to introduce me to future games that eased off in difficulty as time went by. 1993 Space Machine throws you back into the hyper-coloured shorts of your 90’s self and tests your skills in a way they’ve not been tested for over twenty years.
1993 Space Machine provides you with a great deal of ships to choose from, however the only difference they have from one another is the way they look. Different weaponry provides slight advantages and help you overcome sections of the game you thought were otherwise improbable (not impossible).
With a decent amount of levels and different bosses with differing mechanics, 1993 Space Machine does a good job with giving you a nostalgic gaming experience. However, I feel the story itself is a bit lacking and could even be taken out of the game altogether.
Make sure you check out our 1993 Space Machine gameplay and review video above and if you like it, go on and check out the game on Steam via the link at the top of this page!

An interesting MMO. Sure there are other side-scrolling multiplayer games, like Awesomenauts, but that focuses more on team versus matches. With Elsword you have quality visuals, done in an anime-esque cell shading style, character voices are done in Japanesse (text is in English). What's different here is that the vast majority of the time, you don't need your mouse. All combat is controlled from the keyboard, from movement to attacks and the mouse only seems to be used for menus. Also, this game uses a Stamina system; killing monsters in dungeons uses stamina, the more players running that dungeon, the less you use. Stamina refills daily (3am PST), but is unlimited on weekends, and honestly, you can get at least 3-4 hours of dungeon time in on your daily stamina, so it's not a huge deal.
What can be a bit confusing are the costume pieces from the real-money store. While they're nice and they can make your character look decent, they all seem to be limited-time use items. I may be wrong about that, but when you look at them the price is listed twice, one for a 30-day use and one permanent for 2x the 30-day price. You can get by without them, as they only apply stat boost on top of whatever your getting from armor/weapons/ect.
That aside, the game is highly addictive. However, for most quest you seem to have to repeat dungeons over at least 2-3 times, often at specific difficulty levels or higher, but said dungeons have 3 difficulty levels and you can always just join a random group to take on the highest levels or run solo if you're feeling up to it. Dungeons are also split up, with some not letting you progress till all enemies are dead. One gripe I found was in the Skill Notebook quest where I had to run two dungeons over and over again in order to kill one enemy type because I need to collect 20 items, which were rare drops (I'd get 2-3 per run, max with some runs giving none). But most times you're asked to collect 20+ of an item you get it from every avaliable enemy kill, so it's only a problem in specific quests where the item is listed as Rare.
In-game currency is easy to come by. At only 6 hours in I'd already accumulated over 300k, and probably spent even more upgrading my equipment as well, since you can get a lot of use out of equipment via enchanting, enhancing and repairing before you need to get something new.
I haven't delved too deeply into crafting, but item/weapon enhancement is done two different ways, each adding diffrent things, so the system there is robust enough to allow for customization to play prefferences.
In all it's a solid game with solid mechanics, detailed characters, both NPC and your own. My only real gripe is that unless you pay K-Ching (the games real-world money) you're limited to only 3 item quick-slots and 4 skill quick-slots, you're inventory is also limited, with 8 slot upgrades costing 200 K-Ching. However, 1 K-Ching is ~$.01, so it's not that big a cost (This is based off the 500 K-Ching pack costing $5US). But be warned that such upgrades are bought on a per character basis, so it costs about $14 per character to get +16 inventory spaces and all 8 skill quick slots, but you can play just as well with the stock free setup.

The game's concept, while not unique, is really pretty cool. You have an AI-controlled hero exploring a dungeon, which YOU build around him. You place down corridors, monsters, special events, and your hero then acts accordingly. Sounds great, doesn't it? I expected there to be all sorts of tiny differences between hero classes- maybe a Thief would always go for gold, maybe even putting himself into danger? Or a Ranger would probably move themsleves into good sniping positions? I saw myself considering how to place cards so that my hero would survive and level up and that sounded amazing.
Nothing of that. The main idea is: Room with monster is a no-go. Room with same monster and any amount of treasure however: Let's go there. It's almost irrelevant how you place down stuff. Your hero will always act more or less the same.
Even worse: Not only are all heroes the same, even the classes make relatively little difference, at least early on you just don't get that much of a difference between a Bruiser and a Mime, yet on paper they are "Fighter" and "Spellcaster". I admit, I did not play very long, and there probably is more to the class system, but after spending my hour throwing Hero after Hero into a dungeon where my building made little difference, I lost hope a bit.
There's also no permanence to anything. You keep no equipment, your Hero resets to level 1, you just return with some gold. That made it even harder to actually get invested into my tiny AI lemmings.
Still, I admit that the game just disappointed ME, probably because I expected such a lot of it. The core rules are simple and easy to get into. The combat, while simple, works just okay. And the art IS charming as hell.

Although I initially enjoyed this game, in the end I don't think I can recommend it to most players. While the presentation is nice, the gameplay is polished and the general concept well realised, the core of the game design is fundamentally flawed by overreliance on randomness and a lack of player control.
The very shape of the dungeon you explore, and many of the enemies you fight, are determined by placing cards you are randomly dealt each turn. If you're lucky, then the cards you get will lead you to your goal, if not, they won't, which on timed missions can mean you simply fail the mission and need to restart. Similarly, if you can place enemies your hero can defeat, then you can win the battle, level up, and progress. If not then you either skip leveling up and stay too weak to fight the preplaced enemies in the level, or you risk a battle against a too strong enemy, which will likely lead to you dying and needing to restart.
These 2 aspects of the game are made worse by the fact that you cannot control where your hero will actually move. Often the hero will move onto the monsters and treasure you yourself place, while sometimes (usually when it matters the most) the hero will ignore what you've placed  and insist on charging into a powerful enemy and dying. Once again, this is particulalry annoying on timed missions where every move you make is important. The rules for how the hero chooses his path are never explained, so it's possible this can be avoided with clever play, but I never figured out how.
Deck building for combat is also very random, each hero you choose has a gimmick (such as extra effect from healing spells) and a few preset ability cards, but most of your abilities come from equipment that randomly drops in the level after fighting. This means you often end up in battle having to fight with abilities that were randomly chosen from your deck, which itself is filled with abilities that were semi randomly added to it. Once again this leads to frequent situations where you lose battles simply because the RNG didn't give you cards that allowed you to win. Since losing a battle means a restart, the frustration can quickly mount.
If you enjoy the gambling aspect of games, where your fate is 70% determined by the roll of a dice and 30% by the choices you make, and you have a lot of patience, this can be a fun game. The combat is simple, but understandbale and fun, the graphics are nice and the music is good (though the "Lol your hero has died again!" songs eventually caused me to switch off the music entirely). Otherwise, you'll likely find that the frustration of constantly restarting levels due to factors beyond your control will quickly outweigh the fun that the game offers.

The limitations I have encountered so far are:

I've been playing video games for over 38 years. I've bought over 2,000 games in that time. Guild of Dungeoneering is one of the least fun games I've ever played. It's not the worse game, not the worse in terms of how it looks or sounds, but in terms of fun; it's just plain not fun.
I love RPG's, and generally the basic formula of what makes a RPG fun is exploring, killing monsters in entertaining and graphic ways, finding loot, collecting items, and leveling and improving your characters skills and abilities.
The reason GoD isn't fun is because it fails at so many of these "must haves" to make a good RPG.
Exploring: Exploring is kinda fun in this game, but there really isn't much of it. You leave your guild and go directly to a dungeon, which you then build; no real exploring. The building is ... meh ... not so great.
Killing: Killing monsters is pretty much unrewarding as well. The combat system is faily simple; an expanded version of rock / paper / scissors. It's about the best aspect of the game other than the music and the style of the game's artwork. It would be fine if the game was fun or interesting; it's not.
Now for what is really, really bad about this game; ie. everything else.
Loot:  Finding loot ... it's irrelevant, non-existant, a total fail. You have four, COUNT THEM, four item slots for equipping things. No back pack, no storage, no collecting anything. You can equip something you find and use it for the dungeon you are currently in with your current character, but that's it. You leave the dungeon all your equipment is gone! No selling things, no improving them or modifying them, etc. Gone; Poof! So lame. You can use the gold your find to improve your guild hall so you can have the priveledge of finding it randomly in dungeons; YAWN.
Collecting loot: There isn't any to collect. Um what? Yes that's right, no real loot. The basis of every legendary RPG is finding epic gear. GoD thinks it's not a component of a great RPG. Wrong !
Leveling your character and improving skills and abilities: Without this what is a RPG? The answer: Not worth playing. There are no skills, no abilities, and no leveling. You can "temporarily" level up the current chararcter in the current dungeon, but if you survive and go back to town you loose EVERYTHING! You keep nothing. You STAY a level 1 character with no gear, no skills, no abilities; forever. You can improve your guild hall to get a different character class and that gets you a new level 1 character with a different deck of cards to use while fighting. BUT, and that's a big but, that character stays a level 1 too, with no gear, no skills, and no abilities. EPIC FAIL !!!!!
Gee what fun; NOT ! That's the whole point, it's not fun. The game teases you into thinking this looks cool, has a catchy opening musical theme, but that's it, it's a total illusion. It could have been a terrific game if it had any substance to it at all, but it doesn't.  It's not like a castle defense game, or a RTS game, where building up your guild hall is fun and exciting, it's just pointless grinding to get gold to buy more "things" that aren't any more fun than what you had to begin with. I even watched some videos of the game and read as many reviews I could find and I still made the horrible choice of spending money for it. Shame on me, but hopefully you won't be fooled.
Bottom line: If you don't mind spending $15 for 2-4 hours of frustration and disappointment I guess you may want to try it, but it wouldn't be a good choice. I've spend less than $1 on steam sale games that are more fun than GoD, and with 100 times less frustration. It would require a total rework of almost every aspect of this game to make it fun and I seriously doubt that is going to happen. :(

This review assumes no knowledge of D:OS.
The below is spoiler free and story light:
Divinity: Original Sin 2 is an isometric turn-based party RPG for 1-4 players.
I have completed Act 1 (all that is currently available) in a total of 20 hours for a complete (fairly sure) exploration of the zone(s) and utilized a full party to do so (9.18.16) on "classic difficulty".
When I finished the available content my characters were level 8.
As it stands DOS2 is very playable with the combat system particularly shining through as a strong point.
DOS2 emphasizes tactical combat as many systems interact - fire spells touching water/blood puddles creates steam, fire touching oil or poison creates and explosion, explosions generate smoke... I would sotp short of calling it a realistic system but it certainly adds layers of complexity to combat that are missing from less detailed combat engines (any of the CRPG Dungeons and Dragons interpretations for instance).
As it stamds now, the current armor system (physical and magical armor are discrete values, like "shields" in most modern shooters, and are lost before your actual health) seems to favor magic users as few foes had enough magic armor to stand long in withering magical blasts but most melee foes had significant physical armor.
Addendum (10/02/16): I played through as an all physical party and while the early going is rough, once your characters get decent gear and some mobility skills a lot of the issues with physical armor fall away.
The dialogue as it stands is similar to the systems used in many text heavy CRPGs: Characters may have conversations hovering in floating text above their heads but when you engage your options to respond show up in a "summarized" version of a response.  The dialogue currently tends to favor either extreme good or evil, with the occasional cringey bout of lasciviousness.
Some of the dialogue is humorous as are a number of the Non Player reactions.  Several quests were heavy on telegraphing future events, but even when they would have seemingly changed reactions most NPCs still regarded you identically.
As this game is in Alpha, there are a number of small bugs I ran into (nothing that prevented progress) mostly related to typos, placeholder text, and grammatical issues.
While there are a number of systems (inventory standing foremost among them) that bog down progress and gameplay, DOS2 Alpha is still an enjoyable story wrapped in a strategic (if unbalanced) combat system.
The exposed bits of story are setting up for lots of potential which will be rewarding to see played out.
Thank you for the hard work Larian, and I look forward to seeing the future of DOS2!
