-Gifted from a friend-
Firstly I knew little of the game other than knowing it was mini/crazy golf, I have briefly seen some streamers play it whilst flicking around Twitch and was gifted a copy by a friend who wanted me to play.
You don't really need anything fancy when it comes to a mini golf game which is exactly what they've gone for, a nice simple drag and let go style of shooting. Whilst this is normally great it can turn out to be a bit of a pain if you want to use the "full power line" as a guide to line up your shot as when you drag back you will no doubt move either left or right slightly, I am nit picking but it's not really your traditional mini golf game as there are many shortcuts which require some precise shots.
Can't fault the music or sounds effects in the game, it's not generally something I look for especially in a game like this where %99 of the time I will kill the music to chat and listen to friends.
Whilst not so much in the traditional sense of talking about graphics (omg realism) the style suits the game and it does it well, the worlds look beautiful and are very well thought out, one of the main reasons I am eagerly awaiting new updates to see what new things they come up with..bonus points for the glowing balls, they look ace.
I still remember the days of Zany Golf of the Amiga, showing my age slightly, which stir some lovely childhood memories and this game brings back the joy of crazy♥♥♥♥♥golf. Every hole is unique, i've yet to play a hole and think it's similar to another in any way shape or form.
There are 4 (Correct me if I am wrong, it's 8am, not slept) environments to choose from thus far, and looking at the roadmap they already have many more planned. Like the holes they are all very unique, use the environment in completely different ways, for example the new haunted map has you zooming up and down spider webs and dodging ghosts; they're not just pretty sky box's plastered in the background whilst you play mini golf, they draw you into the world and make you feel like you're a ghostbuster taking a break kicking back with a bit of mini golf. Assuming you're on the haunted world of course.
As if that wasn't enough each hole has various "shortcuts" to master to get the all elusive hole in one, there are various ways of doing so and I won't spoil any but what I love about this game so god damn much is that the devs have not put silly borders / respawns on the edge of the holes to force you into playing how they want you to play, they have quite simply gone "F*** it play how you wan't, it's hella more fun that way" (although I belive you can add borders should you want it via options)
Whilst the game from what I have seen currently only offers multiplayer, it does give you a variety of fun options to play with, should you want to mix it up a bit or just competely annoy your friends who think they can watch youtube videos on how to get a hole in one feel free to stick on low gravity, jumping balls, variety shaped balls or even bouncy balls.
Once again, massive props to the devs for not being too serious with the game, these options have made me extremely excited for the future of the game and I hope to see even more wild options to play around with in the near future.
It certainly does need more courses but looking at the game now and the way the devs are handling EA I believe they will honor everything they've put in their roadmap, very few devs these days are open about their plans and it's nice to see a well structered roadmap that IS being worked through bit by bit, keep it up.
This game in my opinion is a must buy for anyone that loves a slightly less serious game to play with their friends / other people online.
The price is exceptionally good value and if I wasn't gifted it I would have bought it myself.
With how dire Early Access games can be (and trust me, I have enough of them) this really is a diamond in the rough and one to watch if you don't want to purchase it now.
This easily is a 10 on the EA scale; it's already well polished and has a lot of content for the price.

So I'm kind of missing a middle option in terms of ratings here.
While it's not a espacially good game. It isn't a bad game either.
In terms of technical aspects. The graphics are nothing mind blowing by any stretch of the imagination, but they aren't bad either. There's a strict 30fps lock going on, which I couldn't find a quick fix to by googling (such as changing a line in some config file) So I just decided to suck it up and enjoy the "console experience".
The gameplay:
The investigating comes down to looking long enough for "clues" and interrogating people afterwards and deciding wether they are
a) lying (and you have proof in form of one of the clues you previously collected)
b) lying (and you don't have proof, but are in fact just suspecting they are lying) - this option is confusingly labeled "doubt"
c) telling the truth
The rest of the gameplay comes down to some shooter-segments, some car chases. Neither of which are particualarly good.
The Main positive about the game in my opinion is the Story, which I actually found pretty interesting. However the actual plot only develops very slowly during the beginning and middle of the playtime. The story gets more interesting towards the end when the plot thickens.
Another Selling Point is the setting of post WW2 America in the late 40s, which isn't beeing explored in very many games. So If you think this sounds like a interesting setting just because it isn't such common theme in video games, then this might be something for you.
So overall I said I don't recommend this game because there is no middle option, cause that is what this game has written all over it in my opinion. And I reserve the "I recommend this game" option for games that I think are actually worth recommending, such as the Witcher 3, Tomb Raider(The Reboot), or Bioshock Infinite,...
This doesn't mean I think LA:Noire is bad, it's just not as good as those games which I just mentioned in my opinion.
And it honestly feels kind of like a♥♥♥♥♥♥move to click the thumb down-button, because I know that people that don't read the review will just think I thought it was a bad game, when really I don't.

As I have said before, the most important feature of an rpg is the story ---- and this game offered by Aldorlea has a great, involving, and interesting story.
You are placed right into the action from the beginning as you follow the tale of 2 sisters who are facing a dilemma of what is really going on, and why. But as time moves along, pieces of this puzzle are revealed, drawing you in as the player. A very well told tale indeed with twists, turns, good humor, and emotion.
Gameplay is pretty straightforward, but there are many secrets to discover along the way ---- so a careful inspection of all areas is advisable.
Artwork is very nicely done, and the music is pleasant and stays in the background, where it should be.
Battle scenes are nicely done, with all the available options apparent and easy to use.

The characters in the game are so fully developed that it could be said that the game is character driven. As you go deeper into the game, it is quite easy to begin to care about Scarllet and Beatrice (the 2 sisters) and several other members of the various parties. And you don't always see that.
I would heartily recommend this game to anyone of any age, especially to those (like myself) that enjoy the old school rpgs. It is a delight in all the important ways. Give this one (and any Aldorlea offering) a chance, and I think you'll be glad you did.

---DETAILS---
This is a card-strategy game with elements of RPG, delver and dungeon building.
The story is prety fun so far and the characters are funny, they actually made me giggle a few times.
Lets split it a bit.
Soundtrack: Simply awesome. Everytime a hero dies, wins a dungeon or when you start the game, the music just blows my mind. It really fits the atmosphere of the game! Congratulations to the developers! 10/10
Graphics: Pretty cool, but not awesome. Its kinda of repetitive, even though whenever you equip a new equipment to a hero it changes the display, everything else stays the same. 8/10
Gameplay:
The gameplay consists on 3 parts:
1. Building your guild.
The gold you get from dungeons you use to upgrade your guild, allowing you to get more heroes, blessings, different loot in dungeons. You can also check your graveyard and trophy room. Nice features, good mechanics to upgrade, but the visual effects and the higher tier upgrades cost are kinda of lame. 9/10
2. Building the dungeon.
At the beggining of the "round" you receive 5 cards. There are creatures cards, dungeos area cards and treasure cards.
You can put 3 of them into play. The idea is to use these 3 cards to build the dungeon, place enemies and treasures for you hero to find. The cards you get are mostly based on luck. Wich SUCKS. Sometimes you only get stupid cards, like 3 areas that only connect to 1 area and 2 creatures that can kick your♥♥♥♥♥as encounters. I got to say that dependiong entirely on luck kinda bummed me out. 7/10.
3. Movement of the hero and battles.
You dont control the hero movement, he ALWAYS take the shortest route to complete the dungeon objective. Easy to understand. The harder the dungeon, the longer the dungeon you must create for him to get there, but the cards you receive to create the dungeon are random, remember? This can SUCK sometimes.
Ok, now for the battle system. Its a card battle system. Each of your heroes start with a deck of cards that is the standard for that "class". You CANNOT change the deck before the dungeon. It's ALWAYS the same. When you win a battle, you will get some sort of equipment. The equipments will then add cards/give more health to your character. All the equipment is lost once you complete/fail a dungeon. So you always start with the same deck.
The battle themselves are fun, but sometimes EXTREMELY frustrating.
You start the battle with 3 cards and you can see the card that you enemy is going to play, with that you can choose the best card for the ocasion.
The battles are in "real time" by that I mean that its not turn based. When you chose your card, yours and the enemies card are used at the same time, unless you use a quick card, wich makes you use it first.
Once again, everything is based on luck, but that is to be expected, since its a card based battle, but it kinda takes a bit of the charm of the game. Since it is luck based you can be defeated by some stupid monsters, that you placed and was sure that was going to defeat it.  8/10
Gamplay overall: 24/30

I've been waiting for the full release of this game for months! The moment I played the tutorial version on the website, I knew I had to pre-order the game. I played the free trail several times and was pretty sad when it was taken down. XD;
On launch my husband actually played the game before I did, commandeering it from our Steam shared account and played it well after I returned home from work. I had to tell him to give me a turn, if that says anything about how fun and compelling this game is.

This is something I appreciated back when I first pre-ordered the game, Gambrinous emailed me a standard thank you with a questionnaire, but then personally emailed me back to chat about the game and release status. I know it can be hard to communicate with the player base with everything that needs to be done, so I appreciate and really support devs who actively communicate with players.
The game is turn based, RPG, rouge-like, with treasure hoarding, card based combat system, and bonuses are applied through upgrading the player's home guild. Lots of people are streaming the game on twitch, so check out a stream if you'd like to see more gameplay before purchasing!

I'm sure Metro 2033 will do just fine in terms of helping you understand the story, but I can't recommend it as I've never played it. However, I have played Metro 2033 Redux and it's an incredible game.
The game takes place one year after the events of Metro 2033. The story continues from the canonical ending, better known as the “bad ending” of 2033. You resume the role of Artyom as he is now a Ranger. After launching the missles and seemingly wiping out the Dark Ones, Artyom's remorse for his actions have led him to having chronic nightmares. But when Khan informs Artyom that he has discovered a surviving Dark One in the Botanical Gardens, there may be one last hope for redemption and the future of humanity. Meanwhile, when word gets out that The Rangers have occupied D6, rival factions gear up to take control of the facility and it's supplies for themselves.
The gameplay in this is amazing. The game switches back and forth between stealth and heavy shooting. It keeps the game fresh and it never feels dull. On some levels you'll be turning lamps out, hiding in the darkness and knocking out soldiers as you quietly try to complete your objective. On other levels, you'll be surrounded by a swarm of mutants as you blast away with your shotgun. Once again, on the stealth levels, stealth isn't mandatory but it's certainly advised and much more fun. But if you absolutely hate stealth, you can blast your way through everyone so long as you aren't playing on a hard difficulty. Just like in 2033 Redux, there are several types of mutants from nosalis to watchers to the occasional demon among others. And just like in 2033 Redux, you'll come across weapon shops periodically where you can spend your military-grade rounds on guns, upgrades for your guns, ammunition, medkits and more. The moral point system returns in this game. It's one of the only things I don't like about the game. I like the idea of playing a role and choosing between good deeds and bad deeds, but this game seems to arbitrarily give you moral points for random things such as discovering a dead body in a dark corner or exploring the level and finding a secret location. Because of this, it's very easy to get the bad ending in this game, much like it was in Metro 2033.
Metro: Last Light Redux includes all of the downloadable content from the original Last Light including the Faction Pack, the Tower Pack, the Developer Pack, the Chronicles Pack, the DLC-exclusive weapons and Survival Mode. There are apparently some graphical upgrades, but I honestly couldn't tell the difference between the look of this game and the original Last Light.
Overall, I'd highly recommend this game to anyone that's a fan of post-apocalyptic games, FPS games or stealth games. The story keeps you interested, the gameplay is great and keeps you hooked, while the graphics are gorgeous and creates an incredible atmosphere throughout. Once again, I would suggest that you play Metro 2033 Redux before this game as it will help you understand the story and it's just as good as it's successor.

Pros:
Has good humour and is a very charming game.
Simple design makes it relatively easy to understand even without any real instruction after a couple goes at a dungeon the Skill system gving you access to cards is clear enough.
Music and voice acting is very well done and enjoyable.
Cons:
It feels very 'gamey' and unnatural after awhile when it becomes apparent the best way to play is to simply grind to 'reset' your character to what you previously had a few time based challenges aside. Which will generally take quite some time given that there is no hard cap on your time limit and you can just indefinately sit in most dungeons walking back and forth between two tiles.
A lot of the game is very counter intuitive.
Examples of this are that it is often wrong to unlock certain item pools, which will do nothing but increase the time you need to spend grinding to reacquire your deck. It's also sometimes, a lot of the time, wrong to take and a equip of a piece of gear with a relatively poor skillset as the cards it will do nothing but dillute your deck.
-The graveyard being shuffled back in as your deck, lack of a resource system and lack of a maximum hand size seeminly make the best strategy to get Aracane IV with the smallest deck size possible so that you can cast Celebrate until you draw your entire deck then heal for 3* (4 as Alchemist) every single turn since the monsters average far less than 3 damage a turn over the course of a game. (If they did it would actually just be impossible given you can't remove chaff like do 1 unblockable damage from your deck).
-There isn't a real feeling permanence with any of your soldiers as they get their stats/equipment reset after every mission.
That said for what the game seems to aim to do it is a good diversion. If I get another couple hours out of it I will be happy with the price point and the concept is really fun. My biggest complaint is that there isn't more depth/levels/items/monsters/cards so clearly the game has struck on something that is very enjoyable. ++

As usual for Artifex Mundi games, also Dark Arcana: The Carnival is about some investigator being dragged into supernatural events that ultimately turn out to be a big threat to all life on earth. At its core, it's a very solid hidden object/puzzle game, with plenty of well-drawn environments and puzzles. The latter are mostly not very spectacular, and neither really hard nor way too easy for the most part. The story in this particular game is actually rather decently written, for a change. It even has a plot twist that I didn't see coming.
What bugs me a little is that you can't get all achievements in one play-through, but need at least two of the latter in order to complete all hidden-object scenes both in hidden-object mode as well as by playing the "Monaco" mini-game instead. Also, the voice acting is as cringe-worthy as in most Artifex Mundi games I have played so far, but given that most voiced sequences may conveniently be skipped (I don't recommend doing it on the first play-through, though), this is a partially negligible annoyance. The game becomes very short, however, when skipping all the pre-rendered animations, being completable within 2-3 hours.
Overall, however, this is one of the more decent games from this publisher, so definitely recommended if you're into Hidden Object games.

Mostly got the game because I like the Halo Story, and on that front it did not disappoint at all in the campaign. There are some pretty cool moments if you are a fan of the series (not gonna spoil them) and with very nice cinematics to boot. As far as the actual gameplay goes, it's rather simple especially when compared to other RTSs: There's only one kind of resource, and the population limit is quite low (Though this can be different in some skrimish modes). However, this also means more dynamic games in terms of actual battles, so if you are interested in RTS games because of the military aspects, this game is definitely for you. There's also quite a diverse set of units, for a game on a rather smaller scale, so there's good room for different approaches to battle tactics. Finally the improved graphics coupled with the rest make very nice looking battles.
Bottom line
Pros:
- Action packed
- Good story and cinematics
- Pretty looking
- Strong on the Military aspect of RTS
Cons:
- Low unit cap
- Very simple on the planning side of RTS
I don't really know what numeric grade I'd give it because it all comes down to how much do you like the different aspects of RTS games, but assuming that all fans of the genre enjoy every aspect to varying degrees, I'd probably say something like 9/10 for the combat-minded and 7/10 for the planning-minded.

At it's core, Elsword is a fun game. The combat is fun, the community is (generally) friendly, and each character feels very different from one another. Once you dive a little deeper though, you're greeted by the plethora of problems that many other games in the same genre face.
Quickly you'll realize that the game heavily encourages microtransactions. For veterans of the genre, these cash grabs won't be anything unusual--enhancing your equipment, having key items, and general cosmetics will all eventually cost you money if you want to reach the endgame. There are plenty of people who have spent hundreds of dollars to keep their gear relevant.
Eventually though, you'll realize that it's not just the microtransactions that's runing the game-- there are problems deep rooted in the game's design as a whole. I'm specifically talking about pvp here-- the game is terribly balanced. Certain characters are just impossible for most of the cast to deal with.
Of course, this isn't really an issue if you're willing to spend massive heaps of cash to max out your weapon. As broken as certain characters are, you can very easily fix the problem by throwing money at it. There is very little put into place to prevent heavily geared players from sweeping the arena. (And very, very little relevant pvp content outside of it).
Elsword has seen better days. I've been playing for more than 4 years now, and I firmly believe that Elsword has ALWAYS had problems. Since I've been playing, there has never been an era where everything was perfect, or even close to it. It's just that in recent years, more issues have arisen, and at this point they've just grown to be unbearable.
At it's core, Elsword is a fun game.
But it isn't worth your time right now.

If you're like me and loved BioShock 1 and Infinite but ignored BioShock 2 because you "heard it sucked", wipe all of those thoughts out of your head. BioShock 2 isn't bad, it's not just okay, hell it's not even good, this game is FANTASTIC. The storytelling is by far better than the first game and has the best gameplay of the three games.
Similar to how BioShock 1 and Infinite are deconstructions of Objectivism and Religous Fanaticism, respectively, 2 has a strong narrative that focuses on and is a deconstruction of Altruism, which is essentially the polar opposite of the Ayn Rand-inspired ideologies of the first game. The villain of BioShock 2 isn't nearly as compelling or interesting as Andrew Ryan  (not like you could ever top him), but the game doesn't suffer as a result of it.
All in all, BioShock 2 is a MUST buy for fans of the series. It IS worthy of the BioShock name, and I'm kicking myself for not playing this game sooner. The first half is a bit of a slog, but after you finish both the game and the absolutely fantastic DLC "Minerva's Den" it will give 1 and Infinite a run for their money in regards to being the best BioShock game.

Divinity: Origional Sin 2 is really good, short at the moment, but good. I played threw just once so far and found myself liking the in and outs of combat. It really sweetens the fun with sneaking and other forms of ways to get the drop on enemies. There is all of the systems from the old game, plus more. New races, and racial skills for each race for example. You have a more diverse way of building a character with the spells you have AND can learn in just the EA alone. Story is solid, not going to ruin it or spoil it but it can really suck you in. As for me it was hard however because there is no voice lines yet, and I, myself can pay attention better with that.
The graphics to the game are run on a great engine, really lush and vibrant colors. Grass moves with a flow, and you can see things here and there you can pick up. The battles are amazing, somewhat breath taking. You throw fire, the land sparks up a blaze in the area of effect with your enemies glowing (if they are on fire). If you use ice/water magic (from Hydro skill), your enemies get wet or freeze! If they're already wet it just doubles the chance for both air (mostly electric), to stun them or the ice to freeze them. With poison items, you can use fire to detonate them into a fiery explosion. A very good synergetic and beautiful display of POWA.
Now we get to some of the things I want in the game. This is just my opinion, so you can skip to the conclusion of you like.
All in all so far has exeeded my expectations, and then some. I will just love to finish the rest of story when it releases. I also hope it can get an Enhanced Edition like the last one for more travel, lore and loot. I really am happy at how much went into this and how much support it got. With the stuff they said would be added it seems to even have the potential to surpass most triple A games. For now, we will have to wait and watch closely at what Larian Studios has for us in the next update.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 is a worthy successor to its predecesor. It allows you to tailor your origins story thus affecting how the world and people will respond to your presence, and the special chat actions characters can have. For the moment there are a few pre-made characters with their own stories from character traits to addictions and flaws. Even if I wasn't able to tinker with the story except character aspect and class; I grew fond of the characters. What itks me is that I cannot make the characters talk with eachother, or banter, just to dog deeper into their origin story.
Combat is just like in Original Sin, but after the improvement of its engine the game now allows a player to interact with the enviroment much more smoothly and with more freedom.
Of course this is an early access, meaning its still rough around the edges and it has bugs. In the game there will be a red text near the minimap saying "Alfa Build". But despite the bugs, the quests that won't update and the bothersome glitching textures from armor or the enviroment; I still greatly enjoyed the hours I spent in the game. I had a few occassions to get off the island but the more you explore the more rewarding it becomes. Even if you stumble over a battle, an ambush, a secret treasure or hidden dungeon; what you find there will help you later on in quests you didn't even get to or expected to be doing.
I do NOT care about the bugs or that it's an Alfa Early Access. This game: Divinity Original Sin 2, has everything you need in an RPG game, except romances. Rewarding exploration, beautiful sound tracks, fun puzzles, challanging battles and a beatifuly detailed world; I would recommend this game to any RPG gamer.

One word: Fun. Fun was had. I love this game's quirky attitude to dungeoneering. You own the guild and build the dungeons, but you don't get to tell your dungeoneer where to go.  You can bribe and cajole him though, with the promise of wealth, glory or death. As long as you take the time to understand his psyche. Dungeoneers are a crazy lot. So you need to be crazier. You need to learn to be better at the game through the delicious process of repeatedly dying when you make bad decisions with your cards. Think before you act. You'll be surprised how well that works! What else about the game I love?  The irreverent writing. The cheeky puns. The endearing artwork. The spirited music. I love strategy games and I like the Endless Universe. Endless Legend is a favorite of mine. Endless Space 2 is something I don't plan on investing any more time in, tho. I'd much rather spend time playing Sins of a Solar Empire, Endless Legend, Age of Wonders, or Civ 5 complete.
The Good
1. Pretty graphics and zooming effects
2. Decent music.
3. Cool universe.
The Bad
1. Boring and stereotypical factions (quirky smart androids, voracious insects, StarCraft humans). I had expected something more after the great factions in Endless Legend.
2. A basically endless number of bonuses that give +50% and +30% and +10 of this. Everything is designed to look super cool and hard-hitting. But it makes the math a nightmare to add up, and it makes the game needlessly complicated.
3. Weapons and ships are generic, bland, and don't really offer any big tactical advantages.
4. No good spying or infiltration system.
5. Incredibly boring combat.
6. Very few and incomplete warfare options.
The Ugly
1. The illusion of freedom. Realizing the game wants you to invest hundreds of hours in a fairly linear way, click after click, and then just optimize that exact same way of winning was when I deleted the game.
Anyway. It's pretty, but it's linear and unpolished. And it tries to hide it behind ridiculous statistics.

This is a truly dark and eerie game with some disturbing moments in it. There is no gore -- this is darkness of a different kind. We get breaks from the intensity of the story via our sweet little monkey helper, which the devs did a beautiful job with.
There are separate sliders for music and sound, plus options for custom cursor, voice overs, and full-screen. Wide-screen adjustments are done automatically. We also have THREE difficulty levels, and the differences are very clearly explained. For example, for Casual mode "HINT and SKIP buttons refill quickly, Active zones glimmer frequently, Hidden Object scenes are indicated, there is no mis-click penalty on Hidden Object Scenes, (and) Locations with an available action are indicated on the Map".
Yes, we do have a MAP, although I didn't have any trouble remembering where I needed to be, and didn't actually use it. Likewise with the Journal (Diary). It has tabs for story and objectives, but there's no extra story in the Notes section, and it didn't mention things I really needed to know (for puzzles, etc). I didn't need help remembering objectives, so the diary was pretty much forgotten along with the map.
There were some interestingly different mini-games scattered throughout the game, but of course there were some of the old standbys, as well. Still, I appreciate the fact that they took the time to make some truly original minis!
We have a couple of great extras that one will not usually find in a non-collector's edition: Achievements and a bonus chapter! Awesome! More bang for the buck, can't beat that! The extra chapter nicely wrapped up a loose thread (so to speak) left over from the main game.
The developers handled the story very well. Our little helper kept things from getting too dark, and the progression of the story kept me interested throughout. It's always great when a tale is not predictable, and this one certainly isn't. I truly enjoyed playing this game all the way through, and recommend it to anyone who enjoys spooky games.

An "old-school" first person style shooting game set in a somewhat futuristic world of large portions of society living in cities underwater.
It's set in 2666 but somehow we are still using gunpwder weapons and non-guided torpedoes, and we don't have any sonar to detect enemy ships?
Being an older game, the presentation is a lot different than modern games in that it doesn't really hold you hand and explain everything.
Steam says a release date of 2003, but my research says Nov 30, 2001. < ?? >
So the game is at least almost 15 years old.
Gamers of this era were expected to read the printed game manual before playing, or at least all the control bindings before setting off.
Using pre-rendered 3D scenes for anything requiring complex navigation or animation, some of the sequences can get a little irratating after seeing your ship go through the same dock sequence for the hundredth time, but luckly, they are skippable.
The game is fully voiced, and the story is pretty fleshed out.
For it's age, this game holds up rather well graphically.
The major problem is that when this game was created, computer mice were not very sensitive and were roller-ball based, so more physical effort and distance was required to move the mouse, hence the sensitivity of the controls is rather high and "floaty" feeling.
Luckly, this problem can be circumvented by turning down the in-game sensitivity.
This game is probably better suited for a flight stick joystick, but I was able to do fairly well with just the keyboard and mouse.
Due to the unforgiving nature of games of this era, I would only recommend this to people who played these older games, or for someone look to dig a little deeper into the game before expecting to actually enjoy it.
Most of the dialogue and plot is cheesy and predictable, but game writers weren't expected to write movie worthy content then either.
As long as you know what you're getting into, the old graphics don't scare you off, and the subject matter interests you, I say go for it. If your a gamer under 25 or so, you might want to read some more reviews or watch some gameplay videos before you decide to pull the trigger on this.

For all it's flaws, I loved L.A. Noire.

For it's time, this is a beautiful, innovative game. The facial models make characters readable and relatable, and the generally minimalist nature of the game - few HUD features popping in or out, heavy reliance on sound rather than visual signposting - allows the game to unfold like a dense TV series rather than a videogame. The atmosphere is exceptional, and period music and vehicles only add to that.
The story is good, although it wanes towards the end. The same goes for the gameplay - it is fun, unique, and rewarding, but also blows its wad off the bat: by the endgame, you're doing the same things you were at the very start.
Even still, a fantastic single-player experience.

I never played Bioshock 2 because of all the people shouting that it wasn't that good compared to the first one. When I got the remastered edition for free, I decided to play through the Bioshock series again and see how teh remasters changed anything. In light of having  recently finished the Bioshock 1 remaster with lots of pain with frequent crashing, I have to say that the Bioshock 2 remaster was much smoother...still with some crashes here and there, but not enough to make me frustrated to the point of the putting the game down for a several days.
As for the game itself...I can see why people dislike the game, but don't necessarily agree. The story is different. The character is different. There's much less mystery as the story progresses than in the first game. But I don't think any of that makes it bad. I thoroughly enjoyed Bioshock 2 (Minerva's Den in particular) because it felt similar without being the same. Mechanics from the first game were more fleshed out with more plasmid upgrades, gene tonics, and some new weapons as well. Not to mention it's a blast running around as a Big Daddy drilling people to death.
I felt that Bioshock 2 added a new dimension to the whole Rapture world because you got to explore the city from a different perspective, doubly so because you got to see it during its collapse (which probably came as a result of the actions of Bioshock 1). I really enjoyed learning more about the different kinds of Big Daddys, the motivations for each kind, the moral outrage against the Little Sisters, etc. Rapture is an intensely interesting setting for a game so I relished in the ability to learn more about it first hand.

The game builds and holds an appealing atmosphere and the shadow mechanics connect well. The story about Didi, a girl whose family is suffering some more or less common problems and thinks Dawn, the character controlled by the player, is Didi's imaginary friend that helps her cope with the situation. The truth, although not completely explained, is more interesting - Einstein is mentioned.
The game is pretty short and may entertain you for an afternoon like it did me. Anyway, I feel like it was time well spent.
The controls are alright but for the games shortness and the ever-changing environments you cannot really learn them, which is fine. You just have to figure out how far a jump gets you in each situation, e.g. while jumping around corners. There were a few cases of me catching on corners where I would have expected to be nudged to the side in order to be able to just run on.
I'd like to know more about the back story of Dawn. Maybe it was a good decision to stop explanations at some point so the story doesn't fall apart but it also allows for a possible sequel. There are possible points to tie that in, e.g. Kat's letter to social services or the family tree.
There is not much left to say. Contrast was short and very enjoyable and I recommend it. I bought this when it was on sale and would wait until it hits the 5 Euro mark to buy it.

This is the most engaging, challenging, agonizing yet ultimately rewarding strategy game I have ever played. For me, the game’s brilliance comes from its open-ended architecture and AI. You play as one of a vast number of medieval rulers, and your goals are completely left up to you. All you need to do is keep your dynasty alive to continue, and that isn’t easy. The AI is aggressive to the point of ruthlessness, which often leads to strings of desperate situations and difficult choices, forcing even the experienced player to concede defeat from time to time. Plots, intrigue, backstabbing and murder are lurking in every shadow. Often your greatest enemy is your AI-controlled close relatives – and they know exactly when to strike. This constant danger needs to color every decision, since you are always one booby-trapped balcony away from death and taking over as your helpless, infant son in the midst of a civil war.
There are ways the game could be improved, such as by adding army rally points, a more powerful people finder, more diplomatic options and so on, but these are all minor points. The game is well executed and extremely re-playable. Like a lot of others, I also came over to Steam recently after playing hundreds of hours with the non-steam version. I still can’t seem to put it down.
If you are into utterly immersive strategy games with a historical foundation, this is the game for you. If you haven’t played Paradox games before and are bit overwhelmed by all the detail, don’t let that scare you. There’s no way to fully learn how to play other than by diving in and making mistakes (though tutorials, videos and AARs are helpful). I believe that learning how to play these games is actually part of the games themselves, and that makes it even more rewarding when you finally are able to pull off what seemed impossible.

Set in 1920's Paris; the City of Lights is an ideal location for a shadow based puzzle platformer. Consistantly testing your perspective of lighting and which dimension you should be within. The game adds an interesting 3D world aswell as a constant 2D platformer which you have to vary between in order to complete puzzles. Having the power to slip between the open 3D world to hopping from shadow to shadow in 2D at your own will opens up some very clever puzzling possibilities.
Throughout the game there's a gripping emotional story line in which follows the main little girl, Didi. As she is always trying to help out her close-to-useless father, having to deal with various mobsters, aswell as an illusionist puzzle master. As Didi’s imaginary friend, you can only see the shadows and hear the voices of the real people within the 3D world, in which Didi interacts with. But again within the 2D world there is great interaction of the real people's shadows and a fulfilling sense of achievment once you complete a puzzle.
As with all medium to low budget puzzle games there are a few bugs/glitches but nothing you can't turn your head at. Some of the puzzels can be very cliche: move a box over a button = door opens. But there was a few interesting ones you'll have to think twice about.
Overall gameplay was enjoyable and certainly made you want to finish the game, yet only being 3-5 hours long depending on collectables and the narrations. It’s hard to say whether Contrast looks better while playing as one of the minimalist silhouettes or running around in full 3D. The graphics are a key aspect of the game, being set in such a hearty destination the overly cartoon design looks great and is consistant throughout.

It doesn't become apparent until you're about 3 hours in, but Guild of Dungeoneering is a pretty linear and repetitive game.  Sure, you can utilize different classes and traits and the randomness of each quest makes things feel different, but overall, you're doing the same exact thing every quest and even using a lot of the same cards quest after quest.
The progression leaves much to be desired. Essentially, you unlock classes, blessings, and random weapon sets. On paper, this seems great, but its progression system is lacking in depth because it's only 3 tiers and each step up doesn't feel like a drastic change. There need to be more options. I think I'm pretty close to the end, but I have the feeling once everything's unlocked, top-level playthroughs will be exactly the same (ie always go with X class, Y blessing, and aim to obtain Z skills in game).
Although I have enjoyed my time with the game, Guild of Dungeoneering doesn't feel complete. It's very close and if it ever gets there, it'll be great. Some of the improvements the dev has discussed seem like a step in the right direction.

Like many before playing this game I was under the impression that this game was blantant YouTube/Twitch bait made to get well known people to sell the game for the developer. But then I actually played the game and I actually have to commend the developer. It's not perfect and it's incredibly oversimplified but it is a fun buisness simulator to play.
So the premise is simple. You start a YouTube channel and rise to fame on the internet. It's a concept that's great since it's a buisness that most people can understand. The problem however is that actually making videos is way too simple. The basic layout to make videos is:
And unfortunately this is the full basics of the game. There's no real way to manage your channel other than seeing statistical information and deciding who to hire and fire when you get bigger.
Another problem is that there are no anomalies in the games. They release and are relevant for videos for a short time and then they're useless. There are no scenarios where you can dedicate your channel to a single game like many gaming channels do now.
The RNG of the editing cards are incredibly punishing as well. It doesn't matter how much stats you get for yourself, there's nothing you can do to medigate getting nothing but incompatable editing cards and making a terribly edited video. If I take the time to discover which symbols go with each segment and I upgrade my stats, I should be able to medigate this issue, not be held hostage by it.
While it's way too simple for some reason it's also incredibly good in making you get obsessed with making videos and monitoring when new game releases to make videos. I found myself coming up with a regular schedule to maximize my idea points to make the best videos I could.
While I know that I listed more bads than goods, I still say that this game was very well made for what it is. I do wonder what it'll look like when it's finished. I hope though that more buisness management elements are added as well.

This game has some really good and fast movement. You can slide, jump high while doing some acrobatic roll, run on walls, latch onto walls, jump on cables, glide through the air in slow motion while shooting like some hitman etc. It's like a mix of Mirror's Edge and Mass Effect on nitrousoxide..
Storywise I can't comment too much since I haven't got that far yet, so far it's been average but I haven't gotten to the so called "good parts" yet. I've heard that Warframe has a decent story, a much better story than your average free to play MMORPG.
Now for the negatives...
Personally I do not like the designs of the guns and warframes, a few are ok but nothing really stands out to me and there is a lot of ugly designs in my opinion. You start out with a very "basic" looking warframe and very few colors, you can buy more colors for in game currency but you can't afford it. Not until you've played a couple of hundred hours maybe. You would have to buy colors or skins for real money but that's to be expected from a f2p game. But hey at least you can grind there if you like the game right?
The biggest downside of Warframe by far is the limitations. It's the most unnecessary and irritating thing I've ever come across in an mmorpg. I will never understand why any game developer would implement such a counterproductive element in a grinder game.
The limitations I have encountered so far are:
You can only rank up by passing a test which you can only do once every 24 hours. Level 1-3 have been easy but should you fail you would have to wait a full 24 hours to try again, or if you passed to take the test for the next level. Most of the weapons are locked to certain levels too. So let's say you wanna play with the "Nikana" Sword because your starting gear looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥ "Yeah! Let's grind tonight to level up so you can try the dank gear and look cool." No. it will take you 4 days before you can even buy, trade or craft it. No matter how much you play. The XP does stack though so if you played one day to get enough XP to climb 2 ranks you can do the next "Mastery Rank up test" immediately after the 24h cooldown from the previous test is over.
Next up is the crafting aspect of the game. Crafting takes anything from 1 hour to 24 hours for each item. You seem to be able to craft many things at once though. But this is just another annoying thing with the game which I think is terrible. Especially since it can limit you from making progress in the game. The game is built up on our solar system, you have a couple of places you can go to on each planet and you have to do some tasks on each planet in order to progress and go to the next one and so on. So crafting can be one of these criterias which has halted my progress in the game and basically forced me to play something else while I wait 2 hours, 8 hours or 12 hours for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to be crafted so the game can let me go to the next planet. It's funny too how the game keeps reminding you to take a break, whenever you have played over 1 hour.
"Sorry sir we are closing the bar now, we have to ask you to leave"
Another negative thing in my opinion is the looting. If you expect a boss to drop some dank loot every now and then like a weapon or something. Don't play this game. The looting is boring as hell. In the start I used to go around the map, open every little container and hidden chest but you only find crafting materials and mods for your warframe or weapon. It's so sad and dissatisfactory.
You can find relics on some missions which are basically like "lootboxes" in cs:go or pubg or any other game that uses them. They are however free to open. You have to do an excavator mission to open them. If you are lucky you will find some part or a blueprint for a weapon or armor.
Playing Warframe makes you feel like you are 12 again and Warframe is your parent telling you to stop playing and go outside.

EDIT: OK, this is the second edit of this review for me, so it's my third go at reviewing this game. Why? Because it's changing, and so is my opinion of it...
My first review was impressed, my second was that i was less impressed, and now, I'm getting impressed again.
1. I was initially impressed because the design itself is great. Great style, great class ideas (on the surface), fun ang quick gameplay.
2. Then, things went sour. The classes weren't quite as diverse as I'd hoped, I realised that to try and balance the game, they wouldn't let you replay any dungeons. This sucks. It REALLY sucks. It makes getting enough gold to buy new rooms hard, and it also means to have replayability, you need to start again from the beginning. This was a massive negative and made it not that much fun after the first few plays.
3. Now that's changing for two reasons. First off, they've added a replay mode for bosses. Not nearly enough, but a start, and one that shows they are listening. Secondly, and this is really important - they are continually evolving and tweaking the gameplay, and adding new features. Sure one way to look at that is they didn't do enough testing/finish before release, but given they are a small dev team, and the fact they take the feedback onboard, this is actually commendable, and they should be supported. (Oh, and they've announced a future game mode that is endless dungeoning - that's not the same as replay, but is actually even better. HUZZAH!
OVERALL: It's a good game, the devs are responsive on the forums, they are improving the game based on feedback, they've published a roadmap, and it really is a fun, quick game to enjoy. Go for it, i say!

I loved this game's predecessor,
and this game was shaping up to be just as good if not better. The story was definitley on par with teh original, and the reversed perspective on the Dark One had me fully immersed. I specifically waited until nightfall to play with headphones in the dark; it was so visceral. The stealth is very fun, as well as the combat mode, Spartan and Ranger respectively. This allows for completely different playstyles to emjpy the same game in different ways, and it had worked beautifully all the way up until the 20th Chapter, Contagion.
Don't get me wrong, each of the levels past the fiery journey through Oktyabrskaya is a great level on it's own, but this sequence of levels is the games downfall. I was playing on Spartan Normal, which means fewer filters and less ammo, but not famine-level like Hardcore. Contagion needs a gasmask the whole time on is in the smoke. As does the next level, and the next, and then one is outside for a whole level, and the again above ground for most of a level. Because as we all know stealth takes time (studying patrol patterns, crouch walking being so much slower, etc.), I was out of filters very fast. I had to resort to sprinting through levels in the hope of finding a spare filter before I asphyxiated, as well as dodging watchmen and Nazi bullets. The way the levels were placed, so many requiring my precious filters in a row, made me abandon my stealth approach to, quite literally, run and gun through each level.
My final complaint would have to be with the some of the boss battles. Some are quite good, and can be completed in different ways, like the battle with the Rhino. However, the Bear was unreasonably diffcicult for, again, a pure stealth player to accomplish. The Bear fight takes place in a completely bare (haha) clearing in the forest. The Bear instantly aggros onto the player and damage can only be avoided by continuously sprinting in a circle. A LOT of damage needs to be done to this bear, which caused me to burn a lot of MGR (a more damaging bullet that also functions as currency in the metro).
I think overall the game is wonderful, and these are minor problems that won't affect half the players who prefer the guns blazing approach, but it made it really hard for me and probably any other stealthy players out there. In a potential sequel, if there is one, I would very much hope that boss battles (if need there be any) be avoidable or able to be completed without dumping MGR into them like a Venice stripper.

Dark Arcana: The Carnival is a hidden object game from Artifex Mundi (they also made, not just published it) with the usual setup: we play a female detective whose expertise is required in solving a mysterious case. The game features a new, alternate method for solving hidden object scenes and features a fairly good story.
In the intro we see the kidnapping of a young woman right next from her daughter in a carnival. There's also a shady and disturbed looking man around, who - as we later find it out - is involved in the criminal act. The villain is probably the timidest one ever seen in a game, seriously, I can't remember seeing a bad guy running away so many times from us as this one. As we progress, we'll encounter the dark side of the carnival and of course it'll turn out that this isn't just a simple kidnapping and there are much greater things at stake. There's also a not so forseeable plot twist towards the end of them game, which makes it even more interesting.
After finishing the main story we can undertake the bonus chapter in which we take the role of the aforementioned shady character and basically continue from the point where we left off. It's great fun and is definitely worthwhile to give it a go.
We'll have the opportunity to travel to the twisted and bizarre version of the carnival (by stepping through mirrors, which function as portals) and these scenes are almost identical to the original ones, except they are usually very disturbing, almost nightmarish locations with the twisted and grotesque equivalents of the real world (this includes a fair bit of dead bodies as well).
The balance between hidden object scenes, minigames and puzzles including item use is fairly good, altough we get to revisit almost every HO scene sooner or later. Most of the minigames are carnival or circues themed and are fairly easy to solve. The monaco game (we have to match adjacent cards displaying the same figures) helps those stuck in hidden object scenes and have hard time finding a particular item (or we can just play solely monaco instead). There are achievements related to monaco exclusively, making the full obtainment of HO achievements impossible, therefore a minimum of 2 playthroughs are required for completionists. For some reason the map travel doesn't work, but since I rarely use it in other games, it didn't really bother me.
We are also introduced to a helpful companion: a monkey, who'll be staying with us most of the time throughout our adventure, assisting us acquiring otherwise unreachable items. As an additional help he also lets out a squeaking sound whenever he can aid us.
Since I mentioned 'child- or family friendliness' before (it is a HOG afterall, with the prime audience being women and children), it's fair if I make it clear: the game can be disturbing and shocking. As a fan of horror games and thrillers, personally I loved it, but it may not be ideal for small children. There are other, cute, but still exciting HOGs out there with great stories (I'll try to review them as well in the future, if I can).
Graphically the surreal imagery works well, with the greenish-yellow colour dominating (in the alternate world), the bizzare and disturbing scenes look very artistic and beautiful. The cutscenes are some of the best I've seen in this genre, there's hardly any pixelation and they look greatly fluid. Maybe some of the facial animation during certain voiceovers appear to be not that good, but these are rare.
The music is generally OK (with a well known carnival-tune), at least it isn't annyoing. The sound effects that co-occur during spooky moments are quite effective and gives a certain additional horror feel to the game.
Dark Arcana: The Carnival a well put together hidden object game with a good plot, interesting characters, some interesting elements (monaco + animal companion) and a surreal art design, which may attract or repulse players. In my opinion, Artifex Mundi did a very good job and I'd certainly recommend it to everyone who'd like to try a quite uncommon looking HOG with light horror elements.
PROS
+ features improvements, such as animal companion and monaco game
+ good storyline
+ interesting bonus chapter
+ fair amount of minigames
CONS
- twice used hidden object scenes
- only mediocre music
RATING
7/10

1. What is Aquanox 2?
Aquanox 2 is the sequel to the sci-fi-underwater shooter Aquanox 1.
2. Do I have to play the first game before I start with Aquanox 2?
No, because Aquanox 2 has its own storyline and you will play as a new main character.
You will meet some characters from the first game, but you won´t miss much if you didn ´t play the first game.
3. Is it worth buying?
If you liked the first game or games like X-Wing vs Tie-Fighter or Wing Commander, you should give this one a try.
4. I played Aquanox 1, what is the difference between the first and the second game?
As I mentioned you will play a new main character. The new storyline is pretty good, more serious and not as cheesy as the first game. The graphics are not as colourful as the first
game, but with better textures and its a little darker now with brown colours. The voice
acting also improved a bit.
5. Can I still choose different ships and upgrade my weapons?
Yes there are not as many ships anymore in the game, but still enough to have a decent variety. The weapons from the first game return and are more easy to shoot (higher bullet velocity and shorter travel speed). You can still upgrade your ships and weapons. You can now sell your equipment or store it outside your ship.
6. What are the missions like?
You will be able to speak to your crew members often before or after the missions. You can prepare yourself and read the mission text before you start. The missions also vary between exploration, destruction, escape or protection. Often you will have some wingmen to help you out.

Hailing from the Artifex Mundi catalog,
isn't probably one of the best games brilliant HOG developer/producer team presented us so far. You see, said publisher has spoiled us to the degree of expecting narrative quality and story consistency from ordinary hidden object games alongside artistic quality in display, so compared to some prior master pieces, this one feels a bit pallid. Yet, it is still a charming enough game to go for in a lazy evening, endowed with your casual Artifex Mundi display quality.
We are yet another lady detective, this time summoned to the place of the local carnival to investigate an unusual case. A little girl's mother has disappeared, leaving her in an anonymous crowd of a carnival, of all places. Usually, it should be the other way around, right? Little girl disappears and the mother pleads that we should find her? Nope, not this time. Presented with the photograph of her mother quite conveniently, we start our search. Through our investigation, we are quick to notice that the only current inhabitant of this colorful yet creepy place, is the master of the carnival: knife-thrower extraordinaire Jim Gibbons. He also has a spectacular talent of avoiding us, so we keep tracking Jim to the point of travelling to a mirror dimension where everything ends up as an eerie, twisted version of the original. This is one persistent detective, I tell you!
Track the victim, learn the reasons of the perpetrator, save the day. Text-book hidden object story pace, alongside the millionth Hollywood action movie. Even though the earlier parts of the game are a bit ambiguous and unrealistic - detective chasing after Jim and casually hopping down into mirror world without even going through "wait, what, alien dimensions are real?" phase - , the game makes up for the most with a neatly arranged plot-twist nearing the middle. The rest is your casual puzzle solving genius, wrapped around a tragic and desperate romance.
The theme of choice is a big plus, if you ask me, considering travelling carnivals have always been the melting pot of the eerie and the spectacular for the Western culture. The Ferris wheel, lion tamer, acrobats, knife-throwers, fortuneteller, freak shows... you name it. Anything extraordinary comes with it, which doesn't necessarily mean safe or reliable. All the artwork here in this game, are accordingly appropriate for the theme: half-way enwrapped in vibrant colors and innocent displays of wonder. Yet, the moment we travel to the mirror world, everything turns into an elegant creep fest. I loved every single scene of it. This package of display comes with decent character animations, believable voice-acting and an efficient soundtrack. Kudos for the display, as always.
Gameplay consists of various HOG scenes, yet you get to visit the same scenes over and over again in their doubles: the original world version and the mirror world version. It becomes a bit annoying after a while. They are fairly easy to go through though, taking just a bit of your attention span. If you are bored of HOG scenes, you are presented with an alternative Monaco gameplay to replace it, which is a nice flavor. Puzzles are not really challenging, most of it is flavor for the setting, nothing more. Which really makes the game lose some points is the excruciating amount of backtracking though. If you are playing in expert difficulty for the sake of the achievement, it becomes a chore to go through all areas that might have opened in the given time.
As the last word,
is an okay HOG with a nice little story, enchanting setting and somewhat tedious gameplay. I'd recommend going for it in a sale, or as the part of a bundle rather than jumping into it. If you are familiar with the developer team, you'll find this one likable anyhow. If not, I strongly recommend a much more well-crafted title to begin. Good day, and good gaming to you!

Imprison relatives! Plot against your benefactors! Declare anti-popes!
It's not about battles, but essentially being an unimportant noble plotting so that your grandson will be the king, and then panicing for a Plan B when he dies in a 'hunting accident'. This usually involves a series of plots, murders, and trying to obtain sufficient popularity to change succession laws.
A nice aspect is that in terms of what individual people think of your character, things actually make sense - everything that you think would influence a character's opinion, actually DOES. For instance, you may wonder why, despite your relaxing taxes and granting extra titles, Count Jeremy doesn't like you. But looking at the details, it turns out he's still bitter that you beheaded his father 20 years ago. Things like that.
It's a little harder to get into at first, and you might not have such a sense of what to do next, but this is an ideal game for imagining that you are a plotter in a world full of AI characters who also have sensible plots and ambitions.

A grand-strategy from the masters of the genre Paradox Development Studio. The game will feel familiar to those that have played other games from the developer, Europa Universalis etc, yet will be refreshing and worthwhile because of its focus on intrigue and dynasties rather than trade and nation level politics.
Crusader Kings II is one of the best, if not the best, grand-strategy game of recent years. The game offers hundreds of hours of gameplay (especially if you have the expansions) because of the vastly different experiences the various religions, cultures and ranks of nobility offer. The RPG elements and focus on your personal dynasty add another layer of depth with the micromanagement of every marriage, alliance and well placed dagger in the unfortunate cousin's back. The game is full of events from restoring the Roman Empire to building a flying machine, which add a lot of flavor and keep the playthroughs interesting and amusing.
The game also has a very good modding community, with mods ranging from the small ones that bring alternate flags and portraits to the total conversion mods such as:
'A song of Ice and Fire' mod:
'Elder Scrolls' mod:
The mods, especially the total conversions, add a lot of value to the game.
The game is not beginner friendly, not by a long shot. Despite being more simple than other games in the genre the information overload will be a lot, especially for new players. If you're willing to take the time to learn the game, it will be an amazing experience.  I recommend the game to anyone who's interested Game of Thrones-esque intrigue.

Few games marry platforing and puzzle elements as well as Contrast. Its shadow mechanic allows for a lot of unique solutions to puzzles, usually requiring the manipulation of the play field to set up platforms or move an object from one area to another. The solutions are fairly intuitive once you get the hang of it, and this keeps the pace of the game brisk. While the game is short (3 hours on my playthrough, with time included for exploration), it's exactly as long as it needs to be for the narrative it's telling.
And oh boy, what a narrative. I admire the decision to tell a story of a troubled couple from their daughter's point of view, and to tell it in a highly Expressionist way. The noirish setting, the importance of casting light onto darkness and viewing events through projection and found documents leaves the player (and Didi) questioning the amount of agency they have in shaping the events occuring around them, but as the game progresses the player's actions do push the narrative forward, leaving one wondering if there's some reality-bending at play or if we're just in a land of childish wish fulfillment. The question is left to the player, as the narrative focuses less on making sense of the universe and more on the emotions of its central characters.
But the experience isn't without a few drawbacks. While I personally found Didi to be a very compelling character, her constant direction can get tiring, as well as break the difficulty of some puzzles. Her guidance may be helpful for younger players or those inexperienced with 3D platformers, but a seasoned player may find themselves wishing for an option to forgo such a built-in hint system. Whether or not you identify with Didi can make or break the game because of this.
The platforming is overall very tight and responsive, and the game grants abilities which ease progression later on. However, it has its moments of challenge which require timing so precise that getting it right may feel more like luck than skill. There is an excellent organic checkpoint system integrated into the mix, so failure is rarely punished and trial-and-error solutions are encouraged, so long as frustration doesn't set in too quickly.
On a rare occasion, my character glitched into a wall or other fixture, but jumping/dashing out of them seems to fix the problem.
Pros:
Cons:
Overall, I found Contrast a fantastic experience, and certainly one that feels artistically-driven. The story and characters are compelling enough to push you forward without bogging the experience down with overlong cutscenes. Collecting all of the found documents in the game reveals an added light to the game's ending, encouraging exploration and abstract thinking, though the core of the game will be Didi's concerns for her father. If you're willing to forgive a young girl asking a lot of favors of you, the unique style and solid gameplay will make the experience worthwhile.

Metro: Last Light Redux Review
Game description
Metro: Last Light  is the sequel to Metro 2033 it continues to take place in post apocalyptic Moscow predominately inside the cities metro system 1 year after the events of the first game. Artyom has been made a Spartan ranger of polis and is sent on a mission to kill the last surviving dark one but thing do not go as planned and he finds himself captured on the other side of the metro. he must now find a way to contact polis as he tries to complete his mission to find a kill the dark one.
Positives
Metro: Last Light  does a number of things right and even improves on some of the things from the first game. It is still amazing looking. it provide an atmosphere similar to the first game which is very nice.  you still get that feeling of being trapped when in the metro and that fear that something or someone will be right around the corner and that they will want to kill you. Like the last game it is incredibly detailed to the point where you can tell how much ammo you have in your gun by looking at the magazine because you can see each bullet depending on the weapon and you can get things like dirt, flies and blood on to your gas mask making it harder to see and shoot.
It is not as intense as the first game in some areas however in the swamps the game provides a different kind of intensity as there are some new mutants lurking around in the waters and the tall grass waiting to jump out and attack. There are new mutants lurking both in and outside the metro such as a new breed of nosalis which is larger and more dangers and is found deep in the metro.
the game play its self has changed very little which is not a bad thing. The fire fights feel really intense and realistic. However it would have been nice if they added one or two more features like being able to pick up and move bodies. One thing that I was really excited for was the truck tone of new guns which can change the way you play. They are as follows.
-Three new sniper rifles. The Preved, the Valve and the VSSK which does not seem to be available in the main game instead only in some of the DLC.
-Two new shotguns. The Saiga-12 and the Ashot
-One new pistol. The Lolife
-Two new assault rifles. The RPK-74 and the AKS-74U
-One new pneumatic weapon. The Tihar
Negatives
However like its predecessor this game like the first game is not perfect.
One problem is that it is far too hard to get the good ending. I played it twice so far and both times I got the bad ending despite the fact that I was the nicest guy ever much nicer than I am in real life. I saved that mutant bear thing ,I did not kill any of the people that betrayed me ,I gave to the poor ,always knocked people out instead of killing them and all sorts but I still got the bad ending.
The worst problem I had really took away from the emersion and was during a part later in the game I which you were supposed to take you gas mask off to save your partner I could shot the guy(where I perhaps should not have been able to) so I instead shot the person holding her hostage he shot back and broke my gas mask and I was unable to find or buy a new one meaning the next time I had to go to the surface I suffocated over and over again to the point where I had to load an old save and take my gas mask off when I was supposed to. This sadly took away from the emersion.
One thing I did not like from the story was the love story between Artyom and his partner Anna. The main reason for this is because in the beginning of the game she is very cold and dismissive of Artyom and then half way through the game she suddenly "loves" him and sleeps with him. it feels like it was forced in to the game  and was only half done. I personally would have preferred it if instead of having a love story they focused on and developed the relationship between Artyom and Ulman from the first game as not much is known about him and he is one of my favourite characters.
Conclusion
In conclusion Metro: Last Light  is a solid sequel to Metro 2033 so if you liked Metro 2033 you will almost certainly enjoy this game. if you have not played the first game I would recommend playing it first. It is not as good as metro 2033 but it is good enough for me to play it twice and to likely play it again.

I played Endless Space 2 in the latter half of the last day of a Free Weekend. With nearly 9 hours on it, you can see I quite enjoyed it, only giving in to sleep when I was absolutely forced to. I won't give a super in depth review of it, telling you the pros and cons and giving it ratings every 5 sentences, but rather tell you what made me quickly decide that I would buy this game when the money was available. It'll still be long, so prepare your butts.
I immediately knew I'd like it just by it being a positively rated space strategy and thought that a few gigabytes on my hard drive would be worth some playtime. After it finished downloading, I loaded it up and began examining all the menus and such as I picked my Galaxy. It was well polished and thought out, but the real quicker came with the races. There was, of course, the simple "Human" Empire, but I fell in love with every other race immediately. All the designs were beyond creative and almost entirely unique.
As with every game with multiple races, the Humans are present, being what I assume to be a jack-of-all-trades. I didn't play them as I was much more interested in everything else, but the "United Empire" as they're called, is easily the most generic of the group at a glance.
The Sophons are a group of small, curious people who love technology and are adverse to war, considering it a distraction from their learning. But they are not to be trifled with. Their advanced weaponry can be dangerous should they be forced to point it at you.
Next are the "Lumeris," a group of amphibious people that are dictated by their economy, which is then controlled by an assortment of families that decide how to run everything. They, along with the Humans and Sophons, are some of the more basic races, if only by comparison.
The most hilarious one was by far "Horatio." A man with super advanced cloning technology and a narcissitic personality so extreme that he made an entire civilization of himself. From this he plans to colonize the universe, forever perfecting it along with himself. They use advanced genetics to create the perfect bodies for themselves.
The Vodyani are some of my favorite, being a warrior culture that was forced into space after their homeplanet's resources, and thus its habitability, were depleted. After finding technology from the long dead "Endless" that allowed them to put themselves into a virtual state of immortality, their populace entirely contained aboard their ark. Because of this, they have a special ability where the population of each system is dictaed by the number of planets times the populace of its Ark. So, for example, if you have 5 planets and 5 people on your Ark, you'l lhave 25 populace. A very unique race, indeed.
The heathans of this diverse group are called the "Cravers." A hivemind populace that was given sentience by the Endless, they scour the galaxy for more food to expand their empire, having recently realized that their world was finite. Diplomacy is a distant thought for them as they prefer to eat their rivals than negotiate.
Another of my favorites are the "Unfallen," a race of sentient plants that had long stayed dormant, prefering to observe peacefully from their home planet. After seeing the destruction and violence of a space battle above their homes, they decided to become the "America" of the galaxy, declaring themselves as the peacekeepers of the universe. Their designs are absolutely beautiful and I adore them beyond most others. Except for this last race.
The race that I chose, both for their design and their story, are the "Riftborn." Originating in another, much more uniform dimension, they were forced into ours after a rift between the two opened, corrupting and killing any of those in their world that was caught in the spread of its chaotic disease. Colonizing an arctic planet reminiscent of their pristine, white universe, they find little comfort beyond the barren planet, taking everything in as a monstrosity compared to their uniform, gemoetric shapes. They slowly adapt to their new homes, realizing that there is no possibility in saving their universe. Timeless in their own universe, they can control it here, allowing them to speed or slow the productions and experience gain of entire systems, three at a time.
My game temporarily ended during a major, galaxy wide quest that I will not spoil. But I cannot wait to continue it. This game is beautiful and anyone with a fondness for space and/or strategy will love this game, too.

Okay, that old review which I wrote yesterday was very short-lived. Out with the old, in with the new. Game beat. Wow.
My god. Aquanox 2 is fantastic. You just float around, doing missions of various kinds, and it stays pretty fresh throughout the whole game. You're constantly finding new weapons ever few missions with which to keep the exploding of enemy subs exciting, and while it starts off pretty easy, the game gets a bit more challenging by the end. There's even a boss fight! It's getting old, how many games today don't have boss fights.
The story is... well, let's be honest. It's interesting. The characters are interesting enough, I guess, despite the fact most of them don't really change very much over the course of the game. Once or twice the dialogue gets... weird. As in, "what the hell was the guy writing this stuff smoking" because of the way it looks, sounds and feels like the two characters are suddenly jumping between two conversations with one another that don't make any sense.
I wouldn't say it's a big deal, but if you don't like listening to and reading a lot of dialogue, this game may not be for you. There's not even that much, but you are forced to click around the ship or city, wherever you are at the time, to talk to every single possible person so you get every available job and trigger whatever other dialogue is coming your way. Or whatever. I personally can easily accept this. Not everyone else can, especially in an FPS which is otherwise considered to be completely action based.
There's no real RPG elements here. But you can choose what weapons you take on any given mission, choose what sub you're taking, as well as choose to invest in different bits and pieces from whatever arsenal you can find. There's only really three or so opportunities to buy or sell though, which is kind of a shame. There's also, like I said, a lot of clicking around before and after missions. So I can see why some might tag this as an RPG - just, you're not roleplaying any old character, you are roleplaying as Captain Drake or whatever.
Anyway, gameplay. It's immaculate. If you have a joystick, and you love your joystick, hey, you can have fun here easy. If you want to use your keyboard, same deal. The controls for both can be swapped on the fly, and you can fly sim with just your keyboard and mouse too, if you really want, for more immersion. I personally stick with the FPS thing because I know it and love it, but, hey.
Torpedoes are good fun, but I generally don't use them. Mostly because they have a relatively long cooldown, can be dodged by buzzers (aka flares to you flight sim guys) and can sometimes just be dodged full stop. This is really kind of a shame if I'm honest, since you'd think they'd work something like bombs. But as it is, especially once you get later into the game, you end up with railguns and stuff that do just as much if not more damage than your average torpedoes.
It's weird to suggest, but the ending cutscene is well worth it. After all of that effort, and you finally get that reward, and it's a big cutscene detailing everything, ending the game perfectly, on a "to be continued" essentially, which I find pretty funny considering we never got a third game... and in fact there's little trace of the Aquanox series anywhere on the internet in terms of story, so I guess nobody will ever really know how it ends or how it even ties into the first game. Just be creative I guess.
I mean, all in all, I could recommend this for the sole reason that it's a fantastically pretty, imaginative, original game made in a genre that today has become more green and stale than hard bread.
If back in the day (like, 2003 lol) people could make games like this, why can't we make new games even half as good as Aquanox?
