Imprison relatives! Plot against your benefactors! Declare anti-popes!
It's not about battles, but essentially being an unimportant noble plotting so that your grandson will be the king, and then panicing for a Plan B when he dies in a 'hunting accident'. This usually involves a series of plots, murders, and trying to obtain sufficient popularity to change succession laws.
A nice aspect is that in terms of what individual people think of your character, things actually make sense - everything that you think would influence a character's opinion, actually DOES. For instance, you may wonder why, despite your relaxing taxes and granting extra titles, Count Jeremy doesn't like you. But looking at the details, it turns out he's still bitter that you beheaded his father 20 years ago. Things like that.
It's a little harder to get into at first, and you might not have such a sense of what to do next, but this is an ideal game for imagining that you are a plotter in a world full of AI characters who also have sensible plots and ambitions.

I backed this game on Kickstarter, and I have to say, it was money well-spent. D:OS 2 is an amazing sequel to the already awesome D:OS 1. It has more soul and fun than many AAA games, and I can feel Larian Studio love and passion for this franchise. Some quick points:
Pros:
- Beautiful graphic
- You can create a custom character, or use default ones. These premade characters each has their own origin, and it will affect how the game world interact with you.
- Run very smoothly for an early access game, even better than many AAA games upon release. I haven't encounter any bugs or glitch yet.
- Offers a lot of freedom to players. There are multiple ways to deal with any given situation, and you will have to face the consequences of your choices. There are also unique choices that only available to certain race / origin of your character, which definitely increases role play value.
- Fun and refined combat. They took the already smooth combat in D:OS 1 and polished it even more.
- INteresting, fully realized characters.
Things to improve:
- Lack of voice acting. Though it's not a big deal and I'm sure they will add it later on.
- Some events can be very linear (no matter what you choose, it still happens exactly the same). Though there aren't many like that, and I understand it is for story telling purpose. Still, it somehwat break the illusion of choice in the game.
- Lack of quest details in Journal. The journals only record the basic task of the quests and certain marked point, not your full progress or all the clues that quest givers and npc gave you along the way, which makes long quests difficult to keep track of. There are also some vague description which leads to unnecessary confusion.
Overall, I think this is a great game, highly recommend. If you like old school RPG or table top boardgames, this is definitely the one for you.

The idea behind this game is great. You build little dungeons and populate them with enemies and treasure for your adventurers to explore. You can guide them by placing treasure or by selecting some corridors over others.
The art is great and looks really cool.
But this game is REALLY lackluster. Not even a demo is this empty. And the price tag of $15 is way too high for what it offers.
The BAD:
- The Game is slow, really slow.
- There are no options at all. Not graphics, difficulty, not even windowed/fullscreen mode. Games made in Unity have this for Cthulu's sake!
- The controls are bad. More than once the game do not register my clicks, making an already slow game, slower.
- The fighting... is really boring. There are no animations, no colors, no anything. There is no difference between attacking with a  spoon or using a fireball beside a small text description at the bottom.
- There isn't a tutorial, encyclopedia or help file to know what everything means (what is a blessing, how to improve statistics, how to level up, etc) nothing is explained.
Conclusion: This game has a lot of potential. Really. But for $15 you expect a more developed game and not something that rival Godus as an Early Access. Shouldn't have been released in this state. I really want to like this game.  I like certain aspects a lot. I bought it for $6 on a Steam sale so didn't have too much to lose. I can't recommend it right now for two reasons though.
1. Difficult to access / join servers
2. Extremely low player base
There are a lot of issues with joining the servers that leave some playes waiting to get into a particular server because it isn't showing up properly in the server browser.  Based on forum activity, it seems that this has been an issue for a long time.
Because of the above issue, as well as other reasons, the player base is really low to non-existant.  I've played a good deal of time on one of the official servers and came across some player built structures but never actually saw another player.
The game itself is actually pretty fun solo if you enjoy the wild west atmosphere.  The looting and crafting is similar to 7 Days to Die where items have a rarity and more rare items are lighter weight and have better stats.
Combat isn't great but it's good enough.
There are PVE and PVP servers.  You can raid on PVP servers but you do so by lockpicks and cannot destroy other people's buildings - can get their loot but their base stays in tact.  I actually like this for this type of game because it makes getting raided not quite so bad.
Overall I've had fun but am frusterated with server connectivity and lack of other players.

One of my favorite RTS games. In this RTS game, instead of focusing on resource gathering and management or building up a base, you have a "deck" of units to work with. You can customize these decks with units you have unlocked. And once you start a match with a deck you can only use those units in the fight. You only have a limited number of each unit so don't just spam tanks or artillery units because you will run out very fast. In order to win you have to achieve a certain amount of points (ex:3500pts). You get points by destroying enemy units. Don't spam units and expect to win. You can't win with only tanks. You have to flank, use combined units to force your way into enemy controlled areas. Does the enemy have a heavily defended sector? Bombard them with artillery to dwindle there force and then move your garrisons in.
You also have to worry about fuel and ammo. You will need a constant supply of ammo trucks to keep your units functional.
Some cons I do have with the game are in fact the decks. It can be kind of tedious or grindy to have to unlock all of the units. It would be much easier to have them all unlocked at the start and just let you build it. But instead you are constantly playing matches to get stars to unlock better units.
Another slight issue would be the learning curve. The game doesn't really explain itself well so trying to figure out what is what and what does what can be confusing at first and may be a turn off for some players.
Over all I would rate this game 8/10. Very fun.

"Deeply disappointing, I wish I could return it."
I hate to have to say that about any game that I spent so much time looking into before buying, but this would be one of them. I have a history with RTS games, and while not my favorite genere, I was looking forward to a 1980's Cold War game that would allow me to move units around and let the computer do all the math for me. I also spent a number of hours watching the Youtube videos about this game and none of the issues that I found are in the vidoes or comments.
Pro's
Its pretty if you zoom in and watch the units, of course to do that you lose contact with the rest of the map.
Con's
The manual holds only the basic functions and does not explain the Deck, Reinforcements, Stars or Points.
The scenarios allow you to gain points which allow you to unlock types of units. From there you should be able to add them to a battle. However when you are in a battle, you get points, but you are limited to a certain number of units, which appear to be a secret cap number. When you unlock the units, yo only seem to get a certain number and they do not seem to be adjustable.
Controls are managble but not easy and often you click a unit assign it and then when you think you are assigning another unit, you are actually redirecting the first unit.
This game is also very hard. Even through the five starter scenarios, it was hair pulling hard. When I tried the AI play at easy, I would continually lose. More importantly, there does not seem to be an improvement each time I play it.
I know that many of these complaints mark me as the fault, but this game does seem to be enjoyable to a very close niche of people. So make sure that you are one of those.
Overall, if you think this will be any type of Cold War simulation type game, you will be disappointed. This is a poorer grade C&C with a Cold War skin. I strongly do not recommend this game, even for the $9.99 that I paid.

Investigating the disappearance of Susan Jones in a fair, you're getting sucked into a world that is a darker version of the place. Jim Gibbons seems to be behind that but why? It's up to you to discover the truth.
The story is well-written and full of twists. While the outcome is expected, the way to attain it is surprising.
Anyway, if you're used to hidden objects games, Dark Arcana isn't a revolution: the hidden objects scenes are really easy, the puzzles aren't too hard. However, the addition of Miles, the little monkey, is nice. He can go grab objects out of your reach for you. And he makes noises when he's needed. However, what is disappointing is the fact that the map isn't used for travelling. After a while, you may be tired to go back and forth between two locations.
As I've said, Dark Arcana is set in a dark world and it's well represented without it being scary. I would have preferred more dark settings as the whole mirror world is yellowish. The soundtrack is also good: while the tune is known to be used in any fair settings, the small remix is enough to show that you're not in a joyful world.
Dark Arcana comes with bonus. I'm not speaking about achievements or trading cards. I'm speaking about the soundtrack you can save, wallpapers, hidden objects scenes, concept art or a bonus chapter, where you're Jim and if I remember well, is a sequel to the events.
Anyway, if Dark Arcana isn't innovative, it's still a very good hidden object from Artifex Mundi. And well, while it has not the quality of Nightmares from the Deep or Grim Legends or even 9 Clues 2: The Ward, it's still better than some other games out there.

Welcome your new $100 game, everybody!
After a long period of Early Access (or "You wanna start making money NOW, Bob? - Uh-huh, SURE!"), and a $20 DLC during that because they ran out of money (and don't forget the attempt to cash in on the Battle Royale hype, ARK: Survival of the fittest, HAHA), they're finally over the hill, with proudly, raised up high price tags. Tamable and ridable dinosaurs was a good novel concept to capitalise on.
In general though, you can put up ARK together will all the other sh!teholes like Rust or Reign of Kings. A single, well-designed Island (the random gen is utter garbage), resource gathering, modular base building, PvP. More or less just the usual treadmill. When it comes to gameplay, it's all bling and no substance. I've seen enough of this run-of-the-mill crap. "It's fun with friends" is about as good an argument as "Feces are technically edible". I wouldn't be surprised if they came out with dinosaur skin DLC at this point, but I guess the heavily priced DLCs  make enough, for now.
As much as they advertise that "it's singleplayer, too!", the game was never and still isn't balanced or built around it. But I have to give it one thing, the amount of customisation and settings you can set for your own world, or your own server is astonishing. That's a truly rare gem among games, you can adjust almost anything to your liking.
They're also not walling off the server software, so you can run your own dedicated server if you have the hardware for it. Meaning, some games only give it to hosting companies for a price. Hosting companies make money by offering and renting servers to people, and the devs/publishers make money off a fee for providing the software. One of the more scumbag moves.
So ARK has its pros and cons, its greedy and generous sides, its shiny moments and downfalls. I'll stick to my overall assessment though, it's every multiplayer island survival open-pvp game ever, when you boil it down.
I honestly couldn't recommend the game at full price, maybe at 75 % or 90 % off. I haven't laid hands on the DLC, but right off the bat I don't feel like they're worth the price either. If you're looking for a good game to play, maybe look around a little bit longer. Perhaps Factorio might strike your fancy?
Strictly my opinion.

This game has so much potential... but sadly falls short on the most important question of all - is it challenging?  And I don't mean "bang your head against the wall with frustration" challenging - but does it provide a reasonable challenge so that you have fun playing it?  The short answer is "no it does not".  The game plays more like a space race simulation than a game... a lot of things are going on... a lot of interesting races... interesting tech trees to click on... interesting planets to explore... and none of it means much of anything because you are GOING to win.  Turn on "conquest" victory conditions where the alien races have to conquer the majority of the galaxy to win... and you may very well win without a single space battle.  How is that possible you ask?  It is possible if the AI begs for an alliance... even when you don't have a military presence.  If pirates don't attack your planets.  If alien races declare war... and then never invade.  All of this you will experience if you play this game.  Adjusting the difficulty level doesn't change the AI behavior, either.  It simply provides more resources to the alien races, which in turn doesn't matter if they don't use those resources to build up their fleets, or expand aggressively, or invade your worlds.
Because the AI does not provide a challenge, at any difficulty level, I simply can't recommend this game.  What fun is a game that you CAN'T lose - no matter how pretty, or how many buttons you have to push?

It's a unique game, where you have to read the motion-captured faces of the characters you're interviewing to determine if they're telling the truth. I enjoyed it, and there aren't many similar experiences made right now.
The setting is 1947 LA, with lots of cars, radio, people and landmark buildings to create an authentic looking world, as if it was a Hollywood movie. You can even change the game into a black-and-white mode, Many of the cases are (loosely) based on real crimes that you can look up online, though I'd try not to spoil the game before playing. A grand-strategy from the masters of the genre Paradox Development Studio. The game will feel familiar to those that have played other games from the developer, Europa Universalis etc, yet will be refreshing and worthwhile because of its focus on intrigue and dynasties rather than trade and nation level politics.
Crusader Kings II is one of the best, if not the best, grand-strategy game of recent years. The game offers hundreds of hours of gameplay (especially if you have the expansions) because of the vastly different experiences the various religions, cultures and ranks of nobility offer. The RPG elements and focus on your personal dynasty add another layer of depth with the micromanagement of every marriage, alliance and well placed dagger in the unfortunate cousin's back. The game is full of events from restoring the Roman Empire to building a flying machine, which add a lot of flavor and keep the playthroughs interesting and amusing.
The game also has a very good modding community, with mods ranging from the small ones that bring alternate flags and portraits to the total conversion mods such as:
'A song of Ice and Fire' mod:
'Elder Scrolls' mod:
The mods, especially the total conversions, add a lot of value to the game.
The game is not beginner friendly, not by a long shot. Despite being more simple than other games in the genre the information overload will be a lot, especially for new players. If you're willing to take the time to learn the game, it will be an amazing experience.  I recommend the game to anyone who's interested Game of Thrones-esque intrigue.

A game built around a couple good ideas--setting, shadow mechanics--and not much else.
The gameplay the entire scenario is built upon can, more than anything else, be described as simply glitchy. It bugs out constantly, leading to unfair deaths or do-overs. Some puzzles, like Vincenzo's workshop, are absolutely agonizing because of this.
The setting is nothing more than an idea: Cabaret. That's it. Nothing more.
The developers seemed to have desperately built everything in this game on those two ideas, turning them into nothing more than gimmicks. The story is nonsense--a mash-up of heart-felt cliches and sexist family drama the player will
care about, with random (--wrong--) references to Einstein and generic ideas of science floating in the background. I guess it's meant to add depth to the universe they're creating, but it doesn't help when a handful of the world-building collectables are called nothing more than "Science Drawing" and are literally just nonsense symbols and images.
The story also just gets in the way: I can't count the number of times I'd move a few feet and have control taken away from me, so the camera can do a stilted, early PS2-era swoop over the surroundings, complete with lots of janky start-stop moments. Speaking of, the controls--movement and camera--also feel like the platformers (e.g., MDK 2) of the early '00s.
Whatever. Everything wrong with this game comes from its creation. It's clear the general ideas of the shadow mechanic and gimmicky cabaret setting were steps 1-10, and everything else was an afterthought.

"Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely."
- Lord Acton
The Medieval Age wasn't the brightest moment in human history. War, Assassination, Torture, Greed, Betrayal; those are merely some of the words associated with the atrocities committed by the rulers of the realm. Some good and honest men have ruled, but most rulers couldn't resist the temptation from the power they wield; the power to rule. They were tempted to gain more power, and they are willing to use even the most atrocious of acts to gain it.
Crusader Kings II gives players a taste of that power.
Starting at any point from 1066 (Or 769 with a certain DLC enabled) to 1453, players are allowed to choose from a very large amount of historical characters that once ruled over a part of Europe and parts of Asia and Africa.
From the lowliest duke to the highest emperor, the game has no final objective whatsoever, leaving players to create their own story and decide their own goals for their dynasty.
Do you want to be the most prestigious family in the world? To work your way up and create an empire that will last for generations? Or simply to make sure your bloodline survives through all the coming conflict?
Grand strategy games typically put players as an eternal invisible guiding force controlling a single country, viewing the world from above as a map as they manage the country’s Politics, Economy, Military, and Diplomacy through various factors. These games use simple visuals to accommodate the large scale gameplay. There are no fancy Total War-like massive battles or anything of sort. Almost every aspect of the game depends on numbers. In other words, the main part gameplay is to manage those numbers and the various factors affecting it to the player’s benefit.
Crusader Kings II offers a sandbox grand strategy experience into a more personal level; giving players control over a single Catholic ruler (later DLCs adds the options to play as Muslim, Pagan, and Jewish rulers) and continue on as his/her heir after passing away.
Instead of dealing with faceless countries, the more personal approach allows the game to have a large amount of characters, be it a lord or a simple courtier. Every character in the game has their own set of skills, traits, and relations with other characters. A major part of the game is managing the relationship between characters by various interactions. You can cement the loyalty of your vassals by keeping them happy with gifts and inviting them to feasts. You can increase the odds of success of an assassination plot by inviting treacherous people within your target's court. You can declare a war for a title your courtier has a claim on. Be wary as other characters could do it to you as well. The best option is to trust no one, not even your friends and relatives. These interactions increase the depth of Crusader King II's strategic gameplay in a very dynamic way.
The trademark Paradox's grand strategy gameplay is still present, even if somewhat simplified by the time period. Politics are mostly done by the character interactions mentioned above; with the addition of a player-manageable council the players can use accomplish certain tasks. Economy is much more simplified, with very little emphasis on trade. Instead of training units to form standing armies, you form a temporary military force in time of war, then disband them when the war is over. Your military comes from raising levies both from your personally owned holdings and from your vassals. (Retinues were added with a DLC).
Religion plays a major role in the game, with each religion having some unique gameplay mechanic that differ them from the rest; such as the Papacy for Catholics and Decadence for Muslims. While the strategy gameplay itself for most the most part lacks depth compared to other Paradox grand strategy titles, Crusader Kings II still stands on its own as a well-made and unique game.
Crusader Kings II is visuals are simple, yet fitting for the game. The map is fully rendered in 3D, it’s nothing breathtaking, but you can still appreciate the beauty of its landscape; although you'll probably spend most of the time using the political map mode. The character portraits are a great mix of realism and cartoony art style which provides a variety of colorful characters faces.
The musical score for the game is also worth praising. While not all the music in the game is memorable, they rarely distract you from the game, and for the most part they complement your playthrough with a variety of beautiful music fitting for the era.
The game is without its flaws, of course. While the tutorial is an improvement from previous Paradox titles, you will still need to learn most of the game’s mechanics on your own by trial or error. While it could be a part of the fun of playing the game, some people may dislike it. I’ve encountered several minor bugs, but the game is fully playable as of now. Another minor complaint is the lack of naval combat. While historically there wasn’t a lot of naval combat at the era, I wish that navies could be more useful such as for blockading ports. But as for the time this review was written, the only use for navies is for troop transport.
Describing everything about Crusader Kings II’s in detail would take a lot of time and energy. Both of which you could be using right now to purchase and experience Crusader Kings II on your own! (Or at least try the demo) Go and create your own story with your dynasty. Be patient and play as an honest, good natured ruler. Or fall to the temptation of power and spill the blood of anyone who stands in your way. The choice is yours.

Combat is just like in Original Sin, but after the improvement of its engine the game now allows a player to interact with the enviroment much more smoothly and with more freedom.
Of course this is an early access, meaning its still rough around the edges and it has bugs. In the game there will be a red text near the minimap saying "Alfa Build". But despite the bugs, the quests that won't update and the bothersome glitching textures from armor or the enviroment; I still greatly enjoyed the hours I spent in the game. I had a few occassions to get off the island but the more you explore the more rewarding it becomes. Even if you stumble over a battle, an ambush, a secret treasure or hidden dungeon; what you find there will help you later on in quests you didn't even get to or expected to be doing.
I do NOT care about the bugs or that it's an Alfa Early Access. This game: Divinity Original Sin 2, has everything you need in an RPG game, except romances. Rewarding exploration, beautiful sound tracks, fun puzzles, challanging battles and a beatifuly detailed world; I would recommend this game to any RPG gamer.

(Big) Edit :
After playing some more hours I find myself beginning to enjoy the game quite better although I still feel disappointed.
So I'll recommand the game in the end if you're not concerned with :
-Character evolution and gears are reinitialised at the start of every mission.
-Only lasting evolutions are unlocked classes, blessings, and lootable gears in missions.
-Personalisation for each mission includes choice of a class (six starting cards), a blessing (little bonus), and then through the mission looting gears of four different types (you can keep only one by type).
No more, no less. Quite enjoyable still but feeling of evolution and variety do not last.
-In my very opinion : evolution is slow and although not that poor in the end still limited, just as variety of missions.
I'll had a special thought for a mechanic I really like : each looted gear do not directly give new cards but rather levels of skills that stack on the character, each level unlocking a new card.
First : it's NOT a BAD game. But...
TL;DR :
-Great game design ideas.
-Globally poor content although sympathic.
-Way too repetitive and boring due to the lack of evolution.
Lovely idea on the paper, building a dungeon with cards around a character that move itself through the rooms you're creating, populating, filling with loot. Then playing cards based combats, making your character evolve, collecting better gears giving better cards. Upgrading your guild with earned golds to unlock new gears and classes.
But...
Very few different gears in my opinion, very limited deck building possibilities (one class and one weapon/offhand/helm/body gear), no lvl or gear conservation through mission makes you start anew everytime, not much novelties to unlock in the guild, at least nothing that feel like...
Very sympathic but get tediously repetitive before the first half-hour.
I have to recognize a great realisation for all the graphic and music parts, very funny narrator and beautiful tracks, very nice paper style design.
But even for 15€ I feel ripped. The game is fun to play but so insanely repetitive. Played four hours, started to struggle to really enjoy myself before end of the first. I can only hope the promised  gifted extension for pre-purchase will really enrich the game but I have few hope.
Great ideas but very unrewarding for the player due to the lack of evolution and real objectives beside. Missions are basically always the same, and even though there are some real tactical aspects they are, well, like all the rest, very poor in the end. Big deception because it's just a funny little time killer where it could have been quite a nice game.

Not a bad little combo for right off the bat.
Conversations have a lot more options with race and origin story adding in more dialog options. A tension meter for when there have been a lot of crimes like theift and murders in an area which effects NPC behaviour, so even if you don't get caught in the act of stealing it could make it harder in the future.
All in all it feels like a much better game (hard to say when the first game was already great) but definitly one where if you liked the first you will love the second, if you didn't like the first odds are there is nothing here that is going to magicly make you like the second unless it was a minor thing that you didn't like that caused you to not like the game (like say not enough dialog options for different characters).
Not much else to say other then the EA is like the first DOS EA, only play it if you don't mind only having access to act 1, if you want to enjoy the entire story all at once for the first time then hold off till the game is actually released.

***PLAYER BEWARE*** Massive grind game ahead.
Fun game, until it isn't. About 10 hours in, maybe less (depending on how fast you progress) you'll find that you're seeing a lot of repeat tilesets, monsters, loot locations, vaults. At first it's cool (you're starting to master the game). You also start collecting blueprints, relics, and unlocking more junctions. Then you start to find out that each planet has the same tileset and for that matter VERY similar levels. You start to want more diversity, perhaps a new change in gear... woops.... you gotta level up that gear first before playing the new levels you just unlocked or prepare to get owned... or better yet let your teamates push through the map for you at lightning speed. RINSE AND REPEAT, RINSE AND REPEAT.... Now lets go farm some blueprints from relics, you've been collecting a lot of components I'm sure theres something decent you can craft. NOT SO FAST!!! Most Prime gear requires you find multiple Prime components from...? You guessed it MORE RELICS!!! I'm bored out of my mind with the the progression of this game past the first 3 planets. Unless you want to start feeding this company money, and I mean not just an initial purchase price between $20-50 which would be reasonable to experience most of the game. In reality that initial purchase price will get you maybe 1 or 2 weapons depending if you have expensive tatste or not. Oh... let's not forget that you have a finite number of character and weapon slots. COUGH*, *COUGH*... either way you eventually start having to pay up. The WORST thing about this game is that the money being pushed into the game is way beyond the server costs, because guess what, if you haven't already been repeated kicked from a map run because the host left (which starts to get beyond annoying if you've farmed a decent amount of MODS and components) BUT YOU GUESSED IT!!! The game sessions are client side hosted by YOU the player. Which means the only infastricture in place is to keep you the player connected to the game is strictrly for statistics, data collection, and authorized purhases.
TLDR
-items are too expensive (especially for how the infastructure of the game is set up)
-gear progression is grindy
-repetitive monsters, tilesets (after experience a few planets)

Metro: Last Light Redux is a wonderful addition to the Survival game genre as well as Horror. Graphics are wonderful for its day and age, and from my experience run well on buisness class pc's and low cost builds, The story is compelling and continues the story of Artyom and the Rangers of the Metro. With the Redux Edition of the game, a full arsenal of DLC and bonuses are avaliable and I recommend getting this game in your library. A FPS game, with a variety of apocalyptic guns that cover varying fields of gameplay. Want to go Solid Snake on this ****? Silence your guns and be one with the dark of the Metro. Are you the player who likes to mess shiste up and go all out warefare on the smallest of foes? Super-powered BB guns can pop open armored units like tin cans. Venture out timidly to the surface, where every step could be your last, where each unfiltered breath fills you with the radioactive fallout of a long-passed war. Survive mutants of varying degrees of difficulty as you walk, wade, and creep through swamps, forests, and the rubble of fallen and lost cities. Yeah..
...go nuts.
Attachments improve and change your guns and can change the way you play the game. And with the Redux Edition gain access to guns not avaliable in the story mode, as well as special missions covering the other stories of the Metro and its inhabitants. Take control of a Fourth Reich heavy-weapons expert and Mow down hordes of Red Army battalions. Look through the scope of a Red Army sniper and clear an enemy Reich outpost. Search for the treasures of the old age and become a worthy Kshatriya soldier. Take the view of a rookie trapped in a spiderbug infested missile silo and search for the way to the surface! Look through the eyes of Artyom's comrades and companions as you divulge into the story of Khan and Anna in their own signurature missions!. Jeez, guys, yeah I sound like the back of the game's box but c'mon, this stuff is gold! There's even a Developer level with models of in-game characters and an AI arena! Did I mention there was a stripper or two involved? Yeah, there is! Love this game, and you should at least give it a shot too!

There is something that maybe the Endless' team could work on: the level of difficulty of the AI. While you can change the handicap you start with, what you can't modify is how smart they are. Because at the end of the early game, you will catch-up with the AI's early bonuses but the AI doesn't change its strategy often. One example: Once the quest for the stellar prisoner pops-up, the AI doesn't recognise it as a priority and you usually ends up being awarded with the quest and the great lvl12 hero while if you were to play with players with such an advantage at the beginning of the game, there is no way you would have it. Therefore maybe in the global quest system, the team could implement a level of importance. If a quest has a level of 1 (most important), the AI should rethink its strategy to integrate it in its build order. This way a player will have more challenges as he will need to consider making sacrifices (e.g. what can I possibly do to have my 3 gravitonal something up and running in the shortest amount of time ?).
Another nice thing would be to integrate the possibility to join a battle that is happening during the turn. Let's say I will fight pirates but in the turn, an AI is supposed to arrive at the location where the fight happens. There would therefore be an option (join the fights with Player or with pirates or fight them both). But that might be harder to integrate in a 4x game
In any case, excellent game, looking forward to see if new races will appear at some point to have even bigger battles !

E=MC²
It's commonly accepted as one of the most elegant and yet profound discoveries of science. There are equasions which Mathematicians and Physicists say put a smile of delight on their faces and which they describe as beautiful. That may seem odd, but they understand the complexities of these acadamic arts and therefore percieve how hard it is to produce something simple yet powerful. For anyone who has an interest in game design - you will have the same reaction to Contrast.
The game is elegant in design, form and presentation. Simple in concept yet profound in its scope and it is a genuine shame that the idea of moving into a world of shadows and back out again hasn't really been explored much in any form of media; be it literiture, movie or gaming. If there was ever a game that deserved a sequel it would be this one. We're talking about the kind of simplicity and genius as when someone said; Lets make a game about wormholes and using them to solve puzzles. Contrast is as unique and creative as Portal without any shadow of a doubt, if you'll excuse the pun.
At it's core it's about puzzle solving, but there is a bit of a storyline in there as well. Although it isn't fleshed out much. The setting itself is the very distinctive Paris of the 1920's but with a weird blend of 20's America as well. I won't ruin the surprize but you'll start to understand that something isn't quite right with the world when you start wandering around the streets. As for the level of difficulty, it isn't too taxing. But the variety of gameplay and novel use of moving into shadows is constantly compelling. This is a short, but perfectly polished gem of a game which is well worth a look.
As an aside, the game can be played with either a pad or the keyboard and mouse. I would suggest using a pad because when using the keyboard there is a weird 'floaty' feel about movement which feels wrong. This may in fact cause frustration, as a number of more tricky platforming sections of the game would be made unpleasently awkward if you use the keyboard and mouse. Once you use a pad however, the controls are rock solid and precise.

Welcome to Halo Wars.
If you're here, you probably like the Halo franchise, RTSs, or both. Either way, you haven't made a bad choice looking here. However, I should mention, this is a rather simple game. If there was an actual entry-level catagory for RTS games, this would fit the bill. Yet this is by no means a bad game. Quite fun in fact. I'm quite picky, and if this can entertain me for years, then something must've been done right.
Let's start with a synopsis of the story. It is assumed you are playing as Captain James Cutter, serving as the Captain on the UNSC Spirit of Fire, early in the Human-Covenant War. You and your crew/soldiers stumble onto an excavation of a Forerunner artifact by Covenant forces being led by the Aribter of that time. This leads to a race to stop the Prophets from activating a Forerunner weapon (that's actually not a Halo installation) that can not only end the war, but the human race entirely.
It's not a boring story. It's nothing truly captivating, but at least it isn't like a Transformers movie: empty. The characters aren't cardboard, and have at least some personality. Best of all though, within the universe, everything actually makes sense. No stupid jumps in the plot. Everything is paced nicely, and the story progresses smoothly, without some dumb Deus Ex Machina to save everything. Plus, it feels like it actually adds to the common story of the Halo universe, and isn't some outlier.
Next up, gameplay. As mentioned, it is rather simple. You scrounge resources in order to set up supply factories (didn't really now what else to call them). You now build units, and complete research. In order to upgrade/access units, upgrade your technology level. (These processes are different for UNSC and Covenant) Balance building units, researching, and upgrading your base(s), as well as making good use of your leader powers/passive abilities (different for each leader), and you are well on your way to victory. Remember these key things though. UNSC units do more damage than their Covanent counterparts, yet the Covenant army size is larger. Also, among the mainline units, Infantry beats air vehicles, air vehicles beat ground vehicles, and ground vehicles beat infantry. Among non-mainline units, this doesn't apply.
The game looks great, and runs smoothly on a potato laptop of all things, even with a ton of units and effects on being rendered at the same time. Mind you, this isn't some game where you crank everything up to the max, and be able to expect to see the warts on a brute, or enough lens flares to drive the world's entire population blind. If you expect this, shove that attitude up your♥♥♥♥♥ and play the game for the fun of it. However, somethings that do look absolutely amazing are the cutscenes in the campaign, as they are done by Blur Studios (Examples here [MINOR-MEDIUM SPOILERS]
.
All in all, this game is surely worth your time, as I found the eight years I've spent playing it was worth mine.

This is a triple A game that is free and its as fun as a 3rd person shooter gets. Haz loot. Haz gunz. Haz swords and bows and maces and knives and throwing stars and MACHINE GUNS and shotguns and.... Haz u controlling a GODLY SPACE NINJA.
This game is as fun as a 3rd person shooter gets.
It has this amazing ability to make you feel powerful when you're controlling your character without making you feel cheap. It accomplishes this by giving your warframe (what the character you control is called) AMAZING mobility. And it's not difficult to pull off, or way too easy. It gets it just right. No complex button combinations to memorize to pull off a soaring jump that flings you forward through the air, glide for a distance, then double jump out of that glide in to another direction, and grabbing on to a ledge.
There's tons of weapons to get your hands on. And different warframes with different abilities as well.
And the best part? It's free. Paying money only serves to get you different weapons and frames NOW. The game has another avenue for these items, and thats loot drops and missions that award different components. Once you farm up your parts, you pop them in to a "Foundry" on your ship and hit the craft button. It will cook for some real world time, and when its done, you have your item. The crafting time ranges from 1 minute for small items like keys or ciphers up to 3 days for completion of a frame. Don't want to wait? Spend some of the game's purchased currency and instantly complete the item. Don't want to farm? Go in to the market through the in game menu to pull up whatever you're looking for and buy it with platinum.
The feeling you get when your warframe or shiny new machine gun is completed after a few days is like christmas morning. It is fun, satisfying, and downright replayable. Frankly, I'm surprised at the vast majority of the negative reviews...
***If you're one of those people who do not want to be a part of frequent bugs, crashes, glitchiness, etc. stay away from ALL Early Access titles!***
Early Access
For those ignorant of what Early Access is actually meant for, it's for games still early in their development, that want to allow players in to playtest (that's play & test) their game, from the very buggy and rock beginnings, to the time it comes out of the Early Access stage.
Most of us have been burned by at least one development studio, but hey, it's a very small investment, whether it's ninety-nine cents, or the AAA price of around sixty bucks (USD) or so. All you're paying for, with ANY game, is entertainment.
So, before anyone gets all super cereal on me, remember, it's all about enjoyment.
According to Webster's:
Definition of game
1
a (1) :  activity engaged in for diversion or amusement
See? No reason to get all cereal ...
By the Way
The team working on Sunset Rangers interact with the community, care about their game, and really, truly, seem to  want to make it an enjoyable experience when all is said and done.
For anyone familiar with creating a piece of software, or playing some integral role in the SDLC of a piece of software, it can be a long, bumpy road, especially for a project such as an MMO.

A Very Important Note
Sunset Rangers is in its early Alpha stage. This is NOT the same as some Early Access titles, because some titles are technically already into their Beta stage of development before they open their game to the general public for purchase and wide-scale testing. This "working Beta", so-to-speak, is a more stable experience than you will generally find in a true early Alpha stage project.
With all of this in mind, I'm having a great time!  Are there bugs, crashes, glitches, and such? Yep! And I'm actually having fun discovering some of them myself!
Now, we all know not everyone enjoys the same things. It's also true that those who do enjoy the same 'things' don't always enjoy them in the same 'way'.
What I'm saying here, is that people know what they like. If you don't like the idea of a true early Alpha stage playtesting experience, then don't playtest. However, do you like the concept of the game, as it's put forth? If so, don't be shy, go ahead and purchase the game; play it later, when it's more stable - when you know you will enjoy it yourself.
Maybe you enjoy playtesting and discovering bugs and exploits and such. Great! Sunset Rangers is truly worth your time and effort doing so.
Ask Yourself These Questions
- Do you enjoy true early Alpha stage game projects, as described above?
No? Do you like the concept of the game as it's put forth?
Yes? Then support this wonderful indie studio, go ahead and grab the game, and check-in now and again to see  what's new!
- Have you been waiting for a great, Western-themed MMO to play, or are you intrigued by such an experience?
No? Okay then
Yes? Then go ahead and grab the game!
- Do you enjoy playtesting games truly early in their development lifecycle; finding and being the first to report those nasty bugs, glitches, broken things of various flavors and description?
No? Oh, well ...
Yes? Then support this wonderful indie studio, go ahead and grab the game, and come playtest with us!
About the Game
Sunset Rangers, at its core gameplay, is headed in a very positive direction. Not only that, the atmosphere is great! It really has the feel of being out in the Old West, roaming the barren wasteland, fending off bandits; running across the occasional ghost town - or is it?
Sunset Rangers has all you would expect in terms of mechanics of gameplay: crafting, PvE, objectives, group objectives, PvP, etc.
You just never know for sure what exactly you'll get from any mob, or craft for that matter, thanks to the randomizer algorithms! This helps to keep these a bit more fresh, and can help build anticipation a bit more!
In Sunset Rangers, you can build positive, or negative, karma - however you choose! Want to be a badass outlaw that no one wants to run into out in the wasteland, or in town, for that matter?! You can do it! No? Oh, so you want to be a badass enforcer of good, that puts the outlaw's face in the dirt - and their corpse six feet under? You can do that too! Wait, you want to craft and PvE? Seriously? Well, you're in luck! Yes, you can do that too!!
Sunset Rangers is aiming at a simple, yet complete MMO experience. You know those small teams that really, truly care about their game? This is one of them.
Folks, at the end of the day, you just gotta ask yourself one thing: "Am I, at all, interested in a game like this?" If that answer is yes, you know what to do.
One of us! One of us! One *BOOM*

I thought I'd let you know what I think is good and not so good about this game if you ever plan on buying it, so here's my Pros and Cons.
Pros:
- The overall environment is excellent. It really meets that feeling I get when I'm in actual deserts, so kudos to the developers for achieving that.
- Exploring is fun. Generally, I don't like exploring much in survival games, but since I adore the desert setting, this was rather enjoyable to explore.
- Graphics are pretty good.
- The tremor-worm thingies or whatever they're called are scary as hell, although I kinda think they're unnecessary to the western genre this game has.
- The guns are neat.
- Menu music is pretty awesome.
Cons:
- Some of the terrain could use some work. However, for the most part, the mountains look pretty good.
- Enemies are absolute bullet sponges, so expect to shoot them a lot before finally killing them.
- This game is in very early access, so expect a sh*t ton of glitches and optimization issues.
- NPCs really don't do much... besides stand around and maybe run after you for a short period of time.
- The world in general feels very empty in general.
Do I recommend this game? Absolutely, but expect to deal with usual early access issues.

I've completed two games of Endless Space 2 and I feel very comfortable stating that it's already one of my favorite 4x strategy games. It may be my absolute favorite one set in space. The soundtrack, graphics, and overall design are practically everything my sense of imagination wanted from the Master of Orion series back in the 90s.
The learning curve is as steep as its predecessor's (or Endless Legend's), but the default difficulty level is much more forgiving. Victorys can be achieved by alliances of factions now, which seems so intuitive that I can't believe I've never seen it in the genre before. If you've played an Amplitude strategy game before, you can probably manage a win on your first playthrough with a little luck and some skilled diplomacy.
I'm slightly disappointed in the variety of playable factions in Endless Space 2 and I wish more of them seemed truly alien in terms of design and how they function in the game. Another minor concern is that the late game seems to discourage a pure conquest victory (especially for players involved in an alliance that may be less than willing to fight a prolonged war at the player's side) and can overall feel sluggish. Especially since there doesn't seem to be an easy way to tell how close other factions may be to a victory condition. Hopefully these very minor issues can addressed with patches and future DLC.

Dark Arcana: The Carnival is a pretty decent HOG game.  It has the usual silly supernatural-romance/horror sort of plot which rolls along at a good clip.  There are plenty of HO screens -- they
repeat, but without respawning the items you collected the previous time, which makes the revisit to the now less-cluttered screen less of an annoyance and more of a gratifying victory lap.
Like some other games, this one offers the option to bail out of the HO screens by playing a mini-game instead; this one a card-matching game called "Monaco".  I've never quite understood
anyone would start up a hidden-object game and then opt to play a boring minigame to avoid having to find hidden objects, but the option is there.  The option was useful at one point where an evident switch of image descriptions had a plate described as a record (and vice versa, in a later screen).  Also, if you're achievement-hunting, you'll need to leave at least one hidden object unfound on each screen, and get it by playing "Monaco" instead, as three achievements are earned through the card game.
Finally, don't be afraid of the "Expert" difficulty setting here.  This game, like the other Artifex Mundi offerings I've tried, leans to the easy end of the scale.  Because of the low difficulty, it goes pretty quickly, but there's a good-sized helping of content, so you should get three hours or so of gameplay, including the bonus chapter.  If you play on Expert and remember to always use "Monaco" to finish off each HO screen, it should be possible to get every achievement in one playthrough.

What to say about Endless Space 2?  It's a turn-based sci-fi strategy game, for a start.  You pick from a list of 8 different space-faring factions, or create your own and try to dominate the galaxy, in some sense of the word.  Either through Diplomacy, Economic supremacy, Scientific advancement, or everyone's favorite, Conquest.  Realistically, you'll use a combination of all of the above, and based on what race you pick, some options might be easier than others.
It's got a nice-looking UI, but don't let that fool you.  For the uninitiated, there's a lot to take in and learn.
of mechanics, many of which the game totally doesn't bother to fully explain to you.  There's a learning curve.  If you're looking for a more stream-lined strategy experience, a la Civ, you're not going to find that here.  That said, the mechanics are fairly intuitive, once you discover that they even exist, which is indeed the trick.  The game asks you to navigate through every single menu it offers in order to master the skills needed to dominate the galaxy.  Each mechanic in and of itself isn't so bad though, but it's where they interact when things start becoming a little more deep.
Speaking of strategy, there's, ironically, not actually much of it.  What is there is meaningful though.  Expand your empire while defending your fronts, weasel your way into back-stabbing some people, schmooze and pay off minor races to be friends with you, and buy your way into developing new planets with which to more efficiently eclipse your foes.  That's really about it.  But how to do all of that, where, and when are all fairly important decisions, and a mistep might leave a key system undefended, a potential ally left as an enemy, or a minor race and their planets getting eaten up by another empire.  As far as the combat goes, not much strategy there either, but again, what is there matters.  You can take two approaches to ship-building in this game;  Brute force it, or prepare for all possible outcomes.  While the ship design itself is fairly simplistic, it's also very fun, and leaves you asking yourself a lot of questions about what enemies you'll be facing, and how you'll face them.  Mix in the ship-building with the tactics cards and how those can affect the course of a battle, and you can find yourself winning fights that normally you shouldn't, through smart strategic planning.  Like I said, what strategy is there matters.
And that's really the name of the game here.  If you're looking for lots of mechanics with a huge amount of depth like a Paradox game, you're going to walk away disappointed.  If you're looking for a set of stream-lined, easy to grasp mechanics that get you conquesterating your foes quickly like in Civ or other similar games, again, you're out of luck.  But if you're looking for what is
a balance point between the two, a wealth of mechanics that aren't necessarily so deep as to have hours and hours of different strategic value to try, but not so simple as to feel like they're wasting your time either, management you can sink your teeth into without it feeling like a chore after the first 10 turns, and some pretty cool space battles with ships, down to little one-man fighters all the way up to the Vodyanoi's big hulking Ark ships that're meant to house entire populations, then this game hits that sweet spot.  It's not so complex as to make you feel like you've just written a college thesis after one game, but not so simple as to make you bored after just one game either, and with enough flavor and differentiation to give quite a good bit of replayability to boot.
It's definitely a pretty decent middle ground between true Grand Strategy titles and the 'more accessible' style of Turn Based Strategy.  And there are other good things to say about it as well, regarding art, stylistic choices, etc etc, but that's all subjective, and it'll either resonate with you or it won't.  But is it a good game?  Yeah, it is, and I think that's a conclusion that can be gotten to a little more objectively.  If a sci-fi strategy is your kind of thing, Endless Space 2 is definitely worth checking out.

HOG (Hidden Object Games) is genre I've never really paid close attention to. I've stayed away mainly because I didn't have 'enough time' to play this kind of games. Reason for avoiding the whole genre is because it was dumbed down on mobile phones and social network platforms, plus the last time I've played it, it was way too simple and rested on eye-hand-spot-and-click coordination.
I've managed to snatch Artifex Mundi 10 games pack super cheap and decided to see what's new in the genre. Dark Arcana: The Carnival for installed first because of the name. Anything that whispers 'paranormal' and has carnival theme, I'm on it.
The storyline is cheap, yet effective, holding attention and progressing nicely, with few dull moments by the end. Also, it contains a 'plot twist' which most players will probably expect, but I didn't think about it, so it rewarded me with pleasant surprise. It's cheesy, but not super cheap.
Beside hidden objects scenes, you also have mini game puzzles and certain aspects of point'n'click adventures. HOG players might find it strange I'm pointing this out, but as I said, I'm not a HOG player and didn't follow progression of the genre. Mini games are easy and fun, usually a different variants of well known puzzling designs. There's an evident difficulty progression which I did like and some puzzles by the end took some more effort, but none of those are frustrating or super hard. When you solve hidden object scene or mini puzzle, you usually get an item you need to use somewhere and most of the time you're well aware where to use it.
Graphically, Dark Arcana is presented via nice, hand drawn backgrounds, music and sounds are appropriate and movie scenes are super cheap and feel like something that came out of the nineties, but they also set the mood in a way, by being what they are. Horror fans will also enjoy different tributes, intentional or unintentional, such as Freddy Krueger's glove, Chucky-like dolls, Frighteners movie inspired villains and so on.
To sum it up, Dark Arcana: The Carnival is short, sweet HOG experience that keeps your attention for three hours which is enough for one walkthrough (and you'll do more if you want to unlock all achievements). I've enjoyed its settings and occasional story silliness and it made me want to play another HOG adventure sometime soon.

Endless Space 2 is a highly entertaining 4x space game that makes it in to my top 5 favorites along with MoO2, Distant Worlds, Stellaris and Sword of the Stars. It’s an easy game to get into with variable levels of in-game tutorials that can accommodate all levels of 4x and Amplitude brand games experience. The visuals are up-to-date and smooth as long as you have the requisite hardware and the audio components range from passable for the music to good for the voice acting.
The game has that ‘just one more turn’ magic that 4x junkies as old as me have learned to crave ever since we first played the original Civilization or MoO. It has all the bells and whistles you’d expect from an A list grand strategy game in terms of customizing maps, opponents and other game play parameters and can be as hard or easy as your game play style requires.
I gave the first Endless Space a reluctant thumbs down for what seemed to me after long hours of play as overly hard wired triggers that undermined immersion and limited replay value. So far those are not a problem in Endless 2. Your strategy and responses to in-game events induce much more realistic responses and while AI players can still suffer from a bit of affective disorder yoyoing from threats to whispering sweet nothings for no apparent reason, there’s none of the flaming manic depressive disorder that broke the first game for me
It’s excellent value for your gaming dollars and another step forward for Amplitude as a leader in strategy titles

Right this way! Come, step right up! See the greatest show on Earth (or at least the part projected to the Earthly plane.  Then investigate the part that is not.)  One of the better off-kilter mystery circus/carnival games I have played.  Though Madame Fate and the sequel Fates Carnival is still among my favorite carnivals (most likely due to over the top characters and body count).
Story: Jim Gibbons, a once famous precision knife thrower, has opened a carnival 25 years after the tragic death of his wife and asssistant, Alice.  One fine day, after taking her daughter to the House of Terror a woman named Susan Jones gets trapped and disappears in the House of Terror.  As a detective, the gamer must find the missing woman and reunite her with her daughter.  Any more storyline would spoil to the story and the surprises.  Concise fast paced storyline without plot holes that is mystery, action and adventure (with quite a bit of the supernatural thrown in).
Gameplay: Let us start with the Hidden Object aspect.  The HO scenes are predominate over the point and click aspect putting it firmly in the HO realm.  The find clues are easy to see and match the area they are found in.  There are a couple of odd clues like windwill (which is a fan).  Unsure if that is a translation error or if windwill is a type of fan.  Shrug.  The HO scenes I would rate on the top side of easy simply because I could actually find all the clues in less then a minute the first time I saw the scene.  (Usually I have to pick up that achievement - Find all clues in less then a minute - during the second playthough and after practicing.)  Not that easy HO scenes are a bad thing.  Helps keep the gamer's mind on the story more then the finding of clues.
This game is broken up into sections and takes place in two separate realms, the earthly plane and the mirror world.  Each section has its own objectives and build and use inventory.  This is a progressive game, so each section needs to be completed before the gamer can move on.  This gives the game a quasi-open world feel as each section's tasks are completed.  There is back and forth movement that occurs within the section, and some sections are larger then others.  There is a map, 3 in fact, but they are not fast travel.  (Fast travel is unnecessary.)  There are penalties for HO word find hints and misclicks when achievement hunting.
Next .... The monkey; your little helper, and what a cute, fuzzy little helper he is.  Once the gamer has the monkey he is quite useful not only for reaching those out of reach places but he "screams/chatters" and waves at you when he has a task that he can perform somewhere.  He is a big hint when something out of reach needs to be found and retrieved.  He is quiet the rest of the time.  The animation of the monkey is unique since he crawls out of his little "use" circle then into the story scene.  Of course like all monkeys he is a lively character and it shows.
Actual puzzles include logic, music, circles, sliders, simple piece puzzles and cooking a turkey.  The basic usual fare with average difficulty.
Last of all there is a required second playthrough for achievement hunters.  And with all Artifex Mundi games there is alternate game instead of the HO scene.  This time the game is Monaco, a strategy matching game.  Here is a hint about the Monaco gameplay for achievement hunters: If the gamer plays the hidden object scene until one or two word finds are left then switches to Monaco and finishes the Monaco game at least two of the achievements regarding Monaco are easy to obtain in that way.
This game comes with extras: wall papers, music, concept art, cut scene replay and a bonus chapter.  The bonus chapter is in many ways an epilogue, but is stand alone in its own right since the character changes as well as that character's objectives and motives.  (No spoilers.)
Fun and easy to play.  Well worth the price.

A great sequel to a fantastic game.  Metro: Last Light picks up where the "Ranger" ending of 2033 left off.  If you are wanting to play this game all I can say is play 2033 (the redux version) first or you'll be missing out!
I have all the same praise for this game that I do for the first (great gameplay, hugely atmospheric and immersive environment, huge attention to detail, diverse npcs and npc interactions, great story).  Like with 2033 you can select any of the four play modes that change how the enemies behave, how much health you have, and how scarce items are.  The original version of Last Light had pretty abundant items (which you can still do with one of  the play modes) but the nice thing about the redux version is you can select the same play mode you used in 2033, which enhances the survival aspect of the game.
While 2033 may have had some atmospheric environments this one goes all out, with incredibly detailed storm systems, and diverse landscapes, not quite as grey as in 2033.  Trudging through the storms with rain pelting down on my gas mask and walking against the gusts of wind, while wiping all the mud and rain from my visor were some of my favorite portions of the game.  The sound effects for this are brilliant to.  There's always a sense of excitement when a storm rolls in since you can see the huge clouds sweeping over the landscape in real time.
The storyline for this one was a bit more interesting than 2033 since your character was a bit more involved with it, whereas in 2033 you are mostly a bystandard or fellow soldier and hadn't done much yet to dinstinguish yourself until the epic ending.
All I can say is I can't wait for the next installment (which I hope there will still be, fingers crossed)!  Play both games and you will not be disappointed.  Easily one of the best singleplayer experiences I've ever had.  Just wish the games were longer!  (10-12 hours each!)

It was fun for awhile but then I began seeing the problems around level 50, and I highly doubt any of that has changed since I lost interest over a year ago. I will add that I did enjoy the music, graphics,  combat and they managed to add more character slots- but that's as far my praise can go. Here's the reality of this game and I suggest you take a good look at the other negative reviews as they tend to go over the cons more thoroughly:
You want to use more than 4 skills from your chosen class and decently sized skill tree? In-game purchase and not account wide.
Need more inventory/bank space? In-game purchase and not account wide.
Want to make your character look cute or badass? In-game purchase, not account wide AND isn't permanent.
Want to reach max level? Prepare to grind a lot, run out of stamina and be forced to either In-game purchase, play another character (which will also face this problem) OR go play a different game.
Want to buy something from another player? Prepare to pay ridiculous amounts of inflated game currency.
Crafting sounds nice but sometimes requires you to purchase needed ingredients from other players or try to grind for them in dungeons which still has that whole stamina meter to deal with.
Dropped gear is probably superior to the crafted stuff anyway but given that the droprate can be terrible and you have that pesky stamina bar to contend with once again... well, you see where this is going.
"That stamina bar sounds awefully annoying and stupid", you might think to yourself... and you're right! But no worries, I believe you can restore it with an In-game purchase!
I hear there's pets and mounts but I'm going to take a guess and say that those come with In-game purchase strings attached in some way or another.
I enjoyed the Gate of Darkness event when you got to defend 2 lanes from waves of increasingly difficult enemies over the course of several minutes. But they went and changed that too.
As a final nail in the coffin and the reason I decided to update and change my review- look at the prices for the DLC they offer! None of that schwag is worth what they're charging unless it set foot on the moon or was involved in some other equally impressive act.
Take this advice from someone who wasted a lot of spare time before realizing what this game is and find a game without restrictions on literally everything. Trust me, such games do exist, even if they're a rare species.

Contrast is a curious combination of pros and cons...
The game has an amazing soundtrack that you can feel at the title screen, even before you do anything. It will be the first thing you will notice.
The second one is it great visual and art from the 1920s. Every character and level are beautiful and the light and shadows effects are pretty nice.
Them you get to know the story and, what a good plot it has, you will enjoy it even more when you get the collectibles and find the hidden pieces of information in the levels.
The problems start when you actually have to make that jump, mixing the 3D and 2D gameplay the game brings. The controls doesn't respond very well and, I must warning you, you will fall to your death many times...
There is only one thing that annoyed me more than fall a dozen times in a row, and her name is Didi. You have to do everything she says all the time, I mean, you must take care of her but Dawn could think a little for her own, it won't hurt.
There are only one or two moments that Didi actually helps you and, after that she is your boss and you must just do what she says. That was the negative point for me.
Contrast is a pretty short game, in about 4 hours you will achieve 100% on it. After all that I still recommend it for the experience, story and the great visual and sound it has, but not at full price, buy it on a special sale.

This is a very tentative recommendation with some BIG caveats – if you are looking to buy this game, I would recommend getting it on sale, as I did, or borrowing off a friend. The reason for this is that the game feels very half-baked.
is only a couple of hours long, ending before the game’s mechanics have really had a chance to flex their muscles. The story also seems to be truncated and cut down from what was originally intended. Further evidence of the game’s apparent rushed development is its controls and mechanics; the third-person camera controls feel very loose and wobbly, which is, to put it lightly, less than ideal for a game that features platforming as a central mechanic. Combine this with some inconsistent “shifting” controls and some poorly-designed puzzles and you are left with a game that often causes frustration where it should instead inspire satisfaction.
So why am I still recommending
in spite of these issues? In short, its central puzzle-platforming system is fascinating, one of the more creative mechanics I have seen in recent memory. As Dawn, the game’s silent protagonist, you have the ability to “shift” yourself and certain objects from the real, 3D world into the 2D world of shadows. This ability is the central focus of the game’s platforming puzzles, which may involve manipulating light sources and shadows to create platforming surfaces in more strategic puzzles, or using the shadows of moving objects to reach an objective in more fast-paced platforming action sequences. This interplay between the worlds of darkness and light forces you, the player, to see the world in a new way by placing shadows (things we often don’t even notice in games or otherwise) at the forefront of a scene. For this reason alone I would recommend this game, if only to game designers looking for interesting ideas.
However, their is a second redeeming quality of
and that is the game’s style. The game’s charming aesthetic and focus on playing as a young girl’s imaginary(?) friend can’t help but make you smile. Additionally, its 1920’s setting, a refreshing change to a period not often depicted in video games, provides us with a nice jazzy, big-band soundtrack. What little story there is features some quality voice acting and an intriguing sub-plot - it’s just a shame Compulsion didn’t have the time or resources to flesh the story out further.
In summary,
is a game that is full of potential but needed a few more months in the oven to be worth the $15-$20 asking price. However, if you’re looking for something that is short, charming, and original,
may very well be right up your alley.

The new combat system, with fewer AP per turn and height-related dis/advantages to damage and range feels very clean. Initially I was turned off to the Armour system but after getting some equipment I realised that it allows players to play more strategically. It makes it easier to reliably apply debuffs to enemies and prevent debuffs being applied to your characters, significantly reducing the amount of dice-rolling and making the game feel more fair.
The addition of new races improves the potential for avid roleplaying -- while that's not my bag, it's nice to have some variation and even the Early Access area has places and events where the character's race or character background mattered.
There is a limited selection of spells in the Early Access release, but they are all powerful when used correctly, with enough complexity and potential for synergy that they are all enjoyable to use. There seems to be a similar amount of equipment types to the first game, so it will be immediately recognisable to players of the original.
The game also looks excellent and is very well optimised, running at 90fps in 1440p at max settings with a GTX980, which is more than acceptable.
In summary, I think the game is in an excellent alpha state which hopefully reflects well on the game's release. If you want to try it out to see for yourself it's a safe purchase at £30, but it's clearly not a finished product and there's a lot of minor polish required. I have absolute faith in Larian to make this game incredible.

My new favourite little casual roguelike to play between bigger/longer games.  Very addictive gameplay with lots of versatility.  The versatility comes with a large castle/base to build on and upgrade which opens up a ton of equipment options.  There's also different classes with their own traits.  The cards you play during combat are modified by the class and also the combination of equipment you have that you gain by exploring.
I'd say it's priced fairly.  10 would be a bargain and 20 too much.  The graphics are crisp and clean.  The artstyle suits the whimsical style of the game and voice overs.
No bugs or issues so far.  I had one initially where the game did not load into fullscreen but I think that was because I launched it directly from the steam install window.  After restarting the game, it's never come up again.
There are no video options but I don't think you need them?  It's cards moving rather than animations so there's really nothing to affect by playing with video options.  Game is capped at 30 fps, which again, it's cards moving, not animations so there's no actual benefit to 60.  I'd rather have it capped at 30 than see frame variance if I'm playing windowed, which I do because of the casual nature of the game, since it's much more jarring.  Plus, I'd rather have it at 30 and see this come out sooner on mobile platforms.  Just a heads up if you're one of those people that needs big options and customzation menus because it's a game on a PC despite it being a small casual game.  The only thing missing is a hard option button for fullscreen/windowed that could even be a toggle on the main menu. I just use keyboard shortcuts because they're quicker and easier.
I don't think you can go wrong with $15 for this if you like the casual or roguelike genres.

A great sequel to a fantastic game.  Metro: Last Light picks up where the "Ranger" ending of 2033 left off.  If you are wanting to play this game all I can say is play 2033 (the redux version) first or you'll be missing out!
I have all the same praise for this game that I do for the first (great gameplay, hugely atmospheric and immersive environment, huge attention to detail, diverse npcs and npc interactions, great story).  Like with 2033 you can select any of the four play modes that change how the enemies behave, how much health you have, and how scarce items are.  The original version of Last Light had pretty abundant items (which you can still do with one of  the play modes) but the nice thing about the redux version is you can select the same play mode you used in 2033, which enhances the survival aspect of the game.
While 2033 may have had some atmospheric environments this one goes all out, with incredibly detailed storm systems, and diverse landscapes, not quite as grey as in 2033.  Trudging through the storms with rain pelting down on my gas mask and walking against the gusts of wind, while wiping all the mud and rain from my visor were some of my favorite portions of the game.  The sound effects for this are brilliant to.  There's always a sense of excitement when a storm rolls in since you can see the huge clouds sweeping over the landscape in real time.
The storyline for this one was a bit more interesting than 2033 since your character was a bit more involved with it, whereas in 2033 you are mostly a bystandard or fellow soldier and hadn't done much yet to dinstinguish yourself until the epic ending.
All I can say is I can't wait for the next installment (which I hope there will still be, fingers crossed)!  Play both games and you will not be disappointed.  Easily one of the best singleplayer experiences I've ever had.  Just wish the games were longer!  (10-12 hours each!)

Take my not recommending this game with a grain of salt. I'm not the biggest fan of Hidden Object games. If you like the genre, then you'll enjoy this.
I bought this game on sale after having played a different Hidden Object game that I enjoyed a fair bit. I'm a sucker for a dark carnival so I decided to give this one a try. I was a bit underwhelmed the whole way through. The locations are well-designed and interesting, but the story didn't grab me. There was a lot less puzzling than I would have liked, and a fair amount of needless backtracking, but for the most part the game progressed at a good pace.
My biggest complaint is that often you'll have to re-visit a Hidden Object location later in the game, with no indication that this is what you should do. That wouldn't be so bad, except that until you trigger a flag, the location comes up as non-interactable once you've done the first Hidden Object pass, so I'd mentally marked it off as "done". Made for some frustration until I figured this out.
Again, overall the game is fine. It just doesn't do anything exceptional, and that's why I can't recommend it. However, if these types of games are your thing, it will definitely scratch enough of the itch for you to enjoy it.

This game may be a few years old now, but it certainly looks and feels as great as ever.
There are a few flaws, of course there are, especially as with something this groundbreaking (which it was at the time and I think a lot of modern games have taken a great deal of inspiration from). But the flaws are minor compared to how many pros there are.
The controls can at times feel a bit clunky and not as quick and snappy as of most video games we play. Truth be told, I enjoy this part of the game. It makes the character feel more realistic, as if you are actually playing as that person and not some physics defying character. A small example is that if you are facing one way and you want to turn around, your character dos not SNAP around, he turns around like a normal person would. A small thing, but I still love that attention to detail.
There is not a great choice of weapons, but this is not a shooting game. This is mostly a detective/exploring game with elements of action in it. So if you were hoping to GTA set in 1940s then you are going to be disapointed.
The attendtion to detail that they have put in to the 1940s era is amazing, right down to the clothes they wear, the language they use and the culture of the time. Every part of it will have you walking around the city checking out the fine details the researchers and developers put in.
Finally the story and characters, both of which are amazing. All the charachters have flaws and rightly so, which is what makes you relate to them and at time sympathise or empathise. The story keeps you entertained and whilst at times can be predictable, the different routes you can take through the game and non linear nature will definitely hold your attention.
One more thing to say. I have completed this game may times and keep coming back to it because it has true replay value. You will not be disapointed.
