The word "contrast" is quite distinct, when I hear the word I imagine spectacular colour palettes of vividly juxtaposed hues and shades. Unfortunately, the type of Contrast presented here appears to have rewritten the definition to fit its drab and dreary canvas. As if someone took the worst parts of the Psychonauts and completely desaturated the visuals, turning bleak a very uniquely bright and eclectic art style.
Contrast is filled with wasted potential and, from the get go, riddled with visual and mechanical glitches. The shadow mechanics are often inconsistent and ham-fisted, causing many a sigh of frustration. If I fail to react accordingly I will often be forced to sit through the same piece of dialogue, waiting for that small window of opportunity to open, only to be forced out of the shadows because I gently touched the wrong thing at the wrong time. I feel my character is too large and agile for such a small set piece, it becomes quite claustrophobic at times.
My main issue isn't the poorly implemented mechanics, but the lack of care I have for the characters within the story and the absence of any exposition that isn't told through the numerous collectibles found in the game. Thankfully Contrast is a very short game as it starts to overstay its welcome by the middle of the second chapter. How many puzzles must be solved by standing on the head of a person's shadow? I'd lost count.

I originally thought that a RPG + Beat 'em up couldn't work too well, but this has changed my opinion quite quickly.
Elsword just looked like another random Free-To-Play thing that was advertised everywhere, but it's actually quite good!
Job diversity takes getting used to (along with a little wait on some releases), little to no lag, able to form groups on the fly, pretty much every boss requiring a different strategy to beat. Much like most other MMOs, Elsword is updated weekly (most of the time...), with the new classes being on the top of that list (is August as I type this). Can't wait for the characters I actually use to get their new advancements.
Only turn offs are that you can only do a certain amount of dungeons a day (not really an issue), cosmetic items vanish after X amount of time, and the plot is negligible to remember at best. Also it, along with many other F2P (Free to play) MMOs, it suffers from a little case known as Pay to Win, though people will trade the in-game currency for the pay-for currency on occasion.
Overall, I'm glad to have found this game, would recommend it to people who like a not-so-typical RPG.
November 2015 Edit:
Even with increased amounts of pay-to-win, I still reccomend this because it's still fun. Though it suffers from burnout REALLY quickly if you don't have friends to play with.
Also, be sure to look up how to play whichever character/class path before putting points into skills, it's a real pain to reset those and there are right and wrong answers... because min-maxing.

I know this game's only been out for two days, I think in my short time i've seen a fair amount of things.
Overall, definitely in an very-early-access state at the moment - it;s good fun but there's not much in it yet.
Oh and I've not tried any crafting yet so can't comment on that.
Pros:
- It's a large scale Old Western MMOPVP/PVE with survival & crafting for a tenner. (£)
- It comes with a PVE-only server option if you get bored of players shooting at you :)
- You can run your own dedicated server instance locally - can confirm this works really well already.
- The graphics are decent enough, the procedural generation seems to be doing it's job. You get a feeling for the vast open space without it being too sparsely populated. Even the medium scale map is huge!
- First Person & Third Person. You can play in both :D!
- The day/night cycles are gorgeous. The sunrise colours the landscape orange and hazily shimmers on the horizon. The days are bright and bleak etc..
- Revolvers!
Cons:
- Currently there's no option to start the game fully clothed, so everyone's running around a desert in their pants right now.
- Joining a geographically distant server seems to REALLY screw with the game - you'll fall through the floor a lot (a lot), movement will be elastic banded. Just start your own dedicated server or join a nearer one and these issues go away almost entirely.
- The enemy AI is... very basic at the moment, The bad guys just seem to stand still until you get close, then they continue to stand still, shooting at you. They will pathfind around objects to get a clear line of sight but there's no attempt at AI cover mechanics.
- the towns aren't exactly populated yet - empty taverns everywhere.
- There are no trains, carriages, horses etc.. you have to walk everywhere.
- Bulletsponges - expect to shoot an NPC about 5 times in the face before he goes down.
- The night time - quite dark. Could do with some ambient lighting around the towns/settlements/camps.
The vision is great, and all of the cons are & could be reasily remedied (some are even in the development roadmap).
I'm impressed with this taster, and genuinely excited for how this will look in a year or two. Good work guys!

I like what's in here so far, it's very promising.  There is a solid foundation of crafting and weapon/quality variation at this time.  Also I was very surprised at the sheer variety of pistol types and unique loading animations/skins for each category.  The atmosphere is sufficently creepy, it's sort of a future post apcolypse type of western with bandits and future tech, but everything is worn in and dusty.  I got a clear  picture of where they are going with the multiplayer landscape, having seen different types of merchants, traders and a player item auctioneer as well.  I assume playing Blacksmith, the class I chose to start with, will be pretty lucrative, putting up pistols and outfits I crafted, as they have a random chance for better quality depending on the toolkit you have equipped and its overall tier.
That said this is stage one alpha. Which means there is zero optimization whatsoever, NPC enemies are in the game but have no real AI yet, so they are derp until that happens.  The game hitches and freezes often when traveling enough distances and sometimes just turning the camera.  It is a mine field of video lag for even the beefiest rig.  As this is common in any game this early in development, I'll look past it for now and see how optimization goes down the line.
To explore the game, I made my own server, locked it and played by myself for a good amount of hours.  I can see the direction they are intending to go with this, and with such a good solid loot foundation and the groundwork for player crafting and enconomy already in, I am confident in my investment here and will be patient to see where this goes.
My final thoughts: Buy this if you want to invest in what it will become.  If you want to actually weather the bugs and annoying glitches with some patience and a bug report to the devs to lend a hand.  But if you want to sink your teeth into something right this moment, you may want to wait for a few updates and watch the forums/news for the game.

EDIT 2
I still haven't managed to get the game to work, properly. But I delved into it, regardless. The first thing I have to say, is the menu's. They're great. I love the integration of them, but I feel like it can get confusing. So something could be done to fix that, perhaps adding pop-up words, as in. When you hover over the inventory icon, you get the word "Inventory".
Next up, the weapons. They straight up look great, and there's a variety of revolvers with different loading animations. Like break action, side-loading, regular-loading. I love the animations. You also spawn with a different revolver, everytime. So the start of every game can get a bit different.

But there's not enough cacti, please add more cacti. (I'm serious.) And, please add more buildings. More npc's, too.

When these issues are fixed, and the frame-rate issues are fixed. I'll gladly make my score higher. All of the people on this indie team are kind, and are human. /Please/. Contnue to improve this game. Even if I can't ever run it, I'll still gladly continue to watch it improve. I might not have seen much, but I'll say this. Good moves so far, keep up the good work.
concept and screenshots look fun. I give this a 5/10 for now.

EDIT 3 : After picking it up a ton of months later, I sadly have to say that, even in this state. The game continues to be a buggy game. Such things I've encountered is my health dropping, but not visibly. Causing me to not know how many hit points I have. And enemies seeming to just stand still once dead. Some not even moving. While most of these were fixed with a quick cache refresh, the glaring ones. Such as the health tick not working, persisted. I wasn't able to play much of the game, due to the unfortunate lack of players on any server. (Played at 11 PM, take that with a grain of salt.)
Regardless, even though I haven't played much. The gun randomization and soundtrack were great pluses. And the feeling of a cartoonish artstyle can appear around sunset. It's a unique game, that unfortunately was released much too early to make any sort of impact. Early access or not, I think this game is a great example of a product released far too early into the market. Though it can be beneficial for extra funding, it can easily affect an overall sense of playercount and purchases down the road. Please. PLEASE. Buy this game, regardless of the overall faults. It's still a decent game at heart, and with much more promise down the road. This company isn't a bad one, and the fact that you can get problems fixed incredibly quick is an insane advantage to other games that don't have a fix, or need you to download random things on the internet to make something work. (See : Fallout 3 on windows 7.)
At any rate, I feel like this review should give you two choices.
If you want to bite the bullet and try it anyways, please. By all means purchase this game and try it out. If the problems are far too much, so on and so forth. You can always try to refund the game.
If you feel like such downsides are too steep, I suggest you purchase it by next year. This game ran incredibly smooth, so I know hardware isn't an issue like previously posted.
This ride isn't a smooth one, infact. Far from it. This is one of the only reviews I've posted that were completely serious on a game. It's just a preference of games. I semi-enjoyed my experience in it so far, but I really can't stand the bugs I've encountered for very long. Please, don't let that subtract from your experience. Guild Of Dungeoneering Review
Guild Of Dungeoneering is the new card-battling, dungeon-building game from indie developer Gambrinous. Taking inspiration from games like Dungeon Keeper, players must build the dungeon around the hero, luring them to the objectives and ensuring that they have faced enough monsters and gathered enough equipment to survive. You bribe, entice, and guide your heroes through dungeons without actually being able to control them directly.
Control wise the game is all clicking and some dragging and dropping. There’s not much to it control wise and by looking at the UI design it has without a doubt been designed for an easy mobile port in the future. I actually think that it would be a perfect game for a mobile port and would do well on iOS and mobile devices. It’s glaringly obvious that the game was created with a mobile version in mind which usually means the PC version can suffer. In terms of usability it doesn’t however the UI can occasionally be unresponsive when clicking a button. However the developers don’t seem to have sacrificed anything from the game to make it touch screen friendly.
It’s a game that’s packed with humor, including a narrator that sings in poetic verse as you get your minions killed, horde for loot, and kill infamous creatures. The game comments on the RPG genre with humor in every aspect, from art design to the hero classes themselves. For example, the Barbarian class in RPG’s is as overused and old as RPG’s themselves, and thus the barbarian in the game is an old man or woman who frequently complains or stops for a cup of tea.
I enjoyed the games cute minimalist art style, the background white graph paper with the pencil shaded graphics not only look good but give reinforce the humor feel to the game. Much of the game is just white and gray but the use of occasional color with vivid reds and blues does work well. The sound of the game is great with the voice acting and the medieval style music working hand in hand. The humour of the game really shines through in the sound design and the only criticism I would have of it is that I want more narration.
Guild of Dungeoneering overall is a fun, well put together card battler. Its dungeon building elements work well and the games humor shines through in everything. It’s certainly worth picking up and is easily enjoyable for what it is. There’s very little to dislike in the game and with the pirates cove dlc on the horizon, there will no doubt be more content to come.

The game, un-officially, is fun. If you have friends to play with and dip into the modded un-official servers, you get to expreience all the game is about. You can build on servers that are moderated by admins and exprience the endgame. You can fight, and play with little restriction. However, if you want to get into the "official" servers, I would tell you not to buy this game.
The devs are way to focused on balancing non-essential issues like turrets and turtles, when they have a problem that has been going on since the very start of official release. Essentially, there are people who play this game a lot. They have maxed levels, and that is fine. They can, however, transfer from official server to official server...AND THEY KEEP THEIR LEVEL. This includes maps that are brand new. In fact, 3 days after aberration was released, I joined an official server because I thought I would take part in their cash prize to down the new boss. When I joined this server, 3 days after released, there were already max level players who not only had multiple high level tames, but pillared the entire map, making it not only impossible to build, but to even set down a campfire or sleeping bag. In this state, the official servers are literally unplayable. The only base you can build is a raft on a tiny lake, and that is if you can survive long enough eating berries and mushrooms while crafting thatch foundations and throwing them away. There is no administration and moderation of these official servers. It is bad.
So, if you want to get this game to join an unoffical server and have fun with a few friends, fine. But if you want the challenge of official servers with no greifing, playing on an even field, look elsewhere.

There were three flaws that did stand out, with one being the repetitiveness of some of the HOG scenes - while the two parallel worlds theme was quite cool, and reusing but warping some of the locations was a good idea, it meant you ended up doing the same scene up to 3 times in some cases, often having to find a bunch of the exact same items in the exact same places - now where the item had changed a lot this sort of worked, but plenty of the items don't significantly change so it just feels too much like a retread.
The other two main negatives were the naming bugs in a couple of the HOG scenes (if you are told to look for a Windwill, it means a fan, and one time you are told to look for a record but it means a plate/large bowl, and in the bonus content the plate they ask you to find is actually a record, etc.) The other issue I had was the puzzles, which were all easy, tending to trivial,

Fantastic. My most played individual game by far. With every patch, every expansion the game has gradually gone from good to just downright fantastic. Take the role of an individual person and lead your dynasty to greatness, control duchies, become king and form a-historical empires as you please. With the added ability to convert a CK2 game into a Europa Universalis IV game the experience is further lengthened and strenghtened. The dev team behind the game is fully in-tuned with the wishes of the fans and their forums show this, as fan's wishes for new expansions are slowly but surely making their way into the game. We've had catholisim fleshed out, Vikings, Islam and the Byzantian empire with more sure to follow.
Sure, there are some negatives. Fear isn't modelled at all, you can't rule based on fear and the constant match-making can get tedious. Rebellion squashing used to be a hassle but has since been made more managable save the few incidents where rebel stacks several times your own personal retinue and combined armed forces stand up to overthrow you it's fairly well balanced. That said, there's a reason for this as well - you're a terrible ruler and you don't deserve to sit on a throne.
A++ would play again, continuing to play.. over a thousand hours to date. That should in all honestly speak for itself.

"Dark Arcana: The Carnival" is a decent Artifex Mundi casual adventure Hiddend Object Game (HOG).  Unfortunately, it's one of their less recent ones.  So, it will require at least two runthroughs to get 100% Achievements (and if you mess up part way through a run, you can't quit and start over -- you'll have to finish the game you started before restarting).  The story and voice acting are decent (well, for a HOG), and the graphics and puzzles are fine.  I did notice quite a few more blatant language issues in the HOGs though.  Three of the most egregious are 1) a record is not a plate, a fan is not a windmill, and the golden mask of King Tut is not a sphinx.  The only other negative I can come up with is that the storyline in the Bonus Chapter is, in a word, dumb.
It took me 3.6 hours to finish my first run of the main game, another 0.7 hours for the Bonus Chapter, and then another 2.1 hours for my second run of the main game to get 100% Achievements.  That's 6.4 hours of decent game play.  So, I'm recommending the game.  But, I'd also recommend finding it on sale for something close to $5.

I'm not the sort to prejudice games over things like their being hidden object puzzlers; and the Artifex Mundi games are by far the best examples of the genre. Nonetheless A.M. has followed the method of if it isn't broke don't fix it, meaning they reuse their puzzles with cosmetic variations from one game to another. This has the unfortunate result that if you've played one of their games you've played them all.
That's O.K. if you think of the games as more visual novels with bonus puzzle content. Granted the writing isn't amazing; but it isn't bad either. I know I've yet to play an A.M. game I could make myself stop playing before the end. That's, on average, over 3 hours in one sitting. And, most of their games include a bonus chapter that extends gameplay another hour.
They do manage to do this without unnecessarily padding game length that overstays its welcome. I know that doesn't sound like much in an industry with triple AAA titles that boast hundred of hours of gameplay. But, for cheap casual games this is an achievement.
My recommendation, because of the "if you've played one you've played them all" problem, is pare your selections down to their better games. That would be Enigmatis 2 (but not the mediocre Enigmatis: the Ghosts of Maple Creek) as a top pick, Grim Legends 1 & 2 if you liked that, and the Nightmares from the Deep trilogy if you just can't get enough of these games.

Endless Space 2 is a good 4x game, and certainly worth the price for the amount of entertainment you get out of it. However, there are many areas that could use improvement, the first being the tutorials. I chose the middle path when prompted by the game for the level of help the game would give me, but after about 5 messages about various things I clicked on, the tutorials shut off completely and left me to fend for myself.
I played the first Endless Space before this one so this wasn't a total loss but there were many events (not quests) that happened during the game over which I had no control over and no clue why they occured.
For example, I reached a point in the game where a message popped up saying I'm going to "win in 4 turns." I figured, "Great, I'll just build up a few more ships in case someone attacks me." Everyone except for the one civilization I'm at peace with attacks me and I easily destroy the ships that advance on my borders. Four turns later, I still haven't won the game and it doesn't tell me what victory condition I fulfilled, nor why I was no longer winning the game (this was before I discovered the Victory Conditions screen the tutorial never told me about - I still don't know how I was "winning" as I know I wasn't fulfilling any of them when I discovered the VC screen later on.)
I began to close in on a domination victory about 10 turns later, setting up two colonies and conquering a system from the AI when suddenly, I'm in an Alliance with the civilization I was formerly friends with even though they never asked me to join or anything. This actually stopped me from winning the game, and I couldn't figure it out why I didn't win until I looked again at the victory screen and it said the alliance needed a bunch more systems to get a domination victory. So I contacted my ally, broke the alliance, and won the game instantly.
This is not a bad game, and I'm still going to give it a thumbs up, but some of what happened was really f'n confusing.

I really hate that I have to call this game terrible, but sadly I do.  For me, it is almost unplayably bad, and I wish I had never wasted my money on it.
The gameplay mechanics are good; it is sometimes difficult to micromanage the orientation of platoons to keep them facing the enemy, and my recon helicopters have an annoying tendency to land whenever they're not actively moving, while I may want them to stay airborne to keep enemy units visible; the inability to set stances, and the rather awkward method of turning off individual weapons on individual units to keep control of who fires what, can be annoying, but I can generally get my units to do what I want.  The graphics are fantastic, making each unit distinct and identifiable.  The music fits the scene nicely, and the single player campaign storyline is nicely plausible.
So why do I call it terrible?  Becuase of the awful, terrible,
AI.  In single player, the game becomes almost unplayable, all thanks to the AI's absolute omniscience.  Don't get me wrong, AIs have been able to see all the units on the field right back to the dawn of the RTS era, but it was generally not that big a deal.  In Wargame, however, recon is a central element of any army's tactics.  It requires careful attention to the type of recon vehicle, and equally careful scouting of suspected enemy strong points to avoid putting your recon vehicle in harms way.  The AI does none of that.  It just drops a full attack force directly on top of you, knowing exactly where all of your forces are at all times.  it is even worse in the campaign, where the AI will face you with overwhelming numbers in every mission, often pre-positioned in ambush sites that you can take no advantage of.  This severely reduces the tactics available, and ends up in a situation where the only way to make any sensible progress is by spamming the Quicksave key every time something doesn't go horribly wrong.
I play single player.  I enjoy playing single player so I can take my time and explore my options.  But this game makes single player a horrible, crippled experience that is more like a chore than a game.  For your own sanity, Avoid at all costs.

This produces significant replay value by varying the races and the shape/constituents of the galaxy.  Hence the >300 hours total.
-Multi-layer complexity: the game is very much a complex 4x space opera, but the learning curve is appropriately gradual.  The nuances are interesting and fun, but not critically imperative.
-Pirates: With the most recent patch the early game pirates are surprisingly strong (likely attenuated in a future patch).  This makes for an early game challenge rather than an outright planet grab.
-Heros: Heros are interesting, adaptable, and helpful.  You will find yourself getting attached to them.
-The developers at Amplitude Studios definitely are committed to being free DLC and improvements, much appreciated.
CONS
-Despite the talk of ranges and ship classes, combat really comes down to who has the highest number of advanced ships in each engagement.  There is some variation; aka missiles work best a Long, compared to short burst projectiles which are best at Short.  But I find myself rarely changing my tactics in any meaningful way.  It is also impossible to intervene once a battle starts.  I find myself rarely watching battles.
-Heros: Heroes have the same basic starship hull from beginning to end.  Not a big deal, but definitely a place for some diversity.
-Quests: The quests are interesting and deep, but few.  A few dozen more (with maybe more varied rewards) would liven up the game play.
-AI: The AI is generally hostile to you, which I find slightly monotone.  Variability would be nice in this area as well.
-After a certain point the game is difficult to lose (Yes, to the chorus of haters, I have continually increased the difficulty).  The game lacks existential obstacles which need negotiated; such as the Black Death or the Mongol Invasion in the Total War series.  As long as you keep your planets happy and have the biggest/most advanced fleet then you will win.
-Most importantly (imho), despite the VERY diverse, interesting races...they all share the same tech tree, same weapons and roughly the same warship hulls (small, medium, large, etc).   Why would a race of Ent-creatures (the Unfallen) use weapons/ships/tactics of a race that is not from their dimension (the Riftborn).  In my humble opinion, this is a failure of vision on behalf of the game designers. Older games, such as Conquest: Frontier Wars, made each race radically different in offensive capabilities, armaments, hull design, etc.  The Vodyani should have sprawling carriers crewed with their subjected races, the United Empire should have massive battleships, and the Cravers should have suicidally under-shielded glass cannons and focus on boarding parties.  Maybe the Unfallen can throw pine cones.
TL;DR: An immersive, streamlined 4x space opera well worth the price tag.  The diverse races provide significant replayability.

Since I have played Metro 2033 Redux it was time to move on to Metro Last Light. I was already experienced in what the world is actually like and knew what to expect from the game. Of course there were few things that I was dissapointed in, but in the end the game was outstanding, and answered my questions on the plot.
The graphics are just amazing. I didn't like the look of the new world, where the Nuclear Winter is slowly ending. I prefered the old world from the Metro 2033. But it doesn't mean that it is bad either! It is still the old, outstanding world, where humans are on the brink of extinction. (for more on the graphics look at my Metro 2033 Redux review)
The main positive point of the Metro Last Light and it is a big improvement over the Metro 2033 is the story. Metro 2033 had a very good story, but Metro Last Light had even better. I felt even more sad and depressed, and made me question of how one stupid move can end all of us. Where in Metro 2033 you mainly battled monsters, in Metro Last Light you battle your own race to prevent the Communist Red Line from taking over the Metro, and destroying humanity. I particularly enjoyed commentary from the Baby Dark One, a child left out as one of the last intelligent mutants. The child was questioning how people may have turned such a beautiful world into something as such, how humans despite being low on numbers still are killing each other, and how humans feel about different things. He highlighted the "evil" people that wanted to kill Artyom, the people that were "good" but ready to kill, and those that didn't want to kill but had to (for example Pavel). And then the final battle for the D6 made me feel proud of who I am in the game. Another thing I have to mention is how Artyom feels guilty for what he has done in the previous game. He now knows that he has done wrong and killed off one of the most peaceful species out there.
But enough of the plot. I don't want to spoil it all for you ;) . And trust me there are plenty of things to talk about.
Since you don't fight mutants as much you won't encounter as interesting beasts as in Metro 2033. Librarians in particular I really miss.
Let's give this game a final score. I believe it deserves a 9/10 for being an improvement of already a beast of the game Metro 2033. Why did I give such a score:
+ Beautiful graphics
+ Plot is outstanding and filled with emotions
+ Baby Dark One is an excellent addition and one of the most interesting characters
+ All characters that you encounter (apart from maybe strippers and civilians you don't talk to) have amazing backgrounds
+ A great final endings
+ Cinematics add a great emotional feel to the game
+ Artyom's guilt made me feel sorry for him
- All women you encounter get naked for some reason (#teenage porn)
- Less mutants
- Romance with Anna sucked (the sex scene was ok at most but even I can make evenings with my missus more romantic when playing War Thunder)
- Strip club (what was the point of it?)
- DRM (what is the point of buying a game on the disc if you will use the disc once?)

Mac and Linux buyers beware.
This game has lots of bugs and glitches that never seem to be fixed properly, but the company is more then happy to push out new (and buggy) expansions and take more of your money. Updates alone can render Mac and Linux clients completely unusable and for a survival game that requires you to login to maintain your stuff, this is totally unacceptable. In fact, it will put you at a huge disadvantage.
I can say it's a pretty game on Windows and if that's your platform it may be worth something. However, if you are a Mac or Linux user, i would highly recommend looking elsewhere until someone at the company learns how to run quality assurance, proper bug testing and just generally cares enough to maintain good working game clients. The game also doesn't look as nice on these platforms and the glitches can make it harder to play. Prime examples are water that looks like cement being mixed in a cement mixer and is impossible to see beneath and lighting glitches that will blind you as you move around.
Game play itself isn't terrible when it works but some aspects are a pain. Like the dinosaur chase ranges being huge or the fact that you can't set this range on your own dinos who will happily run off and never return. It would be nice if you could at least set rally points down so they would return when they do stop chasing stupid people or other dinos. Don't even get me started on the path finding issues.
If the company ever really starts addressing the client bugs and starts actually caring about non-Winodws clients, this game may be worth a look. Until then, i would save your money.

So I've logged almost 1000 hours on the game. I've been playing it on and off steam for about 5-6 years and on multiple platforms for two or three years. While it takes a little time to really get going, the game [obviously] has months and years of content. Before I really get into the review, I want to say that you should take Excalibur, Braton, Lato, and Skana starting out. If you want any of the other starting items, the ones listed above are the most versatile or the hardest to farm (Excalibur is all the way on Pluto so take Excalibur). The developers actually listen to the players, which is really nice especially on a free to play game where they could easily make it about whatever sells best. The content is [mostly] bug free. Even if there is a bug, the developers are on top of it usually within a week. Considering the size of the game and the sheer number of bugs the game used to have, that impresses me. You might have trouble starting out, like your mouse is moving slow and whatnot but the same thing happened to me. Just take a few seconds and mess with your settings because I promise this game is worth it. If you don't like/have the time to spend grinding stuff out and you have a few extra dollars, just wait until you get a 75% discount on platinum and purchase a $100 platinum package for $25. Then you can buy whatever you dont want to farm and thats that. What I like the most is that you arent tied to just one character or one skill set. If you choose something you dont like in the start, hit up recruit chat and have a taxi player take you to a new warframe farm [but remember that a low level player being taken to endgame warframe farms will probably just die over and over again]. You could literally max out as many warframes as you want in one day.
In Review:
Pros:
Great Content
Awesome Developers
Great Graphics
Varied Content
Unique Gaming
Awesome Approach to Character System
Well Worth Time [and Money] Spent
Cons:
Heavy Visual Load (Even lowest graphics can be too heavy for some normal computers)
Takes Time (Especially if you dont want to spend $10-$50 on platinum)
Can Seem Pay to Win (When its really play more to win)
All in all, if you just want a game you can hop on, grab a daily reward, do a few 3-15 minutes missions on and then hop off, this game could be the one you're looking for. Or if you have hours and hours to blow, start prime farming and you could just lose yourself in the game. Either way, Ninjas Play for Free and Warframe is awesome.
Also I wasn't in any way reimbursed or payed or discounted for this review, and I have no affiliation with Warframe, I just honestly think its a great game that only gets better with time.

The game basically has so much information in the form of detailed stats on each class, nation, and type of vehicle that you will have to meticulously study it to get any kind of proficiency when planning your battles. This game requires you to actually resupply and refuel your units with logistics and this is every bit as painstaking as it sounds.  Terrain matters,  unit optics matter, armor matters, weapon range matters, weapon types matter.  It's very complicated, but the satisfaction of success on the field is worth the mind boggling scope of what you have to keep track of, which is why you shouldn't play this alone.  You can team up with 3 other people on one side and work together and this makes it alot easier.

Game Menu Option: Two section – Volume and Miscellaneous settings. The volume section has the following: Music and Sound. The miscellaneous section has the following: Custom Cursor, Voice Overs, Difficulty Mode and Full Screen. Wide Screen is automatically supported in the game.
Game Difficulty Modes: Three game difficulty modes – Casual, Advanced and Expert.
Cinematic/Dialogues: All cinematic scenes can be skipped if you do not want to watch them. They can be watch over again under the cutscene section the extras. There is an option for skipping the entire dialogue scene without having sit through it.
Voiceovers: Nothing much can be said about the voice overs asides from that they are well done.
Game Music/Sounds: Nothing much can be said about the music/sounds asides from that they fit well with the game.
Game Graphics: Nothing much can be said about the graphics asides from that they are nicely drawn with a painted feel to them.
Inventory Panel: There is no lock option for the inventory panel. However, the inventory panel does slides up and down; when the mouse cursor hovers over it.
Notebook: Two sections – Notes and Objectives.
Map: It has useful indicators; map icons/markers. The legend on the map explains the function for each of the map icons.
Hidden Object Gameplay: Traditional word lists with some and/or no interaction required. Most of the hidden object scenes can be replayed in the hidden object section in the extras.
Hidden Object Minigame: It is a match pair games. This optional gameplay instead of go looking for items in the hidden object scenes.
Puzzle Gameplay: Most of the puzzles are fairly easy to solve. Some puzzles has extra puzzles in them to solve. There is a skip button if the puzzle(s) becomes too tasking to solve.
Game Helper: A monkey helper called “Miles” that can carry out certain tasks that the player can’t complete themselves. Like retrieving items that are out of reach.
Game Ending: There is an ending for the main portion of the game. The bonus chapter can be seen as a presequel/sequel to the main portion of the game.
Game Achievements: In game and Steam. There are total of 19 different achievements to earn throughout the game. Each of the achievements has certain requirements before they’re obtained.
Game Bonus Adventure: This only available after the main portion of the game is completed.
Game Concept Art/Wallpapers: 9 concept art and 8 wallpapers.
Game Soundtrack: 6 soundtracks from the game.
Game Trading Card/Badge: This a special feature only available in the Steam’s version of the game. The game drops three different trading cards only once and the rest of the cards: Community Market, Booster Packs and Trading. Contrast is the arty game that gives arty games a bad name.
It's got a really good idea, and squanders it with horrible, unresponsive controls, endless cliche and the kind of poorly envisioned puzzles that make me want to scream at the screen.
Bouncing around on umbrellas and canopies may be a fine game element in a goofy 16 bit platformer, but in a game that dresses, speaks and walks as though it wants you to take it seriously, it doesn't fit, and becomes completely unforgivable when the bad controls and the gimmicky linear level design combine to make the trick virtually impossible.
There is an achievement for failing a wallrun jump near the beginning of the game, and if you play that section, there is no risk whatsoever of missing the achievement, because the controls for initiating the wallrun are so terrible that even if you do hit the right keys, your character will probably tumble off the world before she realizes you want her to actually do something.
Yes, the shadow people are neat, the circus aesthetic is pretty, and running on shadows is a gimmick with a lot of promise; but Contrast is the perfect living proof that a good idea isn't enough to make a good game. I wish it had not been made, so that another developer could have taken on the project, and done it better.
I might return to the game just to enjoy screaming at it. This game might manage to be "so bad it's good", depending on your taste. But it's definitely bad.

I have played 2 long matches in this game now which although doesn't sound like much has ended up with me playing 170 hours. I notice a lot of the positive aspects such as the planet diversity isn't as good as they make it out to be and the so called "balancing" in this game which everybody seems to be ranting and raving about is actually far from it.
Let me tell you why the game is still massively unbalanced, I'll start off with the planet diversity.
If you look at a terraforming tree you will see that you get ice and barren planets which produce science, lava and ash planets which produce industry and then terran, ocean planets which produce food. If you just left it at that then you would think that having a system full of diverse planets would be the best outcome, diversity, right? Well no that's not how it works at all, you see most of the improvements you build on your systems work on population. For example an industry improvement will say +4 industry per pop. Because of this, your best bet is to go for/terraform to planets which hold the most population and when a lava planet has a max population of 5 and a terran planet of the same size has a population cap of 10 this makes a big difference, meaning that once you advance through the technology tree a little bit, your terran planets will end up giving you more industry then lava planets, more science than ice planets and more dust than savannah or toxic planets.
This brings me on to the next problem with balancing, I can pretty much tell you straight up that the way to win this game is to be the best technologically advanced, with technology you can build better ships, construct better improvements  for your systems and move around the galaxy faster than your rivals, whether you want to win by military, economic or social domination, your best bet is to have the technologies to get you there before anyone else.
There is also a massive draw back in the game with the whole happiness of your systems, happiness is too easily influenced and with all the pre made factions in the game the happiness of your systems will always be your main problem as there are certain planets which have a catastrophic blow to your happiness, such as lava or toxic planets giving you -8 happiness per population. This also correlates with the first unbalancing issue I mentioned above.
I have built a custom made faction which produce +12 happiness on sterile planets and +4 happiness on fertile planets, nullifying the planet happiness effects and pretty much guaranteeing that my system happiness will reach 100% ecstatic as my population increases (this also gives a significant food and culture boost).
This race also boosts science output and reduces the cost of science necessary to finish researching a technology. As opposed to when I just used the empire faction in my first match, I have been completing researches in about a quarter of the time it took me to do with empire and this has meant that I am flying well armed dreadnaughts with quantum lasers and have a thriving economy with well established systems that are built so that when population is full, food is converted into industry and I then convert my industry into dust, meaning some systems are giving me up to 7k dust a turn, which alone is enough to support enough fleets to dominate the galaxy.
The game is talked up to prevent people from becoming too dominant, but so far I have not seen any of this implemented at all, not to mention that the space battles which are supposed to be the real cinematic of the game are boring as hell, the ships move slow, there is no real movement going on and the battles go for about 10-15 seconds because a stronger fleet will obliterate the other fleet in no time. The diplomacy system appears to be broken to me, just because you produce more influence than another faction you exert "pressure" on them and can make demands for dust or resources or even technologies, but when another faction had pressure on me nothing happened.
Maybe these issues will be fixed and all in all it is a good game, but as far as I'm concerned it is really just like playing Civilization, but in a space environment and because this game was so talked up and I am disappointed to see that I have pretty much just paid for ANOTHER Civ game, unfortunately I have to give a bad review.

It's not the greatest RTS. There's balance issues and awkward maps and AI pathfinding that makes Daikatana look like an A* masterwork. The missions are♥♥♥♥♥♥easy until you crank it up to Legendary. The way you build bases is strange. Many, MANY UI and design choices let you know this was a console game before it finally shuffled onto the PC.
Yet, I still had fun back then, and I'm having fun now. It's neat to explore the Halo universe in a different way than normal and seeing all of the weapons, vehicles, and characters represented makes it exciting to get a new unit type or upgrade. The AI is competent enough which is good because the online matchmaking is a ghost town populated by tumbleweeds and the occasional reincarnation of Sun Tzu who proceed to school your ignorant undisciplined♥♥♥♥♥then leaves without a word. The best part, though, is the campaign. There's tons of varied missions, the secondary objectives are all nice diversions, and in true Halo form there's incentive for exploration in the form of Black Boxes and Skulls. You can try to beat your scores on higher difficulties and more handicaps via finding Skulls and it can make easy missions suddenly more challenging.
In short, it's not an amazing strategy game but if you like Halo it's a nice addition to its universe and a fun way to kill an afternoon.

Since I have played Metro 2033 Redux it was time to move on to Metro Last Light. I was already experienced in what the world is actually like and knew what to expect from the game. Of course there were few things that I was dissapointed in, but in the end the game was outstanding, and answered my questions on the plot.
The graphics are just amazing. I didn't like the look of the new world, where the Nuclear Winter is slowly ending. I prefered the old world from the Metro 2033. But it doesn't mean that it is bad either! It is still the old, outstanding world, where humans are on the brink of extinction. (for more on the graphics look at my Metro 2033 Redux review)
The main positive point of the Metro Last Light and it is a big improvement over the Metro 2033 is the story. Metro 2033 had a very good story, but Metro Last Light had even better. I felt even more sad and depressed, and made me question of how one stupid move can end all of us. Where in Metro 2033 you mainly battled monsters, in Metro Last Light you battle your own race to prevent the Communist Red Line from taking over the Metro, and destroying humanity. I particularly enjoyed commentary from the Baby Dark One, a child left out as one of the last intelligent mutants. The child was questioning how people may have turned such a beautiful world into something as such, how humans despite being low on numbers still are killing each other, and how humans feel about different things. He highlighted the "evil" people that wanted to kill Artyom, the people that were "good" but ready to kill, and those that didn't want to kill but had to (for example Pavel). And then the final battle for the D6 made me feel proud of who I am in the game. Another thing I have to mention is how Artyom feels guilty for what he has done in the previous game. He now knows that he has done wrong and killed off one of the most peaceful species out there.
But enough of the plot. I don't want to spoil it all for you ;) . And trust me there are plenty of things to talk about.
Since you don't fight mutants as much you won't encounter as interesting beasts as in Metro 2033. Librarians in particular I really miss.
Let's give this game a final score. I believe it deserves a 9/10 for being an improvement of already a beast of the game Metro 2033. Why did I give such a score:
+ Beautiful graphics
+ Plot is outstanding and filled with emotions
+ Baby Dark One is an excellent addition and one of the most interesting characters
+ All characters that you encounter (apart from maybe strippers and civilians you don't talk to) have amazing backgrounds
+ A great final endings
+ Cinematics add a great emotional feel to the game
+ Artyom's guilt made me feel sorry for him
- All women you encounter get naked for some reason (#teenage porn)
- Less mutants
- Romance with Anna sucked (the sex scene was ok at most but even I can make evenings with my missus more romantic when playing War Thunder)
- Strip club (what was the point of it?)
- DRM (what is the point of buying a game on the disc if you will use the disc once?)

After over 2000 hours of being server alpha of Official 384 (Hardcore PVP) I will admit the grind got to be too much. It was literally a second job taking care of no less then 4 of every dino tameable at the time (I stopped right after Redwoods were added to The Island) And when the patch hit that made giga's die within a day of not being fed (And I lost my prized giga at the time among over a dozen others that we had raised from babies) I just lost heart for the grind. Honestly looking at your mods/rules you aren't just removing the grind you are moving key elements of the game. I have a private server running now for my friends and I and in my attempts to remove the grind I just simply x10 harvest gathering/xp/taming speed/breeding and x5 quality in loot chests (This would be the questionable one for removing difficulty but is still a modless adjustment).  Sure this may seem like overkill but the game finally seems peaceful. If I want a super T-Rex I still have to do the grinding of slaughtering Rexes until the right combinations of 140+'s spawn and then breed the hell out of them over and over again to get stats to drop etc. While that seems like a grind as well its more an element of the game. The grind is how long it takes to do the actions you put in work, the wait time. I honestly havent been happier with ark since doing this. We didn't remove any of the difficulty just the 3 weeks of crossbreeding, and the looting 1000 red cave chests to get a few usefull pieces of ascendant gear blueprints. We still have to explore all the caves with the dino's we tame and breed and still have to defeat the challenges laid out before us. We are playing in Ragnarok atm and almost made it to the end of the ice dungeon but realized we didn't pack enough backup armor. We now know for next time and will rise to the challenege.
I do agree that engram points for levels are pretty dumb, and prefer the 7 days to die method, if you can harvest you can craft. (Though they have levels to affect quality as well) but having a high level character on a Hardcore PVP server did mean something more so than on a non Hardcore server. And the character stats tied to the level still makes the level mean something. Honestly though once you get enough blueprints for all the items that roll percenatages (Saddles, weapons, armor etc) You will still have more than enough engram points to craft all the non percentage items in the game comfortably.
This being said the reason there are so many private servers in this game, everyone does have a way they feel it should be set up and played. Which is what makes the game so great and the dev's so great for allowing us such freedom within it (Despite all the bad feedback they seem to get... can't make everyone happy) So enjoy the game how you feel is right, and if you enjoy the game but not an aspect of it maybe find out how you can change that aspect with a private server or whatever else to get your full enjoyment out of the game! Games are meant for relaxing and competition, The grind is there for the competition aspect, the game is there to relax, choose your path and enjoy. There really is enjoyment for almost everyone in this game and especially within their genre.

Last Light is an improvement on the core of the original game in every way. The story ramps up, with Artyom attempting to rectify his major mistake from the first game & uncovering a plot to take over the metro. New weapons include pistols, shotguns, actual sniper rifles & land mines. New locations & characters abound; the Metro has never looked more alive & varied. Levels are larger, more interesting & even less linear (in most cases). If you're a big fan of the "thinking shooters" like Bioshock or the new Fallout games then I suggest you pick this up, along with the redux version of the first game.
The only negative that comes to mind is tonally it's divorced from the first game. The first one had a dower & cold feel, while Last Light is much more "Hollywood" with a lot more explosions & bewbs. I feel that the first metro is superior in that regard.

If you have played any of the newer Artifex Mundi games, then you already know what to expect with this one:
- colourful and beautifully drawn backgrounds
- a cheesy story involving a female protagonist vs. an occult evil enemy
- good voice acting and music
- ugly character designs that make the original Sims look downright sophisticated
- mini-games involving rotating discs and tiles
- intuitive item-based adventure puzzles
- amazingly crisp and clear hidden object screens (HOSs)
- an alternative mini-game option if you don't like the HOSs, in this case Monoco
- a bonus mission that enhances the story (hidden under the "extras" section)
- an animal companion (a monkey) that can be used as an inventory object
- achievements that require playing through the game twice (once for the HOSs, and once for the games of Monoco)
The game starts off feeling a bit boring and railroaded, but it quickly picks up once the occult elements come into play. I like what they did aesthetically with the mirroring of locations and puzzles.
There aren't quite as many HOSs as I would have liked, but I enjoyed the ones that were there, and I liked how they kept getting more and more absurd as the game went on. I honestly never thought I'd be scouring a puzzle to find a "chicken manicure," but this game just said, "You know what? severed chicken feet deserve to feel pretty too." I can respect that.
There were a handful of repeated puzzle screens, but most of the time the game either changed something about the visuals to make it feel fresh, or it had you searching for a different set of items than the first time. The bonus mission got a bit lazy in this regard, though.
There were also a few labeling snafus in the HOSs, such as a vinyl record being labeled as a plate, a bowl being labeled as a record, and a fan being labeled as a "windwill." Just one good beta test would have caught these errors.
As an alternative to the HOSs, you can play a game of Monoco. I had never heard of this game before, and they don't provide you with in-game instructions (unless that was part of the general tutorial that I skipped), so I was a bit lost trying to figure out what to do. Basically, the goal is to clear all of the fancy-bordered tiles by matching them with adjacent tiles that share the same core image. You can also make matches between two normal cards to clear them from the board and shift tiles over, but only the fancy cards count towards solving the puzzle. As you make matches, meters will fill up in the side bar. When a meter is full, you can click on it to clear an entire row, column, or set of symbols from the board.
On the whole, the HOSs and mini-games were too easy, even by genre standards. It almost felt like the game didn't know who its audience was, since the subject matter dealt with horror and death, but the puzzles felt child-like in their simplicity.
Another thing to note about the mini-games is that a few rely on colour recognition. You are able to skip these challenges, but colourblind individuals will have difficulty if they are going for any of the mini-game completion achievements.
In the game, you get a monkey companion who can be used as an object to fetch hard-to-reach items. He will screech on any screen that requires you to use him. I like this game mechanic because it makes more sense in the context of a carnival to be running around with a trained monkey than with an armful of poles, ladders, and grappling hooks.
One side thing that kind of amused me was that the writers of this game know nothing about fires. Rubbing two pieces of flint together will not create a fire, and pouring water on an electric fire will not put it out. Smokey Bear should pay these guys a visit.
Overall, this is a fairly standard formulaic title from Artifex Mundi. If you like their other games, and are looking for something in the same vein, you will not be disappointed. If you are just a fan of HOGs in general, and want to play a game with good graphics, a coherent enough story, very casual puzzles, the ability to play a card game if you get stuck, and built-in bonus content, then definitely give this a try. It doesn't have nearly the same gravitas or challenge level as some of the studio's other games, but it scratches the HOG itch pretty well. I give it a 7.5/10.

Not Artifex Mundi's best effort.  I am a big fan of their previous outings (see my reviews), but this one left much to be desired.  Even on expert mode, it was far too easy and incredibly straightforward.  It's quite a shame given that their track record is typically very good, but I guess they can't all be amazing works.
Dark Arcana is standard Mundi fare with HOGs sandwiched between various puzzles and item fetches.  There's nothing you don't expect in here and naturally, the creepy character models make a triumphant return.  Oddly, the fortune teller is animated very differently with classic "open mouth" animation whereas other characters speak with typical mouth-morphing "lip sync".  At any rate, not that we play these games for story, this one is a bit of a stinker, imo, but more importantly, the puzzles make absolutely no sense.  Granted, in a Mundi game, many puzzles are somewhat out of place in the way you wonder why the police station in Raccoon City is so ridiculously push-blocky.  However, here, there just seems to be a disconnect, moreso than in other Mundi games, and I felt that Dark Arcana was phoned in; even the items in the HOGs don't randomize like they usually do.  What gives?
Finally, the HOG minigame alternative this time is Monaco, a weird match-two game where choosing cards in a row, a column, or diagonally will determine which way the remaining ones shift.  It's largely unfun and keep in mind that I despise shanghai/mahjong when I say this - I would rather play shanghai/mahjong.
Anyways, if you have a choice of Mundi games, I would choose another one, but this one will keep you occupied for a couple of hours.  I wouldn't recommend it at the $10 price point, but if it's in a bundle, might as well grab some achievements.

Dystopia might be the single most complex multiplayer shooter I've ever played. 2 teams of cyberpunk badasses duke it out in a series of immensely complex objective-driven attack/defend maps. Explaining any one of them usually requires 30 minutes and a couple of whiteboards. Explaining some of the weapons requires a notepad. Explaining how something as simple as the respawn timer works still involves a lecture and a couple of diagrams.
Back in its heyday, there were maybe only 1,000 people in the world who actually understood enough of this game to be able to play it. I know more than that are capable, and I'd love to see it re-emerge.

Back when this game first made waves and before Snail games bought out Wildcard and raised the price to $60, it was a joy to play on the official servers and on personal servers with your friends. Eventually progress slowed and the game lost the magic. However, the game has been trending downhill since. While development has been decently consistent the player experience has definantly suffered. The new map expansions were a decent attempt to revitalize the game. The new "DLC" islands are for the more experienced surviavalist and offer a new experience in the early to mid-game, the late game remains fairly unchanged. While I'm not upset about the fact these extra map expansions cost just that much more ontop of a now very expensive game.
In addition the game files for the expansions install regardless of if you own the expansions or not. This turns an already large game into an unnecessarily large game that eats up nearly 109 GB (108791 MB) which is an unrealistic amount of space one should expect casual to moderate players to be able to spare for a single game. Hardcore suvivalists will be willing to spare the harddrive space but most people won't be willing to part with that much memory. This memory burden is also not reflected in the minimum requirements, which at the moment I am writing this review says that for windows I need only 60GB of available space.
As much as I enjoyed my time on the ARK it takes some serious commitment to the game to continue to support the game in its current incarnation.

A hidden object game that has good ideas and nice variety, with very questionable development choices that lead to a severe lack and an overabundance of plot and atmosphere at the same time.
On the surface Dark Arcana: The Carnival is like most hidden object games: it starts by introducing a female investigator who arrives at a strange place to find a missing person. Normally this leads to a stereotypical story, but the writing quickly falls apart: this police detective too casually accepts the existence of a magical mirror world ruled by the Evil One (yes, that really is its name). Still, all is not lost, since the third act has some excellent writing and clever plot twists that make up for the blunders of the first two acts.
The gameplay has a similar dichotomy. The hidden object scenes are either impossibly crowded or too empty. The puzzles are usually easy, but the amount of backtracking is just insane… at least it helps to boost the game time well over three hours.
If you like Artifex Mundi, Dark Arcana is a solid pick, but for the average hidden object game fan it is recommended to play through the publisher’s other games first.

CONS

I want anyone who reads this review to understand that I don't normally, "never" post reviews and that I also feel that a review is only good when you consider the likes and dislikes of the reviewer.
I did receive this game for free as part of the developers Beta testing group.  I did not feel any obligation to post a review until I left my feedback with the game developer and within hours was thoroughly responded back to.  The response gave me confidence that they were taking our feedback seriously and are going to make postive upgrades.
-a little about my likes so you can understand where my review is coming from.
I like strategy games that are open with some micromanaging aspects.  Civ 5, Total War Franchise, etc.  I also like games that allow me to create and progress Characters/Towns.  I fast sim most battles so the lack of fancy graphics for epic battles does not play a role for me.  I don't play multiplayer "I am a happy hermit"
-Alright enough of that now on to Feudalism
-Pros-
*Deep Tech Research
*Ease of control over large amounts of villages
*A lot of Village advancements
*An easy progression into confrontation "hate games that always have some punk attacking me on like the 5th turn"
*Decent Diplomacy "this area has some flaws but is relatively easy to navigate"
*Family Tree "this area also has its flaws but once you learn that giving tasks such as diplomacy to children is a bad idea you will be able to respond to other Factions directly"  Also, just a note on this topic.  I found that giving control of diplomacy, unit building, and facility building can cause actions that you are not expecting. For Example...You are offered a treaty for trade and your kid rejects it before you have a chance to answer.
*Hours of gameplay
-Cons- "Some of which I asked the developer directly about and was given reassurance they would be addressed"
*Tech Tree -  What leads to what?  This is one that the developer told me they were working on providing a guide.
*Factions - What are the pros and cons to each faction?  Also another area that they will be providing a guide.

For the full price - forget about it. When there is a
on, something around 75% off - still think twice. The The whole game is a series of disappointinng shortfalls. Here's my story explaning why:
I noticed Contrast over a year ago and the concept of the game, coupled with what I saw on the trailers and in the screenshots, had me really wanting this game. The price though was a bit steep, so I only got it on sale recently. And I'm mighty glad I waited. Without further ado, here's what's wrong with the game.
First of all, the
feels like scribbled down on a knee five minutes before the writers had a deadline to submit it. Nothing to keep the player interested, just a generic tale of a child and her parents don't quite form a perfect family. The characters, save the protagonist, are shallow, one-dimensional and there's little reason for anyone to form any sort of emotional bond with them. The only chance of livening up the plot
is merely reduced to finding some collectibles and one scene just before the credits.
Secondly, the
is, to put it bluntly, rubbish. Platformers in the 90's offered better game mechanics. The fantasticly promising concept of manipulating lights and shifting between shadows and the 'real' world is there just so you can jump on some platforms and move one or two boxes around. Nothing else. And one more thing here: the player character gains some skills for no apparent reason and then hardly ever uses them.
The
are simple but even there you can find an issue, as the shifting mechanism often has a mind of its own and Dawn gets thrown off the platforms without the fault on the side of the player.
. To be fair, the game looks alright. Nothing remarkable though. The models are edgy, locations deserted for the most part (I'm talking here about items, not characters - the lack of the latter is just part of the game) but the overall feeling is positive. The atmosphere in the locations is nice, kind of gloomy and decadent at the same time.
On the other hand, the
is where the game should deliver and fails completely. The protagonist is said to be an acrobat. Therefore, her moves should be fluent, graceful and light, which they only are when the character is walking slowly or standing still and I'm not convinced that this should be the case in an action game. The animations of Dawn interacting with objects or moving stuff, as well as thhe animations of all other characters feel terribly outdated.
Finally, the
, where the game promises much but delivers little. Despite what you might think having seen the trailers, there is in fact very litle music in the game. Soundtrack activates only when the player apporaches a certain location. Truth be told, the best piece of music was the one in the main menu. Character voicing is just wrong, its highlight being Dawn, who simply says nothing throughout the entire game.
Fortunately, Contrast is a very short game, in jusr 4 hours I manged to obtain a 100% playthrough. I say fortunately because I could not bear any more of the feeling that there's a game that could have been brilliant and turned out mediocre.
Pros:
Cons:
A final note: the ending hints, rather obviously, at a sequel. Unless the developers do some serious work to deliver a more complete experience with a story and gameplay to match its lovely graphics style its going to be, at least for me, a flop. So a word to the producers: Please, please do it right, because I so want the concept to be given the game it deserves.

This one goes right to the top of the "All-Time Best Futuristic/Cyberpunk FPS" list. Despite not building it from scratch and using a very high-quality tool already available in the market, the Dystopia (amateur) team managed to replace virtually all of the artistic assets and core aspects of gameplay on Valve's Half-Life 2 Source graphics/physics engine. Released for free for the first time in 2005, Dystopia delivered an ultra hi-tech, fast paced FPS that takes you into a heavily computerized post-modern world.
The game takes place in 2069 and depicts a world dominated by megacorporations. In its universe, players are spawned as combat clones and fight for two warring factions, either as oppressed renegades (Punk Mercenaries) or private security contractors (Corporate Security Forces).
There are many of them, each with its own agenda and modus operandi. They are essentially any group operating against corporations. While not necessarily outlaws, the vast majority of punks are wanted by governments or corporations around the globe. Punks are organisations of people that can be hired for mercenary missions and/or that operate outside of the "normal boundary" of the law. These groups range from highly trained special forces to the local mafia's hitmen. Any form of contractual mercenary force, operating without proper documentation, is illegal in almost all modern countries. Discovery of a contract can be disastrous to both the client and the punk organisation. This leads to many clandestine meetings in back-alleys between corporate and punk representitives. It is dangerous to make connections with a punk organisation, not only because of legal reasons but also because of the unpredictability and secrecy of the groups. Hired Punk factions can be allied with a rival organisation of the client. Revenge killings are not unknown. Double-crossing is also disastrous, occuring when a Punk faction accepts contracts from opposing forces, and secretly sabotages both, while taking both payments.
There are tens of thousands of registered corporations around the world, operating on different fields of industry and following distinct guidelines. Some are huge like WalkTek or DataTrust. Most single corporations are owned by other, larger corporations.
It's tempting to say that in 2069 the Mega Corporations have taken all the power from the world governments, but this is not entirely true. The relationship is usually symbiotic and governments are completely dependant on corporate trade, technology and security to maintain their peace and economy. Without the corporations, many nations would literally wither out and die. At the same time, corporations have no desire to govern. In fact much of their strength stems from not ruling. They, instead, delegate this task to the governments of the world, which maintain the social order and public infrastructure necessary for a stable economy. The governments create a place in which the corporations can thrive.
Along with the backstory and highly detailed environments, one of the great features you'll notice as soon as you login to Dystopia is a kickass soundtrack by techno artist Bioxeed. It really adds up to the immersion.
The primary game mode is asymmetrical and objective driven, one team holds out while the other fights against the clock. Players battle against each other in both the physical world (known commonly as meatspace) and the virtual world (cyberspace), with actions in one having an effect on the other. Every map contains a sequence of objectives. Each of these objectives is unique, located in its own area, and associated with multiple interactive devices. The offensive team must complete every objective on the map to win a round.
Because of
, each environment is dual-layered and demands coordinated action from both teams. Cyberspace is a three-dimensional manifestation of computer networks, a second world sprung from technological advancement. Deckers use cerebral implants to leave their meat-sacks behind and fight over the tangible, digital realm. As avatars, they traverse the memory of servers, execute programs (up to 13 of them are available), align with different protocols and pass through data links. Servers contain nodes that house the control panels of crucial devices. Programs let players interact with these nodes, dissolve opposing avatars, and accelerate their own movement.
Bloody carnage fills
. In this future, organizations get away with murder, but for clones, respawn technology means death is temporary. Keeping the enemy dead and teammates alive requires superior aim, tactical positioning, and communication. Loadouts are fully customizable, and with every respawn comes a chance to change armor class, primary weapon, and implant selection.
Light, Medium, and Heavy Augmented Armors are available - each have with their own unique strengths and weaknesses with varying amounts of health and armor. Choose up to four primary weapons and further customize your selected class by equipping different class based special abilities - implants.
with more armor jump higher, have more health, and have more powerful weapons. Classes with less armor are smaller, have more implant diversity, move faster, and have shorter respawn penalties.
Each class has different
, and every player respawns with a primary weapon, a melee weapon, some grenades, a machine pistol and some ammo. There are 18 destructive weapons in total, 12 high powered primary weapons, as well as special dispensers that resupply ammo for them and the machine pistol.
You can choose between 14
to customize your loadout. Active implants drain energy, and are triggered by the player. They won't work without enough energy. Passive implants do not drain energy, and don't need to be triggered. They can all be temporarily disabled by the blast of an EMP grenade.
There are two implant groups: head and body. Lights and mediums have a different number of head and body implant slots. Players may change implants each time they spawn.
There are 14
and a large amount of
in Dystopia. Players are free to develop and submit their own, however they must ensure they integrate well within the game universe, and that they're the highest quality possible. To see a walkthrough for a map, you can navigate to its page and click the "Walkthrough" link. These walkthroughs help familiarize new players with the relatively complex map gameplay found in Dystopia.
Dystopia's team oriented gameplay is extremely suitable for
, and teams have continued to form and participate in Dystopia’s clan scene since the mod's release. A persistent statistics tracking system keeps track of every players combat stats across all active Dystopia servers. Several tournaments and leagues have been organized, and the developer tries to keep the game competitive and balanced with each update.
Team Dystopia is an amateur team that has worked their asses off on their spare time to create this highly detailed, immersive, futuristic, action-packed cyberpunk multiplayer game. It's completely free to play and they're even working slowly on an Unreal Engine 4
upgrade, so go ahead and assume the role of a heavily-augmented combat mercenary armed to the teeth with the latest in combat technology, or a twitch-reflex cyberdecker rushing to infiltrate cyberspace nodes! Jack in and kick some as$!

Halo: Wars is definitely an RTS made for Halo fans. Extremely little variety in just about every aspect. There's only two playable factions, the UNSC and the Covenant, and each faction has three interchangeable heroes who offer a very limited change in units and abilities. I mean, we're talking it changes almost nothing about how you play. On top of that, maps only get as big as 3v3, and I don't even think you can do free for alls? There's hardly any map options, and when compared to an RTS like Warcraft III, that's much older than it, it simply isn't worth the money. Not even at the discounted price of 11 something I got it at. The campaign is the only thing of substance here, if you like the Halo universe it's cool. But if you're here more for the RTS aspect I can't recommend it.
Now if they REALLY wanted to make this interesting, they could've added so many other things. More maps, more units, more playable races, more heroes. Battle for Middle-Earth II would have been a great example for them to follow. Yeah, sure. Isengard, Morder, and Goblins are all working for the forces of evil under Sauron. But they have enough creative ideas and liberties that they could make them all interesting factions on their own. They didn't even attempt that with this. We could've gotten a Flood race like the Zerg from Starcraft. Hell, maybe divide the Covenant up into two or three different factions. Like with the Banished in 2, it's not hard to get creative and add more flavor to your game. This is just lazy.
Tl;dr if you're looking for a great RTS, look elsewhere. If you're looking for a Halo game, just stick with the FPS. But if you're really excited about the concept of a Halo RTS, then yeah. Pick it up. You got no other options :(

I got this game for free about an hour ago and I love doing first impression reviews. Some think that below an hour can't tell you anything, I say it is helpful when a game just released and its all you have to go on. I am here to give you the first look before buying on a whim.
I certaintly wouldn't call this game amazing or better than many other 4x games. It does however do its job. You expand your empire, you build facilities in villages to expand from within and of course you can expand through military domination.
The best way to explain this game's...okayness..is through the age old pro con list:
+Turn-Based Strategy fits well
+A lot to research and advance
+Military Strategy and Formations which a lot of strategy games seem to be lacking these days
+Dynasty System
+Espionage works wonders
+It's not early access but, this has a lot of promise if devs stick with it
+So far, no gamebreaking bugs
+Events and other notifications has cool, feudal period art
+You can customize your victory conditions. Like instead of winning when you have 100% of tech, you can make it 25%
-No Achievements
-I suffer lag often when weather changes or I switch to a new board [I'll get more into that in a second]
-No option to turn off music
-Combat is really clunky and hard to really tell whats going on. Tutorial does not teach combat
-Speaking of Tutorial, it covers only the basics
-Colonizing other boards is confusing...how do I populate the colonies? Tutorial says nothing
-Diplomacy is bad
-UI and Graphics are an eye sore
-You can't scroll through the notifications, think Civ V, you right click to dismiss notifications to see all of them...can't do that here

First off, something I usually look forward to in a game: the soundtrack. It's absolutely amazing! Right from the tutorial level, I got excited just hearing the music, and couldnt wait to hear the rest of the game's soundtrack.
The game itself looks very visually stunning. Something I like is that each level has its own theme, and when selecting levels, you also get to jump around the environment to get to the levels, which gives you an idea what the actual levels themselves will be like. Each environment has a different thing you have to clean; There's sludge for one level, leaves for another, etc. etc.. I thought that was a nice touch. But the whole game is nicely animated and well-drawn!! <3
Now to the important part: Gameplay. This has to be the best part of the game; The controls actually may take a bit used to get to, but practicing is fun!! You have to be quick when finishing levels (as well as making sure you don't mess up), since breaking your combo will give you a lower score. This gets a bit frustrating if you want perfect scores on the levels, but it's hard to stay frustrated at this game, since the visuals are amazing and the music is rather calming. There are plenty of levels to play, so don't worry about the game being too short. If you're a completionist who loves platformers, I reccomend you pick up this game! There's alot to offer!
Overall, I'd give this game an 8/10. Great soundtrack combined with stunning visuals, though the controls can take a bit of practice, I'd say you should definantly get this game if you like platforming games!! (and possibly if you're a clean-freak)
