Before I came across CK2 my experience of strategy games was mostly with the Total War franchise, which I loved. I really enjoyed the campaign map gameplay too. So when I played CK2 I was awestruck by the level of detail and scope the game gives you. Firstly, you can choose to start at any year between 1066 and 1322 (I think), so there is so much to look at and so much choice. I found myself just facinated at what happened in each year before I played the actual game. Then, you can also play as and ruler in Europe, North Africa, and the Middle-East within this timeframe. But it gets better. You can play as ANY ruler, so you can even play as a count within a kingdom or empire, under a duke, king or emperor. Any level except barons are playable. Add all this to the sheer unpredictability of the game and how things happen differently with each playthrough, there is so much replay-ability in the game.
There are loads of interesting details that I could go on about forever, but in short, you can take parrt in a number of things such as, crusades, factions, rebellion, political intrigue, plots, role-playing, and so much more.
Though the positives for the game are countless, to be fair I've got to mention the problems/issues. Firstly, you will need a period of time to get used to the game given its complex nature, so don't expect to be a pro anytime before about 30-40 hours. Secondly, the main problem with this game actually is more to do with the way its given to us. If you look, there an incredible amount of DLC, so many little extras and expansion packs to buy to add on. Its well over £100's worth of DLC, so if you want the whole package definitely wait for a sale (do so anyway really, it will be on eventually). Don't bother with the Republics or Aztecs expansions because they are rubbish and pretty much a waste of money, unless you get the complete pack. The way they try to get money out of you through DLC is actually shameful, but it doesnt change how good a game it is.

I bought this game when the price droped as I did not have the time to invest to play this against other players.
The more modern equipment made me want this game as I like the cold war military stuff.
But the game seems to have a pretty steep learning curve and I get the idea you must exacly do what the developer wants while playing the campaign or you are not going to make it.
The realism is nice but I would have prefered some player preference options like showing the visibility range of a selected unit like we could in Ruse or weapons ranges would also have made the game a bit more enjoyable for me.
For example I was playing on a level with a hill and the units  hidden in the trees would not engage a command unit sitting at the base of the hill for no clear reason , but i suspect there was an issue with visibility.
Another improvement would have been some clarification of weapons, unless your are really into military equipment you have no idea what the weapon does except for what you can make from its name and picture.
The campaign missions can easily take you an hour and more to complete.
You also must try to loose as few units as possible because those units can not be "bought" in next campaigns when lost.
Here too I would have liked to see a player preference option as it can suck the fun out of the game.
But these cons are not enough to give up so I keep trying to complete the campaign levels.
Thats why I would recommend this game but only to players who are looking for a more complex micromanagement heavy game in a cold war setting.

Clicker heroes, the modern masterpiece is one of the greatest games to ever exist on planet earth, released on the 6th of August 2014, created by the amazing company, Playsaurus, receiving an astounding 9/10 on steam for its near perfection, to this day three years later people are still as close to the end of the game as they were when they started, because the game is literally endless, the simple yet addicting gameplay is what makes this game cherished and loved throughout the world, the feeling of satisfaction of reaching unheard damage, earning an amount of money that surpasses the amount of particles in the universe... That is what makes this game, simply perfect.
Playsaurus not only nailed the gameplay aspect of Clicker Heroes, but revolutionised the idle clicker genre for years to come, introducing the ingenious mechanic of ascension and ancients, a mechanic that allows the game to continue on forever, and you don’t have to be there for the entire game, if you don’t have enough time on your hands, all it takes is a few minutes to open the game, upgrade your heroes, and thats it, thats all you need to do, and then you will progress and you can check on it later. The gameplay is simple, you click, which can be boring, but compared to the amount of time you’ll feel like an unstoppable force for, that beginning part is miniscule. As soon as you reach level 100 you are able to ascend, allowing you to buy ancients, allowing you to then increase idle damage, making it advised to not click in the game, and after gaining all those numbers and seeing how quickly things fall to your damage is satisfying to say the least.
I’ll get this part over with done, this game does have some flaws, if only 1 or 2. To begin with, transcendence (restarting the game to gain more hero souls) makes the game boring, like start of the game boring, but all you gotta do is to get to level 100 again and it’s back to tremendous damage and money, also another problem with the game is that it’s free, which isn’t the problem, but the fact that there is microtransactions to speed up the game are included, but that isn’t a big problem, you can easily avoid them by playing the actual game and being patient.
One great part of clicker heroes is that literally anyone can play it, it has no favoured audience allowing for anyone to play it, from school students to full time working adults, it can be easily accessed by anyone and everyone, at school, at home, doesn’t matter where you are, as long as you have a computer or a phone you can play this incredible piece of art.
So overall, I’d easily give this game a 10/10, the perfect blend of clicking and being idle, making the game boring but taking you right out of it as soon it starts to go that way, the simple concept and the brilliance used to execute it, the satisfaction of reaching unnamed numbers, the fact that it will never end, and it will never get boring is the reason this would be one of my favourite games for years to come, and the best part is, Clicker Heroes, the instant classic, is getting a sequel.

Yes and No,
No for the simple fact that this game is a rushed port from console and the controls aren't as fluid as they should really be and also for the fact that the game is very simplistic and rather shallow for content.
And yes for being simplistic it is relatively easy to pick up and play hence why it was developed for the 360 years ago, because consoles do not have the correct input devices for truely deep Real-time strategy games. The game is fun and hosts a medium-long campaign testing your capabilities to handle certain situations, In addition this game hosts a simple combat effectiveness system:
Some units are good against Air.
Some units are good against Vehicles.
Some units are good against Infantry.
Some units are for utility.
Some units are all around good.

I'd consider "Contrast" one of the "Indie gems" of our time.
It's a modern game with some fresh ideas, but also obvious roots in some classics.
The whole design, the art, the music, the story, the levels, the mechanics, it all plays together very well, creating a rounded experience.
The story soon became more intense than I expected, driving me forwards, wanting to know what happens next.
The levels, puzzles and platform sequenses aren't very big or difficult, though sometimes there are little to no indicators what to do next, just a little exploration or trial should provide the solution.
The main mechanic of using light and shadow is just amazing, used in various ways, keeping it interesting, only sometimes it seems a little rough/ glitchy.
The only "negative" i could say about the whole game is that i would've wished for some more of it all, a little bit more story, a little bit more gameplay to go through, (even) more things that could've been done with the mechanics and a bit more smoothing out the little edges of the game. So i would wish for a bigger, second part, or a spinoff or something, but that's not even really a bad thing to say about "Contrast" itself.

How and where to begin this review? Like most story driven games, I shall begin with the plot and the setting. Both of these strive very well indeed; however, due to the game's short length (roughly four hours for me), the story unravels greatly towards the end. You can see where Compulsion Games were wanting to go with it, but unforunately the developers were told to wrap it up, and it shows in Act III.
It was disappointing because the noir setting was surperb, and the story soars in Acts I and II. The music and voice acting are top notch. I also loved the idea of Dawn being an imaginary friend and the concept of traveling from the real world to the shadow world.
However, the controls in this game is what did it for me. The game is a platformer, which I admit that I am okay at them. Dawn would not stop getting stuck on little things or would pop out the shadow world even when there weren't any conflicting shadows nearby. There were also numerous times in which you should be able to jump onto a simple ledge in the 3D world that was only waist high; however, Dawn would refuse to jump onto it. And due to the game's short length the puzzles weren't that hard to solve. The mouse is what controls your camera angle, and it felt like you had to barely move it or else everything goes haywire.
All in all, Contrast is a game that had so much potential and soars through the air in the first two Acts. Then, it faceplants in the third act. I did buy this during the Steam Summer, so for just $7.99 (got the soundtrack as well) I did get my money's worth....just wished that there were tighter controls and a longer game length.

This is the first F2P game i have seen that is done right, and for that Digital Extremes have my utmost respect.
I first picked this up around mid 2013 if i remember correctly but i quickly got bored with it, because in my honest opinion, at that time it was not that enjoyable. My brother however, stuck around, kept playing. Fast forward to mid 2016. Ive recently returned from a year abroad, and my brother is urging me to pick up Warframe again. At first im hesitant, but as i do im blown away by how far this game has come. I started playing more and by now i can say, i wont be stopping anytime soon.
So lets get this done. Yes the game is free to play but NO it is not pay to win. You can spend money on it, which is fair since DE has paychecks to fill after all. Therefore you obviously can spend lots of money on Warframe, but the balance is so good, that you dont have to pay to advance at a reasonable pace but you also get rewarded for paying nevertheless. There are no paywalls whatsoever but if you are impatient or simply cant invest as much time as youd like, there is the option to pay real money for that.
Also dont get me started on the lore. There is so much hidden info in this game, that even now, after completing all quests and sorta unterstanding what has been given out so far, i still have questions, i still want to find out more about the Tenno and their world.
DE have created a masterpiece of a game here, and i highly urge you to give it a try too, if you can tolerate some levels of grind along the way. So far im very impressed by what DE have done and how much thought they have put into this.
If there is one game that shows how much good potential the Free 2 Play genre has, its Warframe.

Unlike traditional shoot 'em ups, you don't have to start from the beginning when you lose. You don't even run out of continues. You keep going until you beat the level or decide you've had enough.
One benefit in this game is the local co-op multi-player. You can have up to four people playing with you at once. And it's a blast.
The graphics won't wow you, but they're pretty. The polygons remind me of the PS1/PS2 era of gaming. The look reminds me of anime, which shouldn't surprise you since you're playing a mech. While you won't mistake this as having a "retro" look, it is definitely nostalgic.
The music is a high point as it should be since at once point you're fighting a
. Regarding the sound effects, the best it can be described is as "arcade-y". It's fun!
I've tested this game on a variety of hardware: an i7 tower with a GTX 1050 Ti running Windows, a Thinkpad T440p running Ubuntu with integrated graphics, and an HP Stream 11 running Windows with integrated graphics. It runs with flying colours on all three. It runs well with low and hi resolution graphics. If you bought virtually any new computer within the past 5 years, you should be able to run this.
I bought this in a bundle, so I didn't pay anywhere near the full price. That said, the value largely wrests on who you are. If you're an old hand at shoot 'em ups, you could probably find cheaper games that scratch that itch. However, if you're looking for a good game to buy a child, or are just looking for short co-op action with a friend, then this is well worth the money.
It was a fun few hours that I spent with this game. The graphics and sound were nice. Though there's nothing innovative going on with this game, the formula works. Certainly some people might find this too easy, but then again, hard shoot 'em ups are plentiful. Score: 4/5

Wargame:EE is a mostly realistic RTS of which the setting is Europe during 1965-1975. You play as either a PACT or NATO country during the Cold War when all hell brakes loose. You use everything but Navy and Air Force in this game, to control strategic points, control high ground and set up ambushes on your enemy. You need to strategically place everything from ATGM's to recon units to almost every significant tank variant in the world at that time (T-55, T-62, T-72, T-80, M48 Super, M1 Abrams, Leopard 2A1) or you will lose. This isn't the type of RTS you can spam factories and a single unit and win, there are no factories and you need strategy. You also have to worry about logistics, for example, a ATGM soldier only carries from 6-12 rockets, you will need supply trucks close by to keep him full on ammo. All in all they created a pretty good game 8/10, my only quarrel with it is the command stars system, It takes entirely way too long unlock your multiplayer "deck" so you suffer with low level tanks as others still playing mp are running full decks, that, and the units you unlock in the difficult campaign do not carry over, but still very minor annoyances.

I loved 2033 for its immersiveness and relatively not-hand-holding gameplay. The levels were basically linear but with a bunch of little nooks and crannies and dead ends you could wander off into and find ammo or medkits or whatever, basically straight from the start of the game. You could carry a small arsenal with a bunch of random grenades and knives and it felt like playing a real packrat, possibly the most immersive FPS I've ever played. Everything felt meaty and real.
I gave Last Light an hour, and in that time it showed none of the charm of the first game. The first thing that struck me once I got out into the game with free reign on my weapons was the knife was no longer its own weapon. The knife in 2033 wasn't particularly good from a gameplay standpoint but it felt like a real knife, you had to manually pull it out and it had a weight to it. In Last Light it's replaced with the magical lightning fast quick melee that too many games have these days, tap V and your knife teleports into your hand, slashes instantly and teleports back to its sheathe all in around a second. There's a place for quick melee in games, but I don't think it's here. The same thing happened when I got some throwing knives in a prison, tap C and whip a knife with no weight to it out of nowhere. The movement felt similarly disappointing, it's slow but doesn't feel like a natural slowness, just like someone took Half Life or whatever and halved the walking speed. All in all the gameplay just felt cheaper and less real.
The level design was similarly disappointing, I looked in every single corner I could find and scrounged up nothing but a couple journals that rather than being notes people actually left behind were apparently just diary entries Artyom somehow managed to leave in places he'd never been before. No hidden ammo or anything else. The game also started off with disappointing areas in general, 2033 opened with exploring above ground ruins while Last Light drops you in a big bland featureless grey bog or something, which you walk slowly across one open area of before walking through a ditch and going into a cutscene. Then it goes to forced stealth through a nazi camp, mirroring the worst parts of 2033 and I lost all desire to keep playing.
It feels like Call of Duty: Russian Sewers and I wasn't immersed in the slightest.

is a fun, neat little platformer. In
, you play Dawn, the silent 'imaginary' friend of a young girl named Didi, whose mother is a cabaret singer. Throughout the game you help her solve puzzles and get past obstacles by using Dawn's ability to 'shadow walk' in 2.5 style platforming sequences.
While the game is not a technical marvel,
oozes atmosphere. Inspired by a 1920's vaudeville style, the game features impressive if somewhat linear levels. The choice to make almost all of the characters actually shadows of themselves thrown on to a wall Dawn is platforming across is a very nice touch that allows for almost all of the story to be explained while you're playing the game, so cutscenes are down to a minimum(in fact, there are only two or three actual 3d models of characters in the entire game, one of them being Dawn, the player character) while giving you something to pay attention to in cooperation with the gameplay.
Gameplay wise,
is fun, but is hampered somewhat by glitches and clipping issues. Some parts can be aggravating simply because Dawn clips weirdly into a shadow or hits a part of a wall that randomly ejects her from her shadow persona, usually over a bottomless pit that resets you at the start of the current section. Despite this, the shadow puzzles are well thought out and interesting, and despite hearing a lot of complaints in the reviews on the camera, I found that the developers managed to make the camera do what the player wanted(many times I found the camera 'locked' to a certain axis, which made platformer easier and highlighted spots I should be focusing on). There are many times when Dawn got caught on pieces of the level, or clipped at the edge of a shadow and simply threw me back out again, failing the puzzle. However, these issues were minor enough that there were only one or two times I truly felt the game was entirely at fault.
's level design is pretty solid, though very linear, with the world well conceptualized to mix between shadow movements and 3d overworld sections, which serve to move you from one section to another. Occasionally I did find sections where it wasn't clear where I was supposed to go(In one, I had to resort to a walkthrough simply because the game's lighting hadn't highlited a jump point properly)
This is not a very long game, but I think I like that(the entire game and all collectibles took a few hours at best). Not every game has to be 60 hours of content. Like a movie, this game has a story to tell and it's good at pacing itself for that story without dragging. The best description I can give for the playthrough is 'comfy'. It's not particularly hard, but a few of the puzzles make you think. And that's really
's largest failing, in that the game is relatively
for these sorts of games. I think this is by design, as it feels like some things were made simpler for a younger audience. Collectibles are sprinkled directly in paths you'll be heading anyway, and simply add little flairs to the story exposition wouldn't be able too, so I have no complaint with them.
All in all,
is a pretty decent buy for the price, though some leery of its short play time might want to consider wishlisting and waiting for a steam sale.

I purchased this game based on the recommendation of Extra Credits. They described it as a turn-based strategy that plays like a grand strategy, but is much more accessible. They said it was easy to jump in and play.
I enjoy Civ-type strategy games, but grand strategies have always turned me off. I don't have a lot of time to devote to any single game. The idea of spending +100hrs to master a game is something that's never appealed to me. But I do enjoy the strategy genre; so I've always stuck to strategy-lite games. The screen shots on this game looked like a grand strategy, but it wasn't tagged on Steam as such, wasn't recommended as such, and had some reviewers saying the game was too easy; so I jumped in the pool.
Commander: The Great War was recommended as an easy strategy game. It is not. After only an hour of gameplay I can see this game is not something you just jump into and pick right up. After losing 3 times in less than an hour I decided to look up a guide. The guide said expect to loose 20 or 30 times before you get the hang of it... Wait, that sounds like a grand strategy.
I'm sure this game is probably good and those who took the time to learn it certainly can attest to such. But for me, I'm not that guy. I enjoy playing a multitude of games, not focusing on mastering just one. I work at a job that has me navigate the world of federal and financial regulations. My movements at work are a grand strategy. When I come home I want to unwind and enjoy an experience. What I don't want to do is spend hours reading manuals, guides, and trail and error gameplay.
So it's not for me. That isn't the fault of the game, but the recommendation I based it's purchase on. Still I hope someone else, with tastes like mine, finds this review. Every game isn't for everyone.

Halo wars takes the Halo universe into the RTS settings.
The Good
=======
1. Halo Universe - Nice to finally play Halo in the RTS view. Controlling a number of units that you would remember in the Halo series such as marines , ODST and Spartans...oh yeah and the countless number of vehicles.
2. World - The maps are nicely made with the looks and feel of the locations your at.
3. Music - The halo music is back and feels nice to each situation your dealing with.
4. Factions - Being able to play as the UNSC or the covenant is awesome especially each having unique leaders with special abilities and sometimes units....god I love that Scarab tank
5. Story - I enjoyed the story along with the characters as it brought some familiar faces back into the fight and keeps the pacing nice so that you feel interested to keep moving on.
========
The Bad
========
1. Ai Pathfinding - I found a few path finding issues where my units would wonder off even though they are asked to move a few setps forward, other times they would wonder way off even into a enemy base if you click to close to a cliff side or a rock.
2. Lack of Unit control - I found there isn't much options to control your units such as asking them to hold location (very annoying when a enemy comes and runs off taking half your force with it as they follow), patrol (setting waypoints for your units to patrol back and forth (would be useful on those defending missions) and so on.
3. Zoom - I found a few maps you are zoomed right  in without the ability to zoom out. Other times I found I'm zoom to far out and not able to zoom in. So a really annoying distancing issue.

I liked the first Turbo Pug game, so I thought I would give this one a shot too. I definitely prefer the original to this, mainly because it was so much more simple and I feel like Turbo Pug DX added a lot of (what seemed like) interesting features to it that just aren't necessary.
I liked having the pug coins unlock new playable characters, but it just kind of bothers me that after collecting everyone the coins do nothing... I think being able to buy more customizable items or powerups would have been pretty cool. (Maybe eventually??)
My other issue is that it seems like the game lags a bit sometimes, but usually for me, it's worse on my first play and after that, it smooths out a bit. I think that there's very little leeway when it comes to avoiding obstacles... but that's probably just me being terrible at this game! c:
Having achievements to reach is nice, despite needing to commit several hours to the game to get them.
The last thing- pretty much my only real issue with the game- is the changing colors in the background. It may just be me being old and having issues with my eyesight, but sometimes I struggle seeing where the pug is compared to obstacles and boxes that I need to jump over and onto. Using a custom BG helps a lot, so if you decide to play and have this problem, I definitely recommend doing that in the options setting.
If you don't like casual, simple games, you probably won't like this game. But if you're like me and play games to kill some time, you'll probably enjoy Turbo Pug DX.

This is a wonderful shoot-em-up game with a campaign mode that is unfortunately too short, but there is quite a bit of replay value if you are a completionist. There is also the gauntlet mode which is very similar to endless, but I have yet to reach the end of a gauntlet, at this point in time, to know if it is endless or not.
You get to play 5 different mechs that each have their own unique capabilities and suitabilities to how you play. A decent variety of weapon for you to choose from and each having their own pros and cons. Having tried all the mechs and different variations of each weapon, I definitely know I prefer a certain combination of weapons compared to others. The base stats are all the same for each mech and all the upgrades will apply to the mech you select before the start of the campaign. Some of the upgrades are interesting and quite helpful depending on if you are playing solo or co-op. Because it's a couch co-op game, it'll most likely be a solo campaign for me most of the time so a few upgrades are not as high priority for me than others.
The game's music is very nice and I think carries the right beats and mood for each stage in the campaign. While there is a very minimal story plot in this game, it was amusing to progress through the game with it, but definitely not story-rich. The context did make me a laugh a bit, but that's about it. (It's a shoot-em-up game, take it for what it is!)
I think the custom difficulty adds a nice touch to the game. Haven't tried it yet, but being able to customize the game's difficulty would make the game appeal more to a much wider variety of gamers - aside from the preset difficulties in the game.
Overall, I did finish the game once on sunday stroll mode just to learn the game and practice how I want to play before the harder modes. Definitely will go back and forth playing this game between others to complete all the upgrades and maybe unlock all the achievements. 8.5/10!

Simply put, it is the best, most interesting 4X right now.
At first glance, it's gorgeous. Charming. Galaxies are beautiful to watch. The music is soothing and sticks (i would love to hear more). It's like immersing yourself into a warm bath.
Then, you discover a really interesting 4X, that is also beautiful under the hood. The races are completely different, they play differently, they each have a story. The mechanics are well oiled and work. The technological wheel is rich and, as it progresses, unlocks different challenges at different stages of the game. Diplomacy has become much more interesting in the last update, with good ideas finally working, like pressure, influence, etc.
The AI still needs working on as it sometimes acts like a dummy, like all AIs in those games (except maybe Galciv3's, which is quite ok). But nothing serious enough to diminish playing pleasure in my opinion.
All in all, it is a joy to play.
There are still things that would need improving / changing. I would say the economic part is still a bit unbalanced. The space combat part seems, to me at least, a bit overkill for what it is. I would rather have a simpler system than this whole lot of stuff which only artificially deepens an already deep game.
But looking at how the devs work on this, giving massive free updates (of course this should be normal and not even worth mentioning, but in our DLC era, especially when you look at what others do, it IS worth mentioning), i'm sure that this gem will even get better in the future.
PS : for those concerned by initial launch problems, thoses are gone and well gone.
For me, it's the best space 4X available right now, and i played them all.

Dustforce is a challenging action arcade platformer in the same vein as Super Meat Boy.  The graphics are serviceable, and the music is exceptionally well done.  I appreciate the fact that the developers attempted to harken back to old style 8-bit audio without actually giving us the terribly awful reality of it (like in Wizorb).  Though the game does work with the Steam Overlay and supports widescreen, the gamepad support is not very well implemented and will require the player to manually reconfigure the control scheme to work.  I found the the native keyboard controls to be cramped and non-intuitive, particularly for a game that requires fast reflexes.  Other users on the forums have reported they prefer the keyboard for later in the game, but I have not progressed far enough to have an opinion one way or another.  Dustforce in short, is a quality indie game that will resonate with fans of Super Meat Boy or VVVVVVvvvvVVVV.

I've played this game for about a year now, I got a good bit of fun out of it, skirmishing in the desert sands of the Middle East, Running the Western front meatgrinder, Driving across the Russian plains, Sinking hundreds of tonnage in ships. It was all quite nice.
But after going through it a few times, the game started to feel empty, after you learn what the game will demand of you and when you realize how the AI can lose. I was about to put it down when on a whim, I look at the old forum for this game.
Thats when I found what needs to be recognized as the unnoficial free expansion to this game, The Potzblitz Mod.
Potzblitz reconized the emptyness of the game and in response, gave this old game long a breath of new life.
Redone game mechanics, retweaking the stats of Units mades the static nature of war more apparent, moral and manpower make the war into the one of attrition it was.
New Collapse point statistic accounts for crippling events the war with afflict you with, Leader Dead? Offensive Failed? Crop Failure? all of these and more will make your will to fight decrease due to collapse points.
Rebalenced tech trees make the race for new weapons specialized and event specific, you may hit the jackpot from the minds of Ernest Swindon, Anthony Fokker and Fritz Haber.
New cities, forts and battle locations on the map. Ypre, Rheims, Metz, Anzac Beach, Lublin, what was once vast nothingness now is a minefield of strategic defense points and soon to be points of attack.
New events added flavour and replayability to the repetition, Potzblitz gives us the what-if and for want of a nail moments that hindsight deprive us of. British invasion of the Netherlands? Finnish Civil War? Irish Uprising? Middle East Antics, Spanish Flu, Influencing U.S. Elections?!
Extra Commanders and special ways to unlock them. For part of the games title, you only had half a dozen of these historic figures throughout the entire game. Potzblitz gives us more of these unique leaders to help break the monotony, both with historical info and their troop bonuses. You can also now lose your commanders due to politics, retirement or death on the field of battle.
The Potzblitz transformed this game in a way I don't see often, and it accounts for well over half of my playtime in Commander. A game thats been abandoned for two years, but due to its modability, has continuous been improved.
I had no part in this mods development, nor have I been asked to endorse it, its only due to my appreciation of it improving the game and its relative obscurity (I found this on a whim on a forum for a 5 year old game.) If you want more from this game, The Potzblitz Mod is the way to go.

I think this game is a very accurate association of how our society would behave after a nuclear war:
Getting rid of all the different ideologies when there are mutants at the doorstep? Nah, better get the good ol' nazicommunist thing going again!
Solidarity for a new and better future? Nah, better kill off each other over some pre-war bullets..
God-like mutants that could make the difference in establishing a new society? KILL IT WITH FIRE!
Use every available ressource for a better everyday life? Nah, better craft buttloads of weapons and live in crappy wooden shacks..
But despite all the unneccessary war mongery resulting out of human stubborness it is interesting to see how the normal people try to get along with their lives: building towns, voting majors, getting supplies and so on
All in all I really like this game franchise and there are  a lot of things to discover in the world of post-apocalyptic moscow. A must play for all FPS Lovers!

It's great. It's just... it's great. It's beautiful, it's creative, and it's lovely.
I was asked if the puzzles got repetitive, because most of them are "move box to thing." And that is true, but the game was only a few hours long. If it went on much longer, I feel like it would have gotten repetitive, but as it was, it was the perfect length to not get boring.
There were a few puzzles that were kind of dumb, where I felt like I was kind of cheating by doing it the way I was, because I couldn't figure out what it wanted me to do. None of them were really frustrating, and the one time that I looked up how to do something, it was simply because I overlooked it.
I'm all about collectables, so it was really jarring for me to collect something, which was something like the 15th out of 20, when the previous one I had was maybe the 8th. Then later, as I progressed, suddenly I got those bits. It looked as if I had forgotten them, and the way they were ordered for the second half of the game made me constantly question if I got everything.
There were also a few occational blips in the graphics, where it suddenly felt like an early Playstation game with how things moved or reacted, and I caught a couple T-poses if I got caught on something. Certainly nothing game-breaking though - just took me a step back from the magic. Sometimes shifting into the shadows would be aggrivating as well, and it just... wouldn't. I would do it again and again and suddenly it would work, and then it wouldn't do it again when I wanted it to. Frustrating, but nothing worth quitting it over
Dispite these things, the game is lovely. The art is lovely. The world is lovely. I wish that there was more going on, a sequal in the same space, or something. Maybe a second episode. I want more of this world and this cool ability, but maybe with a different puzzle designer. I would totally reccomend buying it if it's on sale, that's for sure. It's absolutely worth the few bucks. Ful price, ehhhhh. Didn't quite fall in love with it, but certainly had a big crush on it and made it my wallpaper for a day or two.

I was just writing a post in the forums that sums up my thoughs so I decided to add it here as a review.
(Some one in the forums asked why the AI tranfers troops, leaving gaps, and does other wierd things).
The AI does some wierd things. You would think in the year 2017, AI would really kick butt. I have only played (and won) a few times as the central powers, and every time my wins are based on the AI doing stupid things. Mainly it is the AI transfering forces to other fronts.
In my last win, France send troops to Italy as I was smashing their forces in northern france. A few turns later I notice Italy sending troops to France, even though France still had troops in Italy. In the same game, Russia sent tons of troops to Turkish borders to repell a tiny invasion, which opened the eastern front to my German troops. Britain, dont get me started on Britain. Britain decided to do an all-out defense of Egypt. My Turkish troops (after some initial losses) smashed through the Sinai, destroying 3 British armies and 3 british fighter units.
Russia fell first after they desided to totally man and occupy the Turkish border. My German  troops walked to Petrograd and surrounded many single units in the center. France fell next after they tranfered units to Italy. They left every hex north of Paris open. My troops rushed into the gap and France was never able to recover. Pretty soon I had a 2 to 1 advantage in France. Also Britain decided not to send troops to France (only a couple early on).
It is as if the AI is only capable of making strategic desisions based on large blocks of troops. I think the AI is only strategically able to plan and move block equal to 25% or so of a country's total forces. So, for example, if the French strategic AI decides Italy needs help it moves one block of troops to Italy (this block seems to equal about 25% of Frances forces). This "block" of troops always seems to occupy part of the front line. Its as if these blocks of troops are slices of the front. The AI doesnt form (or it doesnt have) a strategic reserve, so when it needs to move troops it just takes one 25% slice out of the front line. The AI does not seem capable of taking a few units off of the rear of their own line. This is dangerous when the AI does not prioritize fronts or strategic objectives.
As for Britain in Egypt, my Trukish troops killed every Brit in the Sinai and formed a front line at the Suez canal. When I moved up my fighter unit, it revealed that the Brits had armies, fighters, and artillery units stacked 4 hexs deep in Egypt of all places. That is when I knew I would win the game. Oddly the AI decided build 3 artillery units and 3 fighter units and stick them in Egypt.  That is another AI problem - the AI builds the wrong units.

‘Constrast’ is a game of the platformer variety, centred around a puzzle mechanic which uses light and shadows as a mean of switching between a 3D and 2D environment, but it becomes completely irredeemable by committing the capital sin for platformers : bad controls. The game simply doesn’t work at what it is trying to do and, as such, is utterly unrecommendable.
It starts… bad, and only gets worse. The game has no rebindable keys, the mouse cursor doesn’t work in every menu (like restarting a checkpoint or leaving the game), but it does offer very lacklustre graphic options. Although I like the style of the game, I really disliked its graphics quality. The textures aren’t pretty, and there is nothing to distract from them, as the environments are lifeless and empty. Even the music doesn’t help, as it is barely even present while you are exploring or solving puzzles. Worse, one of the main mechanics of the game requires you to play with shadows, but even they are barebones at best. In the days of soft focus shadows, that’s a big no-no if your main mechanic revolves around them. All the cutscenes and story bits are shown through the shadows too, so you get to experience bad graphics on top of very stick figure-like animations, not even remotely human. Not that it really matters as the story holds no water, but I will get to that in a minute.
But alright, let’s give it the benefit of the doubt, what else is there? Any other nitpicks? Well, even though I’m a native French speaker, I preferred the English dub, but the collectibles, with press articles and other, supposedly, world building information extracts, aren’t fully translated! That’s disappointing.
What about the gameplay? Well, the controls aren’t rebindable, the camera is atrocious, -which doesn’t help-, and the animation of the character is stiff and “mechanic”. Clunky really, fast and yet without precision. When the camera switches mode, between locked in 2D shadow world and free 3D exploration, it is feels horrible: during the transitions, it is either too quick or too slow, but feels unnatural either way, jarring. You don’t feel in control, you are at the mercy of the game’s whims.
So let me get this straight. It is a puzzle platformer with bad controls and bad camera, where you have to jump on platforms made from poorly rendered shadows, from which you will end up sliding off for the smallest offense. This will lead to some frustration since… well, you character doesn’t move like you want it to or the game just refuses to acknowledge your input, for whatever reason, and getting sacked for it, unfairly, is rather infuriating. It is actually so bad, I landed in a secret area one time, one I hadn’t neither seen nor planned on jumping into. Thanks for that I guess, but it isn’t gonna make up for all the bad jump related deaths.
As said before, even the story didn’t hold my attention. In all honesty, I had a hard time sympathizing with the dad figure. Because he was trying, although he put his family in harm’s way, that makes every alright? When you stand in the rain, you get wet. Don’t. Stand. In. The. Rain. Or least, don’t ask for my sympathy when you complain about getting drenched. The story didn’t resonate with me.
The nail in the coffin was one particular moment that is reminiscent of Limbo. Except, you know, Limbo kind of works. So now I have a better game in my mind that I could be playing on top of all this nonsense. Anyway, it was too obvious, with the spider and all… You haven’t earned that game, the right to make an ‘homage’ like that. And even if you did, you have a game that is three hours short (and thank god for that! I wouldn’t have been able to play any more of it), and you basically have so little to put in it that you lift levels from another game. That doesn’t come across as very endearing to me.
There is definitely an interesting concept at the core of the game, with the change between 3D and 2D platformer, and that’s where the puzzles are I suppose, if you can call them that. It is a proof of concept, sure, but that’s not enough for a good game. And it is actually possible to break the puzzles, making them impossible to solve, forcing you to reload if you aren’t careful enough, which you can’t be because of the horrendous controls! At times, it does feel like an endless cycle of displeasure. Certainly, that concept deserved better. As it stands, the game is a demo I would present to my boss in order to get funding for a project based around the shown concept, not a final product I would charge money for.
All in all, what I am seeing here is a game that had a great gameplay concept, and a great art style, but failed to get to the finish line with them. The game feels rushed, empty in a lot of aspect, barely functional sometimes, without any form of polish whatsoever, and it makes it all the more disappointing when the game does finally decide to work, when, very rarely, there are some “sparks” and it clicks. From time to time, things work out alright, and the puzzles and their solutions aren’t hampered by the flaws of the game, but those shining moments, where the transition from an open world to one of shadows stimulates your brain and gives you the satisfaction of actually solving a problem in a clever way, without the frustration of dealing with force outside your reach, are far too few to justify any consideration of purchase, no matter the price.

3. It is a game where you can play on...
- Easy - which makes enemies brainless so you can learn the game
- Normal - where they show signs of aggression so you can step up your game against an enemy
- Heroic - where the enemy starts getting aggressive much earlier introducing some rushing elements to challenge you
- Legendary - which allows you to harness your ability to maximize on time, resources, and rotating units
4. It feels like Halo without it being Halo. I can build Spartans and they be a presence as they take vehicles. Scorpion tanks feel and sound like they should. Banshees feel like they should. It doesn't feel like it's just a reskinned game to look like Halo.
5. Introduces new vehicles and units that challenge certain army builds and counter others.
6. You get all of the DLCs, which includes more than a handful of maps and modes, and it adds to the game.

It requires you find games already set up in a pool of players that was small from the day it was released because of how you have to find lobbies with people. The random matchmaking element that was on the console version is gone. :(

I recommend original Bioshock 2. Game was fun (albeit really difficult for casual gamers that play more for story then difficulty. Easy mode can be considered "normal mode" for casual gamers).
Anyways, I don't recommend remastered for two reasons:
1) the textures they didn't remaster stick out like sore thumbs. There are some more detailed textures and effects. But, then you walk up to a texture on a bulkhead or a wall and it's just a blurred mess. Seems they remastered part of the game, but not all. So, the parts they didn't touch start to stick out and look ugly.
2) The crashes... dear god ... the crashes. The game randomly commits suicide. The remaster comes out after a period of time when players are used to games auto-saving their progress now. Bioshock 2 only auto-saves your progress between major levels. Major levels take hours to plow through. So, you need to spam the quick-save key every 10 minutes or so or end up losing an hour+ of progress when a crash sneaks up on you like a ninja. There's no rhyme or reason to the crashes either. You get a crash in one area, then play through it again crash-free. These are the worst kinds of crashes, because they are so random. If you knew what caused them then you could perhaps do something about them. But, no... random. They haven't patched or updated the game to fix this stuff. So...yeah.
I liked Bioshock 2 (original). It was an ok game. I would recommend it for players that like interesting story. But, the remaster doesn't add enough to warrant purchase, and the crashes it introduces create a net loss in value for the game. So, avoid the remaster. Get the original (if it's still sold). If not, then get the remaster and buckle in for some rage-inducing crashes.

So I've logged almost 1000 hours on the game. I've been playing it on and off steam for about 5-6 years and on multiple platforms for two or three years. While it takes a little time to really get going, the game [obviously] has months and years of content. Before I really get into the review, I want to say that you should take Excalibur, Braton, Lato, and Skana starting out. If you want any of the other starting items, the ones listed above are the most versatile or the hardest to farm (Excalibur is all the way on Pluto so take Excalibur). The developers actually listen to the players, which is really nice especially on a free to play game where they could easily make it about whatever sells best. The content is [mostly] bug free. Even if there is a bug, the developers are on top of it usually within a week. Considering the size of the game and the sheer number of bugs the game used to have, that impresses me. You might have trouble starting out, like your mouse is moving slow and whatnot but the same thing happened to me. Just take a few seconds and mess with your settings because I promise this game is worth it. If you don't like/have the time to spend grinding stuff out and you have a few extra dollars, just wait until you get a 75% discount on platinum and purchase a $100 platinum package for $25. Then you can buy whatever you dont want to farm and thats that. What I like the most is that you arent tied to just one character or one skill set. If you choose something you dont like in the start, hit up recruit chat and have a taxi player take you to a new warframe farm [but remember that a low level player being taken to endgame warframe farms will probably just die over and over again]. You could literally max out as many warframes as you want in one day.
In Review:
Pros:
Great Content
Awesome Developers
Great Graphics
Varied Content
Unique Gaming
Awesome Approach to Character System
Well Worth Time [and Money] Spent
Cons:
Heavy Visual Load (Even lowest graphics can be too heavy for some normal computers)
Takes Time (Especially if you dont want to spend $10-$50 on platinum)
Can Seem Pay to Win (When its really play more to win)
All in all, if you just want a game you can hop on, grab a daily reward, do a few 3-15 minutes missions on and then hop off, this game could be the one you're looking for. Or if you have hours and hours to blow, start prime farming and you could just lose yourself in the game. Either way, Ninjas Play for Free and Warframe is awesome.
Also I wasn't in any way reimbursed or payed or discounted for this review, and I have no affiliation with Warframe, I just honestly think its a great game that only gets better with time.

Controls were an absolute pain. I had to mash buttons to figure out that 'confirm' was mapped to the 'B' button on my controller. Huh, who uses 'B' for selection? There weren't any controller icons until halfway through the tutorial, so stuff like movement was never explained. Control rebinding is the standard Unity method (aka absolutely terrible) and makes me wish the author had just pulled a controller plugin off the Unity Asset Store.
For actual gameplay, you use one set of controls to rotate your ship in 3D and another set to turn the barrel-shaped map clockwise or counterclockwise. That sounds ok on paper, but it's absolutely terrible in practice. Most 3D platformers use a complex system of shadows to help players know where they are and where key items are, but Underwater Adventure can't do this because there isn't any ground. The result is that you'll think you're hitting an item over and over only to flip the camera and realize you're still a good twenty feet away. Well, that's if you can stop ramming into the bounds of the level in the first place. The player ship is so small that you can barely tell which way you're headed and you can cross the screen in two seconds, meaning getting stuck is a likelihood.
I like what I see in the promotional material, but the game just feels wrong to play. In addition to some serious quality-of-life improvements, the game probably needs to be less of a '3D adventure'. Maybe just make it 2.5d? Maybe restrict movement to the camera's x-axis and y-axis? I don't know, but getting through the tutorial used up all my good will for this game.

I watched several youtube "Lets plays" for this game and it looked like fun. I've always enjoyed turn based strategy games and I thought I would enjoy this one as well. Boy was I wrong. Let's start off on a positive note.
Pro's
The games music soundtrack is pretty good and captures the time period
The graphics, while not great by any means, are pretty good for a game of this caliber
You can play as either the Allied Entente or the Central Powers
and that's all of the pro's I could come up with. Now for the negative aspects.
Con's
Games balance is horribly HORRIBLY off. By this I mean you have a couple different units, garrison (nearly worthless in every possible aspect), cavalry (completely and utterly worthless in 90% of combat), aicraft and blimps (words can not describe how bad these units are at EVERYTHING) and front line infantry (which are decent but takes much longer to train and costs alot more resources).
The AI's units are ALWAYS stronger than yours. Their garrison units often will stop you fonrt line infantry cold in their tracks and will hold you off indifinitely. Once the AI's front line infantry begin attacking you en masse, the game is pretty much over.
You would think that the dev's would make it where the Central Entente would have some hope of winning but that's not going to happen ever with this game. When playing as the Central Entente, it's more or less 'I wonder how long I can hold them off until I am defeated'
The Allied navy will crush your navy before you have a chance to do anything
Russia produces a never ending stream of units and since AI units will always outperform yours in combat (which was not the case in real life as German soldiers were far superior than Russian and Austrian untis were far superior to Serbian untis) so you'll slowly lose ground int he East to the limitless supply of troops. It's almost as if the AI is so badly coded, that it defaults to producing infantry in every case.
The game sometimes crashes despite being a 'released version' (i.e. out of Beta)
The AI turns are excruciatingly slow. I'm a programmer by profession and there simply is no reason an AI turn calculated by a computer should take 2 minutes. It shouldn't even take 2 seconds with todays computers. It's almost as if the Dev's put in timers just to slow the game down.
All in all, I am very unimpressed with this game. I wanted to like it so much as I have never found a turn based stratgey game I disliked until now. Save yourself the money or if you MUST have a turned based strategy game, find an old copy of Civil War Generals 2 from the late 1990's. It's far superior than Commander ever hopes to be.

Yo, why are you reading recommendations? Just go play it. You've got nothing to lose since it's free to play. Go.
Wait... you're still here? Still not too sure about it, huh? So, you wanna hear more? Fair enough. Well, this is a game that does "Free to Play" the right way. Yessir. There's no locked content or anything that would prevent you from enjoying the game unless you'd pay. There's an item store where you can buy cool costumes for your character with real money, but they DON'T affect the gameplay since they're just costumes. Y'know, cosmetics. But you're gonna want them, because the game is a hell of a lot of fun and you care about the way your character looks in a fun game. Especially when it's not a FPS. I mean, look at TF2 for instance. If you have hats in TF2, then you're definitely gonna want to have some cosmetics in this game, because you can actually see your character at all times here.
Now, you might be asking yourself, "yeah but what if I don't want to pay real money, will I still look decent?" Well my dear reader, you'll be glad to hear that yes, you will be able to have your own style and look decent even if you don't pay. Sure, you'll be less fancy or less over-the-top, but there's a lot of different clothes that you can drop, and another cool thing about this game is that you can enchant and give attributes to your items. This means that your old dusty shirt you love and cherish can actually be good for a lot longer than you might imagine. You get quite a reasonable amount of in-game money by simply playing the game normally, so you can actually enhance your equipment pretty easily and it's fun to experiment with that.
What else is there to say? Wait, you're right, I haven't even talked about the actual combat yet. Well, this game uses a basic melee combo system and a spell system that uses Mana. Your Mana regenerates faster as you do melee combos. So what you do is you combine your melee combos with your spells and it's super fun and satisfying. There are many classes to choose from, so that makes the game very replayable. Oh, and the surprisingly great music adds a lot to the intense, fast-paced combat.

First off. I know people are going to read this and go "You have 1.5k HOURS IN THIS GAME HOW CAN YOU GIVE IT A NEGATIVE REVIEW?"
Easy. I've played the ♥♥♥♥ out of this game. I love it. I split the time playing it between myself and a family member. Interacting with dinosaurs? Amazing. Building a base? Amazing. The overall concept of the game? Amazing.
The difficulty? There are so many times in this game where something stupid happens and it literally has a domino effect on everything else. It's immersive. You take ONE moment for granted while you're mining, or picking some berries and out of NO WHERE you'll get bum rushed by a large dinosaur who's hungry and wants YOU and your TAMED animal for dinner. Within moments the flying mount you've spent HOURS taming can be gone. It's infuriating. You get so mad, and then you go back, and you rebuild. You go find another dinosaur to tame. YOU won't get beat by the game. Even at higher levels it's difficult. It's unforgiving, and for that I appreciate the game itself.
Why can't I recommend this game? It's broken. I've been playing since Alpha and there are STILL snapping issues with buildings. You have structures that have clipping issues and make it difficult building things next to each other. You know minor things that can be fixed relatively easily that have just been overlooked.
Some of the dinosaurs are incredibly unbalanced. MicroRaptors  are hands down the worst thing ever introduced to this game. You literally have no way to combat them and they often come out of no where and are found near numerous other dinosaurs that have no issue taking a nibble out of you and your mount while you're stun locked for 10 seconds. It's hard enough being knocked off of your mount. This is just one of the examples I can give as far as how over powered some of the dinosaurs abilities are.
Constant bugs. This game had NO business exiting early access. I can honestly say that. Every single time you roll out a patch you're breaking something within the game. It doesn't necessarily have to be a large patch like the recent one with aberration. Often times it's small little patches that cripple the game system to the point where it's unplayable. I recall a patch not long ago where anytime you went to harvest stone the game would just hard crash each and ever single time.
Stuff like this shouldn't be happening to a game that's out of Early Access.
Quite simply. This game was not ready for a full release. It still is not ready for a full release. You shouldn't have game breaking bugs every single time you release a patch. A proper game that is ready for release is Polished. It functions. This game does not fit either of those criteria. It's understandable to have SOME issues with each major patch, and we appreciate how often Wildcard releases patches and adds things to this game, but this game is still by all means an Early Access title.
For that reason, and that reason alone. I cannot recommend that others buy this game. Not until Wildcard fixes some of the glaring stability issues that it has.

Contrast is a linear game, with lots of platforming and puzzle elements that tie together very well with your shadow shifting abilities. If you're looking for a game with great story that you can just sit and finish in 3-4 hours, this is the game for you.

If you prefer to take your time, take some screenshots, there's plenty to see. The story is so well written with a surprising ending as well as a hidden storyline that hints at past events. The most interesting part of the game, in my opinion, was the fact that everyone is a shadow. You never see their faces, only Didi's who is the main character. You can't interact with any character directly, yet you can manipulate their shadows to help you achieve objectives. All that has made for a wonderfully atmospheric game that you can really immerse yourself in.
On the downside, if you're looking for a game you can play over and over again, skip this game. It's a sit through and play once type of thing. Also, controller highly recommended.

Not bad, considering this is their first game.  The soundtrack is great, the choice for weapons is nice, enemy variety is nice, but it really shows that this is their first game  Level progression is different backgrounds with enemies flying towards you in waves.  There's even an endless wave mode you can play, which is nice to have.  Bosses are okay.  They aren't amazing, but they aren't bad.  Overall, for their first shmup, it's passable.  I feel I got my money's worth, though I also somewhat feel the soundtrack is as valuable as the game.  The amount of options with regards to customizing the game is also nice, but I feel in the end it may have hurt them as I would rather have a very polished single form game than an unpolished "you can do anything" game.  The story is stupid, but I enjoyed it because it was self aware.  However, nowadays, the "I hold up my spork" kind of random stories are a dime a dozen.
That said, I feel there is a lack of polish on some things, which I imagine occurred due to this game being an amalgamation of ideas and the little bumps haven't been ironed out.  The many pieces of the game don't really fit together.  They're just...there.  Like the different mech's special attacks.  Largely unneeded as it's better to prioritize shooting your main weapon.  The game needs focus.
This game is not a slow moving bullet hell like touhou (which I am glad for, as I do not enjoy that game), it's not a score/coin reward game like giga wing, and it's also not a strong level progression game like r-type or jamestown (though jamestown is a mix of story and coins, which was very highly polished).
I think that its main problem.  It's not quite sure what it wants to be.  Numbers pop up like crazy, so is it a reward kinda game?  There's no coins, so my brain's reward center isn't happy.  Level progression is lame and consists of different enemies on a slow moving background.  There's no level elements like barriers or a finely detailed background that goes along with the enemies.  At times it is a fast moving bullet hell game, which is great as the recharging shield mechanic makes the game frantic, but it's missing that polish to tie it all together.
The stupid story is kind of the epitome of this game - forgetable.  But, it's ten dollars forgetable, and most importantly, it's not bad, so I feel I more than got my money's worth out of it.  If they make a sequel I would be very highly interested, provided the above points were addressed.

IMO Warframe is the current pinnacle of Free2play grinding/internet gaming. Certainly you can spend money to gain warframes (classes) instead of grinding for parts but there is no incentive to do so. Warframe is focused on PVE, you and friends or clan mates fight hordes of enemies in various game modes to attain pieces of new weapons/frames/gear to assemble. There are story missions you play as you go that explain who you are and why you fight the various enemies but the game is focused on being an item grist mill. You grind for items, better items or just prettier items, and hop from planet to planet chasing the pieces needed to assemble those items. Paying real money to buy the fully assembled item is a shortcut and alleviates the grinding, but as the grind is the game it is pointless to waste the money.
The PVP, which is where you would normally see a p2w situation, is miniscule and doesn't matter to most of the community. The few who do play it are unlikely to do it exclusively. In addition you have different loadouts for PVP so it largely doesn't affect and isn't affected by the PVE. I wouldn't claim it is a walled garden but the times a change in PVP affects PVE is rare.
Essentially the only reason to spend money in the game is to buy boosters that accelerate the leveling of the warframes you own (in Warframe you never level up the various weapons, companions, and warframes gain levels). Which is understandable but not necessary as leveling isn't an onerous process. If an impatient gamer were to take up this game it could become quite expensive but I would advise them to walk away.
Overall, Warframe can be a lot of fun. You play space ninjas with powers that vary from shooting lightning to turning invisible to summoning forth tentacles to attack enemies. All warframes have their uses, some are stronger in certain game modes than others, but all get a chance to shine.

I ran across the game after searching for some WW1 strategy games.  I had just finished listening to Dan Carlin's 18+ Hour long series on the first World War so my opinion is obviously not without its' biases. I'm usually not too big a fan of turn based strategy, but this one(and CIV5) are pretty fun. It's different from CIV5 in the sense that it isn't building based. You get a certain amount of income per country per turn depending on how much of your population you haven't drafted into your armies.
This game isn't like RTS games or CIV5 where you send your units straight into combat, trying to kill enemy units one on one. 90% of success in this game comes from positioning your units and stocking up artillery ammo for taking out one or two enemy units on there flanks and then trying to turn that flank in on itself.
If you like the WW1 theme and like grand scale turn based strategy I'd recommend this game, it is very satisfying after playing 6 hours on veteran as the central powers haha, beating back Russia into submission, swinging down and stomping out the Serbian rebels and all while holding back England France and Italy in the west.
You'll like this game if you're into almost chess like games, where time is really a factor, you play your units as best as you see fit and wait for the enemy to react, and vice versa. A fun back and forth, plus after u defeat the Allies I always try to land the Kaiser's Troops in America hahaha! (after taking Portugal and Spain for there ports ofcourse ;) )

To whom it may concern (presumably wargamers)
This is a hex based grand strategy game set in what is generally referred to as the First World War (some believe the Seven Years War fits the description far better, and I think on the whole I would concur). This game is initially difficult to get into as at first glance it appears as if someone just made a WW I themed Panzer Corps mod which was unnecessarily diffici;t and excessively expensive. However, this can be an extremely addictive game once you have given enough time for the mechanics to become sufficiently intuitive. It does reproduce the deadlock of the western front quite well, while also allowing for large scale encirclements and manuevering in the east. It also attempts to simulate other broader concerns such as production and technological research (the homefront). The British naval blockade is also featured although I think it does understate the damaging effects of the Turnip Winter in Germany. The only other flaw would be the representation of the early clashes in 1914 as it was hard to really obtain any result which appeared to resemble the Battle of the Frontiers or Tannenburg. However, after the first clashes it does get quite interesting and difficult to tear oneself away.
I recommend this game wholeheartedly to anyone who would like something historical and on a grand scale and I hope that you have found this review both useful and strangely written.
Sincerely

The pros:
- The story is fantastic, and the voice acting is well done. The main character, Didi, is particularly good considering her age
- The music creates a wonderful atmosphere, and the world is creatively put together. There are fascinating details throughout, that make you want to explore every nook and cranny
- The platforming is clever, and for the most part the mechanics work. A few hiccups here and there, but usually there are work-arounds if you're patient enough
The cons:
- It doesn't say a controller is mandatory, but it should. You should be able to get through the first Act with just a mouse and keyboard, but after that it becomes more challenging. A controller will give you the freedom to maneuver that you're looking for.
- Exploration is all but banned. Step too far to get a good look at something and a solid road may actually cause you to fall through the world. There's a lot of hand-holding, particularly in the quest objective that you can never remove from the screen. This is a pity, because it's tempting to take a lot of beautiful screenshots, but you can't without "Follow Didi" and "Go back and meet Didi" being scrawled on the upper right-hand side almost constantly.
- There are few save points, no checkpoints, and no manual saves. This means that if you break a puzzle (it's possible) then resetting from the last save may put you behind a couple hours' worth of work, forcing you to do conquered puzzles over again.
Overall, though, this very a very good game and very imaginative. Since the developers plan to make another game (though not a sequel) it will be interesting to see what they have in store.

The bosses are standard fare, you will die a few times learning their patterns but none of them are tough once you know how to dodge their attacks.
The game took me just shy of 2 hours to beat, there are also leaderboards for time trials if you are into that sort of thing. Definitely worth a buy.

Here’s an indie title that took me by surprise: Salmon Ninja! The name may not say much upon first glance, but the actual game states otherwise. It’s a challenging platformer that is not unlike that of Super Meat Boy. Like the aforementioned title, it’s kind of a good game to say the least.
Story
The story in Salmon Ninja is a simple one. Our ninja character here is lost and wants to find his way home. There are cutscenes at the beginning and ending of each world that provide some character interactions as a means of substance for the minimal story. While I do wish a couple of the characters spoke English, the dialogue is otherwise amusing and almost makes me wish the respective speakers had more screen time.
Graphics
I never tire of the pixel art in these games. The graphical style in Salmon Ninja in particular is an enchanting use of pre-16-Bit-esque visuals. It helps that the performance is at no less than sixty frames per second! Considering how the game does thrive on being difficult and giving the player several looks at the death screen, it’s a treat to realize that the transitions between everything are as instant as they could ever be. There are no loading screens; the action is front and center – as it should be! Speaking of, the animations and special effects are fluid and can be dazzling in their own right even if portions of the level get painted red with enemy or player blood.
Audio
The music is whimsical and atmospheric. The sound effects complement the pixel art. Together, this creates for a distinct kind of sound only some of the top-tier indie games seem to enjoy displaying. It gives off a bit of a Thomas Was Alone vibe to it. Although Salmon Ninja obviously doesn’t play by the same rules as that game, the atmosphere does display a feel of something grand thanks to the audio complementing the scale of the level layouts.
Gameplay
Salmon Ninja, as said earlier, takes quite a lot of inspiration from Super Meat Boy. There are four worlds, and each world contains several levels that are more-or-less bite-sized platforming gauntlets. The ninja has wall-jumping abilities, a sword, and a grappling hook at his disposal to help progress through unscathed. He’s also a glass cannon, however, so one hit from anything and he’s done for! Thankfully, each level has a generous amount of checkpoints. That way, no level ever gets too frustrating.
I was actually pretty surprised how I managed to play through this one. Since players use the mouse to wield the sword or fire the grappling hook, I thought I was in for a danger zone I could never be able to finish playing through. In theory, it seemed like the mouse functions would only complicate the precise platforming players have to go through. But you know what? The game actually works wonders with the tools provided! Granted, the default button for jumping shouldn’t have been the spacebar, but interchangeable controls make this a nonissue; I found myself being comfortable with using W for jumping and A and D for moving.
Salmon Ninja also has a solid degree of challenge. There is admittedly an emphasis on trial-and-error in a few places, but the checkpoint generosity and the magnificently swift transitioning from death to respawn drastically diminish the problems I typically have with trial-and-error gameplay. It assists in shifting the focus to what obstacles lie straight ahead and how the player should overcome them. Basically, legit challenge and not fake difficulty. Adding to the fun factor is the abundance of interesting enemies, obstacles, and clever design layouts.
Verdict
The overall result is an awesome title that is well worth your time! Salmon Ninja has all the right elements for a great Meat Boy-ish game, and it used them properly and triumphantly! I highly recommend it to players looking for a good ol’ hardcore stroll.

I stumbled onto this game while looking at upcoming releases. It looked fun and engaging, so I bought it pretty much immediately on release. I have to say, though, I'm left more on the disappointed side so far.
On the up side, the game has some definite style in its visuals and sound, coming across like a sleek upgrade of a retro game, with fluid-looking movement and eye-popping colors. In terms of gameplay, it obviously draws a lot of inspiration from Super Meat Boy, but its central difference is the grappling hook, which is part of what caught my eye. But I'm left unsure of how to feel about the hook.
For the purpose of specific aiming of the hook, you need keyboard and mouse controls, which feel a little awkward during certain fast-paced segments and contributes to some of the difficulty if you're more of a controller gamer (like me). But for all that, the hook doesn't even seem like the central gameplay gimmick. Most of the early levels just focus on your ability to execute precision jumps. It feels like the hook should have been made a bit more necessary if it was going to be part of the game.
The thing that really bothers me is the progression. One could argue that dying a lot is definitely expected in a game like this, but at times because of the fast movement and perilous obstacles, you'll find yourself dying a lot if you're not the most skilled gamer (somehow that little ninja can be very slippery sometimes!). Here's the biggest problem with that: your ability to progress in the game and clear worlds is dependent on getting gold medals by clearing the levels effectively and efficiently. This means that progression in the game is essentially more of a "hardcore" feature than a "casual" feature, meaning a lot of your potential audience may be shut out from experiencing the game if they don't feel like re-running the levels to get them just right. Things like leaderboards and achievements and their in-game bonuses are great features for rewarding players who really polish their skills.
Overall I can tell there's a lot of heart here, and pieces of a really fun game. But what stops it from being a classic is that clearing levels alone isn't enough; you have to master them, meaning that a lot of the game's content might end up being replaying the same levels, which I don't personally find to be fun enough. It ends up feeling like the sort of Flash game I would have played on Newgrounds back in the day and thought was cool, but I after a few minutes of retrying the same level I'd probably get bored and find something else to do.
I think tweaking that alone would be the difference between me recommending it or not.
EDIT: Based on feedback, the medal requirement was removed. The game is still super challenging, but it feels much more accessible now. If you're going into it knowing it won't be easy, then I definitely recommend giving it a try!

cons: post launch DLC's are hidden on the "chapters" panel on the main launch menu ("Q - new missions"), no windowed full screen mode, game won't even launch sometimes (requires a "safe mode" launch which diverts the game to 720 resolution, you would have to re-apply your video settings), won't allow you to skip logo animations during game launch, invisible walls & extremely linear progression, quick time events, some scripted events bugged out, clunky AI movements & odd facial animations, most characters are uninspired & not compelling, redux isn't as visually impressive as I expected it to be overall (although some parts are), the game randomly switches to military grade bullets, unable to kill flying monsters (which is a complete waste of bullets on the illusion of hitting flying targets), immersion breaking monster spawns (some monster are unkillable for the sake of scripted events), underwhelming rewards for exploration, annoying water submersion animation (just let me ♥♥♥♥ing swim), won't allow you to carry more than 3 guns at a time, unable to interact with objects in the world during reload or filter change animations, clunky way to pick up ammo/equipment on body piles (why not just auto pick up ammo when walking next to them...), clunky ladder climbing, repetitive stealth kill animations, only ONE save file - does not allow you to save/load multiple save files (single player & DLC's share the exact same save file... ive read on the forums that you have to manually copy/paste your current save files from the game folder so you don't lose your save when starting a new game and/or DLC mission), ending was underwhelming
DLC's: -Heavy Squad: basically a TF2 heavy weapons guy spray & pray simulator, with annoying lens flares at every direction
-Sniper Team: you have to wait for a 2min scripted event until you can actually start to shoot anything, a sub-par Vassili Zaitsev experience
-Kshatriya: annoying & immersion breaking random spawns of monsters when opening the base door (so damn stupid...), immersion breaking clown-car spawn points for mutant rats, my ability to select weapons & interact with objects bugged out when going in & out of base, bullet sponge librarians, a librarian basically teleports to the door outside of where you obtain the last object...
-Tower Pack: boring & uninspired wave defense. Blue pill or red pill neo?
-Spider Lair: a linear vent crawling, lighter, blowtorch simulator. Although executed much better than alan wake
-Developer Pack: has a museum to see 3d models & animations of characters & monsters, has a shooting range with time challenges (worthwhile to attempt), & arena that allows you to pit monsters against monsters (hit or miss)
-Pavel: a descent mini chapter where you try to escape after being held captive
-Khan: great narrative & paranormal/anomalies! More compelling than most of what is on the main story line
-Anna: a better sniper chapter than "Sniper Team" in my opinion. Overlaps anna's encounter with atryom on the main story line
Overall, a drastic improvement from metro 2033 (a game I found unbearable). This game is rough around the edges which needed a lot more polish, definitely a wasted opportunity for a more open world game, but a above-average experience all the way to the end. This game could of been so much more if not for the terrible game design decisions that held it back. Some DLC chapters are worth the look.
