Contrast is a great, non-violent 3D and 2D platformer.
Much of the gameplay involves navigating the protaganist Dawn around a 3D 1920s city.  The boundaries of the city are warped in a twisted MC Escher way which is a far more stylish way of focusing the player in the playable space than invisible walls would be.  Dawn is led around this space by another character Didi to various areas where the player is to overcome various platforming puzzles to advance the story.
The platforming is very clever.  Against most walls on which shadows are cast, Dawn can phase into the wall becoming a silhouette that can jump on the shadows cast by objects in 3D.  Prior to phasing in, Dawn can interact with objects to move the shadows into more traversable platforms.  She can also phase some 3D objects into the shadows with her to help solve puzzles and reach collectible items.  The 3D navigation is occasionally interrupted with a jittery camera and the player will occasionally pop out of shadows while phased without notice.  It seems the idea is to keep the camera perpendicluar to the wall while phased, but at bends or corners in the wall, this can get tricky.  Other than that, the controls are decent.
The story is touching with a focus on family and the characters are unique, except for Dawn who is essentially a mute avatar.  Didi, the child who accompanies and directs Dawn, is adorable and determined to help her father Johnny.  Johnny is the reformed tramp that to whom the player immediately yields his sympathy.  Kat is at her wit's end with the unreliable Johnny as she raises Didi on her own.  Didi's--more so than Dawn's--resourcefulness and her comments--especially during the puppet show--highlight a theme of female empowerment without being heavy-handed in its delivery.
I completed this game in four hours and would recommend it, especially at the going rate of a movie ticket.  The energetic Didi helps move the heartwarming story along in a stylish world with many ledges and crannies to explore.  Phasing from 3D into a 2D environment is a treat and the creatvity with which the 2D shadow puzzles were designed is impressive.  Despite camera and control issues in the 2D space, it would have been nice to explore this mechanic with more puzzles, but even so Contrast is a standout title.
If you like medieval combat, extreme gore, improving thyself, and an amusing community who will make formal gatherings in the midst of all this, this game will surely entertain you.

PINEVIEW DRIVE: This contains no spoilers, just gameplay instructions that I felt would of helped me when I played this game. Please do play Pineview drive. The sound design, atmosphere, and graphics are some of the most amazing i've seen in the horror game scene in a few years. The more you react to scares and do different things in the game it will adapt and attempt to scare you more. The health system is also based on this and how you react to scares.The scares and sounds will lead you to the next objective. This game does not hold your hand, you need to learn the twisting hallways of the house and where each room is, locked and unlocked. At some point it will become clear where to go or try as an objective, but it takes time to learn the house and plot to get there. You will arrive at a house that is almost completely locked up. You will need to find a keys over a total of 30 days to explore the house and property, on average unlocking a door or two a day. The day ends when you find a note that will expand on the story. The game takes patience. You will need to manage your light sources (match sticks and flashlight batteries). Flashlight starts to become unusable at 1 battery level. You will need to rely on lighting candles and jumping to and from lightsources to avoid losing health in the dark. Many who dislike the game run out of light sources and are lost in the darkness. You start each day with what you have left. There are additional spawns of batteries and matchsticks over the days throughout the already explored house. You can relight candle sticks. They will go out at the end of the night and they also have a chance of being blown out. The game has a day and night system, with the night coming sooner every passing day. If you take long enough and are unable to progress your character will remark about hearing a noise in a portion of the house or grounds to clue you where to go. The trick is to know where that is and how to get there. I found that it helped to find a place to hang out in the middle of the house conserving light sources and standing by a lit candle until your character gives you the clue to progress. I used a food storage room that opened from one side with a candle by the door and faced away from the window on nights I found I did not have enough light source to progress on my own and needed help. Even though this is in essence a key finding simulator, it takes a degree of skill to progress efficiently. After completing the game I had several critiques to the ending(the last night) as all the way to there I was blown away by the quality of the game. I felt the very tip of the end was lacking, but after understanding the plot and end, I accept it. On a side note in my opinion I wish the developer had put a limit on the matchsticks and candles to increase the difficulty and dismay camping. For instance candles would be spawned in a random condition (full stick, half stick, stub) that could hold a total of 3 times lighted by a matchstick and would degrade each time until they are unusable for the rest of the game. They would go out at the end of each night, and stay in the condition you left them in (3 use candle-> use-> lit-> chance of being blown out or night end->next day->2 use candle is there). I also would like if using a matchstick did not always work. The strike and spark, no fire (1/10 probability). It would make the decision to add a light or explore an area much more treacherous increasing the risk of taking a chance to find the keys. It also adds a level of punishment to new players who then learn throughout the nights that the candle resources are running out and would further push the player to learn how to conserve the resources and make smart decisions regarding paths to take through the house, learning new paths as shortcuts open up, and memorizing the layout of the house and candles. The game is full of easter eggs and is drawn from many horror sources. Enjoy!

]
Endless runners typically have two extremes when it comes to quality: One end of the spectrum being addictive and enjoyable to play for hours on end while the other end runs it course and becomes dull and drab before long. Turbopug DX mostly certainly falls into the latter category while also suffering from being just not fun to play. It’s cute motif and deceptively alright soundtrack may be attractive to some along with its low price, but there are certainly much better games of this genre out there.
Turbopug DX follows the typical formula as other endless runners in which your character moves forward constantly and must avoid obstacles while gathering collectibles and going for a high score. Said collectibles come in the form of letters that spells out ‘Turbopug DX’ along with pug tokens that come in counts of one, five and twenty five which goes towards unlocking new types of pugs and animals to play as - This is all simple stuff that gives the game something to work towards while going for high scores, but unfortunately it falls apart when you actually start playing the game. To start, even with the game being controllable with a single button, I encountered many instances where my input would be eaten upon having my pug land on the ground and try to jump again immediately, like I had to wait for my jump to ‘cool down’ for a fleeting moment. This had runs frequently be robbed from me since the game runs rather quickly and requires jumps with tricky timing that need to be strung together, and often require the right landing otherwise your jump will be too early or too late and your pug will run headfirst into an obstacle. Jumping simply doesn’t feel good because of the game’s speed, with very little hang time once airborne before your pug plummets like a stone in water.
The overall issue with Turbopug DX however is that it simply becomes dull and painfully repetitive after twenty minutes once the cute charm has worn off. The level proceeds with obstacle ‘sets’, but these sets are limited and any sense of surprise is brief, making the game feel awfully stale in no time. The game does cycle between visual styles and even has a whole system to create, share and play with custom skins that are applied over the level, but that can only go so far when the game itself becomes boring and artificial means have to be used in order to freshen things up. Collecting letters to spell out the title of the game does let you play a minigame as a change of pace, but the issues here are twofold: For one, collecting those letters is based off of lucky spawn rates which means that when you’re missing one or two letters you’ll run into repeats more often than not, and split paths in the level can make you miss a needed one. Secondly, failing the minigame once kicks you back to the main menu and you have to collecting all the letters again to have another shot - Completing these minigames grants achievements, so by that margin it’s really not worth the hassle.
Even with a peppy soundtrack, very little saves Turbopug DX from being a cheap yet painfully drab experience. The cute aesthetic is strangely subverted with the fact that your pug can die, not limited to spikes and sawblades that have blood coating some of them - And that’s on the default visual skin. The game is $1.09 (Canadian) so purchasing it will certainly not break the bank, but considering how there are endless runner games on mobile platforms for free that’re better than this, there’s no way I can recommend Turbopug DX unless you’re a fanatic for pugs, endless runner or score attack games - Even then, this one is a hard sell due to being far too generic.

Do I recommend this game? Yes
Before starting I would just like to outline that even though I haven't played this extensively on Steam I have clocked roughly 70 Hours on the Xbox 360 version many moons ago! So that will also form the basis for this review. Enjoy.
- Simplistic style, would act as a good starter for those new to the strategy genre
- Good variety of units accessible by certain characters based on what the user chooses
- Its release in 2009 would suggest that it has aged incredibly well, aesthetically is very pleasing
- The graphics have been updated from the Xbox 360 version
- Includes all DLC from the original edition as seen on consoles
- Engaging campaign, which I feel is a great edition to the Halo series
- Ability to play as both Covenant and UNSC offering different perspectives from both sides
- Dissapointing difficulty system (Lacks an inbetween difficulty) / This will likely vary from player to player
- Unit inbalancing, Covenant Scarab is easily obtained and very few units can withstand it effectively making Covenant a better choice
- Its simplicity, although a positive, can be seen negaively by some more familiar strategy players. The inability to have larger amounts of units and not being able to set up bases anywhere can leave users feeling somewhat restricted
- Very few maps, 18 in total, but some cannot be accessed in certain scenarios. For instance, 4 of those maps are only available for 3v3 games, and 7 maps for 2v2 and 1v1.
I recommend Halo Wars to you if you enjoy a more simplistic playstyle, but be warned there are a few restrictions in the game which might leave you unsatisfied, especially if you are coming from much more familiar titles suc as Supreme Commander, Ashes of the Singularity, Planetary Annihilation and Stellaris.

Lumino City is a short, sweet and simple game. You solve puzzles and click your way across a beautiful handmade city looking for your lost grandfather, meeting a couple of interesting characters along the way. The puzzles are mildly difficult, but there are some which are nearly impossible to figure out without a guide or walkthrough, such as the
. The visual style is cute and carefully crafted and the soundtrack is quite peaceful and relaxing.
Pros-
-Adorable hand-made visuals
-Not too challenging puzzles
-Funky and relaxing soundtrack- I purchased it and listen to it frequently
-Simple, feel-good story with bits of dry, British wit interspersed within it
-A generally enjoyable, relaxing, casual game
Cons-
-Quite a few bugs, some crash-inducing.
-Restricted movement- Any place you wish to reach must be clicked.
-Some impossible puzzles, with little to no hints on how to solve them, I.E.
.
[EDIT: It appears that I may be overstating this a bit- The Handy Manual which you recieve at the start of the game acts as a sort of a book of hints, however it is indeed over 900 pages long, so you may or may not wish to spend your time sifting through it.]
-$20 price tag- It is a bit steep for a game like this, but had I known how much I'd enjoy it, I would've paid the full price.
-One of the most point-and-click-ey games out there- If you aren't a fan of the genre, you won't enjoy this one (I daresay it is much better than the entire FNAF series combined, no offense to FNAF fans).
Overall, I would give this game an 8.5/10. It would be better without the little annoying bugs along with the crash-inducing ones, and it would be perfect with less restricted movement and fewer impossible puzzles. The game's creators really poured their souls into this little game, and the effort has been rewarded with a mostly smooth and visually appealing experience.
On a side note, this game made me want fish and chips very badly.

Игра, которая на первый взгляд казалась очередным клоном GTA, Mafia и прочих, оказалась очень и очень приятным сюрпризом.
Плюсы:
1) Геймплей. Сцены расследования и вдумчивого поиска улик вовремя сменяются погонями и перестрелками, и наоборот. Ни от того, ни от другого заскучать не успеваешь.
2) Графика. Дело даже не самой графике, которую я на 100% не оценил из-за не слишком сильного железа, а в лицевой анимации. Персонажи проговаривают каждое слово, эмоции переданы очень и очень достоверно. Впервые вижу такой высокий уровень исполнения.
3) Миссии. Они всегда увлекательные и интересные, со своей предысторией. За кровавым убийством обязательно скрывается драма, бармен не хочет выкладывать на-гора всю информацию, похищение оказывается следствием кризиса между супругами, а плохой парень в итоге оказывается хорошим. Даже побочные квесты, которые можно принимать при движении по городу, не повторяются, и их действительно интересно проходить. В этом отношении Rockstar, как всегда, не подкачали.
4) Музыка. И та, что играет на радио, и та, что звучит во время расследований - уместно, атмосферно, выполнено на высоком уровне.
Минусы:
1) Первый и главный минус - Rockstar Games Social Club. Отвратительное дeрьмо, которое постоянно забывает мой пароль, лагает, просит зайти снова, в общем, всячески мешает играть. Если бы можно было приступить к игре, не заморачиваясь с регистрацией, стало бы только лучше.
2) Еще один минус, менее существенный, но все же заметный - открытый мир. Песочница тут довольно-таки безжизненная, но основная проблема не в этом, а в том, что открытый мир тут не играет никакой роли, мы бы запросто могли обойтись и без него, автоматически перемещаясь по локациям, связанным с текущим расследованием. I enjoyed Endless Space 2 right from the beginning.   I tried it out over a review weekend and bought it to keep going.  Before I understood much of what I was doing, it was already scratching the 'just one more turn' itch.
The game is pretty.  Most things are animated in some detail, and the main map view has a great live feeling.  The UI is mostly clear and not confusing.
Space ship battles are neat, with detailed animated destruction, but they're kind of long after a few of them.  I like to watch big ones, at least for a bit.  You can cancel out of watching them and let the game tell you how it went or skip them entirely.  The ground battles, on the other hand are flat icons sliding around and going boom.  Yet, somehow I felt like I needed to watch these to get a sense of gravity about planetary invasions.  That's probably just me.
There are a couple of things that are not obvious and could be improved.  For instance, there's one flavor of icon that I did not find in a place where I could mouse over it for a tooltip when I first encouintered it, and I was not confident until I looked it up elsewhere that it was a composite icon for multiple earned resources.  Seemed kind of obvious once I knew, but at first it was used as if it were already explained.
The other main issue was finding out that there were game options that were completely unavailable until I turned off the tutorial, which I only left on because it came up with good information any time I tried a new task. It turns out you can tell a ship to guard a star system.  Good luck with that if you have the tutorial on.
I definitely recommend Endless Space 2 to eat up days' worth of your 'free' time.

I'll start with the end first.
If you like the idea of trading in a pretty large scale, then this game probably fits your taste.
When it comes to the actual trading aspect of the game, it's pretty straight forward. Different towns have different produce and needs. You buy where it's cheap and sell where it's expensive. The more goods you buy of a particular type in a town, the more it rises in cost and vice versa. Later on it seems to get a bit more complex, you'll be able to establish trade routes and so on, but on the grand scale of all, it's simply buying and selling.
But there is so much more baked in. Maintaining reputation, new ships, crew, equipment, battling pirates and different factions, plundering, gathering influence in a town so you can start your own production, managing settlements, doing quests. I was incredibly surprised by the sheer massiveness of a game that seemed so simple.
My only "gripe" with this game is that the different ways you can lose is not emphasized enough. 4 hours in and I was almost completly wrecked. The game went from "this is to easy" to "is this the same game?!!" in such a small time window. Still, I'm looking forward to restarting as much as it takes to win (Shogun 2 player haha).

So it's a Cold War strategy game. Yay.
More seriously, it's actually fairly decent, and at times unforgivingly difficult. This game goes for more "realism" in that it depends heavily on spotting your enemies and then shooting them before they see you. Charging into an open field in this game without any idea where your enemy is is just asking to get your people killed. And in this game that is not something you can really afford, since your troop numbers are limited, even moreso in the singleplayer campaigns where you use the same units from mission to mission. So if you lose them... your next mission will suck, as will all the others after it. Which is kinda neat, since it rewards good gameplay and hits you if you are too reckless.
I'm not sure how the multiplayer scene is now. It's prolly deserted since AirLand Battle is out. But... it was good when I played it. Only thing is that you need "stars" to unlock units, which you only get from the singleplayer campaign or by doing lots of multiplayer. I got 100% completion in this game so having units to use was no problem for me, but it can be for others. The Singleplayer is one of the toughest in any game i've played, but it is pretty good.
Anyway, it's an RTS more about strategy and less about APM (actions per minute). There's no base-building here. It's all about taking and holding ground, and bringing in reinforcements to help with that. It also is a game where combined arms is critical, because having a weakness in any area is just asking for your enemies to expoit it. Anti-air is particularly important, since Helicopters will tear you apart otherwise.
Anyway, it's pretty good. If I made this game sound interesting, then you may as well check it out. :o

Early review -
I've been a wargamer for a long long time, so I perhaps have a bias towards games like this.  This is a grand operational level game where you control one of the two alliances in WW1, with a choice of 5 start dates.  It's a bit like Panzer General etc. in that it's turn based - you move and attack with all your units one at a time, then your opponent takes his turn and does the same.  It's
like PG in that it is one continuous campaign - no linked scenarios with core units gaining xp,  Also, you have to control both land and naval units, as well as manage research and unit production.  There is multiplayer, but I haven't tried it so far, and there is only AI for your opponent (you're thrown in the deep end - you have to manage everything for your side yourself).
I suggest you check out some of the let's plays by RiotHouseLP if you want to see what the gameplay is like.  One thing about those LP's though - they're a year old, and it looks like the game has had one or more updates since then.
The AI is reasonably competent - on land it knows how to break through weak spots in your line and encircle and cut off units.  My advice on either side of the 1914 start is focus on cranking out cheap garrison units until you have enough to maintain continuous fronts with some reserves.  The AI wasn't so good with the German Navy though - when I loaded up my first BEF units to cross the channel, it sent a battleship and cruiser into the channel to attack a transport.  This might have been ok if he was certain to sink it, but he didn't, and anyway I don't think it's worth sacrificing a battleship just to kill one land unit.  So the AI doesn't know the value to the Germans of just keeping a fleet in being.  It seemed to handle the Allied fleets better.
OK, back to my 5th start - maybe this time I can make it through the end of 1914 at least ;)
Update:
After another couple tries starting as CP in 1914, I've given up for now trying to win with them until I get better at the game.  One of the things I like most about historical wargames is when by playing them you can learn a real historical lesson.  In this case, the lesson is that the Central Powers have almost no chance of winning if they can't knock out at least one of their 3 opponents in the first year.  After that, the numbers are all on the side of the Entente for winning any war of attrition.
I've now played a complete game as the Entente.  I won through to a complete victory in 1917.  I defeated Germany and Austria-Hungary early in 1916, but the pesky Ottomans wouldn't surrender until I moved some armies all the way across the map to Egypt and the Caucasus to start putting a hurt on them.  It was worthwhile though because learned how to perform an amphibious invasion and I got to see the importance of massed airpower, artillery, and shore bombardment in punching through otherwise hopelessly strong static trench defenses.
So, a definite thumbs up!

Absolutely excellent game! Today, the 30th of December, I can with certainty say this is my game of the year. It has completely captivated me, so much so that I've so far spent 91 hours playing it, even after only owning it for little over a week!
The game itself is a real time grand strategy where the focus is placed on the actual people in your kingdom, and not just warring. It has a very "Game of Thrones" element to it where to succeed you have to combine plotting, diplomacy, wars, land management (church, city, county, duchy, kingdom & empire) and execute it perfectly.
When you start, you can select to be a normal lowborn all the way up to emperor. If you select to be the Earl of a single county, you will in most cases report to your liege. You liege reports to his Duke and that Duke reports to his King. Using Marriage and other tricks you can position your family members so that at some point in the game your family inherits more land and titles. Once you have enough power you can then use war to take future land.
Overall this game has endless depth to it and many unique ways to replay it.
The game is very hard to understand at first and you will spend a lot of time on google trying to find out what you are meant to be doing, but once you grasp the methods, it really does come alive.
My only gripe with the game is the DLC is expensive for what you get. Dont buy it up front until you have played through the game enough to understand what you are getting with the DLC.
You will like this game if you enjoyed the Strategy map gameplay in Total War (not the battles) and if you liked Civilisation V. Those games are very simple and casual compared to Crusader Kings 2, so if you found those games hard or boring, then don’t bother playing Crusader Kings 2. If you don’t like slow games with 90% reading, then don’t bother buying this. Otherwise it is excellent and I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys grand strategy games.

At this point, please take my advice... KEEP GOING. I have never had so much fun losing in a game, and the sense of discovery when you figure this game out is some of the greatest moments I've had in gaming. Another great thing about this game is that it actually gets you interested in the time period! I can't tell you how many times I've paused the game and went to look up a character or country. So if you want a game with a terrible learning curve that turns into a wonderous experience, CK2 will serve just fine.

Best of all, it rewards skill: for each level you clear perfectly you gain a key which you can use to unlock a harder level of your choice, making it feel as though you're actually progressing. I enjoy video games. I like the thrill of shooting monsters and solving sliding puzzles, I relish exploring the world and having adventures in it, I love seeing my cities and theme parks grow because I made them just so. Crawling through dungeons, directing your minions strategically to best your foe, sneaking around conspiracy theory-laden faculties – video games are a rich medium with terrific entries in all kinds of experience. And even though I don’t particularly enjoy role-playing games, I can see why it’s pleasing to build and personalize a character of your making and vanquish your enemies. Even in a world with such a varied library of enterprises, there’s a single holy grail for me: finesse.
Let’s use my favorite game of 2012, Dustforce, to illustrate. Dustforce is a platformer made Hitbox Team, a group of four people. It stars four janitors (the eponymous “Dustforce”) who are put up against stages filled with leaves, rubbish, slime, and other waste that they can aptly clean up by swinging their broom (which involves walking over it). They’re not your average grumpy, unshaven, high school brutes though – they’re agile acrobats who can climb walls, hang on ceilings and traverse the most dangerous of environments. However, it’s not the dangerous environments that are the main objective of the game (though they will certainly test you, especially later), it’s finishing the stages completely clean – and herein lies the game’s greatest strength. The game measures two things, and rates you, at the end of the stage, accordingly: completion and finesse. Completion is the percentage of dust you cleaned up and enemies you defeated. Finesse is how often you lost your combo, preferably never – it’s a meter at the bottom of the screen that tracks how long it has been since you last dutifully scraped the last specks off the floor, and you lose it after a given amount of time. These two combined make for a drive to hone your abilities and learn every stage so that you sweep through it both smoothly and flawlessly.
The levels themselves are created in such a way that doing it right will give you a great flow through it, never really slowing down or losing a beat, making for a great sense of satisfaction when you finish them thoroughly. Not only that, but the stages gently go from very easy but enjoyable to an excruciating but very gratifying hard. If you happen to run into the later stages when you’re still a rookie cleaner, they will seem daunting to you, almost impossible. When you come back later, however, you suddenly realize how it’s done, and after a few runs, you will be able to beat that which looked to be so insurmountable to you earlier. It’s this “I can’t believe I did that” feeling, this ascendancy, that is so bliss. And it’s never because you upgraded your fanciful armor at a merchant, or upgraded your cannon with gems, it’s just you. You, physically, became more dexterous and skilled at this game. Your character didn’t gain any new abilities, he didn’t become stronger, you did. The realization of this is an amazing feeling, because it’s so fair – you put time into this, and you reaped the benefits by knocking out the obstacles in ways you earlier never thought possible.
Reinforcing this sentiment in Dustforce is the sleek graphic style, emphasizing the player’s action through a simple, but well animated, cel shaded style which make the janitors a joy to look at while they bounce through the environment. These environments, too, look great – while clearly being what they are (a city, a mountainous forest, a laboratory, and a crumbling mansion) they are presented in stylish, sometimes almost surreal ways, making for an aestethically pleasing journey through them. Also accompanying these is a terrific soundtrack, which never gets monotonous or annoying, even if you spend hours perfecting those later levels. It’s these elements that make mastering Dustforce a real joy, and here’s hoping many more follow its ways.

The soundtrack only adds to the adorable atmosphere created by the handcrafted levels. The game is just a lot of fun, and I love the devs attempt at being innovative. Really, this game is the pinnacle of clever design.
Lumino City is a really refreshing game. If you got a thing for puzzle games and would like to try something new, then this game is a must-have.

Tired of people spamming Half-Life mods and fan games? want something that has little to do with Half-Life other than the fact that it's running on Source? well, welcome to Dystopia! a game that isn't trying to be yet another Half-Life fan fiction!
Now you may be full of rage thinking: "Peter! it's ♥♥♥♥ing Half-Life! how dare you speak words of heresy against our all mighty internet god Gaben!" guys, I love HL like everyone else, but if you are subscribed to the Source engine group on Steam look at the long♥♥♥♥♥list of Half-Life: 2 "mods" I'm tired of it.
So now that I am done lighting the internet on fire. What is Dystopia? it is a small free to play class based game set in a cyber punk future. You can join two factions: Punks, VS Corps
But this time it's a bit different. Now you can choose implants that will boost your abilities in combat or hack(deck) computer terminals on the map supporting your fellow soldiers virtually without getting messy in reality.

Hacking: there is a slight difference between Dystopia's hacking and other game's hacking. Hacking in games generally result in being a little mini-game
you instead enter what is called "Cyber-space" while in this instance you fly around tunnels getting from place to place looking for the enemy's security controls. If you have played System Shock: 1 it look's a lot like that minus the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls of SS:1. But there are two things you must worry about while in Cyber-space: the enemy team's hacker, or the enemy team all together back in Meat-space. Your body in reality is completely defenseless so make sure you have your team covering you while you hack. You should also watch out for enemy players within Cyber-space defending/attacking the objective.
Implants: you're probably thinking "F2P+implants=P2W business model!" this game is 100% free. And before you ask, yes, implants are surprisingly well balanced
When you first enter the game you will be given a step by step menu, for instance: Choose your faction, now choose your class, select your weapon of choice, now pick out which implants you want. You can select a number of implants depending on how many points you spend this can also be changed at any point within the match.
Classes: there are a total of 3 very simple classes all three can be customized with implants and weapons. Starting with the Light: fast, heavy hitting, can't take♥♥♥♥♥♥ The class makes a good medic if you installed the healing implant or a decker since he can get in and out of situations easily assuming you installed the decking implant along with stealth. As for his weapons the shotgun and the melee weapon is all you need since both of those weapons are incredibly strong

Medium: the medium armored class is slow (but definitely faster than the heavy) and useful for defensive/offensive situations. In other words he's an adaptable class. Equiped with a selection of weapons such as the Grenade launcher, Assault Rifle, Scout Rifle, and that shocky...Orby thing I can't remember the name of....It's useful when dealing with heavies, that's all you need to know (don't judge me bro!)
Heavy: the heavy class serves as a tank, soaking up damage for the other two classes while dishing out massive blows of destruction at the same time. It's only flaws are lack of speed and no hands
the heavy cannot deck like the other two classes making him primerally a defense class. He has the option to only choose 3-4 implants (depending on what you installed) and his weapons of mass destruction are: the chaingun, the rocket launcher, the rail gun and the shotgun/grenade launcher claw of robo fapping.
Final verdict: And that's pretty much it! my only gripes with this game is: no player model customization, lack of weapons, (because there just needs to be MORE GUN!!!) and the sad limit of only a couple maps. However it's well balanced, has a nice funny community and it's just generally fun with anybody. You will of course meet some dumbass kids along the way

Bioshock 2 got a bit of a mixed reception when it released, for good reason. It's shorter than Bioshock 1, you can't backtrack to get things you missed, the EVE hypos and health packs are more limited and less useful (you can't reload your plasmids manually, for example), and I'm sure most people who have played it agree that one of the moral choices is a little questionably moral. The game tends to assume that the player is an idiot, like having a door with the code written on the window display the code on a little piece of paper when you go to the keypad in case you somehow missed it, or the game introducing Sophia Lamb like three times to you, or explaining what hacking a door does every time you hack a door. And unlike the first game where everything in the world felt like it had a place in it, Bioshock 2 tends to feel a little gamey - why does a Big Daddy need to use a weapons upgrade station, and why would they even make those stations be able to upgrade those weapons? Why is Delta just able to use the gene modification that lets him restore little sisters for no explainable reason? How does he eat potato chips with that helmet on? In terms of the remaster, the game is more stable than Bioshock 1's remaster, but also lacks the bonus features like the developer commentary tracks.
At the same time, looking back, I think we didn't know how good we had it. At least Bioshock 2 wasn't a series of linear corridors. At least hacking wasn't turned into an automatic plasmid. At least the weapons were fun to use, and still allowed you to set up traps and plan things out and gave you reasons to bother doing so. At least the world still felt a little bit alive, and didn't present you with a world where you were the only thing that mattered and every living creature existed to live and breathe wanting you dead. By now some of you are probably looking at Bioshock Infinite in your steam library with the same sense of regret that I do. Instead, Bioshock 2 took a familiar great game and played it a little safe, adding some nice new features like dual-wielding plasmids and guns while keeping the overall formula pretty similar. You don't get the bonus challenge maps that Bioshock 1 had, but in its place you get Minerva's Den, a generally praised side story DLC. And while Sophia Lamb ultimately isn't really as good of a character as Andrew Ryan and nothing quite tops an evening with Sander Cohen, Bioshock 2 still has a fair amount of memorable characters in its cast. Is Bioshock 2 as good as Bioshock 1? No, but at least it's not as boring as Bioshock Infinite, and I think that's what really counts.

This game is short and sweet. Can really be played through in one sitting without a problem (especially if you don't go on a hunt for the random collectibles which some made no sense and said things as nondescript as 'science photo'- I had to find them because completionist)
Some of the movement within the shadows can be finicky at times, but isn't much of an issue since there aren't really load screens or repercussions for dying. Just a fun puzzler that follows the active imagination of a young girl and her love for her family.

Contrast is one of those games that's unique and memorable at the same time, as it drags you into a shadow world in the 1920s Paris in the role of Dawn, young Didi's best friend who possesses the ability of shifting between the 3D material world and the 2D shadow world, making Contrast one of most ideas-filled titles of this year. Didi is also the only person who can see Dawn, but the actions you perform around the city will have an impact on the real world that is seen as shadows from Dawn's eyes as well. Even though Dawn is an interesting character on her own that you'd definitely become interested in as the game goes, this is the story of Didi's parents, who are constantly arguing after Didi's father left and her mother is too busy working at night, leaving her unattended - a perfect opportunity for her to sneak out and fix things around the city with Dawn's help. The bad thing about Contrast is that it will end too soon, rushing through the events of the story just to get to the ending, and even though following the plot is satisfying as it is, there are lots of moments that could've been detailed more, making the game longer and the lasting experience more satisfying in the end. Without doubt Contrast nails its presentation, having a simple menu that will almost instantly take you into the action, while still offering you plenty of options to manage things such as collectibles or taking a look over your stats. Starting with the purely astonishing art work and the detailed characters and moving on to the shadows that have an important role in the gameplay, but offer an incredible visual effect as well, the game is constantly reminding you how awesome its core idea truly is. The problem with that idea however is that it hasn't reached its full potential, as the moment when you get most comfortable with the control and the idea of the game is the same moment the game will reach its denouement. There are so many ideas that are simply rushed inside the game, such as walking up the shadows of Didi's parents in order to reach a location and listening to their speech while doing so; those are the kind of moments that make Contrast feel unique and make you desire more out of this game.
The idea of shifting between the real 3D world and the world of shadows is without doubt one of the most unique and innovating ideas of this year and Contrast takes great advantage of this idea, creating some amazing puzzles that will leave you satisfied each time you complete one and move in to the next area, but the best thing about those puzzles is their deductibility, forcing you to analyse each one of them, but offering the solution if you stare at them long enough as it is sometimes more than obvious. Each new location you visit will introduce new puzzle concepts, some trickier than others, but same as the story those are rushed, never taking full advantage of their potential, as the game will quickly move from one concept to another, leaving abilities such as the shadow dash to be used only a few times in the entire game. There are the occasional glitches that will stop you from making a move in your first try, but there isn't any sort of time pressure on the gameplay so you have all the time in the world to find your way around a puzzle and reach your destination. The 3D world puzzles are enjoyable and the shadow puzzles even more, but the real magic begins when the game combines those elements to create some amazing areas that you will have to scout first, try different approaches and only then decide on a final solution that will take you to your destination, but all this time spent looking around an area is well spent as you will constantly be excited about where one thing should go or how the positioning of some objects will help you reach a higher point. Walking up the shadows of Didi's parents is an amazing concept as you get to listen to a part of the story while you're slowly making your way to a location that's related to that story, constantly keeping you on the edge about what's gonna happen next as you climb higher and higher and eventually reach a location that will unlock further mysteries. There is a lot of great stuff in here and because it is so great it leaves you with a thirst for more and unfortunately there isn't anything else.
Contrast on the PlayStation 4 looks amazing, making the city of Paris come to life at night with the use of those same shadows that make the gameplay so enjoyable, as the little bit of light that is available in an area will reflect objects in the precise direction, something that affects the gameplay as well as the overall beauty of this title. Even if you only get to see Dawn and Didi as full characters, as the rest of the cast is seen as shadows, they are both incredibly detailed and fit into the world perfectly. The visual effects are okay, with a few things that could use some work, but what is really impressive is the reflection of certain things on the pavement of the street as it is wet and seeing that no matter where you go is impressive.
The voice acting is top notch, as the entire cast including Didi, her parents and Vincenzo take advantage of some amazing voice work that truly helps sell the story and the emotional road it takes once you get to know Didi better. The sound effects are just as good, making the world come to life and give Dawn's powers a great background; the best thing however, comes in the soundtrack, as from the start of the game you will be greeted with a noire classic, a perfect fit for the city of Paris in the early '20s, and the list goes on and on as you progress through the game.
Unfortunately, the main campaign is the only thing that the game provides and that will be over in less than 6 hours, depending on how much time you take to solve each puzzle, and even though the game has collectibles you can find those easily in your first playthrough if you just look around, so unless you wanna replay the game a few weeks after just to relive the awesomeness, there isn't anything else to keep you around.
Contrast is one of the best experiences you can have this year, not only because it is unique, but because it works wonders, providing some great puzzles, amazing exploration and a story worth hearing, unfortunately that will only last a few hours, so if you were looking for something to keep you around your PS4 a lot more, this will come as a disappointment, but either way Contrast is a game worth playing at some point, even if it isn't your priority for the new console.

This is a Resident Evil/Call of Duty cross with just a nod to Metro 2033.  If you played Last Light there's nothing new in the Redux.  If you a fan of the original Metro 2033, not the Last Light wannabe that Metro 2033 Redux was, you won't enjoy this one.  Everything that was great in the original is lost here.  This game is just a mindless shooter like the resident Evil and Call of Duty games.  As matter of fact this game actually has Boss battles like Resident Evil.  What do creature Boss battles have to do with Metro games?
This is a heavily scripted game with a convoluted story that only serves to get you to the next round of shooting.  The AI is amazingly dumb and can't see you even if they are in front of you.  It seemed to me that the mutants were harder to kill only because the weapons damage was inconsistent.  In Metro 2033 you could rely on your weapons because the damage they doled out was consistent.  In Last Light Redux it seems to be arbitrary.  Even the sniper rifles were inconsistent in their damage; usually one shot to the head with a sniper rifle is an instant kill in in most games but not in this one.  Even the pneumatic weapons like the Tihar that were so deadly in Metro 2033, so much so that you could kill the Librarians easily with them, are hit and miss in this game.  Sometimes one shot to the head will do it and sometime you have to just keep blasting away.
I never found Metro 2033 to be too linear of a game even though you were in tunnels going from tunnel to another.  The same can't be said for Metro Last Light Redux it feels very linear.  You simply shoot your way from point A to point B.  Like the Boss battles in Resident Evil you just need to figure out what the key is.  In one laughable Boss battle the oversized mutant needed to knock down columns in order to bring down the ceiling so it was just a matter of running around in circles and letting the mutant knock them down, thereby saving my ammo.
There were too many of these scripted click a button and fend off the mutants until whatever is supposed to happen finally happens.  In those scenarios I found that I could save ammo by just running around in circles, like a fool, shooting the odd Nosalis that got in my way while waiting for the event to finish, i.e. the boat arrives for you to jump on to make your escape.  It’s basically one obviously scripted scene after another.
Also way too many cut scenes, a significant amount of the game is made up of cut scenes that you can't skip.  Most of this is story exposition, because the story was convoluted and very artificial.  Metro 2033, being based on the novel, had a very simple, straightforward plot and it was good at story telling.  However, even though the same author wrote the story line for Last Light, it really had the feeling of being a slapped together plot to justify the Metro Last Light sequel.
Bottom line if your Metro 2033 fans you will be disappointed in Last Light.  But if you’re a Resident Evil / Call of Duty fan there are plenty of mutants (just not the weird Resident Evil kind) and soldiers to shoot at.  So if you're just looking for a linear FPS shooter with fantastic graphics, and don't really care about the plot then you won't be disappointed in this game.

Each of the game's "worlds" contain plenty of pre-unlocked levels to master as you meander your way through them one after another to unlock the rest of the more challenging and meaty ones. As boring as collecting dust sounds, the mechanic of picking it up without letting your combo meter drop makes every level challenging and fun. Dustforce is an excellent and subtely-challenging game that I definitely recommend picking up.

Beautiful re-skin, like for Bioshock, interesting 180 perspective on philosophies, some new mechanics from BS1.  Lots of crashing issues in Siren Alley, frustrating keyboard setup, and not quite as good as the first game. Worth getting? Depends on if you like waves of zombies *cough* splicers constantly coming after you.
Bioshock 2 basically takes you to the other side of Rapture, the side that no one wanted to talk about.  It was the brothel, down-on-your-luck, Skid Row area that you navigate through, shooting splicers and others, trying to find your specific little sister.
The re-skin is beautiful, compared to the original PC version, one hell of an improvement.  But, considering how...ugly...the area you're traversing through is, it doesn't make that much of a difference overall...
Objectivisim (the individual) vs Communism (the collective) was an interesting thing, in that how differently they treat each other, yet are inherently flawed thanks to human nature being dissatisfied with "perfection".  It doesn't help how corrupted the convictions of their leaders became (see: Siren Alley).
There are some new Plasmids for you to get, new weapons to find, and a different way to help the Little Sisters.  But, this is where it starts falling apart for me and why I can understand how this game can be considered by some groups to be "non-cannon".
Bioshock 1 is the superior game in my opinion; the story was tighter, the splicer fights a lot more "meaningful", and while there was respawning, it wasn't a crowd, it was one or two.  In Bioshock 2, they decided to make almost everything a huge fight, with wave after wave of splicers coming at you.
Theoretically, most of the people in Rapture should have died out after Jack's antics 8-10 years ago.  Fresh and canned food, clean water, medicine, all of that should have run out, while others would have drowned from collapsed buildings.  If not, they should have fought themselves to death.  It makes no sense that there are that many splicers left to attack Delta when he's helping a Little Sister harvest ADAM.
This sequel is pure shoot-'em-up, survival, throw-everything-but-the-kitchen-sink at the player, which I didn't like nearly as much.  Bioshock 1 placed the splicer waves at strategic points, while Bioshock 2 tried to put them in as many places as they could.  When it comes to the weapons, I stick to the machine gun and the rivet gun; the rest just don't work for my play style.
I miss the hacking from the first game; that was fun.  The needle seems to hate me, and my reflexes are pretty bad (I play on easy; yes, I suck that badly). Let's not mention how difficult it can be to find the freaking hack darts...
I had to go through and change all of the keyboard keys to what they were in Bioshock 1; why they changed the layout, I will never know.  That's pretty minor compared to the crashes.
The crashes, oh the crashes.  I started playing after the second patch, as I was still finishing up the original Bioshock.  The crashes seemed to happen in Siren Alley (which I
just finished), mostly around the third Little Sister.  She seemed to be the catalyst for the crashes; if the Big Daddy exits the door, the game will crash; if he goes another way, it won't.  When you have the Little Sister, you can't harvest this one body first, or it's a crash for you.  If you put her through this vent, and are fighting the Big Sister, KABOOM.  You use the key, the issue starts, and the sound is half-there; two splicers later, BOOSH.  Ignore the one splicer and you're golden.  Hell, I was fighting an "immortal" spider splicer at one point!  Then my charged up plasmid doesn't want to discharge and I had to switch plasmids to release it!
There are other random crashes, but those are the ones that really stuck out for me.
I honestly wish that there was a "kind/sort of" or "maybe" button for the reviews; it's not a favourite of mine, but has some interesting points to make.  It really was like
where it was a sequel just to be a sequel, like someone said "Oh man, Game X is super popular, we need to push out a follow-up as soon as we can to capitalise on it!", so Subject Delta's story was born.  It's one of those take it or leave it games for me; I'm playing it because it's part of the series, but as I said before, I can understand why some people consider it non-cannon, as it doesn't
fit within the Bioshock 1 universe.  It was shoehorned in, and it shows.
Play it for yourself, and come to your own conclusion; other people think that this is better than the original; I'm on the other side of that coin.

Absolutely amazing !
Now, I have to say that having a game like this be free to play is already enough. The game looks and runs better than most AAA titles out there these days, the grafics are stunning and the story is realy immersive. BUT this is not your typical ''Free To Play'' game, this is fully fledged grinding material right there. You can choose if you want to pay for in-game stuff, however it is completely optional. No Pay To Win, no real in-game advantage gained by paying. It's all mostly cosmetics and the choise of player.
If THAT is not enough to sell the game to you, which is free by the way, the there's much more ! The PVP is amazing, making you feel like real Tenno, not extremely easy, not extremely hard. Just enough to make you feel super powerful and part of the Warframe universe. Combat mechanics are interesting, each Tenno has his own set of skills and combos to make, you can play the game how you want it to play. If you choose not to put any real money in the game, it's gonna cost you pretty decent time to catch up on the loot, but thats your choise, theres no real advantage lost or gained.
The community....ahhh the community. It's something special when you compare it to, let's say, Overwatch community. When I first started the game, I was realy confused on what should I do. I asked a few people and they turned out to be realy helpful and friendly. For the est. 52 hours I've played I never saw any real toxicity in chat or in game at all. Don't be afraid to ask a fellow veteran player in chat for a tip to a newcome, Im sure someone will help you with your problem or confusion.
Over all, if I should show someone a free to play game, this is what I would propably choose. It's fun, fast paced, strategic and most of all realy free to play. Games like these are what still keeps Valve running, and I am happy to be part of the community that enjoys it as well as I do.

I actually think the game looks a bit better on "low" because the colour filter is removed, but with it so are the pretty lighting effects. The story is quite compelling, and it has a unique take on interactive story-telling. The music and sounds are nice, fitting and well-implemented, the game-feel is pretty good and for the most part I can recommend this game to anyone who likes puzzle games or platformers...
But I do have one enormous gripe with it. It has an obnoxious tendency to constantly take control away from the player. This is very common with games nowadays but it is so bad here that I got annoyed and stopped playing at one point, just because of it. I don't think there is a single 5 minute stretch of gameplay without a cutscene, or extremely slow camera-pan across a level to point something out. Even standing on buttons triggers a bloody cutscene, and not just the first time; every time. I get that you need to show the player what each button triggers, but it's better to naturally design the level so that the player can notice it in-game. Or at least only have the cutscene play the first time.
Most of the triggered cutscenes are there for seemingly no reason, and the game would have looked almost identical if it just played out in-game. Sometimes the game simply freezes you in place while a character speaks with absolutely no camera angle changes.
If it wasn't for this one annoying tendency, I would have absolutely adored this game.

When it comes to horror games, Pineview Drive is an interesting breed of game.
The Initial Feeling
- When you boot up the game and get into it, you're treated with an annoying start.  You're outside this large gate with a mansion just teasing you over the edge.  It takes a moment for you to find the key you need to open up the gate and dive into things.  An awkward start, though don't let that fool you into thinking you wasted your money.
Cons
- It 'can' be hard to see the jump scares, this is true.  There are a lot of things happening, sometimes you don't even see it.  A ghost is behind you and touches you (I think that's what happened) or something was on the other side of the door and you turned away missing it.  For a horror game, that can get annoying.  Though, a lot of it is repetive stuff you'll most likely see...  eventually.
- The 'Fear' mechanic of the game (The bar in the top left) is, admittedly, the downfall of this game.  Initially, I thought, 'Wow, this is new!'.  For one, I typically avoid horror games I'm unable to fight back.  They're not immersive enough for me, though I do play them from time to time due to a horrible lack of 'Good' horror titles.  Anyways, the 'Fear' mechanic in this seems to be far to random to be reliable.  Essentially (The game doesn't tell you this), when a jump scare happens, such as a phone ringing, a ghost appearing, something flying in your face, the game will pick up your actions via the mouse and keyboard.  This determines whether or not that meter drops down.  If it goes away, you die, presumably.  After much testing this mechanic, it seemed like it was far to random for you to become conditioned to not jump at various things, thus being able to progress.  Some things just drain your meter no matter what.  While being an interesting feature, it would be much more interesting if it had some consistency to it.
- It can be frustrating to try and figure out where to go.   This game pretty much requires you to wear headphones with the volume as high as your ears can stand.  I found myself wandering around most nights going 'Where do I go?'.  Eventually, the main character would give a hint then I could finally go and progress because I couldn't hear whatever I was supposed to be hearing.
- It takes...  way to long to get to the most frightening parts.  Initially it's just your cliche paranormal things before it advances into a hellish jump scare mayhem.  While the later part of that is good for the game, the first 20 nights feel more like the ghosts aren't even trying.
Pros
- It is a beautiful game, the developer should be proud of their work.  The rain looks nice, the mansion looks nice, and the weather effects do add quite a bit to the game.
- The atmosphere is spot on, with the little noises here and there to make you always wonder 'Should I be worried about?'.  You feel like you're immersed with the noises in a haunted mansion.
- Upon reaching the later nights the game becomes rather frightening.  It just takes time to get to those points.  I won't say any spoilers of what those scares are but I found them to be well done, even if some are. admittedly, hard to witness.
Final Verdict
I'd set this game as a 6/10 final review.  It's good for a one time full playthrough, if you don't become to annoyed with the 'Fear' meter.  If you can manage to get that to cooperate, the game is fairly well made.  If the 'Fear' meter worked better this could easily be an 8, if not a 9, out of ten.  Give it a try.  I'd recomeend snagging it on a Special Deal day.  Twenty bucks isn't to bad but there is no replay value and the buggy Fear can cause more frustration than enjoyment.

A good horror game. It has a slow start and a few issues that hinder the game's potential, but the game picks up later on and definitely becomes a much scarier game. It's a game where actually too scared actually does cause your character to die.
Talking about the cons first...
Among the game's issues, two of them stand out. The first of them is that the game can be really confusing. Basically, during most of the game, you'll be looking for keys to open doors and find notes - each time you read a note, you advance one day, and on the way you'll be collecting batteries for your flashlight and matches to light candles.
The first issue is that actually finding the keys can often be an issue. Right off the start of the game, you have to find a key to unlock the main gate... Which is lying right on the ground. But actually spotting the key is hard, because the color of the key slightly blends with the color of the ground. The game does spot items with a red contour, but only if you get really close to them - which isn't saying the game should just make items shine in the dark and make things too easy, specially since most of the game is about exploring the mansion, but the game does make it hard sometimes to find the necessary items. There were times I triggered events that were supposed to reveal keys to me and I still couldn't spot them. I admit I actually almost gave up on the game on the beginning because I was running all around the mansion and couldn't find the keys I had to find.
On this note, I should also add that using the keys will add slightly to the confusion, because the game doesn't tell them apart - it just tells you how many keys you're holding, but you have to try out each door until you find the one the key opens. However, I don't consider this a flaw. It's part of how the game works as, once again, exploration is a big part of the game.
The second issue is pacing and knowing what's the next step to take during the game. As I've mentioned at the beginning of this review, the game has a slow start. During the beginning, there's a lot of frustration involved while you're going around looking for keys to open doors and finding notes and it takes a while before things actually start to get creepy. The game is divided between 30 days and some of them are longer than others - there are days that are actually pretty easy, short and scareless to beat, while others can be a lot longer and scarier. The game's story that you learn from the notes you find don't help much in telling you where to go next. Sometimes you read a note and you think you know where to go on the next day, but then you find out you were wrong. In fact, very often it's actually better to just sit near a candle light and wait for the character to talk to himself, which is when you get tips on what to do next, so you know where to go or what to do.
Now, for the pros - which is where the game actually gets really good.
After you get past the game's slow start, you find out how scary the game can be. The game successfully creates a creepy atmosphere with a combination of elements in all the right places - statues, paintings, objects, everything makes the player feel like everything is observing him/her or that everything could be a trigger for a jump scare - even objects reflecting light in the distance can look like something creepy, like a pair of glowing eyes. As you explore the house, you'll run into certain events, some of which are pre-determined for each day, while others are random, and they're meant to, as you'd expect, scare you. And the game actually tries to measure how much you're scared, based on your response to those events. If the game detects you're scared, you lose health, so you have to do your best to stay put while the game tries to surprise you, in order to stay alive. (The problem with this "scare-o-meter" in the game is that it could actually be improved, as sometimes it doesn't work as intended. I won't spoil the actual mechanics, but I've read how it works and tried it out and there are times when I lost health even though I had no response to some events.)
There are different events that will try to undermine your health. It's not about running away from ghosts or hiding from monsters, but actually a little of everything. You never know if there is something behind the next door you open. Even events like a phone ringing all of a sudden or a whisper coming from behind you can be enough to take away your health. As you progress further on, you'll unlock more places inside the mansion and the more you explore, the more room the game has to try and catch you by surprise and the more events will be available to do so. Closer to the end of the game, actually trying to stay put in order to not lose health becomes quite challenging. You do recover health at the start of each day, but only a portion of it, so if you get scared a lot during each day, eventually the character will die. You can try to make use of daylight when a new day begins, but it lasts very little and soon everything is all dark again. And in some cases, you have to wait for night time anyway.
Even after you beat the game, there is still an extra playable mode (two, actually, but one of them is just a mode to freely explore the mansion) that adds a little more to the game. In this mode, you have to find the 8 Scarecrow letters while avoiding the Scarecrow (inspired by Slenderman, apparently). It doesn't use the health system, so getting scared is no longer a problem, but then the game is fully randomized in this mode, with no pre-determined events and random locations for items. And I'll admit that while I finished the main game without quitting at any time, this extra mode actually made me nope out of the game, which is quite an achievement since only one other game made me do it before.
I've been reading about Pineview Drive II and, personally, I believe there's a lot of potential for a sequel. If they can address the game's current issues (keys that are hard to find, knowing what to do next and the health system not always working as intended) for the next game, I could easily see Pineview Drive II becoming one of my favorite horror games.

This game is a gorgeous experience of a point and click adventure. Everything in the game is hand-made out of cardboard, presenting a really special looking, unique style.
The story itself is really simple. You are Lumi, and you're looking for your grandfather who disappeared, and you solve puzzles to continue your journey while helping the citizens of the town.  There are barely any items to pick up, most of the puzzles are self-contained, or take place in a very small environment, like in a room. The puzzles themselves are pretty hard compared to the average point and click game, but mind you, in Lumino City the gameplay is centered around them, not on finding and combining items. This means the game is short if you know what you're doing, the game's focus is on style, atmosphere and puzzle-solving, with minimum fluff and gameplaytime inflation.
It's a short, but intense game puzzle-wise in an everchanging environment in a nutshell, and it does a perfect job at it.
And as an extra, I'd love to mention it's guide system because it's incredible. You get the book with all the hints, and another ~ 470-480 pages. The contents page tells you that if you're at the gears puzzle, then take the number of gears, multiply it by 9 then add 5 and that's the page where the solution is. Besides that (though didn't check each and every) pages are filled with high resolution texts from manuals, it's looks incredible :)

The character design is less brilliant, with characters being reduced to toilet-male-female-icon like simplistic collage, and no personality or story to back them up.
Gameplay wise, it's a point and click with strong emphasis on varied puzzles,  some being fun and original and some annoying or stale. The point and click parts aren't great, with the controls being sluggish and being hard to determine with precision where you need to click.
Theres a neatly designed in game manual with the complete solution to all puzzles. Unfortunately it doesnt have the solution to the absurd point and click riddles - which is where it was most needed.
And this is where the review ends: I encountered a game breaking bug in one of the point and click bits, where you need to bring 3 items to a captain. Well, after failing to progress despite restarting the chapter twice I looked it up and it turns out you need to bring the 3 items in a specific order, if you do not you get stuck (despite the character telling you you can proceed) and need to restart the whole chapter again and do it in the "correct" order.
It turns out the devs acknowledged this was a problem back in 2015, but never addressed the issue. Upon search there are other 100% crashes and game breaking progression bugs. Yet the game continues to be sold at a premium.
Given that you are probably going to encounter some of these issues as you go along, and that your money will obviously not go towards getting this game the critical update that it needs, I absolutely cannot recommend that anyone buys this product.
A real shame.

~Some Pros/cons I compiled. ~

Port Royale 3 is a good game, but it is unfortunately marred with some serious design issues and is lacking basic information.
Overall, the game is not user friendly at all with little to no explanation of how to do anything anything in the game and where it does actually explain how things work, it doesn't even use the correct terminology for many screens/fields/controls. For example, there is a "tutorial" objective in the trader campaign that tells you to set up a trade route with another convoy, but it does not tell you how to make a new convoy, or where to set up the trade route. Most modern games provide some type of walkthrough tutorial that guides and teaches the basic gameplay to new users (Known as the First-Time User Experience). It also suggests that you set up with convoy with a specific strategy, but the strategy is called something else. Basically, if you are not familiar with the previous games, you will simply need to fumble around through screens in order to figure out how to do practically anything.
The UI is clunky and confusing. The pause button in the upper left doesn't actually pause the game. basic features (and information) are spread across various screens with no way to quickly tab through to find what you need, which is important for economic/sim/tycoon games.
The general gameplay is fairly solid, but (especially the trader campaign) is very slow and quite boring until you get further into the game... When I say boring, I mean compared to similar games (like Patrician IV). Combat is pretty lacking as well (from what little I have played). The player should have much more control over their fleet. With the backdrop on the main menu, I honestly expected to see detailed 3D combat (Like Age of Sail II). What it didn't expect is how it feels like all you are doing is watching the ships fight, with very little control other than setting the behaviour of your ships (which in my opinion is simply horrible design).

Based on all the supiciously postive revies, I must be missing something, but I could not get into this game.  In fact, I hated it so much I'm going to write a review which I never ever do.  I read the reviews and though, "Great, a nice graphic strategy game.  I like and am good at strategy games, and it's $2!  What a steal!"  I want my money back.  As someone else pointed out, there's a reason they don't offer a demo for this game.
The user starting interface looks like it came chronologically before Command and Conquer, and built on a budget.  It's so bad there's a tutorial in the game for how to use it.  As for strategy, I tried using my light vehicles for recon like they instructed, but learned the hard way that rushing is always better.  Honestly, there is more strategy in tic-tac-toe.  Touching on pacing, "slow and strategic"?  Are we playing different games?  One review sums it up when they wrote that the tanks would have to be doing 200mph to do the speeds they do in the game.  It's like controlling a million little racecars that all blend into the terrian and all have spec sheets that are longer than your arm.
And the tutorial throws things at you so fast and so poorly that your eyes will go cross trying to figure it all out.  "Press this button to group units"?  Why don't we send every enemy unit at you while you sort through our complicated menu screen to find that button.  I just gave up trying to find it, not that it mattered as rushing seems to be the better strategy anyway.  The learning curve on this game is more like a right angle!  As an example of how bad the tutorial is, I don't normally use tutorials as I can just figure out the game on my own, but the tutorial is preprogramed so I thought I'd give it it's go.  It took me almost 6 minutes into the first mission before I found my troops and were able to move them as the tutorial kept trying to point out ally units that were totally pointless to the whole mission, and my units blended in so well I couldn't see them.
Additionally, the mini-map is by far the worst I've ever seen.  I felt like I needed a mini-map to understand what I was looking at on the mini-map!  It kept trying to show me what I can only imagine is the angle that my camera was rotated to in such a way to show what my field of vision would be if I was looking at the main map.  If that made sense to you, you might like this game, but I kept having to furiously scroll around on the mini-map to get it to go over the red blobs that were attacking me that I just gave up on the whole mini-map.
Now, I love strategy games, and I have played MANY of them, both new and old.  But this game doesn't even rank in my top 50.  Want a good strategy game with realism and a myriad units?  I suggest Company of Heroes, and I would wager that CoH2 will also be good.  Can't be worse than this.

There are two campaigns and a Free Game mode. The campaigns serve more like tutorials. Besides, each of them has a story. The first campaign will guide you in a path of a trader, in the second you will take a role of an adventurer. After you complete them, they will transform to a free game, so you can continue playing them if you wish.
The principle of trading remains the same. Buy cheap, sell as expensive as you can. After some time, you can build your factories, hire workers and build residences for them. The products will go in your warehouse. In Port Royale 3, you can hire a steward for your warehouse. This will automate the warehouse and make your life easier. You can tell him to sell goods, buy raw materials for your factories, keep raw materials so he won't sell them or specify which products should stay in the warehouse(and the amount of it too). Trade routes are now easier to manage. You just choose a convoy, select towns which will the convoy trade with and choose a script. Then activate the route and watch how your wealth grows. But if you wish, you can still create your own script and tell your captain where, what and how much to buy/sell or transfer between convoy and warehouse. In my opinion, this is not necessary, as the scripts are well made. There is even script for supplying your factories and selling the goods they produce. This makes life of a merchant in PR3 much easier.
The path of an adventurer includes many naval fights, attacking towns and pirates hideout. Frankly, the combat system from the first Port Royale is still unbeaten, as there you could use all your ships in a naval fight. Here, you can select a maximum of three ships from your convoy that can fight. But at least you can use them simultaneously, unlike in Port Royale 2, where you can only use one ship at the same time.  Convoys will have the basic crew available automatically. But it's vital to hire more sailors if you want to fight other convoys. There are three types of ammunition. In Port Royale 3, you don't have to buy the basic cannon balls, as they are always available. The other ammunition types are chain-shots and grape-shots, which you have to buy in towns, along with sabers and muskets. The rest of combat is very similiar to the games predecessors. You can sink, plunder or take ships from enemies convoys.
You can also marry a viceroys daughter, as you can in the previous games. But first, you must have your own manor in a town which you rule. You can obtain your own town either from a viceroy, or by force. A viceroy will give you a town if you are popular there, if the status of the town is Prosperity(the satisfaction of citizens is 75% or higher), if you have enough workers there. In addition, your popularity in the nation of which town you want to rule must be also quite high. A viceroy will not give you command of a town when the nation have 5 or less towns in possession. I don't know if you are able to have your own hideout, like you was in the first Port Royale. I think yes, since I believe you can become a pirate in PR3.
Another novelty lies in acquiring higher ranks. In the previous games, you only had to increase your wealth. Now, you also have to hire more workers and enlarge the storage in your convoys(which you can do simply by buying more ships to the convoys).  The rest of the game is the same as the previous ones. You can buy pieces of maps, save castaways on sea, etc.
In general, I find Port Royale 3 a good game. In my opinion, it's better than Port Royale 2, but the first Port Royale is still the best from the franchise because of the combat system. Port Royale 3 is the easiest game from the franchise. The campaigns won't last long. I finished the trading campaign in 3 days(cca 9 hours) and the adventure campaign in one day(cca 3 hours). The only problem I have with this game is the flickering when I turned on anisotropic filtering. That I think is problem related do AMD graphics cards.

Pineview Drive, in my opinion, is a mediocre horror game that had the potential to be much better than it is. It’s not really a bad game, but it has some major flaws that really drag it down. The good things about the game are: The atmosphere is great for a horror game. The music and sound effects are excellent and really add to the game’s creepiness. The graphics are great. And the game has some well done scares. The major flaws about the game are: The game is WAY TOO DARK even with the game's brightness setting set to its highest level. You do get a flashlight but it doesn’t last long enough. And flashlight batteries in the game are few and far between. You may have to turn up the brightness and the contrast on your monitor to their highest levels just to barely see anything when your flashlight is low on battery power. When you start up the game, you can’t skip the introduction screens. And they are fairly lengthy introduction screens. You can’t rebind the keys either. It would have been nice if the game had a built in map of the mansion to help the player with finding their way around as you progress through the game’s 30 days of terror. It would have been nice if each door had its own specific name that relates to the room that it’s for. And also if the game told you which door each key is for when you find a key. These are major flaws that make me just barely recommend Pineview Drive. It’s not bad, but it’s not great either. It’s just mediocre to me
