Pineview Drive is a game that is designed to be a story driven thriller, it's designed to make you think that something isn't quite right and that if you round the next corner something may jump out at you. In most cases this is correct & every door is a new gateway into hell.
While this game is designed on Horror there's nothing in it that can physically hurt your character, there is only mental tricks that can end the game & in a majority of those cases the game pulls this off quite well with its sharp and shrill audio tones, it's nice graphics during the day and night & many other things that this game did well to capture the immersion.
It's a rather enjoyable experience & it's also quite a long experience with 30 days to play through & each of those days becomes a little more intense.
Pineview Drive is a well paced & well designed peice of Software that performs nicely & manages to capture you with it's good horror designs but it's story is pretty average.
There are so many things that were good and bad about this game but where to start?
For starters i think we should get the story out of the road.
The Story has you (the main character) attempting to figure out what happened to your wife and why she went missing at the Mansion.
Maybe it was something i missed or maybe because by the end of the game things felt a bit meh & i stopped caring so much but i was still left not understanding what the hell happened to her. All i got was a cinematic of you holding something and her running away into the forest, is this supposed to explain to me what happened? Cause it's done a bad job explaining.
Overall the story is pretty poor, but what about the rest of the game?
The gameplay of this game is very similar to other Horror games you are required to find different keys and items to help you progress in the game, but here's where things change a bit unlike general Horror Games this one doesn't rely on monsters to scare you it rely's on your reactions to random noises or ghostly figures to do the damage rather than a monster chasing you down the corridor and needing to hide.
Although this mechanic is good and worked well, this game really needed more to it rather than just reaction avoidance. Most of the time i'd rather have reacted to the thing that made the noise and relied on it to scare me rather than "oh something made a noise better not look or it'll cause me to lose sanity". They could have REALLY done something great here and instead of just losing health with no signs of what caused it, they could used these ques to generate a random Ghost or something of that nature to terrify the player. (Really disappointed about that).
The dark atmosphere in this game is superb but it was lacking a few things here and there that could've made the game better, the more you played the game the more obvious it become that things weren't going to change up much after the power goes out and you have to rely on the Flashlight or Matches to light candles. This would have been PERFECT if and only IF you used the power outage much later in the game when things started to get more scary.
One thing this game did pretty nicely was the fact that it made sure you didn't miss the bigger scares because every night you had to find the biggest scares to progress further and collect the valuable keys you needed to open locked doors and find the diary entries. (Good Idea!)
This game had potential to be something more and sometimes it showed like the new feature of using just scares to make you go insane rather than using a random monster.
Or it's unique idea of not just relying on jump scares all the time but actually making sure you're getting scared by forcing you to endure them to find the keys.
Using a pretty normal setting not like most settings and making it creepy with atmosphere and not just a run down old building.
Not branching out much and after a while things got pretty repeatative, not enough variation with the scares.
Around about the last 5 days things seemed to start being rushed it took maby a minute to complete them from 25 - 29, 3 of the days from 26 - 29 involved finding a peice of photo with absolutely no new scares to endure between finding them? Come on seriously it's meant to be a horror game not a find and seek game.
Removing players use of interactive light switches too early in the game to increase the scare factor before things actually started to get scary, it would have been better removed after the scary stuff really began around day 15 or so.
No clues as to where you are supposed to go or what you're meant to be doing until the clock reaches 5:00AM it really doesn't help, try adding a quick vocal que to the beginning giving the player just a little hint as to what they should be doing.
It changed from day to night really quickly, like 2 minutes of day and about 20 minutes of night or so, and once you reach a certain point in time at about 5:00AM ingame time the clock just stops, you really could have used this feature much better and made it a time limit, if you missedthe deadline then you miss part of the story and won't get the full picture of what happened.
Although i did enjoy the experience of this game it's going to receive a very low score because there was just so much more i expected from this and didn't end up receiving it.
I give this game a 5/10 because while it brought something new and interesting to try & experience there was just too late here to warrent anything more than a 5.
There was scares, i did jump a few times but more often than not i ended up just walking around going "Oh was that meant to be scary?" As i said earlier in the review instead of expecting people to not react to the games scares you should have expected them to react and then used this to generate a more terrifying experience.
While the game had beautiful graphics for the most part, it was a bit lacking in other parts the lighting and the atmosphere during the night was great & the transition between day and night was beautiful to watch.
I find it hard to recommend this game due to the fact that there was just so many things that could have been there to make it a more enjoyable experience but for the most part it was just lacking in things to make it scary.
If you think you'll enjoy it then give it a go but don't expect much unless you're easily scared.

(Disclaimer on technical aspect: I haven't played the non-Redux versions of the games, and this was written with 2033 Redux in mind; mostly for comparisons.)
I'm not going to deny that appreciating the Metro duology was not easy; I started with 2033, but I'm not going to write a review for that one since I'm pretty mixed with the whole game. Last Light was different. My previous complaints with the first game, such as guns feeling weak and the whole combat experience being drab, was all heartily addressed in Last Light - with a few better weapons, excellent stealth segments, and more varied level types and objectives. I understand that 2033 was meant to be more of a surivival horror experience, but anyone who's gone through the levels Regina, Undercity, and Dead City could probably agree with me that Last Light was a bit more unnerving.
(Huge props to Undercity for the Splatterhouse-esque, macabre experience!)
Most importantly, maybe this is on a personal level, but Last Light's story is more engaging, and the ending more satisfying compared to 2033. 2033's story isn't bad or uninteresting, but I'd like to think it went like that as a necessary step to build Artyom's character first. Last Light's story and pacing has some of the best bits I've experienced in survival horrors - the Church catacombs, the Dark One's revelations, the overarching plan of the Red Line, and more that can surely spoil the story.
Great game, really enjoyed the gameplay and story. While I feel Last Light can stand on its own, getting it with 2033 and going through that first will definitely improve the Last Light experience.

So I just finished playing this game, so my opinion might be heavily influenced by how the game ended. I will try not to spoil anything in the opener, and talk about the game mechanics first.
Sound: So at first the sound in the game is alright, the music is there to creep you out and create an atmosphere. However, the music is constantly there and it feels out of place at most times.  At times, the music will get intense as well, and loud noises will come out of nowhere, which again feels out of place most of the time and is overused in my opinion. There are a lot of sounds that are there to disturb you, example at times you’ll hear footsteps near you, or someone “Psst”-ing. Personally I don’t think these are out of place and makes sense to use, and they aren’t really overused to the point where they become an annoyance
Graphics: Graphics were okay, I don’t have anything to add to this since I didn’t really expect AAA game graphics in the first place. Some textures were weird, but it’s nothing to really focus on.
Gameplay: Gameplay wasn’t that interesting. Opening the same doors to the same rooms every day, trying to find out which room is going to have any “Action” or events happening in them is not as interesting as it may sound. It was alright the first couple of days when there weren’t that many rooms to look through, but once you unlock almost every door it gets irritating to put up with, because the game basically requires that you re-visit every room every day. If you run around confused for a prolonged time, the person you’re controlling will give you a clue, which is nice, but I still feel like it’s annoying that you have to walk around every room all the time.
Level-design: The level design isn’t TOO bad, but it does fall short on some parts. Some rooms connect weirdly, though it does help you getting around the house easily once you have all the doors opened. Still, it’s an annoyance walking around, and you will often find yourself being lost in all the rooms that you can visit, and will probably miss some every now and then. That being said, the rooms were nicely decorated and they helped with the atmosphere.
Atmosphere: So I guess we can all agree that atmosphere is the most important thing in a horror game, and Pineview does get away with it pretty nicely I’d say. There are the annoyingly repetitive sounds I mentioned earlier, but if you look past that, the game does succeed in having that horror feel to it. Some of the props helped nicely and were put to good use. Overall I’d say that Pineview does capture a good scary atmosphere and there’s not a lot to really touch on here.
Story
: So I decided to split this up in to two, because the story annoys me to no end. It starts off by the main person arriving to the house where some stuff has gone down. Linda, the wife I’m assuming, has died in the house and “No one has survived in the house for 30 days” and you have to find out what happened to Linda. Simple stuff, though from there the story kind of falls short, and I can’t go in to detail without spoiling the game, but you basically find letters scattered around the house that tells you what has been going on in the house back when the incident with Linda happened. That’s it, that’s the basic storyline.
Story
: Right, so moving on, this is where the game falls short and REALLY disappoints me. Note that this section will spoil the entire “Surprise” of the game, so read with caution. During the game you find some notes which help you finding out what happened to Linda, and you find notes explaining what has been going on around the house, like the clown being moved around and then appearing in its original place, and that Linda had been hearing strange noises in the house. Though, the notes doesn’t seem to tell all that much until you start gathering the pieces of a picture, which then reminds the main person about a doll. A doll that is evil, and, assumingly, is buried with Linda. On day 29 you gain access to the cemetery, and enter Linda’s tomb, and in that tomb you’re going to face the game’s biggest disappointment. You’d expect everything to be cleared up, an open ending, or some sort of explanation as to why the house is being haunted, why the clown is moving around, why the scarecrow will chase you, why the shadows of the girls appear at random times or get to know something about Linda’s death. But no. The game ends weirdly, abruptly and in a very strange fashion. As you walk in Linda’s tomb you suddenly find a machine. There’s no explanation as to what this machine does, and you have to turn it on. Once you do, the game ends with a video which I assume is a continued version of the video in the very beginning of the game. This still clears nothing at all, and the machine still feels weirdly out of place.
Edit: This is the first time I have actually taken my time to write a lenghty review for a game, and I would love some feedback. Thanks in advance.

For those that remember and loved the Police Quest games this one is up your ally.  La Noire lets you find clues, question suspects, do crazy car chases and lots of shoot'em ups with the bad guys.
The game engine used for this game is massive!!  There are so many streets to drive place to see, that doing all the 21 mission (DLC included) will not let you experience the whole map of L.A.  What is also nice is the small little details in the game.  The radio music playing while your drive or the news broadcasts are specific to the time of the game.  The cars also all handle differently from each other.
On the hunt for some of the collectibles in the game I left my partner behind, after stopping in another part of the city a black and white police car stopped sirens blaring.  My partner got out and had some choice words for me leaving him behind.  This brings me to the voice acting which is really good for a game on this scale.  The small talk between your character and you partner on the specific desk can be a times really amusing.
The annoying parts of the game are 2 achievements that you need to get to complete the game 100%.  One is the hunt for the golden films reels and the other is driving all the 95 vehicles in the game.  The film reels are movies related to the time, but they are hidden in such places that you will never find them during normal game play.  A quick Google will net you clues and maps to where all the golden film reels are.
The other pain is driving all the vechiles in the game. :(  This took me a couple of days to complete.  In the end I found a site that made it easier to get some of the vehicles.  For this you need to go to the Extras in the Main Menu, then the vehicle show room.  Move to the blacked out vechile and press ENTER for about 20 seconds. Escape to the Main Menu again and go to Cases and Select the Homocide Desk (Free Roam).  As soon as the map is loaded get out of the car and you will see the car that you need drive by.  For this you will need to Google to find a picture of the car needed.  If the car does not drive by check the parking lot across from the police station to see if it is there.  Some of the cars are mission specific and will only be found in certain missions or street crimes.  This will also only work for the 2 door and 4 door types of cars.
All in all this is an amazing game.  If you follow your clues and check your suspects facial expression you may become a top rated detective.

Hesitant non-recommendation. More neutral if that was a thing on Steam.
This game is pretty fun early on. Figuring out people's tells and searching for clues to use against them keeps cases moving in an organic direction. Each case is roughly 45-60 minutes long which is perfect for short stints. Unfortunately, the game starts to feel pretty tedious about midway through. You'll notice a cycle of find clues, talk to guy, find more clues, talk to next guy, talk to another guy, put bad guy away. Throw in some car chases and shootouts and I've described every LA Noire case progression.
And that brings us to the biggest negative. You are a detective and yet there is VERY LITTLE DEDUCTION IN LA NOIRE. Seriously. You can't lose a case - you just get different ranks. But it's not because you as the player discovered anything. It's because you picked up clues that obviously lead to the next point in the case. And holy crap do you find a lot of matchboxes to lead you to the next point in the case.
The overall story doesn't even really get going until halfway through. But by then the game has already worn out its welcome. This game needed to be 10 hours, not 20+ hours. Even though the individual cases in the DLC are solid, I'd avoid them because it makes an already too long game even longer.
There is fun to be had in LA Noire, but don't buy this detective game expecting to deduce anything like Sherlock Holmes. You're really just a human lie detector that wins no matter what at the end of the day anyway.

I grew up playing Port Royale 2. This game is a huge disappointment compared to that, you don't need to ever trade manually, you can simply start out with a strong trade route on the first day that generates 20k gold each month. If you try to fight pirates, you need to get at least 400k-500k gold to spend on warships to have a chance of defeating the weakest convoys even on the first day they appear.
The campaign maps are horrible, they're just long tutorials (and can be finished within an hour or two).
If you haven't played PR2 and are looking for a trading sim, this game might be good for you, though I'd still recommend trying to get a working version of Port Royale 2 instead.
So, what does the game offer?
Trading around the Caribbean, production differs in each city, prices change with supply and demand.
Possibility to attack convoys and cities to plunder or even capture them.
Missions (get X amount of Y goods in a month, find something on the ocean with some hints and deliver it), treasure maps, random "drops" you might find in the water (and you have to spot it and pick it up because it disappears after some time).
Dynamic wars between the 4 nations, respect with each of them and reputation in every city (modifies possible missions).
Setting up production facilities in cities to create your own goods (which is cheaper than buying them, so more profit).
Events in cities like plague or gold rush, they modify production, life quality, demand for some resources.
Control over multiple fleets (based on rank), each having one or more ships, they can be set on automated traderoutes (very easy to set up a profitable one, once you've done it it's AFK Simulator 2000).
Mutliplayer (haven't tried it, can't say anything about it) - the only thing Port Royale 2 does not have.
the only thing it lacks is a titan or superdreadnought class capital ship. Three sizes are far too minimalistic for me. Otherwise 10/10 would blow up cosmic mafia planet again

Crusader Kings II is an excellent grand strategy game. It is delightfully complex, deep and realistic, even though that is also one of it's downsides, because it is extremely hard to get into. I highly recommend watching the first couple of episodes from a god CK let's player on youtube, because he (or she) will usualy give a good explanation of the base concepts. The game has you invested for days in all kinds of enormous goals like glorious conquest or dishonarable scheming. It may seem a bit slow paced to Civilization players, and the Casus Belis (valid reasons to go to war) and dynasty centered gameplay might seem restricting, but know this, if you embrace Crusader Kings II, you will never be able to go back to a game so "simple" as Civilization or the like. And if you just want war there is of course the Old Gods DLC where the only reason required to go to war, is that you want to.
Conclusion: If you like complex games, grand strategy (if you've ever played a board game like RISK and liked it, you probably like grand strategy) and the medieval ages, then CK is the game for you, but if you don't like one or more of those, then this is probably not the game for you.

It may come as a surprise to see that I have, I believe, no hours in Dystopia. Yet, I'm writing a review for it. This is because I played the old version of Dystopia, before it had a store page. Dystopia is an incredibly important game to me, in that it is the game that got me to play PC games. Before Dystopia, I didn't know that PC was really a gaming platform. I remember being at my Mom's boyfriend's house, and hanging out with his child (who was almost twice my age) and watching him play it. I was blown away by the futuristic look of everything, and all the little secrets he knew about in the community-made levels. Not to mention, watching him hack whilst in cyberspace just seemed incredible to the eight or nine year old me. So, I wanted to play it. So I got Steam. But I couldn't play it, because it wasn't a stand-alone game. It was a mod. So I needed Half-Life 2. But I couldn't run Half-Life 2, and by proxy Dystopia, because my PC was trash at the time. Finally, I obtained a PC that I could play Dystopia on, and... it was dead. Hardly anyone played it. The game had died by the time I was finally able to get around to playing it. So there I was, 11 or so years old, unable to properly play the game I had up until then so longed to play and I thought to myself, "Well... I guess I could try out this Half-Life 2 game. Maybe it will be alright. The guy on the cover looks like a nerd though..."
So that's why Dystopia is important to me. Not only did it get me to start playing PC games in general, but it got me to start playing PC games on what is perhaps the greatest game of all time. So, even if it's still dead, I have to thank it for that. And maybe, just maybe, some day it will be revived and I'll be able to -really- play the game.

In many ways Dystopia feels like a HL1 mod. It's clearly old, the maps are dark, the sounds headache inducing, the gameplay is reminiscent of Quake and Unreal Tournament... It's from 2007 and feels like it was meant for HL1.
Game is so blatanly unbalanced I was asked not to use one of the weapons because it was considered overpowered.
Matches oftenly got to a point where every team was so set in their positions it wasn't possible for any of them to get a definitive edge, thus dragging the game way longer than should have been. This is because of the map design and of how respawn works in those games. If you want to see respawn done well see League of Legends and Dota 2.
The level design is often terrible. Many chokepoints will just result in a 20 minutes struggle between the two teams with no clear winner. The lighting is either too bright or too dark, most of the time creating a contrast higher than acceptable. The layouts can be quite confusing as they tend to be really open and identical corridors don't help.
As for the sound the footsteps of the heavy class is too loud, too clunky, too abrupt, etc not to give me a headache, making it impossible for me to play the class for long.
Given such major flaws I cannot recommend this game to anyone but to the most curious and to game designers because it's easier to learn from a bad game than from a good one.

I love Halo series and this is no different. Chronologically within the Halo universe, this is the first game of the entire series, which means that you get additional stories from before the other Halo games. Now to this game alone; it is a tactical RTS with 6 different heroes to choose from (3 covenant, 3 UNSC) with differing specialties and abilites. Here is a Pro/Con list:
Pro:
RTS
Each hero better/worse at different combat situations
Well polished
More background story
Con:
When using the Spirit of Fire (the UNSC's way to use Hero abilities) abilities, the screen is extremely sensitive unless you move very slowly. (Compared to Xbox where the SoF targetting screen was fast, but controllable)
"Unit to unit, the UNSC are slightly superior to the Covenant in every way" -Direct quote from the game itself
The selection box can be misplaced, i.e.: start holding LMB right behind a unit, and drag, only to have the box start being drawn infront of the unit
Regardless of the cons, this game is very engaging, and entertaining. It is definately well worth the $20.

I tried to make it through this game in the interest of being open minded and writing a fair review, but it was so mind bogglingly dull I just couldn't take it anymore. The atmosphere and darkness are indeed creepy but the pacing was terrible, and the scares were so laughably unfrightening, few, and far between that it felt like a poor reward for all the aimless circling ( done at a snails pace walk ) to obtain them. I don't mind a slow start but this went on with no clear rise in the pace of activity for 10 agonizingly slow levels. I felt more annoyed than anything as I made my nightly rounds, hoping against hope to stumble across the door behind which something would finally happen quickly. The story is delivered in single sentences and is, so far, too vague and without unity to be engaging. Yeah, yeah, some creepy stuff happened, but there's no character or conflict or mystery or anything motivating me to find out what happens next. If you don't have action or puzzles you have to have a really good story. A game can't sustain interest on atmosphere alone. Perhaps all of these things improve later in the game, but without some kind of hook in the first few levels that teases at something  mysterious or surprising or scary or dramatic etc. I have to presume after 10 levels without change that this is what I can expect from the rest of the game.

Metro: Last Light is a First Person Shooter that takes place in post-apocalyptic Russia, years and years after a nuclear war has struck, the now wasteland filled, radioactive ruin. Your objectives are to secure to tunnelways and metros, while helping your friends stop what they are called the 'Dark Ones'. And just so as it turns out, you have the capability to contact and communicate with these creatures, which happens to be getting in the way of what everybody else thinks of them. No matter what difficulty you play on, Light, or even the darkness is your best friend, depending on who you're fighting. Checking on ammo, making sure your oxygen supply is sufficient, and assuring that those wretched hallways filled with monsters and other things that lurk doesn't try to eat you alive is all part of what is great from what Metro: Last Light has to offer, being one of the best survival horror games to date.

I've played this for about 2 hours so far and I've reached day 10 of 30. I was expecting it to be a lot scarier. Unfortunately I found it a bit slow. But it hasn't been a bad experience and it was reasonably enjoyable.
First thing you do in the is game is search for the key that opens the front gate. This becomes a pattern in this game, find keys and figure out which door they open. I thought that running and turning around quickly when you hear sounds is what would be classified as 'getting yourself worked up' and causing you to take damage. So I spent most of the game walking slowly around. However there wasn't a clear indication that doing so meant I was taking less damage from hazards. So really I think moving around slowly just meant that I took a lot longer to progress through the game. So I just started to run whenever I could to save time, because I backtracked an awful lot in this game. I basically got stuck every day of the game trying to find the daily journal entry which brings each night to an end. I found myself revisiting pretty much every room in the house each day, and mind you there are a reasonably large amount of them! This was because I didn't know what else to do or where else to go. The game will give you a clue on what to do next in the form of dialogue by the character. This seems happen after a certain amount of time. However I wish the game would give you hints much earlier because I found that I spent the majority of my time just being lost. It wasn't even really scary most of the time to make up for that fact. I think the infrequency of scares could possibly have been because I played very cautiously and illuminated every room I entered. This may have prevented more frighting events to occur, but I don't know for sure. The contents of the journal entries don't really seem to have a lot relevance to what to what you need to do every day. It helped a little when I got the hang of remembering which rooms had locked doors. But I think that a map which has locked door's marked on it or some other feature could be pretty handy here. There are occasionally scary moment's such as seemingly random noises beside you which may cause you to take damage if you look in their direction. And there are apparently scripted events at certain points in the game where you would see ghosts and take damage. I couldn't see a clear way to avoid taking damage in some situations, even though I thought there would be a way to do so. As described on the store page 'you will need steady nerves if you want to survive the game unscathed'. I thought it meant you need to steady your nerves and control your character calmly. But I even seemed to to take damage when I apparently completely missed whatever was supposed to have scared me e.g. when I was looking the wrong way.
The game looks good overall. You have sort of imperfections such as shadows of objects being cast through solid objects and stuff like that. The game isn't full of cheap scares but it probably doesn't try hard enough to really scare you as often as it should. But in general it definitely has a creepy atmosphere to it, the ambient sounds and music are generally good for this. Unfortunately I think that some of the visual events can be missed completely if your view is obstructed or if you are just looking away when they happen. One thing that was bit unusual was that when there were lightning storms there was no accompanying sound of thunder.

Here's my initial first look Let's Play. TL;DR and in-depth thoughts underneath:
TL;DR: It's a good game made for the most part by just two people. The lighting and sounds are great and definitely atmospheric. The graphics are good but it is a big game made in Unity, so the limitations of the engine does mean it can lag a bit but it's not too bad at all. Gameplay is simple as it revolves around finding things and exploring the place, but the experience is there and can get very tense. Would recommend.
More in-depth:
The gameplay so far seems to be based around finding keys to unlock doors, with rooms that have things in them that pertain to the story. There are a number of things to interact with including candles and light switches, and things to find like keys. The house actually seems quite large and I've only gone into a small part of it so far, so I imagine key finding plays an integral part in the exploration of the game. This is a bit of pain though as sometimes it can be easy to miss the key so you will have to take a good look around in each place you visit otherwise you will be walking around back and forth for ages in frustration wondering why the story isn't advancing and trying to find where the damn key is (Look low AND high!). It's hard to say how much of the game has changed for me based on my moves and reactions as mentioned in the features list but I have noticed things such as furnature being different when I go back to visit a room again, things get added or removed etc all based on what seems to be where else you've been during the level. I do feel like there isn't too much option to stray from the storyline though as keys for doors can appear at any point on any level. This does mean going back and forth as you will have to revisit an old room in order to find something new to advance.
I think the graphics are what you'd expect from your average horror title. Textures are pretty good, and the models have fair amounts of detail when needed and nothing looks too low poly or low res. As for things such as lighting in the game: When it's night time and you are in a dark room with the candles on, it does create quite an interesting atmosphere. These lights are surprisingly weak however, and often aren't enough to fill the room so even at night with the lights on you will find it to be VERY dark. This makes it very difficult to play in a lit room at certain points, and is one of the reasons why I found it hard to spot items sometimes. Maybe that's intentional and will force you to play in a darkened room, though. I imagine that would only heighten the effect of horror. If you're using a flashlight, the huge shadows you cast can actually make you jump if you happen to catch the cornice and it casts a huge shadow you weren't expecting! One negative about the graphics is that I don't feel it's very well optimised. My framerate can go from 60 to 15 purely from turning around and looking at certain things.
The other quip I have about the graphics is the door animation. They often open towards you and go through you, which is rather disconcerting. This does seem to be a sign of a UIG game though. They are yet to figure out how doors should work in a game.
The sounds in the game seem very fitting and add to the atmosphere and help to build tension and fear. Lots of tense ambient sounds, momentus music, things like breathing, which I assume is coming from the character you're playing, and things like wood creaking and even one sound that sounds like someone walking around in leather trousers, which is rather odd. I have come across a couple of things that made me jump. The screen flashed white and there was a sudden noise, although I won't say from what to spoil the game. The way momentum builds from the sounds really set you up in anticipation of a sudden noise or something, and it definitely got my heart racing. At the very start of the game there is a health warning suggesting you should avoid the game if you have a known heart and/or circulator disease, or if you're a pregnant women, which seems reasonable enough for any horror game really and not just this one. There is also narration in this game (I believe in both English and German) that narrates a story when you reach certain parts.
Whilst this review is purely based on my first impressions, it does make me want to play on to see what else is in store as it does seem like it's been well thought out. I do have a slight bit of concern for the fact the whole game is revolved around one house, wondering if maybe you could get bored of your environment before long, but as there were a lot of rooms left for me to explore in different parts of the mansion I think it should be fine and fit in with the story well. The relatively low graphics optmization that gave me some moments of low framerates is another cause for concern but I imagine if you just turn down the graphics a bit you should be okay. It was still playable for me but having a smoother framerate would have been nicer. Either way, if you're into your horror games I'd definitely say to give a try.

If I was to only review the hint system alone.  This game would be a recommend, but the game that includes that hint system still receives extremely high marks.   While it's not perfect, it's a fun little game, and my only complaint is the price.
To start with, this is yet another point and click adventure.  However what stands out in this game is the graphics.  This game isn't just beautiful, it's stylized and gorgeous.  Everything has a feeling of depth, and the papercraft style it, and that's because it was.  Literally this game was made out of cardboard and paper, and then photographed, and holy crap, this game look unbelievable.
The one negative thing I could say is the player character kind of looks weak against this unbelievably gorgeous world.  I mean this game is astonishing.   It's just that good looking.
The puzzles in this game though are good, but they almost don't live up to the graphics.  The graphics are a solid 10, the puzzles are 7 or 8.  They're good mind you, but they can range from almost too easy to insanely hard due to the wrong reasons.  For instance there was a puzzle I just couldn't figure out, I couldn't figure out how to make a boat rock.  I solved two other puzzles, and I was feeling damn good about myself.  Then I finally had to look up a guide, and it turned out I was missing a hatch on the boat, I spent at least 10 minutes just trying to find a way to rock the boat, and it was something that almost blended in with the screen.
A similar issue happened at another point (I missed a tool).   But these are the exception.  There's very little pixel hunting required.  Most times you need an item it's blatantly obvious what you need (or maybe I'm just that lucky), but I was stymied twice so far.
However for the puzzles themselves if you get stuck the game has something special.  There's a book that you're given at the beginning of the game, and while it looks confusing at first, the table of contents actually is intended to work.  The book has over a thousand pages of random stuff, but it also contains solutions for the puzzles in the game.  To look up a solution, there's usually a question related to the puzzle, that leads to a small math problem that tells the player which page to look up.
The only flaw with this hint system is it gives a complete solution.  There's no hint, if you go to that page, you're going to see a decent (about 5 percent) of the game's puzzles' solution exposed.  It's mostly in order, so if you can avoid scanning the whole page you might be ok, but it's still VERY spoiler.  However it allows the gamer to not have to look up solutions... as long as you have all the items to get you to that solution (for instance it doesn't mention the location of the spanner I was missing.)
I just love the idea of the hint book however, and I will rave about it, because it's actually quite fun to have to look up a solution, since there's very little chance you'll run across solutions for other puzzles while you find yours.
Now the one thing I wasn't a huge fan of is the sound.  The game is gorgeous, and fun to play, but there's nothing special about the sound.  There's no voice acting and almost nothing going on with the sound design.  There's nice music, but that's about it.  Just songs, and silence.   A shame, because visually this game is a feast, but the sound seems to lag behind.
The one big negative though for this game is length.  And that's about the only place I think this game falls short.   It's a gorgeous feast for the eyes, but only about 4-5 hours long, less if you use the hint system relentlessly.   That's ok, but at 20 bucks, this game is WELL overpriced.  However this game does go on sale often, and it would be a "must buy" for less, but at 20 bucks, that's a value question each gamer is going to have to decide.   I got this game through a humble bundle, so that wasn't a big issue for me, but it definitely deserves a mention as it's short for 20 bucks.
Overall though, I'd recommend Lumino city if you can get at a discount.  10 dollars is probably worth it, 5 dollars is an easy purchase.  This game is just unbelievably beautiful that I can't stress it enough, the only issue is eventually the game comes to an end, and I don't think I'll be returning for a second playthrough any time soon.  But for those four or five hours, it's really incredible.

I played this game a lot on the free weekend. It was pretty good. I'm going to review in in comparison to the first Endless space game, which I played a fair amount and is the only other Endless game I have played. Also: I only ever play single-player.
Pros:
* This game looks great
* The quests are a nice addition
* Moving around with the keyboard or the mouse is so much better. There were lots of annoyances in the original. There are some Mac-specific improvements here, too.
* The choices you make when picking ship loadouts feels better explained
* I like the new investigation / discovering anomalies mechanic
* AI negotiations are better
Cons:
* The population types would be great if micromanaging them wasn't so awful. A preview to show what the effects of moves might be? An overview of who is where? There should be some better way to let you see into what is happening, whatever that might look like. The notification about them dying in transit was so cryptic it took me most of a game to figure out what it meant, much less why it was happening.
* In the original, you could make a some adjustments to your strategy mid-battle. The opportunity to do so came slow enough that it didn't feel like an RTS shoehorned in to where it didn't belong. In comparison, many other reviews here comment on how poorly done battles are in this sequel. The ship battles may look interesting for a minute. There's nothing to do, and it's very hard to figure out what's happening. There's a mode where you can turn on statistics, which tells you how fast you're winning or loosing, but it's hard to otherwise tell how well your strategies are paying off. With the statistics off, it's still not immersive or gripping. It's generally pointless.
* The end game was more polished in he original. How to win and how much longer it was likely to take you was much clearer.
As a last con, which I hate in all games of this genre -- there's no good in-game mechanism to help you pick up where you left off if you want to save a game and come back to it days or a week later. Sure, I could pick up a pen and paper and write it down, but shouldn't my notes about the game stay with the game itself? I'm mystified why nobody ever does this.
All in all, if you like 4X space games like this, this is a solid entry into the genre. Nothing felt groundbreaking, but it's still hours and hours of fun.

I got this on sale with all 3 DLC expansion packs for 10.19 during the Black Friday sale. I'm an avid fan of the Port Royale series, and loved Port Royale 2. I was nervous getting this will all the mixed reviews, so it took me well over a year to finally go through with it.
Overall, I thought it was pretty good. For anyone wanting a comparison of this to Port Royale 2, they are very similar in most aspects, with some differences good and bad. First off, trading in port looks very different. There's a slider to select the amount, as well as green and red bars to tell you how over or understocked (and priced) a particular item is. A lot of people hate this new layout, but it's really not that bad if you can get used to it. The town palace now holds both a town administrator and sometimes a governor to hand out distinct missions. This is a bit unbalanced, especially once you advance in rank, as bringing lets say 67 crates of tobacco can get you a hundred thousand dollar bonus. One thing I HATED was the nation's reputation system. It drops way too quickly on it's own, that unless you're constantly doing missions you're going to be stuck at 25. Also, when two nations form an alliance, your reputation between them gets averaged. This is the most frustrating thing when you're trying to take over a town economically and suddenly your 100% reputation gets dropped down to sixty because your mother nation decides to form a treaty. Fortunately, this also means that nations that hate you get bored pretty quick. Still, they can pack quite a nasty punch if you're not prepared. War is also completely different, but in a way I enjoy. Each convoy uses 3 armed ships each battle, and you control all 3. It's a bit tougher to fight and board enemy ships, but now you can't make a fortune capturing and selling Ship of the Lines. There's a really dumbed down system for attacking in the harbors. Most nations will first have anywhere between 3 and 10 military convoys you have to fight through to make it to the harbor, instead of the max of 1 in the previous game. And thank goodness they got rid of those annoying harbor cannons that would completely obliterate your fleet one ship at a time. Instead, you send in your three ships that park, bomb the heck out of a fort, and then unload your soldiers for a land battle. Pirates have no fort, just a gazillion soldiers. Luckily, they are a lot easier to take down this way later on, if not more difficult in the early stages. The last part I really like is that you can take over pre-existing towns forming your own nation (Long live the free people of America!). This can be done either economically (own 75% of a prosperous town, and then go whine to the Viceroy and he'll probably just give it to you). Or you can attack the town and annex it for yourself! If the nation you attacked liked you enough before, they'll let you keep it. Also, there is no more waiting til a nation is weak enough to annex a town.
The only DLCs that seem to do much is Harbor Master. None of the campaigns seem to amount to much compared to the sandbox game. Still, the new buildings are very effective in preventing droughts, outbreaks, pirate attacks, etc. Ship building is pretty cool, if not expensive and time consuming. Still, it's better than having to travel port to port searching for that particular ship you want.
Overall I recommend giving this game a shot. Not sure if it's all worth $30, but if you get it during a good sale I say go for it!

The internet claims that this is a mediocre game, and I disagree.  In fact I disagree enough to positively recommend this game.  Port Royale 3 is a trading and economy simulator with minor RTS elements.  It's not a perfect game, of course: boat combat is best left on autopilot, as is most of your trade empire.  That said, the challenge lies in learning the somewhat mystifying AI, fanaggling trade routes to suit the needs of the economy, and so on.
If you are an econ nerd like me or simply fall for the simple charm of the story spun around Elena, daughter of the Viceroy of Port Royale, then give this game a try.  At its sale price, it's not too shabby.
I would be remiss to not address the Metacritic score of 54 however.  Upon review of, uh, these reviews, I have determined that most of Port Royale 3's detractors succumb to puerile "it's not as good as Port Royale 2" grognardism.  For better or worse, I never played Port Royale 2 and therefore take this game solely on its own merit.  And for what it is, this game has been enjoyable.

That's one of the best games I've encountered during the last couple of years. Despite starting to play a buggy and unstable release, I really enjoyed it. The gameplay is amazing, in my opinion, and by now all the bugs are gone (as far as I can tell, at least).
The main idea in the game is to either be a pirate and build your own naval empire, or be a trader (my personal preferred choice) and build a huge merchant fleet, and later on gain control over cities.
The game takes place in the Caribbeans, during the European colonization in America. Therefore, you can choose to be either Spanish, English, French or Dutch, but you're not limited to trading just with your country's own colonies. Also, even for people like me, who aren't die-hard fans of "Pirates Of The Caribbeans", it's impossible to miss the connection. :)
The trading mechanism is quite realistic, and is a lot of fun, as you need to start small, trading stuff yourself, until you get rich and famous enough to buy more ships and more goods, so you can buy more ships and build businesses in cities, so you can manufacture goods yourself, which is obviously cheaper than buying them from someone else.
If you're into trading simulation, get this game. You won't be sorry.

Games like Command & Conquer, Total War and Age of Empires are much better representatives of the genre and are, lets be honest here, much more successful ones at that. However, they are extremely functional and easy to understand and utilize. It is certainly, as so many others say (as much as I loathe to say it myself), a good introduction into the genre. But the lack of depth and features that the other RTS games previously mentioned have can potentially makes this a double-edged sword and drive people AWAY from the genre all-together.

Here are the cliffnotes of a review I wrote for this game elswhere:
I’ve had this game on my Steam wishlist for a few months now and decided to grab it during the Winter Sale last week. I’m glad I did because, in retrospect, I wouldn’t have wanted to waste more money than I already did on it.
This is not something that I would call a puzzle game. A puzzle implies that there is an intricate mental test to perform that has a rewarding outcome if you can find and place all the pieces. To solve the puzzles in this game you just have to perform trial and error because there really is no intuitive puzzle to be had. You platform around as a shadow on the wall to perform an arbitrary task and that’s about it. The “puzzle” aspect comes in, I GUESS, when you turn a wheel or press a button and the shadows move and you continue platforming. Maybe it’s that some of the buttons are on timers? I suppose some people would consider that a puzzle……But if you find those people, please, remind them to take the plastic bag off of their head once in awhile.
Bottom line: I wouldn’t recommend this game unless you have a big hard-on for platformers….But there ARE better platformers…..Much better.

Although, I am very interesting in art history and amazed about Art Deco, I didnt play Bioshock 2 since I finished the first Bioshock years ago. So, I was very excited when I heard this game's remastered version announced. What I remembered is, when Bioshock 2 came out years ago, many reviews didnt like game's visual and they mainly critisized about game's engine which seemed a bit old when game came out at 2010.
So, remastered version of the game is a really jackpot for me, cause several days ago, I downloaded old Bioshock 2 to play; then I waited remastered version's relase.
And now, I finished this awesome game and I am very grateful and pleased. This game is a real master piece, with Bioshock of course.
Generally speaking, Bioshock 2 is telling us a new story about Rapture City after Bioshock and this game is filling the blanks of first Bioshock very succesfully. But, actually, Bioshock 2 is giving us an opposite perspective view of a society order, than Bioshock. Instead of Andrew Ryan's self obsessed, individual focused freedom and community thoughts and "individual should be existed for their own", "freedom of the individual to succed or fail on one's own merits idea", we observe Sophia Lamb's altruist, selfless and collective "family" idea, "individual belongs to others".
This two opposite ideas mixed with the flavor of art deco, sanity and awesome soundtrack; Bioshock series born. In these stories, we tested these "idologies" several times and observed their change, evolve and corruption. They tell you definetely some real and solid basic principles. I think, everybody should examine these ideas.
About gameplay, there are several mistakes and fails. As visual experience, especially the remastered version could be better and we need definetely more graphic options but these fails won't bother you much while you are playing as a Big Daddy this game.
There are lots of details to make you fullify yourself with the story, you should listen the all audio tapes. Examine and experience the world, the enviroment in this game. Observe the posters, readings, maps and splicier's behaviours and chats. You need to listen this awesome soundtrack. This game is not one of the a "you are a gun; go kill it." games, you need to live it.
Trust me, and definetely give a shot to this serie. Play Bioshock first, and then play this game. You won't regret.

I wish I could give percentual review rather then yes no, because frankly, I wish I wouldn't have bought the game. On the other hand, I can't bring myself to give it negative review, because it's just too interesting.
Sounds conflicted? It is. I'll try to keep things brief - the game has a lot of interesting idea and improvements. It's heavily oriented towards empire building, in the first half or even two thirds, you always have something to do, exploring anomalies, colonizing planets, building structures. And yes, fighting sometimes. Someone added a combat as afterthought.
Combat is my first accustation towards the game. You can design your own spaceships, because it's the coolest idea since master of orion. After first few battles, I didn't bother, because I just don't feel the designs matter. It has guns and it has defense, that's pretty much about it. Maybe there is a way to exploit the cannon/beam/missile mechanic, but I haven't discovered it. Just stuff your ships with the best guns and send them into combat. First five times you'll watch how the ships fly around and shoot at each other. Then you'll just turn it off and click on button to resolve the battle, shrug and go on. Combat is bland, boring and uninteresting.
My second accusation is endgame. I have troubles achieving victory. Not because the game is difficult, I'm just so horribly bored by the endgame that I end up leave it unfinished and starting anew. You have tons of resources, you can build ships quickly, you can pretty much conquer anyone you like, the only question is, why bother? Ships dwaddle around (sloooowly) and after a boring battle and just as boring planet invasion, you have another planet. Yay. Except you don't need resources, you don't need production, you already have a ton of planets that are producing nothing, because you've built everything on them already and you don't need another swarm of battleships.
The game is typical "endless" game. Packed with interesting options, but lacking to provide any challange to use them, so it quickly becomes boring. Shame on me for buying it (50% discount was too tempting). I've had few hours of fun, but in the end, the game becomes repetitive and ultimately boring. Buy at your own risk.

When I first started Endless Space 2, I was a little overwhelmed with the number of features. I probably should have paid more attention to the tutorial. I’m glad I stuck with it though, because this might be my favourite 4x game ever.
• The soundtrack and visuals are very atmospheric and set the tone well.
• There are a number of different races, with different playstyles to suit your preferences.
• You can customize each match from the map type, the size of the map, the number of AI opponents, victory conditions, pirate strength, resource abundance and so on.
• Besides just building your empire, you receive a number of short quests which can be solo, cooperative or competitive.
• I love exploring the galaxy, discovering new worlds, new minor factions, new curiosities on the planets you find.
As a heads up, there are a few minor gripes I have with the game, but they are easily overlooked.
• When playing with a friend we would become desynced from time to time and have to reload a save. It’s not a big problem since the game tells you when you desync and it autosaves every turn, and reloading only takes a few seconds.
• Some of the AI behaviors can be very annoying – like when they get mad at you for having a fleet somewhere in the same hemisphere as them, or when they call you a warmonger for sending a scout into their territory. They’ll go to war with you over the slightest offense it seems and it’s very hard to win back their favor.
• There isn’t really a way to communicate or coordinate with your AI allies. They’ll say they’re on their way to help you with an enemy, but it’s rare. So, it’s best to play with a friend instead.

So, remastered version of the game is a really jackpot for me, cause several days ago, I downloaded old Bioshock 2 to play; then I waited remastered version's relase.

Generally speaking, Bioshock 2 is telling us a new story about Rapture City after Bioshock and this game is filling the blanks of first Bioshock very succesfully. But, actually, Bioshock 2 is giving us an opposite perspective view of a society order, than Bioshock. Instead of Andrew Ryan's self obsessed, individual focused freedom and community thoughts and "individual should be existed for their own", "freedom of the individual to succed or fail on one's own merits idea", we observe Sophia Lamb's altruist, selfless and collective "family" idea, "individual belongs to others".
This two opposite ideas mixed with the flavor of art deco, sanity and awesome soundtrack; Bioshock series born. In these stories, we tested these "idologies" several times and observed their change, evolve and corruption. They tell you definetely some real and solid basic principles. I think, everybody should examine these ideas.
About gameplay, there are several mistakes and fails. As visual experience, especially the remastered version could be better and we need definetely more graphic options but these fails won't bother you much while you are playing as a Big Daddy this game.
There are lots of details to make you fullify yourself with the story, you should listen the all audio tapes. Examine and experience the world, the enviroment in this game. Observe the posters, readings, maps and splicier's behaviours and chats. You need to listen this awesome soundtrack. This game is not one of the a "you are a gun; go kill it." games, you need to live it.
Trust me, and definetely give a shot to this serie. Play Bioshock first, and then play this game. You won't regret.

I was a huge fan back in the Xbox 360 days, so I decided to pick this game up for nostalgia sake. In short, it's everything I remembered, but keep one thing in mind while playing this game:
It was designed for consoles and controllers. NOT for keyboards and mouses.
For the most bit, the game performs quite well and is a great game for newer players looking to get into the RTS genre. However, if you've been spoiled by PC RTS games, you might notice some glaring flaws.
Normally, the game pacing is pretty balanced, with my only gripe being that the Covenant gets access to Vehicles and Aircraft after Teching once, compared to the UNSC, who has to tech twice, making Wraith Rushes quite dangerous if the player hasn't trained Spartans or built AT-Turrets.
However: if you play a map with empty reactors, this HEAVILY favours the Covenant faction, as they get a free tech upgrade while they would otherwise have to spend 2000 resources, compared to the UNSC's 1200. The UNSC also has to reach Tier 4 tech compared to Covenant Tier 3, and Covanent troops gain access to many of their units and Tier 1 upgrades simply by building a Temple, which also provides them with their Leader unit.
It may sound like the game is unbalanced in favour of the Covanent, but fortunately, UNSC troops outperform their Alien counterparts and they have access to some excellent abilities, which helps even the playing field. You'll likely not notice anything that's blatantly unfair, other than the Reactor situation.
In terms of AI programming, the biggest threat to you is actually friendly AI leaders, with the Covanent Leaders being the worst of the lot. The AI Brute Chieftain and the Prophet of Regret will ALWAYS spam their unique units until mid game, making them extremely easy to defeat with Flamer Rushes. Only the Arbiter is semi-competent, as his unique unit (the Suicide Grunt) has horrible sustain (for obvious reasons) as such, he rarely builds them. Even with this glaring programming flaw, your allies will likely not build UNSC Troops, instead attempting to rush Vehicles and Aircraft, which often results in their bases being overrun. The friendly AI also has terrible situational awareness compared to enemy AI, as enemies will often coordinate a defense or attack with each other, whereas the friendly AI has poor expansion, often ignoring free bases, will attack enemies even if the odds are against them, resulting in a lot of extra work for the player.
As for the rest of the game, it comes with a solid Campaign with Coop mode, something I believe is sorely lacking in modern games, especially RTS games. The cutscenes are extremely well rendered, which I applaud the devs for. The story and characters are well-written (though I'm not a huge fan of Forge, but that's my opinion).
I recommend purchasing if you're a fan of the series or enjoy a casual RTS game. If you're a competitive RTS gamer, however, you may find this game to be less than you're accustomed to.

Crusader Kings II is an excellent grand strategy game. It is delightfully complex, deep and realistic, even though that is also one of it's downsides, because it is extremely hard to get into. I highly recommend watching the first couple of episodes from a god CK let's player on youtube, because he (or she) will usualy give a good explanation of the base concepts. The game has you invested for days in all kinds of enormous goals like glorious conquest or dishonarable scheming. It may seem a bit slow paced to Civilization players, and the Casus Belis (valid reasons to go to war) and dynasty centered gameplay might seem restricting, but know this, if you embrace Crusader Kings II, you will never be able to go back to a game so "simple" as Civilization or the like. And if you just want war there is of course the Old Gods DLC where the only reason required to go to war, is that you want to.
Conclusion: If you like complex games, grand strategy (if you've ever played a board game like RISK and liked it, you probably like grand strategy) and the medieval ages, then CK is the game for you, but if you don't like one or more of those, then this is probably not the game for you.

Game was really short, not too difficult, and maybe a bit glitchy.
It had an interesting concept but the puzzles aren't that difficult to figure out once you figure out all the items at your disposal.  You could do alot with the game but it didn't really last long enough to really amaze me with a whole lot.  Phasing into the shadows is fun but its annoying getting kicked out of the shadows when it seems like you should be fine.  At one point during the Merry-go-round, there was clearly open space that kept kicking me out of the shadows for no reason, and after going around and taking another route, it stopped doing it.  There's far more that could be done than simply putting boxes into the shadows, then moving the spotlight around.  Outside of getting kicked out of the shadows at random sometimes, the puzzles aren't overall too difficult to figure out once you pick out every option at your disposal.  The last stage introduces the idea to focus the spotlight but you cant keep it focused and is only used to raise a box higher and its only used once.  Its fairly useless to introduce something out of nowhere just to solve one puzzle, especially since you need to tell the player the controls so you're basically telling them what to do
On top of getting forced out of the shadows at odd times, the models for the shadows are clearly screwed up.  Johnny's hat is often floating half off of his head, the character's limbs seem to disconnect, and you can see glitches like this even with Dawn in the shadows.  It was most noticable when you had to float down on an umbrella and it disappeared whenever I faced a specific direction.
The game overall seemed a bit like Vincenzo's act in the end.  His act seemed cool but I could only see the shadows of it, and it was also over very quickly.  In fact, he seems to hint that there may be monsters in the Shadows that could prove to be an obstacle for Dawn but its never followed up on cause all thats left to do in the game is follow Didi then its over.  The game was very interesting, especially for the concept, but again, it only took 2 hours to complete.  Judging from the other reviews, it seems I may have gotten it down quickly, but in order to get 10 hours of gameplay, you would have to be looking for every luminary and every collectable, or have played through the game multiple times.  The game does have some good music and a good story, but its far too short and gameplay wise, not interesting enough to be worth the $17 (canadian) it costs normally.  I got it during a sale but even then, there's other games you could spend your money on instead

Set one year after the events of Metro 2033, 21 year old Artyum must travel to the Botanical Gardens - home of the former Dark Ones' City to find a youthling to help restore the balance of power and to stop his nightmares about his choices from happening again. Were the Dark Ones really sent here to save us all, and is this the last of the Angels? I suppose you'll have to play the game to find out!
Metro: Last Light Redux is a technical update from the original game which features improved texture sizes and even some additional content as well as all DLC released for the original game. Almost anybody who isn't adeptly aware of everything in the game will more than likely not be able to distinguish the differences, and that's understandable.
I love this series and its other medium, It's based on a series of novels which tell the tale of Earth and mroe specifically Moscow Russia following the events of a Nuclear Winter. 2033 introduced us to this world, and one year later we have the events which unfold in Last Light. Where Khan finds a child of the race which Artyum foolishly destroyed, and it's up to Artyum to restore or destroy the balance for the next game.
The game has been updated, refined and developed by 4A, and it's developed by Russians based on a Russian story. The level of detail is such of that, that no two play-throughs are the same. I can say this confidently, as I really have lost count of how many times I've completed the series. The weapon choice is unique, diverse and generous, and you more than likely won't get to use every weapon in a single playthrough, The environments are the best part of the series, they're so immersive you could get lost and of you'd be fooling to not appreciate these environments.
It should also be noted that the available DLC for the most part ties in with the story directly, telling the events of certain situations happening as they happened through the perspective of other characters. This helps with the telling of the story, and naturally gives you insight to other key characters. Most DLC packages released fail in this respect to add value to a story or game, but simply layer information which was originally not planned into a title. The DLC in this case is worth playing once you've completed the game.
Sure, post-apololyptic games are considered a cliche. 4A really have done an incredible job with refining this game into the vision set by its creator who helped the vision come to light. You need to play this game, Redux or otehrwise, so stop reading and get engrossed in the Metro.

As someone who got this remaster free, I can't complain too much - but I can advise those who may be considering the purchase to hold off.
First, as others have stated, the game crashes... sometimes several times in a row, other times, it crashes randomly after a solid 35 minutes of gameplay. Sometimes it didn't crash at all - which leads me to believe that the issues that I experienced weren't hardare driven, but rather, just part of an unpolished console port. I can't comment many technical issues, aside from some intermittent texturing issues where consumable items would blink when approaching them.
Because of this, my feelings towards the remaster are mostly positive, but still mixed. However, unlike my review for Bioshock where I said that the remaster looked like only a minor tweaking of the texture/skins, the remaster really glows in Bioshock 2. Environments, weapons, enemies, and objects that can be moved/interacted with all look great. Environment lighing is less harsh than the original, which makes the gameplay more organic than the original release of Bioshock 2. Now given, the game is very old now, so while some things look fantastic, other things look smoothed out, but still generic. However, enemy characters like other Big Daddies, Big Sisters, and splicers look more polished than the original, and the Minerva's Den DLC looks great as well.

In the end, the game crashed 4 times for me out of the 9 times that I launched it for a single playthrough, and it was annoying, but it didn't kill me. I still enjoyed the remaster. But with hundreds of negative reviews based upon playability problems, I would say that if you don’t currently own the title, you may want to wait until the majority of problems have been addressed before you purchase... or at least, wait until the Steam Holiday sale.

Halo Wars was first released on February 26, 2009 exclusively for the Xbox 360. This was a dark day for Halo fans who played on the PC, since Halo Wars was an RTS and lets face it, nothing does an RTS better than a computer; sadly it was not meant to be. With the greedy console peasant mentality, Microsoft decided to hold Halo Wars hostage as a "console exclusive" in an attempt (just like all other "exclusives' [nothing more than holding games hostage]) to garner more sales of the Xbox 360 itself. Now I, being a fan of both Halo and RTS games had been waiting a long time for something like this; though when I saw it was being held for ransom and would only be set free if I bought a crappy Xbox 360 I sadly had to let go of my dream of playing a great Halo RTS. I had never played the original game, and have never seen anything of it more than some short teasing footage (I wanted to keep away from spoilers in the very off chance it was ever ported over to PC).
Fast forward to December 20, 2016. Halo Wars was given a sleek HD release followed by an immediate port to the glorious PC! Now, I only realized yesterday (5/20/2017) that it was remastered and released to us on steam, and of course the moment I saw that my dream had finally come true I threw my (rather nicely priced) $20 at steam and acquired my copy. Now before I continue I want to state for the record that I have been playing RTS games since Age of Mythology (released back in 2002), and have developed an avid love of RTS games ever since. While I am not the best, I have been able to play and dominate rather well on various RTS games of varying complexity (some moderate, some advanced).
So now that that bit of needed information is out of the way we can continue with my review. After it installed I began my first experience of the game early in the morning. It wasn't long until I found hours had vanished as if they were minutes. Now I want to make something perfectly clear; I have not played the story. For me the story in RTS games is good, but its not what I come for. I come for the instant aciton of solo or team conquest against my opponents; so naturally I hopped immediately into Skirmish mode (after making sure the game was set to maximum visuals) without even looking at the tutorials. After quickly selecting the covenant for my ally and myself and setting up team two as the UNSC it was straight into the action.
My immediate reaction was to be taken aback by just how beautiful the game looks. Now I play on my Alienware 14, which has a Nvidia GTX 765M, 16GB of RAM, and a 4th gen i7-4710MQ  processor; so needless to say this baby packs a punch given its a few years old now. With maximum settings (for me that's 1920x1080 with AA of 8x) this game looks and runs beautifully. By far one of the nicest looking RTS games I have seen, and high attention to detail (and by far a good improvement over the original Halo Wars).
After the visuals, the next thing I noticed was the audio. Now, the audio I hold some mixed feelings for. On one hand the audio has some of the best sounding background music and special effects implemented in a RTS game (at least from the long list of ones I have played), while on the other hand I had to turn my volume way up in order to really hear and enjoy the audio. See, the intro to the game and opening credits were plenty loud, and even after triple checking my audio settings in and out of game, the BGM and SFX were much too soft. This is definitely something I feel should be patched, but it is by no means a deal breaker. Just disappointing and annoying that if I go watch a cinematic or exit the game and forget to lower the volume my ears will get blown out.
Now we move on to game-play. Now this is something that may bother some people... the game-play is pretty simple. It is a very easy to play RTS. Now that is not to say the game cant/wont be challenging, it is merely to say that the mechanics are much more laxed. For example, resources gain automatically, and the speed of which they are gathered can be increased by constructing more of a specific building. In many other RTS games your currencies (as most have multiple) require units to go and gather them, so some hard core RTS fans may not like the recourse simplicity as much. Personally, I don't mind it at all. It lets me focus more on the action, and I think it fits better for this type of game. Like how credits passively generated for Empire at War; these types of RTS games fit better without having units go and hunt down resources in my opinion.
Additionally, your bases could only be placed in certain locations. Now some people hate this, some love it, and others don't care either way. I don't care either way; after all, my first RTS was Age of Mythology and in that game you could only place your town centers over predetermined settlements. So again, another aspect I don't mind. Now, buildings can only be placed in specific slots around your base, and towers/turrets have a limited placement that are also attached to the base. This I was disappointed on due to being used to placing my buildings strategically in other games, but it's not too bad.
One thing that did seriously frustrate me was that keybindings are limited in what can be re-bound. Now, for a PC RTS game, port or not, we should have full access to keybindings. So for me this is a decent negative. Now, the controls are simple and easy to learn, but that doesn't excuse such basic customization options that should be a staple in these types of games. Though I do love how WSAD let me move the camera... that's right, I'm looking at you Age of Mythology.
When selecting a building a circular menu appears with all available options for that structure; units, upgrades, ect... It's a little odd at first, but looks rather nice and seems to just fit nicely with the games design and setup. Very easy to use and very clear about what everything does. Everything has a tooltip that can be read to give you everything you need to know before constructing the unit, building, or upgrade.  Oh, speaking of upgrades... everything can be upgraded. I mean everything. I absolutely love it! There are so many units and subsequent upgrades that it offers various styles of play with unique combinations to your army that can be altered every game. You have three infantry units, three vehicle units, thee air units, one leader (hero, ect...), and various special units depending on faction/leader. Essentially, leader included, each  one you select will have roughly 12 units available to chose from. While not the largest variety, it holds very true to the lore of Halo offering high levels of accuracy while still offering relatively varied armies.
Now for the things you need to manage. You have your population (which is capped at 50 for all game modes aside from Deathmatch; I love Deathmatch), your technology level (which can be upgraded to level 3 by default, while buildings can be captured that can push your technology level beyond that), and your resources (which are passively generated, can be gathered by units when they stumble upon resource crates scattered across the map, or can be traded between allies). Simple, sweet, and gives you a small task of managing those three things while conquering the field your in.
The A.I. in this game is alright. Though what I really love is how you can almost fully command your A.I. allies. I found the A.I. in this game to be much more useful than in other RTS games. While in other games they will offer limited help and mostly do their own thing, in this game you can direct them to scout, attack, reinforce, guard, provide resources, ect... They are fast, responsive, and and work rather well. Additionally, I have played up to Heroic difficulty and found the combat between teams to be fun, while offering a challenge at times. Also, huge map selection with each one beautifully detailed.
All in all, I rate this HD Remake a 8.8/10

In Contrast you play as Dawn, who may, or may not, be the imaginary friend of a young girl called Didi. The game is set in a surreal fantasy city with strong tones of 1920’s Paris. Your role in the game is to accompany and guide Didi on her adventures around the city. The story takes place during a single night when Didi has snuck out, to try and reunite her mother and her estranged father.
Contrast is a platform game with environment traversal puzzles. The game is fully 3D, but its unique feature is the ability to shift into the 2D world of shadows cast upon walls. Dawn uses the shadows to reach areas inaccessible in the 3D ‘real’ world.
Contrast is a short game, I finished it in two sittings over the course of a weekend. Far from a criticism, the longevity was one of the aspects I appreciated most. It never outstayed its welcome or outlived its enjoyment. Unlike most games I finished it because I enjoyed it and wanted to see how it ended, rather than feeling obliged to grind on to the finish line hours after it ceased being fun.
Contrast is also a fairly easy game. No 3D platform game is without a few tricky jumping sections and Contrast is no exception. But I never encountered anything that caused me to quit in frustration and I never felt lost in the game world or became stuck overlong on any particular puzzle. I never encountered any bugs, crashes, glitches or clipping errors during my play through.
I enjoyed Contrast, particularly the art style and character design. I have a feeling that I would have enjoyed it less if it had been longer. But as it stands it was the perfect length for me. I would definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a fun and beautiful platform-game experience that doesn’t require a substantial investment of time.
